This story is part of an investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project. Read the other stories here.
In January 1966, a South African ship caught fire at sea. In port in Bristol, England, after firefighters pried open the smoking container, the conflagration spread and burned for five days. A little over a month later, a Liberian steamship caught fire near Rotterdam, ignited a storage area with barrels of petrol and sank. The month after that, a Danish ship caught fire off Long Beach, California, injuring three firefighters, killing a longshoreman and causing over a million dollars in estimated damages.
The culprit in each fire was fishmeal, a dark yellow powder made by drying and pulverizing fish that, if left untreated, is known for spontaneously combusting as it decays and oxidizes.
Tied to at least 90 ship and plant fires from the 1950s through the 1970s, fishmeal’s combustibility was a serious worry for seafarers, insurers and dock workers, according to a sweep of historical news coverage by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C.
In 1967, American feed producer Cargill announced a solution: ethoxyquin.
A fire retardant previously used to keep rubber tires from drying out and applied as a preservative on fruits and alfalfa, production of the antioxidant was soon ramped up.
“Antioxidant treatment has made bulk handling an easy matter,” the director of the Canadian Department of Fisheries told an industry publication in 1966, arguing it should be required for fishmeal shipments.
The chemical was highly effective. By the 1970s, press-reported fires dropped sharply—from a typical 16 ship fires a year, according to the Liverpool Underwriters Association, to five.
By 1976, the U.S. Coast Guard imposed mandatory ethoxyquin treatment on fishmeal shipments, and three years later, the United Nations body that oversees maritime activity recommended fishmeal be treated with it “to prevent spontaneous combustion.”
But there was a problem: Ethoxyquin is a carcinogen.
“Toxic effects had been observed in laboratory animals fed high concentrations of ethoxyquin,” said a 1969 paper by U.N. food and agriculture authorities.
As its use in animal feeds and aquaculture grew, a 1987 study by British researchers found the chemical “caused severe damage” and had a potentially “carcinogenic effect” in rats. In 2015, the European Food Safety Authority said an impurity within ethoxyquin, known as p-phenetidine, was capable of causing mutations in genetic material.
There is a lack of scientific consensus on whether it is safe to eat farmed seafood raised on feed treated with ethoxyquin, but some countries have considered the risk to be high enough to justify banning or limiting the use of the chemical. In 2017, the European Commission suspended authorization for its use in animal feed across the European Union.
Today, ethoxyquin has been banned in the U.K. and by members of the European Economic Area, including Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. But ethoxyquin, within limits, is still permitted in animal feed in Australia, Japan, South Korea and the U.S.
With more than half of the seafood eaten worldwide now coming from fish farms, and with the majority of such species fed fishmeal and fish oil, studying the chemicals added to feed is critical for understanding the possible contamination of our global food supply.
Although ethoxyquin is not banned in the U.S., it has been at the center of a half-dozen lawsuits, typically involving claims of false advertising. Some lawsuits targeted seafood companies for marketing their products as “sustainable” even though they contained ethoxyquin, while others
highlighted the potential risks that the additive poses to the environment.
In 2022, a New York resident brought a class-action lawsuit against Aldi Inc., a German supermarket chain with stores in the U.S., alleging its Atlantic salmon products were falsely labeled as “sustainable” due to “environmentally destructive” practices. The complaint cited the EU’s ban on the chemical and a study linking ethoxyquin to mortality and deformations in fish and crustaceans, noting the chemical “poses a risk for aquatic life.” The case was settled out of court.
The same year, a New York and a California resident jointly sued Gorton’s Inc., a seafood company, for labeling its frozen tilapia as “sustainably sourced” despite containing ethoxyquin. This lawsuit also cited the “risk for aquatic life” and the European Union’s ban, and was settled out of court.
In Canada, the country’s Food Inspection Agency requires feeds containing ethoxyquin to carry a label declaring that it meets the legal limits, but the agency does not specify how it tests for the chemical in feeds. Inspectors also do not check whether ethoxyquin ends up in the seafood itself, according to the agency’s latest food inspection report from 2022.
And a 2024 audit of the Canadian agency by the EU found it completed only about 40 percent of its planned inspections, citing “systematic and significant under-delivery” in terms of testing seafood products.
Cargill said in a statement that it has assessed alternative antioxidants since 2005 and no longer uses ethoxyquin in its global salmon feed business or in any market where ethoxyquin is not authorized for use in aquafeed. The company also noted that it did not develop ethoxyquin. Globally, producers and feed makers have also increasingly shifted to alternatives, including natural additives such as rosemary extract and vitamin E compounds.
“More and more destinations are not accepting ethoxyquin, starting with our local Peruvian market,” said James Frank, managing director of the Peruvian fishmeal company MSICeres, during a 2022 webinar. He added that 100 percent of Peru’s fishmeal exports to Europe, Canada, the U.S. and Australia are now ethoxyquin-free, a shift also seen among companies in the U.K. and Norway.

42a741cd61db.text: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) delivered another debate performance tailor-made for social media Tuesday night, feeding the presidential speculation he insists is entirely misplaced. Why it matters: A darling of the Democratic internet and a favorite to win the party's nomination in 2028, Ossoff emphatically ruled out a White House bid and pledged to serve a full six-year Senate term if re-elected. "He is running. He's going to be your DSA candidate," Republican challenger Rep. Mike Collins countered, seeking to paint Ossoff as a socialist with ambitions beyond Georgia. The big picture: Georgia was one of three battleground states hosting Senate debates Tuesday night, with candidates in Iowa and Maine also clashing over President Trump's foreign policy, the cost of living and their records in Washington. In Georgia, Ossoff and Collins traded vicious personal attacks throughout their second and final debate, reprising a feud that has become a viral spectacle online. "Will you commit tonight that for the remainder of this campaign — it's just three weeks, Mike — you won't allow any more neo-Nazi propaganda to be produced from your house?" Ossoff demanded , referring to Collins' son-in-law, an alleged white nationalist influencer. Collins accused Ossoff of inciting threats against his family, then attacked him over campaign support from billionaire Reid Hoffman, who had ties to Jeffrey Epstein. "Mike, you really want to bring up the Epstein files?" Ossoff shot back , pointing to Collins' initial vote against releasing the documents — a position he reversed after Trump changed course. In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins cast her independence from Trump as a political asset, arguing that her willingness to challenge the president — and work with him when necessary — has delivered for her state. Collins cited her nine votes to end the Iran war, opposition to Trump's Big Beautiful Bill and roughly $1.5 billion in federal funding secured for Maine projects. Democratic challenger Troy Jackson argued that Collins has spent years helping Trump advance policies that hurt Maine, only to express "concern" and claim credit for mitigating the damage. In his closing statement , Jackson invoked a fatal ICE shooting in Maine to accuse Collins of enabling Trump's immigration crackdown: "Sen. Collins paid for the bullets at Donald Trump's command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger." In Iowa, GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic challenger Josh Turek squared off in a race that has Republicans on edge , as Trump's tariffs and soaring farm costs threaten their grip on a state he carried by 13 points. Hinson broke with Trump over his deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel , saying she believed there were ways to lower fuel prices without empowering Vladimir Putin and his war in Ukraine. Turek accused Hinson of helping drive Iowa toward a "second farm crisis" through her support for Trump's tariffs and votes against congressional efforts to end the Iran war. Hinson said the war should end "as quickly as possible" but rejected another congressional resolution, arguing Trump and the military could bring the conflict to a close themselves.

11cb4cc98038.text: By — Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/new-york-plans-to-ban-central-parks-horse-drawn-carriages-after-teens-death Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter New York plans to ban Central Park's horse-drawn carriages after teen's death Nation Oct 14, 2026 2:18 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — New York City lawmakers plan to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park, ending their more than 150-year run as an iconic, old-timey tourist attraction, following decades of opposition from animal welfare activists and the death of a teenage tourist last spring. The City Council is expected to approve a bill next week that would end the rides by 2028. Three consecutive mayors had called for an end to the carriage rides because of safety concerns, only to have lawmakers yank back the reins. A spokesperson for Julie Menin, the council speaker, confirmed the incoming vote and said the proposal had enough support to pass. Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office said he had reached a deal with the speaker on the legislation. "The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City," Mamdani said in a social media post. Teen's death reignited debate over carriage rides The latest push for a ban started in June, when 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, visiting the city from India, died after jumping from a runaway horse carriage during a ride with family members. His death, which appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park, reignited the debate over whether carriages, a romantic throwback to the city's past, have a place in a modern metropolis. Mahajan's family has appeared at City Hall, in person and through videoconference calls from India, begging the city to finally end the rides. "We are shattered, our whole family shattered. The pain does not go away," his father, Deepak Mahajan, told city council members via a videocall during a hearing for the bill last summer, saying his son leapt from the carriage to try and help his mother, who was flung from her seat, after the horse bolted. "Every morning we wake up and think of nothing but the loss of our son." For decades, animal welfare activists and other critics have decried the carriage industry, arguing horses shouldn't be hauling tourists around busy streets and Central Park while having to navigate bustling traffic and gawking passersby. In the past, horses have collapsed, gotten startled and run off, hitting cars or other objects, with each accident resulting in fresh calls for a ban. READ MORE: How horses whinny has long eluded scientists. A new study reveals the answer "The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable. Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City's history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability," Menin said in a statement. The industry and its supporters have long cast the rides as a way for visitors to experience the New York they know from classic movies and television. Fred Astaire and Cyd Charisse danced into one of the carriages in "The Band Wagon." Robert Redford and Jane Fonda rode one in "Barefoot in the Park." Macaulay Culkin escaped bandits in a carriage in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York." "Taking a horse and carriage ride in New York City is one of the most iconic things to do in New York City and people from all over the world know about us and travel to New York to go to a carriage ride in New York," Conor McHugh, a longtime carriage driver, told the Council earlier this year. Mayors have faced pushback in efforts to ban rides Efforts to close down the industry have been met with pushback from unions and influential supporters, often resulting in tiresome political fights that have seen mayors throw up their hands over nagging worries about putting carriage drivers out of work and what to do with the horses if they can no longer work. Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen said the Council's bill has "no meaningful economic relief for workers" and that Menin "used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis." "This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families' livelihoods are being destroyed. This entire situation is reprehensible," he said in a statement. The proposal as written would require the mayor's office to develop a workforce transition plan for drivers, and includes a measure that would allow the city to consider some kind of compensation for industry workers. Carriage owners could not sell their horses off for slaughter, according to the bill's language, which requires that horses be disposed of in a "humane manner." "I think we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry," Mamdani told reporters Wednesday. The mayor's predecessor, Eric Adams, called for ending the industry during the waning days of his administration, but the proposal went nowhere. The mayor before that, Bill de Blasio, had pledged to eliminate the rides on day one of his administration but abandoned the crusade after heavy opposition from unions and a media blitz involving actor Liam Neeson. Over the years, the city has placed various safety regulations around the industry, including a requirement that the horses get at least five weeks of vacation a year outside of city limits with daily access to a pasture. The horses are inspected by a veterinarian twice a year, and the maximum age they can work at is 26, according to city regulations. And they don't work when it is hotter than 89 degrees. a097cdd4c219.text: By — Jaimie Ding, Associated Press Jaimie Ding, Associated Press By — Dylan Lovan, Associated Press Dylan Lovan, Associated Press By — Sudhin Thanawala, Associated Press Sudhin Thanawala, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/roller-coaster-riders-death-puts-spotlight-on-safety-of-ever-more-thrilling-rides Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Roller coaster rider's death puts spotlight on safety of ever more thrilling rides Nation Oct 14, 2026 2:09 PM EDT The horrific death of a man who was ejected from a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia is drawing attention to the safety of amusement park rides that have become increasingly faster and steeper in their quest for the biggest thrill. READ MORE: Man killed on a Six Flags roller coaster was thrown from the ride and hit other patrons, police say Deaths on roller coasters are still extremely rare, and Georgia officials have said little about what happened Monday when Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old school employee from Atlanta, was thrown from his seat while riding the Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia before striking other patrons and then landing below the ride. Goliath uses a sheer drop from 200 feet (61 meters) to reach top speeds of 70 mph (112 kph). It focuses on velocity and downhill plunges rather than turning riders upside down through loops or corkscrews. It has operated at the park for two decades. Six Flags temporarily closed nine similar coasters across North America following the death, saying it was doing so out of an abundance of caution. Ride manufacturer Bolliger & Mabillard said it is "actively investigating the incident and will not comment further until we have a better understanding of what happened." The U.S. has a patchwork of rules regarding rides In the U.S., roller coasters and other rides at major amusement parks such as Six Flags are not regulated by the federal government. That responsibility falls to states. Some say this has led to an inconsistent patchwork of rules where some states have strict regulations and others have little to no oversight. U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has repeatedly introduced legislation to close what he calls a "loophole" in federal law that allows U.S. safety officials to regulate mobile rides but prevents the Consumer Product Safety Commission from overseeing stationary rides like those at major amusement parks. Brian Avery, a University of Florida professor and amusement ride safety expert, agrees that more federal regulations are needed. "Who's watching those in these organizations to ensure that they are adequately trained, that they are compliant, that they are monitoring these rides to the level which the standards have established?" Avery said. Georgia's Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which oversees annual ride inspections in the state, is "conducting an in‑depth and comprehensive review" of what happened Monday at Six Flags, said Garrison Bennett, a spokesperson. Amusement park industry has set its own safety standards Amusement park operators worldwide generally adhere to what are known as ASTM standards set by industry experts, which cover everything from ride design and construction to how much acceleration and force each rider is allowed to experience. The industry has multiple layers of inspection, said Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, a trade group. Park operators are under pressure from insurance carriers that could face a hefty payout if something goes wrong. "With the checks and balances that are put in place, theme parks are really one of the safest places to be on the planet," he said in a phone interview Tuesday. In 2024, the rate of serious and reportable injuries per million roller coaster rides was 1.27, according to the trade group. For all amusement park rides, "guest behavior" contributed to 66% of the injuries that year, with 9% attributable to operational factors and 15% to technical factors, the group said. Jakob Wahl, the trade group's current president, extended condolences to Kariem's family in a statement on Wednesday. Experts say roller coaster safety mechanisms are 'dependable' Martin Lewison, a roller coaster expert and a professor at Farmingdale State College, said it was difficult to imagine there being a mechanical malfunction on a roller coaster such as Goliath because of its design. The ride features a pull-down lap restraint called a "clamshell" that works with a ratchet mechanism that makes clicking sounds as you press it down over your hips. They have multiple disks to ensure redundancy if one fails, Lewison said. "They're dependable. They're not so technically advanced that theme parks have difficulty with operations," Lewison said. The operator then has a safety system that displays a green "go" light for every seat on the train before it can be dispatched. The train should theoretically not be allowed to proceed unless all restraints are locked, Lewison said. But few things are 100% safe. In 2022, a 14-year-old Missouri boy fell to his death from an Orlando amusement park ride when the harness didn't lock properly due to his size. In 2013, a 52-year-old Dallas woman was killed when she slipped out of her seat on the Texas Giant ride at Six Flags Over Texas. Six Flags has since added redesigned restraint-bar pads, seat belts and a coaster seat at the ride's entrance so guests can check whether they fit safely into the cars before getting on. Nick Mendenhall, who has been on the Goliath more than a dozen times in recent weeks and witnessed Monday's death, said he saw Six Flags staff check the restraints each time he rode it. "There are two employees, one on either side of the train, and with their hands they push down and they make sure it locks every time. I've never seen them not do it," Mendenhall said. Hegseth, service secretaries discuss ‘generational change’ of Autonomous Warfare Command
Each of the services will also stand up a component command, defense secretary said.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s vision for the planned Autonomous Warfare Command over the next two years “is that we're still iterating, we're still adapting, we're still learning, and we're moving faster and faster because we're doing it. We understand how to do it better with each iteration.”
Hegseth sat down to discuss the Defense Department’s efforts to advance its autonomous capabilities with the service secretaries and the Pentagon’s top civilian for special operations during a panel Wednesday at AUSA’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C., but the discussion offered few details on what the forthcoming AUTOWARCOM, scheduled to activate by Oct. 1, 2027, will look like and how it will accomplish its mission.
The secretary, who has ordered cuts to and flag officer positions across the military services, was asked why a four-star combatant command is the correct vehicle to speed up acquisition and fielding of autonomous systems. He said that sometimes a general is the best person to get the job done.
“Let's put rank where we need it to ensure we can drive change quickly,” Hegseth said. “We're going to use rank to drive change with the right people in those positions, but not just legacy formations and commands which have gathered over time and haven't led to battlefield efforts.”
He did not say whether a search is on for commander candidates and what kind of experience he’s looking for.
The Army on Tuesday announced it would rename its Futures and Concepts Command, headed by Lt. Gen. Mac McCurry, to Futures and Autonomy Command, which will be the service’s component command nested under AUTOWARCOM.
The other services haven’t made any announcements about their own forthcoming autonomy commands. The Navy did not immediately respond to a query from Defense One on its plans. The Air Force referred questions to Hegseth’s office.
Much of the discussion focused on the services’ current use of unmanned platforms, as distinct from autonomous systems, which generally function without a human operator.
Hegseth said that AUTOWARCOM would deal not just with procurement, but also with training and doctrine around unmanned systems.
Two of the speakers mentioned an Army effort to open up its test ranges to private companies that make “drone, counter-drone, and long-ranges fires solutions.” Announced in August, the Army Permissive Test Range Expansion effort includes a website that promises a response within four weeks to companies that apply to use the ranges.
“Before, we kept these test ranges to ourselves for our own purposes. We were prioritizing and micromanaging the use of these ranges,” Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said Wednesday. “To the degree that our bureaucracy is living in the way of our most innovative people from iterating quickly, it's a shame.”
The Army is also working to open “theater innovation labs” outside the United States, said Derrick Anderson, assistant defense secretary for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict. Anderson said the labs, which are being launched in conjunction with U.S. Special Operations Command, meant that “operators sitting here stateside iterating on these autonomous systems” would have a “place to go and iterate” when they go abroad as well.
Anderson added that the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group run by the Defense Innovation Unit will be folded into SOCOM’s new Task Force Autonomous Warfare.
One day before Hegseth took the AUSA spotlight, Army officials had offered some insight into their plans for autonomous warfare on Tuesday, including “appropriate levels of human judgment,” Army Chief Technology Officer Alex Miller said during a panel.
“Things like counter-battery fire, things like air and missile defense, things that happen at a superhuman speed and scale—want to have humans on the loop for decisions, but then we cannot be limited by you know the 20 watts that have up here,” Miller said, pointing to his head. “If we are taking thousands of drones or hundreds of rounds, we can't put that on a human. We want to enable them to be a crew chief for superintelligence and autonomy.”
On Wednesday’s panel, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said his service is experimenting with autonomous fighter aircraft at Creech Air Force Base in Nevada.
Last year, the Pentagon came under fire for its intentions around autonomous capabilities when AI company Anthropic, then a vendor to the Defense Department, protested the potential use of its models in support of lethal autonomous weapons and mass domestic surveillance.
Currently, artificial intelligence is used in collecting intelligence, identifying battlefield and data management. AUTOWARCOM would ostensibly be an entire combatant command built around autonomous platforms, but none of the senior officials on stage Wednesday identified any of the advancements the department hopes to make in their use.
“It will be a leader in the way we fight going forward, and I think we'll look back and say that was a no-brainer,” Hegseth said. “We should have done it 10 years earlier, but at least we did it.”
Lauren Williams contributed to this report.

5d28cbd9da7b.text:
Coral-fringed tropical atolls are among the landforms most threatened by global warming, but many have a potential superpower: Healthy ecosystems may help them keep pace with rising seas.
Atoll islands with native vegetation and thriving seabird populations are “naturally active systems that can change and adapt to their environmental conditions if they are allowed to do so,” said Nick Graham, a marine ecologist at Lancaster University in the United Kingdom, who led an international team of scientists that studied island resilience across 28 atoll islands in the Pacific and Indian oceans.
Their paper, published Wednesday in Science Advances, shows that restoring atoll ecosystems reinforces their growth. Seabirds ferry nutrients from the open ocean and deposit them on the atolls as guano that nurtures land plants, marine life and coral growth. This provides more material for reef building, as parrotfish and other reef feeders turn dead coral into sand to maintain beaches, while native plants with extensive root networks stabilize sediments.
Eradicating rats and replacing coconut plantations with native forests and brush could give some atolls a “fighting chance” to persist at the rate of sea-level rise expected toward the end of the century with about 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming, Graham said.
The findings provide more evidence that nature restoration can buffer the impacts of global warming. For example, restoring wetlands and forests dampens swings between wet and dry spells, reducing flood and fire hazards. Restoration efforts can also slow global warming by supporting natural carbon storage.
On the 28 atoll islands Graham’s team studied, strengthening the dynamic system of seabirds, native vegetation and reef systems starts a virtuous cycle, as ecosystems become better able to sustain themselves and build resilience to growing impacts. 
The research included data from islands in the Seychelles and Chagos archipelagos in the Indian Ocean, and Tetiaroa, an atoll in French Polynesia in the Pacific Ocean. Graham said terrestrial ecologists, marine ecologists and geomorphologists combined measurements of seabird populations, native vegetation and coral and reef organisms to trace how energy moves through the ecosystems.
The scientific approach, called ecosystem energetics, uses energy flow as a common currency to connect organisms typically studied in isolation.
Seabirds link the open ocean, where they feed, to the land, where they nest. Thousands of birds swarm out across vast seas and the food they digest is concentrated into a nutrient-rich guano. Islands with greater seabird nutrient input tended to have more productive coral communities and a higher energy flow.
Parrotfish and other reef nibblers also contribute to energy flow by scraping the coral to feed on dead organisms and excreting sand-sized particles. Calcifying algae, other reef organisms and shellfish help build the reef framework upward, helping reefs continue to buffer islands from waves.
In the terrestrial part of the cycle, restoring native vegetation that coconut plantations replace is crucial. Coconut palms have small, unstable rootballs that leave the surrounding soil vulnerable to erosion. Native plants, by contrast, have huge networks of finely meshed roots that bind and stabilize the shallow, porous soil, and also provide better habitat for seabirds.
Restoring the nutrient cycle also means eliminating invasive rats brought by colonizers and have devastated seabird colonies for centuries. This cycle has been sustaining atoll ecosystems at least since the end of the last ice age. A 2026 study of 288 reef core growth records found that most kept pace with rising seas, although that capacity varied by location and is not guaranteed at the current rate of warming.
The new study measures the “‘reef accretion potential” for the islands, showing it to be twice as high on lagoonal and ocean-facing reefs around rat-free islands with abundant seabirds as around rat-infested islands. That would be “sufficient to closely keep up with predicted sea-level rises to the end of the century under a 2 degree Celsius warming scenario,” said co-author Casey Benkwitt, a California-based restoration scientist with The Nature Conservancy.
Reef growth rates without seabird populations are less likely to keep pace with projected sea-level rise, she added.
Graham cautioned that the study doesn’t imply a miracle solution for global warming impacts to low-lying islands. It didn’t make direct before-and-after restoration comparisons, and the data came from islands with different levels of seabird abundance and rat infestations, differences the research team tried to smooth out with an ecosystem energetics framework.
And reef accretion doesn’t always mean an atoll is growing vertically, because global warming is also changing waves, winds and currents that affect where the material ends up. The study also focused on mostly uninhabited or sparsely populated islands with room for native ecosystems. On developed atolls, he said, restoration efforts can help but won’t replace the need for engineering solutions.
The study helps show a nearly complete loop, “from ocean-foraging seabirds, through native forests and coral reefs, back to the construction and stabilization of the islands on which the birds breed,” ecologist Hillary Young wrote in a Science Advances Focus commentary. Quantifying the loop provides “much-needed evidence that the fate of an atoll cannot be understood or managed by treating its land and sea separately,” she wrote.
Local conservation can influence physical resilience to rising seas, but, she wrote, “rapid reductions in greenhouse-gas emissions remain essential to long-term viability of these systems.”

Trump admin's retreat from foreign-influence fight is weakening US defenses, sources say
States and industry report getting less help from the federal government ahead of the midterms—even as AI gives foreign operatives a boost.
The Trump administration’s retreat from programs that track foreign influence operations has weakened various cross-sector relationships used to identify and confront those campaigns as midterm elections fast approach — even as artificial intelligence makes those operations easier to deploy — multiple sources told Nextgov/FCW.
State officials say they are receiving fewer election-specific federal briefings than in previous cycles, while others who track foreign influence have observed routine exchanges with government and technology companies fall away. Some also note that federal workforce departures have weakened cooperation with outside partners, including social media platforms, to track false information online.
While the federal government continues to gather intelligence on foreign threats to U.S. elections, some of those who lean on those findings say federal agencies are less reliably sharing information with non-federal researchers and state officials responsible for countering those campaigns. That cooperation began to weaken before President Donald Trump returned to office, and his administration has since dismantled several programs dedicated to countering the problem.
This story is based on interviews with current and former federal officials, state election officials and specialists in cybersecurity and influence operations. Several people spoke on the condition of anonymity to be candid about their views and for fear of retribution. Their concerns come as fast-evolving AI tools now allow foreign influence operators to do more than just generate fake images or audio, instead helping them produce plausible-sounding messages, find audiences to target and autonomously adjust campaigns at a scale not seen before.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions about foreign malign influence to the Justice Department, saying that influence operations fall outside CISA’s mission. DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“Election security is national security, and protecting our critical infrastructure remains a top priority for the Trump Administration, DHS, and CISA,” a CISA spokesperson said. “CISA works closely with intelligence and law enforcement partners to monitor threats to U.S. critical infrastructure, including election infrastructure.”
The spokesperson added that the agency is committed to supporting state and local election officials “to protect election infrastructure and safeguard our democracy.”
The Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not respond to a request for comment.
Foreign influence operations aim to shape what people believe and how they act, often without revealing who is behind the message. Around elections, that can mean spreading false voting information, stoking political divisions or casting doubt on results. Such messages can be harder to question when they appear to come from or be amplified by fellow Americans and reinforce views people already hold.
One election nonprofit official told Nextgov/FCW that, during the November 2024 election, they received an early-morning text from a colleague in Georgia asking about bomb threats at voting sites, which U.S. officials later deemed may have been tied to Russia. The official was sitting in CISA’s election operations room. Finding out whether other jurisdictions were facing similar threats meant simply walking across the room and asking federal personnel.
“Any time you have federal support to help connect the dots, it’s a game-changer,” the official said, noting that they have not been alerted to or invited to a CISA elections operations room for the coming midterms.
The CISA spokesperson said that, before and during Election Day, the agency will “activate an Incident Coordination Group to establish a unified operational picture, rapidly share critical information, coordinate essential services for stakeholders in the field and strengthen incident response within its mission and authorities.”
Bret Schafer, senior director of policy and research for information operations at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, said efforts to bring government, technology companies and researchers together grew during Trump’s first term, after Russia’s interference attempts in the 2016 election exposed gaps in their understanding of foreign campaigns.
Each could see activity the others could not. Sharing those findings helped them recognize operations that might otherwise go unnoticed, Schafer said last week on a panel at a national-security law conference hosted by the American Bar Association.
Those routine exchanges with the government have become harder to sustain. Now, “civil society is out on both sides,” he said, adding that he had gone at least two years without an information-sharing conversation with a relevant technology company, and a couple of years without one involving the government.
Much of that cooling began in the Biden administration, when GOP litigation over federal interactions with social media companies made participants more cautious. The Trump administration has gone further. It shuttered CISA work focused on election disinformation, disbanded the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force and closed the State Department’s office for countering foreign information threats, all largely on censorship grounds. The ODNI Foreign Malign Influence Center also faced a similar fate last August under then-director Tulsi Gabbard.
An office can retain its responsibilities while losing the relationships that helped it do the work, according to a person familiar with U.S. efforts to address influence operations. More than 1 billion people per year were exposed to heat waves and fire pollution at the same time from 2010-2019, a sharp jump from the decade before it, according to a new study that highlights the growing public health crisis caused by global warming.
The research, published in Science Advances on Wednesday, is the largest global assessment to date of how many people have been exposed to heat waves and fires—particularly wildfires—at the same time.
“There are two reasons why the total number of days people spend exposed to both hazards can increase: more people are exposed, or people experience these conditions more often,” said lead author Yao Wu, a postdoctoral research fellow at Monash University in Australia, in a written statement to Inside Climate News.
“Our findings show that the second reason plays a much bigger role,” Wu added, noting that “the problem is growing mainly because people are experiencing these two hazards together more often, not simply because there are more people.”
Researchers used detailed environmental data on hourly temperature, fire emissions and air quality, along with population information to map where and when people faced both hazards.
They found that the number of people exposed to at least one day of heat and fire pollution rose from 761 million per year in 2000–2009 to more than 1 billion per year in 2010–2019, with some of the highest exposures in countries that have fewer resources to cope with the problems.
The researchers, from universities in China in addition to Australia, described the trend as “alarming.” Public health plans to address one climate-related hazard at a time aren’t sufficient as disasters increasingly overlap, they said in their study.
Tarik Benmarhnia, a professor of climate epidemiology who was not involved in the study, said the research highlights a growing challenge for public health.
“This study captures how climate change is actually showing up in people’s lives today, and how it will increasingly affect communities in the future: not one hazard at a time, but several at once,” Benmarhnia, at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California San Diego, said in a written statement to Inside Climate News.
Climate hazards, which also include events like floods, dust storms and drought, can additionally follow one another in rapid succession, he added.
The hazards covered in the study—fire pollution and heat—can both be deadly. Extreme heat overwhelms the body’s natural systems. The heart strains to move blood, sweating depletes fluids and heatstroke can damage internal organs, including the brain. Wildfire smoke, meanwhile, carries toxic fine particles linked to a wide range of health woes.
The cumulative impacts of simultaneous exposure to heat and fire are not well known and need to be better studied, the researchers said. Benmarhnia also stressed that big research gaps remain, but noted that a handful of studies have found overlapping heat and smoke events send people to emergency rooms with worse heart and lung problems than either hazard would cause in isolation.
The new analysis found the annual average number of days with both heat and fire exposure rose sharply per person, from one day during 2000–2009 to 1.7 days during 2010–2019.
Zambia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Malawi, Guatemala and Burundi had the highest exposures on a per-person basis, with Zambians having nearly a month of exposure per person every year, according to the study. Measured this way, smaller countries with frequent exposure tend to top the list.
The study also looked at the total exposure days across each country’s population. By this measure, more populous countries tend to rank higher because many residents are affected, even if each person is only exposed for relatively few days. The Democratic Republic of Congo, Indonesia, Mexico, Brazil and Russia collectively accounted for more than half of all global exposure days to both hazards between 2010 and 2019, the study found.
Countries with lower living standards, including poorer health and less education, had the highest exposure per person and the largest increases, the researchers said.
They added that lower-income countries often have less capacity to prepare for and adapt to climate risks, and that fire-related air pollution in low-income countries is four times worse than in wealthy countries.

The study highlighted how climate change, heat waves and fires affect one another.
Human-caused climate change is shifting global fire patterns. In the past, fires were more strongly influenced by how much rain an area received. But today, rising temperatures play a larger role, the researchers said.
Hotter temperatures, drier air and parched soil make fires more likely to start and spread quickly. In turn, fires can worsen heat waves by releasing heat and pollution into the air, making conditions even hotter and drier.
“These processes create a positive feedback loop in which heatwaves and fires amplify one another,” the researchers said.
Global warming also makes heat waves and large fires more likely to happen at the same time. The researchers pointed to the 2021 record-breaking fires in Western Canada and the United States that burned 3.2 million hectares. A heat dome contributed to between 21 percent and 34 percent of the area burned.
The study also cited the 2022 heat-fueled fires that blazed across Portugal, Spain and France, along with the 2020 fire season in Brazil’s Pantanal, which, worsened by heat and drought, destroyed about a third of the world’s largest tropical freshwater wetland.

Reedâs view
One of the most profound takeaways from my interview with Reflection AI co-founder and CTO Ioannis Antonoglou this week on Semaforâs Future Proof is his declaration that the AI era will force us to redefine what each business actually does and rebuild it from the ground up, using AI as scaffolding. And that is going to take decades, a lot longer than most people in Silicon Valley project.
Right now, we are thinking about data all wrong. Today, businesses mostly capture data thatâs measurable or the result of some kind of work product. Whatâs usually not captured is the work itself â the difficult-to-define causal link that connects all of the actions that a company takes. âA lot of the context is like, âwe jump on a call, or someone shared something or said somethingââ Antonoglou told me.
Iâve been thinking about that challenge with my own work. How can a journalist capture gut feelings about what might make a good story? (Itâs a bit like that famous 1960s US Supreme Court case on pornography, âyou know it when you see it.â) What about capturing how reporters decide who to call first, or what questions to ask to get the most revealing answers?
In the AI era, Antonoglou told me, companies have to throw out what theyâve done for decades and come up with new ways to measure and carry out their work. Thatâs part of what Antonoglou is trying to help customers do with his companyâs open-weight models. âIt will take maybe a decade or two decades before people really rethink how things are done and how they can just do them with AI in mind,â he said.
It wonât happen in every industry at the same time â probably a good thing for the economyâs stability â but it does provide another new entry for startups that move faster than incumbents to spring ahead.

177d2da12729.text: By — Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/iowas-water-quality-and-cancer-rates-forced-into-forefront-of-state-politics Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Iowa's water quality and cancer rates forced into forefront of state politics Politics Oct 14, 2026 1:48 PM EDT DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Iowa is facing a budget deficit, high costs and economic strain from trade disputes that have squeezed farmers. But problems that have simmered for decades — water quality and cancer rates — have been forced to the forefront of state politics this year. They are the focus of debate questions, roundtable events and campaign advertisements for candidates from both parties, up and down the ballot. The issue has historically been politically taboo to avoid pointing fingers at the powerful agricultural industry in Iowa, one of the country's top producers of corn, soybeans and hogs. Chemical fertilizers and animal waste contain nitrates and phosphorus that can get washed with rain or snowmelt into the state's web of rivers. The problem has long caused tension between Iowa's more liberal urban centers, which rely on rivers and lakes for drinking water, and mostly conservative stewards of its rich farmland. Farmers are increasingly participating in practices to prevent runoff, although critics say the lack of regulation forces downstream Iowans to pay for the pollution. The spotlight has grown — and the political calculus has shifted — after back-to-back years of restrictions on water use in the Des Moines area coupled with a burgeoning "Make America Healthy Again" movement in Iowa's small towns and rural communities. Cancer rates are a growing problem in Iowa Iowa has the second highest rate of newly diagnosed cancers in the country. Specific diagnoses, like prostate, breast and lung cancer, are increasing in Iowa faster than in the U.S. overall. It's affecting urban and rural parts of the state. New state-funded research at the University of Iowa shows most — but not all — of Iowa's above-normal rates for five cancers can be explained by demographic and behavioral factors, such as smoking and binge drinking. Researchers next assess environmental factors, including nitrate levels. "The real issue is the water and the nitrates," said Democrat Josh Turek, who is running for U.S. Senate, as he talked with cancer patients last week. "Every Iowan deserves when they turn on the tap to ensure that their water is clean and not giving them cancer." WATCH: As cancer rates fall nationally, Iowa sees a troubling rise in diagnoses Some studies have found a link between nitrates in drinking water and certain diseases, but it remains an area of debate. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency does not currently classify nitrates as a cancer risk. The agency initiated a plan to review that assessment in 2017, but it's been stalled, revived and stalled again under different White House administrations. The Republican congresswoman running against Turek, Ashley Hinson, recently gathered farmers, researchers and local officials to discuss Iowa's water problems. She said there is an ongoing need for investments in infrastructure, water quality monitoring and conservation programs to ensure Iowans have safe drinking water. She also said people can feel safe because treated tap water meets federal regulations. "We all know that we have some challenges here in Iowa," she said. "I don't think water quality is a partisan issue." Farm runoff is a key contributor to river pollution — and political tensions It's been more than a decade since the Des Moines area's water utility, fed up with paying roughly $16,000 per day to remove nitrates from water, sued counties further upstream to get them to help cover the cost. The complaint was ultimately dismissed, and Iowa's Republican leaders celebrated the ruling. Last year, Central Iowa Water Works issued its first-ever ban on lawn watering to reduce demand on its nitrate removal facilities, and state politicians rejected any suggestion of a "blame game" that would implicate farmers. Iowa had been investing nearly $100 million annually in its nutrient reduction strategy in recent years. WATCH: U.S. House candidates James, Mitchell debate in Iowa in race to replace Hinson In May, though, Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds and lawmakers committed an additional $320 million for water infrastructure, conservation initiative incentives and other projects, including millions to Central Iowa Water Works to update equipment. "Water quality isn't a farm issue. It isn't a city issue, and it isn't a political issue," Reynolds said. "But it absolutely is non-negotiable." Still, criticism of slow progress has continued, including from candidates running to replace Reynolds. Governor candidates make the issue central Republican Zach Lahn and Democrat Rob Sand both emphasize that the state needs to better prioritize the water problem, though neither have called for mandating farming conservation practices that reduce runoff. Lahn, who was endorsed early in his primary by political committee MAHA Action, has diverged from many of his Republican peers in directly linking polluted water and agrochemicals to Iowa's cancer crisis. At Lahn's agriculture-focused town hall in northeast Iowa in August, one attendee raised the issue. "Right now the farmers, I would say, are really getting blamed for the high cancer rate in Iowa," she said. "Even our daughter calls from Des Moines and says: 'Should we be drinking this water?'" Lahn said he knows certain agrochemicals are important "tools in the tool chest." "We're not here to ban products," he said, "but we do have to address the water quality issue." In the span of weeks, AI altered the video game industry with mashups, which allow people to combine multiple popular games into one â and Xbox is leaning in.
AI-coding models have crossed new capability thresholds that allow users to reverse-engineer and recreate complex game code that would have taken humans years to do. People have created mashups that allow Minecraft characters to play in Elden Ring, or skateboard through Call of Duty.
âThese experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry,â an Xbox executive said in a memo sent to employees and posted Tuesday on the companyâs website, adding that the viral mashups mean gamers have become creators. âThese are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.â
The video game giant announced Xbox Labs, which will aim to work with users as well as its own developers and engineers to make games and experiences stemming from the new AI-fueled creations.

365db38b7d7e.text: ICE is rejecting a Government Accountability Office recommendation for technology that automatically activates body cameras when weapons are drawn and safeguards to ensure agents record arrests, searches and detentions when required. Why it matters: The GAO warns that ICE risks losing crucial evidence on what happened during incidents involving force amid growing distrust over agent accountability in the wake of multiple fatal ICE shootings . The big picture: The GAO report found both CBP and ICE are struggling to manage their body-camera programs amid shifting deployment plans. CBP and ICE haven't updated their camera plans since 2022 and 2024, respectively. The plans fail to account for funding changes, expanded deployment needs and pauses in camera rollouts following one of Trump's executive orders that rescinded a Biden-era federal body-camera mandate. ICE's camera activation dispute is the central flashpoint in the GAO review, as DHS accepted all six other recommendations. CBP uses technology that automatically activates body cameras when officers draw firearms or turn on emergency lights, but ICE doesn't. Zoom in: At six of the 10 locations GAO reviewed, CBP and ICE personnel said they were unsure when they had to turn on their cameras. Some said camera use is "not mandated," "up to interpretation," and "has gray areas." Agents specifically reported uncertainty about whether they should record during "subpoena issuance, in-custody interviews, vehicle searches, undercover operations, and detainee transports." At five sites, people said they weren't sure how to use a newer camera model. The other side: DHS rejected the recommendation, arguing that automatic activation "presents significant operational risks, including inadvertent or false activations during routine movement." DHS warned that accidental activation could expose sensitive interactions with informants and victims or record people engaged in protected First Amendment activities. GAO pushed back, noting that DHS offered no alternative safeguards despite the risks of critical encounters going unrecorded. DHS didn't respond to Axios' request for comment. Worth noting: ICE issued no written reprimands for failing to comply with camera policies from the program's launch through September 2025. CBP issued just one. The bottom line: Both CBP and ICE say their body-camera programs are meant to improve public trust, officer safety and accountability. But without clear standards, the agencies can't determine whether their programs are meeting those goals, GAO found. Go deeper: ICE says all its offices will have body cams in 60 days

1bcb2bcb02fa.text: President Trump has directed his White House counsel to examine explosive allegations dropped on him Friday in the Oval Office: Former Trump attorney Alina Habba told the president that another one of his top advisers — former Kennedy Center leader Ric Grenell — failed to deposit a multimillion-dollar donation that her billionaire husband made to the center a year ago, according to four senior administration officials and three insiders briefed on the controversy. Grenell denied the accusations as "absurd" and a "lie." Habba and her husband, Turhan Mildon, declined to comment through a spokesperson. Why it matters: The extraordinary row between the two top-tier presidential advisers and former allies provides a rare and acrimonious behind-the-scenes glimpse into the intersection of power, influence and money in Trump's Washington. The total value of the contribution in question: nearly $6 million, White House sources said Habba told them. A senior administration official cautioned that "these are only allegations. We don't know if they're true. This could be a misunderstanding." Said another: "POTUS doesn't want to deal with this. Of course, he's concerned. But if there is missing money, this is a big, big problem." Just a few months ago , Grenell was friends with Mildon and Habba. But he was notably absent from their $10 million wedding that was attended by Trump world officials, power brokers and luminaries last month. "This is the ultimate MAGA blood feud," said one Trump world insider with knowledge of the conflict. Zoom in: The dispute grew out of a friendship between Grenell and Mildon, sources familiar with the conflict say. The men had mutual interests in Venezuela in early 2025, immediately after Trump returned to the White House. Grenell, as a Trump special envoy, was advocating for normalizing U.S. relations with Venezuela's leader at the time, Nicolas Maduro. Mildon, a Turkish national, had extensive Venezuelan business interests that were threatened by Secretary of State Marco Rubio's hardline pressure campaign targeting Maduro. The intrigue: In the spring of 2025, Grenell persuaded Mildon to include a multimillion-dollar Kennedy Center donation in a lump-sum $17.6 million payment for a business deal involving a U.S. company, Habba told the president and White House staffers, two sources said. Habba's attorneys plan to give the White House documentation — reviewed by Axios — to support her allegations about Grenell soliciting a Kennedy Center donation from Mildon to go to a private company in the spring of 2025. "The White House counsel has asked for documents and proof. None has come so far," a White House official said. Grenell called the statements from Habba to Trump "Absurd. I've never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I've never received any payment from him at all. Make him give proof to what he is saying, not make these absurd allegations." When Habba initially leveled her accusations against Grenell, she said the total amount of the Kennedy Center contribution was $17 million, the sources said. But as she learned of the specifics from her husband, she said the amount of the contribution in question was $5.6 million. "This has been hard to track because numbers have changed," the White House official said. After making his alleged contribution , Mildon never checked to see if it was deposited. He believed it had been credited because he was treated like a VIP donor at the Kennedy Center, where he met Habba in late 2025 before their whirlwind romance and marriage, those sources said. Friction point: Mildon and Habba, the sources said, discovered the issue after their business relationship frayed with Grenell, who lost an internal administration power struggle with Rubio that culminated in the U.S. seizing Maduro on Jan. 3 and taking him to New York City to face narcotics charges. In June, Maduro's successor, Delcy Rodriguez, issued an order revoking one of Mildon's company contracts to operate state-owned cement plants in Venezuela, the New York Times reported Monday. A source familiar with the situation told Axios this summer that her action was partly due to the U.S. government's prodding. Rodriguez then reversed herself, the Times reported, after learning of Mildon's new relationship with Habba because the Venezuelan leader believed Mildon therefore had Trump's backing. Amid the Times' reporting into Mildon's contract, Habba discovered that Mildon's supposed donation never made it to the Kennedy Center, the sources said. Inside the room: Habba then headed to the White House last Friday to tell the president about the situation. "Alina hit the roof" when her husband told her that he hadn't donated the money directly to the Kennedy Center, whose records indicate that Mildon actually owed a $270,000 pledged donation. There was no record of Mildon giving anything close to $5.6 million, officials said. Mildon on Tuesday paid the $270,000, records show, to the Kennedy Center. In partial confirmation of Habba's story , Kennedy Center staff reported that late last year there was a search for Mildon's contribution — then thought to be $6 million — but that it couldn't be found, an official said. But Lisa Dale, who handled finances for the Kennedy Center then, said the only record in her books connected to Mildon showed he owed $270,000. "There was nothing about $6 million," she told Axios. "I would have heard about that." Context: Habba and Grenell trace their roots to Trump's first administration. Grenell was Trump's ambassador to Germany and then his acting director of national intelligence. Habba was Trump's private attorney and briefly was U.S. attorney in New Jersey during this term. Between the lines: The Kennedy Center has been an ongoing sore spot for Trump, beset by controversy over his efforts to put his name on the building and fundraising woes. e81812d62949.text: By — Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press By — Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/republicans-retreat-from-battleground-districts-as-lines-shift-in-house-races Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Republicans retreat from battleground districts as lines shift in House races Politics Oct 14, 2026 1:30 PM EDT DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Republicans were retreating Tuesday from a handful of battleground U.S. House races while Democrats were racing to raise money to boost candidates who seemed like long shots earlier this year. The Congressional Leadership Fund, the leading House Republican super PAC, canceled spending in four races from the Midwest to the East Coast and increased its investment in 16 other races from Texas to Pennsylvania. Another super PAC allied with President Donald Trump is cutting back in a battleground district in the Las Vegas area. The decisions were disclosed by three Republican campaign officials familiar with the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity to share private strategy conversations. Meanwhile, Democrats' House campaign committee is eyeing openings in Republican-held districts and hoping to raise millions of dollars in the next week to fuel a late round of advertising that they say could net at least a half dozen more seats. The shifting money in the final three weeks of midterm campaigns points to an increasingly defensive posture by Republicans, who have already trimmed their expectations in U.S. Senate races, and new aggression from Democrats, who are trying to capitalize on President Donald Trump's weak approval ratings. "You can tell now where people are competing based on where they're putting the money," said Stu Sandler, a Republican strategist working on House and statewide races this year. David McIntosh, president of the conservative Club For Growth, said there are only a few places where Republicans could pick up seats this year. "The economic environment has not been good," he said. "Voters are dissatisfied with their Republican majority and the base is also dissatisfied with that they weren't able to get the SAVE America Act passed," referring to Trump's plan for a strict proof-of-citizenship voting bill. "It looked like Republicans were weak," McIntosh said, "and so you've seen a lot of drop-off in enthusiasm." Republicans cut back in front-line districts The Congressional Leadership Fund is no longer spending on advertising in Iowa's 1st District, where three-term Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks is defending her seat against Democrat Christina Bohannan. Bohannan is running for her third time against Miller-Meeks. Last time, the race was decided by only 799 votes, making it the second-closest in the country. It's an eastern Iowa district where congressional cuts to Medicaid have been linked to hospital service closures and high diesel prices have been a challenge for farmers. Likewise, the officials said the group won't keep spending in New Jersey's 7th District, where second-term Republican Rep. Tom Kean is facing off against Democrat Rebecca Bennett. Kean has been under scrutiny for his four-month absence from Congress, which he left unexplained until disclosing a mental health crisis upon his return. Kean, who won by 5.4 percentage points two years ago, has also faced questions over his support for Trump's tariffs and the Iran war. These races, as well as one in the Cincinnati, Ohio, area and one in east-central Michigan, have accounted for $13.3 million in Congressional Leadership Fund spending, more than 12% of its total through Oct. 13. The group will instead reinforce districts where Trump beat Democrat Kamala Harris by narrow margins in 2024. Safety and Affordability, an offshoot of MAGA Inc., pulled nearly $1 million in ad spending aimed at helping Republican Marty O'Donnell's campaign in Nevada's 3rd District. Republicans had hoped that Trump's tax-cut legislation — specifically no taxes on tips — would resonate in Las Vegas and help defeat Democratic Rep. Susie Lee, who voted against the bill. Sandler said his party needs to turn out voters who usually participate in presidential elections but often stay home in the midterms. READ MORE: Can Democrats win the Senate? Here are some pathways "One thing you can't say is that they've been under-resourced," he said. "Republican resources are at a high. They've never been this well-funded in the midterm." Democrats try to scrounge up more money As House Republicans have retrenched, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee believes at least a dozen more races could be within striking distance. However, they need more money to take advantage. The committee launched a $17 million fundraising drive, with a deadline of Oct. 22, to pump advertising onto the air in districts that were once seen as out of reach. "It's not that we need the money to win in the districts where we have been running to get to 218 seats," said Courtney Rice, the committee's communication director. "We're talking about the next level." One is Ohio's 10th, a Dayton-area district represented by 12-term Republican Rep. Mike Turner. Democrats see Turner as beatable despite the former Dayton mayor's durability and 18 percentage-point victory two years ago. Trump carried the district by six percentage points in 2024. Turner didn't begin advertising until late September, according to AdImpact, later than most competitive House incumbents, and the National Republican Congressional Committee started spending there this week. If the Democratic committee reaches its goal, it would also start spending in the Miami area, suburban St. Louis, Missouri and the Little Rock, Arkansas, area. Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola, 10 days after a businessman died of the virus after he had travelled to the East African nation from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The new patient, a 39-year-old man, is a close relative of the first case and was already in quarantine when he fell ill on Tuesday, Kenya's health ministry says.
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Detecting his illness early had improved his chances of recovery and limited the chance of him passing the virus on to others, the ministry said, as it urged the public to "stay calm but vigilant".
"Both cases are linked, and there is no evidence of spread in the wider community," the ministry said.
"Kenya remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings", it added.
The 40-year-old Kenyan man who died on 5 October was diagnosed with Ebola shortly after being admitted to hospital in the capital, Nairobi.
A relative had taken him there shortly after picking him up at the airport. He had travelled from DR Congo, through Uganda to Kenya without his illness being detected.
Since his death, officials had determined that he had been in contact with 128 people - and since Tuesday 113 of them had been found, the health ministry said.
Of these, 108 were in quarantine in Kenya and tracing of the remaining 15 continued, it said.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
"Anyone with fever, unusual tiredness, muscle or joint pains, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding should seek care promptly at the nearest health facility," Kenya's health ministry said.
The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died.
However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the continent's leading public health agency, has reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements for the six weeks leading up to his death.
It revealed that he first started feeling unwell in DR Congo on 15 September - and showed how several opportunities to detect the infection were missed, including during several visits to Congolese medical facilities.
He then managed to travel through Uganda to Kenya - and was again not detected at airports screenings.
Health experts say it highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.

Trump is expected to speak at 3 p.m. EDT. Watch live in our player above. The visits come as the Republican president works to bolster his party in Nov. 3 elections that will determine control of Congress, and they follow stops earlier this week in Ohio and Alaska. In Bullhead City, Arizona, Trump will be rallying support for Rep. Andy Biggs, who is seeking to defeat incumbent Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs. Afterward, Trump is set to travel to Western Montana's 1st District to try to boost Aaron Flint, a former aide to retiring Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke, who served as Interior secretary in Trump's first-term Cabinet. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump has kept up a brisk pace of hour-plus-long rallies — new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia called it a "midterm blitz" — in his effort to stem expected Republican losses and fight a historical trend in which the president's party typically loses seats in elections halfway through their term in the White House. Arizona stands out as the lone swing state among the president's recent stops, though the airport rally will be in an area of the state known as a Republican stronghold. His other visits so far in October have taken him into traditionally solid Republican territory — Alabama, Nebraska, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas — as he weathers low approval ratings, rising costs and the Iran war. With under three weeks left in the campaign, the Western swing comes as Trump's party has begun retreating from a handful of battleground U.S. House races and Democrats aim to raise money for candidates who seemed like long shots earlier this year. The shifting money in the final weeks of midterm campaigns reflects an increasingly defensive posture by Republicans, who have already trimmed their expectations in U.S. Senate races, and new aggression from Democrats, who are trying to capitalize on Trump's low public approval. Trump twice won Arizona, in 2016 and 2024, but lost the state in 2020. Montana's 1st District is slightly less Republican overall than the state, which voted for Trump by double digits in each of his three presidential campaigns. Biggs, of Arizona, has been a stalwart ally of the president and assisted Trump's attempt to block certification by the House of Trump's 2020 election defeat. A one-time head of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, he's represented a safe GOP seat since winning election in 2016. He faces Hobbs, who narrowly defeated Republican Kari Lake in the governor's race four years ago in a state that has increasingly elected Democrats to statewide office. In Montana, Flint won the president's and Zinke's endorsement during the June primary. An Army veteran and talk-radio host, Flint assails progressive Democrats like Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as part of his campaign. Flint's opponent is Sam Forstag, a Democratic labor union leader and Forest Service smokejumper, a specialized firefighter who gets to fires by aircraft and parachute. Catalini reported from Morrisville, Pennsylvania. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. “Exponentially exploding,” mathematician Thomas Bloom told me by phone, describing the flood of new results in his field. Little did he know that hours later, OpenAI was going to post 722 mathematical manuscripts an unreleased AI model had produced.
The firehose of new work lends new urgency to the question: How is AI changing mathematical discovery? In their race for headline-grabbing breakthroughs, AI companies typically do not disclose their methods and data. That competition among AI companies threatens to overwhelm human collaboration and understanding.
This tension had been playing out in miniature on a website Bloom runs that tracks progress on more than 1,000 problems originally posed and collected by Paul Erdős, one of the 20th century’s most prolific mathematicians. Here, people used to collaborate to discuss open problems, or ones for which the best solution either hasn’t been found or isn’t known to the greater math community. But increasingly, visitors were competing to close open problems with AI proofs that they often didn’t understand. Bloom, a mathematician at the University of Manchester in England, doesn’t want to spend his days refereeing AI-generated work. So, soon after we spoke, and before he knew that OpenAI would be announcing its latest results, Bloom posted that he’d no longer tag problems as open or solved, and he also closed comments.
It’s definitely exciting that AI can tackle so many open problems so quickly. But can it help mathematicians understand the answers and build on them?
Just two days after OpenAI’s deluge of results, the peer-reviewed edition of a Google DeepMind study became public. First reported in a preprint earlier this year, it offers an inside look at how one AI system tackles open math problems. The system called AlphaProof Nexus solved 9 Erdős problems and made a number of other interesting mathematical advances, researchers report October 8 in Science.
The report includes a detailed description of how the results were obtained. Plus, human mathematicians vetted many of the proofs. That’s “quite different” from how OpenAI and Anthropic are handling their math results, Bloom says.
“The ultimate objective of any AI for math research,” says research scientist and study co-author Swarat Chaudhuri of Google DeepMind in London, should be “to advance mathematics as done by human mathematicians.”
A look inside an AI math machine
In the recently published study Chaudhuri and his colleagues tested different configurations of their system. To tackle a collection of 353 open Erdős problems, they used multiple agents powered by the Gemini language model. These could call on AlphaProof, an AI model specially trained to do math, and the inspiration for the name of the overall system, for difficult steps. The agents also relied on Lean, math software that identifies steps that remain unproven, to check their logic. The agents shared their work, circulating promising proof attempts and discarding ones that weren’t going well.
The team also tested a simpler setup on the nine problems the full system solved. Independent Gemini agents worked through proofs using Lean’s feedback, without sharing attempts or consulting AlphaProof. That setup solved all nine, too. It was cheaper—using fewer computing resources—than the full system on easy problems and more expensive on the two toughest ones. The team did not establish whether the simpler setup would solve any of the problems the full system had missed.
The fact that the simpler setup could solve the same nine problems as the full system surprised Chaudhuri. It suggests that increasingly capable language models can tackle research mathematics with relatively simple checking tools.
But computer-checking comes with a caveat. Lean checks only the statement it’s given, as it is written in its code. And a mathematical statement may be incorrectly translated to or from Lean code. An October 6 preprint shows why this translation matters. In the paper, the researchers pinpoint mismatches between parts of OpenAI’s written Navier–Stokes proof and its Lean counterpart. The mismatches do not mean the written proof is wrong, the team writes, but they note that a valid Lean proof does not automatically validate an AI-generated math paper.
That’s why the vetting human mathematicians did for the DeepMind publication is so important. “The human mathematician has to really think through the problem and set goals for the system,” Chaudhuri says. And even if the system failed to finish a proof, its checked steps helped mathematicians focus on the remaining gaps. “Math is ultimately a human art,” Chaudhuri says. “The system enhances the human user’s insights, and the human user is able to guide the system with new ideas.”
With math ability comes responsibility
The mathematical results that the AlphaProof Nexus system achieved are “not really at the top level of importance,” says Bloom, who wasn’t involved with the work. But that underscores the team’s more measured approach. Google DeepMind, he says, is “trying to be more responsible with the science,” while companies like OpenAI are using math to showcase their software. OpenAI’s papers and accompanying Lean proofs were entirely AI-generated, leaving it up to the math community to work out what’s useful or useless.
OpenAI says they worked with an independent advisory group to develop best practices on how to share their AI math results. But that group has said their advice was to not test unreleased AI models on advanced math, guidance the company clearly ignored.
The company’s fast-moving, competitive approach continues to alienate mathematicians such as Bryna Kra of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill. She says the company made some improvements in their efforts to cite past literature. And she’s excited about AI’s potential to solve important problems in math.
