Australia has been awarded its first Michelin stars, with 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia receiving the distinction.
Magill Estate Restaurant in Adelaide was the only venue to receive two stars, while 10 others were awarded one star each.
South Australia's government paid for incognito inspectors to visit the state, according to national broadcaster ABC, which is why no spots have been recognised in other parts of the country.
The announcement comes more than a century after the Michelin Guide was first published in France and following years of unsuccessful attempts to bring it to Australia.
Michelin has approached the national tourism board about bringing the guide to the country more than once, with no luck.
South Australia decided to go it alone and pursued its own deal. The state government has not disclosed how much it paid, but Tourism Minister Emily Bourke defended the investment in an interview with ABC News.
"It is enabling us to create a tourism destination and put us on the world map," she said.
The move follows Michelin's expansion into New Zealand, which became the first destination in Oceania to feature in the guide in July, agreeing to pay NZ$6.3m (Â£2.7m; $3.5m) over three years for its inclusion.
Created by brothers AndrÃ© and Ãdouard Michelin in 1900, the guide was originally designed to encourage motorists to travel - ultimately boosting their core business of selling tyres. It offered drivers maps and recommendations for places to eat and stay, before evolving into one of the best-known names in restaurant recognition.
Michelin stars were introduced in 1926 and have since become a major distinction for chefs and restaurants around the world.
One star recognises high-quality cooking, two stars indicate excellent cooking worth a detour, while three stars are reserved for exceptional cuisine worth a special journey.
Among the one-star recipients is ArkhÃ© in Norwood, which specialises in open-fire cooking, while Aptos in Adelaide serves a tasting menu focused on native Australian ingredients. Here is the full list:
Two Michelin stars
- Magill Estate Restaurant, Rosslyn Park
One Michelin star
- Anvers Restaurant, Kangarilla
- Maxwell Restaurant, McLaren Vale
- Botanic, Adelaide
- ArkhÃ©, Norwood
- Esmay, Adelaide
- Aurora at ILA, Adelaide
- Hentley Farm, Seppeltsfield
- LVN Restaurant at Bird in Hand, Woodside
- Aptos, Stirling
- Skillogalee Barrel House, Sevenhill
The wider guide includes more than 70 other South Australian restaurants, with some recognised through the Bib Gourmand category, which highlights restaurants offering good food at more moderate prices.

The ease in which England saw off Greece in round one of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs showed just how inefficient the structure currently is.
The two-time European champions were superior in every sense as they won 8-1 on aggregate against a Greece side ranked 55 places lower in the world.
Realistically, Greece stood little chance in a two-legged tie against Sarina Wiegman's side despite performing well in their home 3-1 defeat.
England's resounding victory was not a one-off as Europe's other top nations, who were forced to drop into the play-offs, also met lower-ranked opposition and won emphatically.
It was not an evening that truly reflects the growth of European women's football, which has become more competitive than ever in recent years.
It was, however, indicative that the qualification process perhaps needs reviewing by Uefa.
Why did we see heavy scorelines?
One of the main reasons for Tuesday night's results was that only one team from the league phase groups received automatic qualification.
The Netherlands, 2017 European champions, finished second in their group behind France, ranked sixth in the world. They went on to beat Hungary 11-0 on aggregate.
Norway, World Cup winners in 1995 and six-time European finalists, lost out to giants Germany in their group and ended up beating Romania 8-0.
Other League A fallouts Sweden and the Republic of Ireland thrashed their opponents 15-0 and 12-0 respectively.
So it was no surprise when back-to-back European champions England, who were drawn in the same group as world champions Spain, went on to record another heavy victory against much weaker opposition from League C in their play-off.
"Of course we wanted to qualify straight away, that's not the case," said England manager Wiegman when asked about the qualification process again on Tuesday.
"For us now, the facts are that we are in the play-offs, we have played Greece, now we're through, and now we're going to play Ukraine. That's what my focus is on.
"Uefa will review how things are set up and see whether they think it works or it should be better, or different. I don't think it's my place now to review that."
The Lionesses still have another two-legged tie against Ukraine to play, with the first leg taking place away from home on 1 December and the return fixture at Wembley Stadium on 5 December.
Ukraine are a side who England beat twice in the league phase by an aggregate score of 9-1.
It seems absurd that they should have to beat the same team on at least three occasions as part of their qualification process.
England have won seven of their last eight qualifying matches, scoring 21 goals, conceding just six times, and their only defeat was away from home against world champions Spain.
They came runners-up in League A3 only on their head-to-head record with the best team in the world - they even beat Spain 1-0 at Wembley.
England's overall tally of 15 points in the league phase was beaten by just three other teams - Germany, Switzerland and Hungary.
Switzerland and Hungary were also in qualifying groups in League B and League C that did not include a single team from the world's top 45 ranked nations.
In contrast England, who were seeded in League A, had Iceland - ranked 13th - as a tricky opponent, and world number one Spain in their four-team group.
Is the competition good enough?
When qualifying for the 2023 Women's World Cup, England beat Latvia on two occasions, winning 20-0 and 10-0 .
That tournament saw an increase from 24 to 32 teams and while qualification was still one-sided, the showpiece in Australia and New Zealand was a different story.
England were tested against debutants Haiti in the group stages, narrowly winning 1-0, and by Colombia in their quarter-final, despite the South American side failing to qualify for the previous tournament.
The level of competition was growing and it was evident even more so across Europe with England failing to qualify for the 2024 Olympic Games on behalf of Team GB after finishing second to the Netherlands in their Nations League group.
A draw with Portugal and defeat by Belgium were suffered by England the following year, while they were forced to overcome two penalty shootouts in Euro 2025.
There is no denying that England's competition has improved but they were still dealt a rough hand in this year's World Cup qualifying campaign.
Following their costly 4-0 defeat by Spain in June, Wiegman said: "The competition in Europe is really high.
"What I'm disappointed about is that we win five games, we have 15 points and we're in a group with the world champions and then you can't qualify.
"I'm happy with the performances but not the result of us having to go into the play-offs. That's just the way it is."
What is frustrating for England is that while they picked up a routine win over Greece and now prepare to face an opponent they have already played twice in 2026, their potential World Cup rivals are getting to play matches against top-tier teams.
Two of the tournament favourites Germany and Japan met in a friendly match on Tuesday night; Brazil and Argentina played out a 2-2 draw and four-time world champions USA played Spain twice in five days in a mouth-watering meeting.
Fifa has announced that the 2031 Women's World Cup will be expanded from 32 to 48 teams and it is too early to know if that is the right decision.
But while larger scorelines remain, it is clear it is more a direct result of a European qualification process that doesn't benefit the majority.

8126cc7715c5.text: Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios U.S. inflation picked up in September as soaring energy prices added to already stubborn price pressures, the Labor Department said on Wednesday. Why it matters: The latest Consumer Price Index shows that the inflation fight is far from over — and makes further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes more likely as Americans struggle with higher costs. By the numbers: CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, with the annual inflation rate at 3.7%, the government said. That compares with a 0.4% monthly increase and a 3.4% annual rate in August. Core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy costs, gained 0.3% on the month, compared with a similar monthly gain in August. In the 12 months through September, core CPI rose 2.6%, up from 2.4% the prior month. Zoom in: The latest figures capture the toll of the Middle East war on American consumers as disruptions to global energy supplies push up fuel prices. Gasoline prices spiked 9.1% in September after climbing 3.9% in August, when they accounted for more than a third of the monthly increase in consumer prices. Prices for shelter, one of the largest components of the index, increased 0.4%, compared with a 0.3% gain in August. Food prices were flat, compared with a slight 0.1% increase the previous month. Zoom out: The surge in fuel prices has prompted extraordinary measures from the Trump administration, particularly as soaring diesel costs threaten to push up prices for goods transported across the country . President Trump temporarily eased restrictions on tax-exempt diesel and lifted some U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel to boost global diesel supplies. Airline fares surged 1.2% in September — bringing the annual increase to 22% — as higher jet fuel costs put pressure on ticket prices. What to watch: The Social Security Administration is set to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for millions of retirees, based on inflation figures released on Wednesday. The increase will take effect in January. The big picture: The report comes as Federal Reserve officials weigh how soon to raise interest rates again , with policymakers divided over the persistence of inflation. In a speech on Monday, Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack warned that inflation pressures extend well beyond energy — citing tariffs, AI investment and rising services prices. Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg on Tuesday that higher Treasury yields are already helping restrain economic activity, possibly reducing the urgency of another rate hike this month. New York Fed president John Williams said one more increase might be ahead this year, though he cautioned the central bank might not have to raise again in 2027. The bottom line: In the wake of the inflation report, financial markets are now betting that an interest rate increase is more likely when the Fed meets later this month. Odds of October rate hike jumped to 44% from 22% Tuesday, according to CME FedWatch data. The yield on the two-year Treasury note — the security most reactive to Fed policy expectations — jumped 12 basis points, while the 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

70b6d5998e60.text: By — Franklin Briceno, Associated Press Franklin Briceno, Associated Press By — Isabel DeBre, Associated Press Isabel DeBre, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/south-americans-pray-for-pope-leos-recovery-as-uncertainty-hangs-over-his-visit Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter South Americans pray for Pope Leo's recovery as uncertainty hangs over his visit World Oct 14, 2026 6:07 PM EDT LIMA, Peru (AP) — Roman Catholics across South America responded to news of Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer diagnosis with an outpouring of prayers and support, along with concerns about whether the first American pope would go ahead with his highly anticipated and physically demanding visit to the region next month. Across the three countries on his itinerary — secular Uruguay, predominantly Catholic Argentina and Leo's adopted homeland of Peru — government officials wished the pontiff a swift recovery, church leaders urged patience and worshippers gathered to pray. WATCH: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer and prognosis The Vatican said Wednesday that Leo was recuperating as expected after surgery and that the trip remained on his schedule. But Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori sounded a more cautious note, telling reporters that his recovery could take "several weeks, longer than expected," potentially forcing changes to the Nov. 6-17 itinerary. The trip would follow an ambitious itinerary The 12-day South American tour would be the longest of Leo's papacy so far, covering more than 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles) on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides. Across Uruguay and Argentina — two countries last visited by a pope in the 1980s — Leo would celebrate Masses and meet with worshippers, clergy and political leaders in six cities. The longest leg of the trip would take Leo, 71, to Peru, where he spent 20 years as a missionary and bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo. From the capital, Lima, he is scheduled to travel north to his former diocese, then on to the ancient Inca capital of Cusco high in the Andes and the Amazonian city of Pucallpa. The thin mountain air in Cusco, roughly 3,400 meters (11,150 feet) above sea level, could pose a particular challenge so soon after Leo's lung surgery. READ MORE: Pope will retrace his missionary footsteps in Peru and finally visit Argentina in November Church officials in Argentina, the homeland of Leo's predecessor Pope Francis, urged parishioners to put the pontiff's well-being ahead of their excitement over the country's first papal visit in four decades. "Sometimes we think selfishly about his coming, but the first thing we need to think about is his health," said Cardinal Ángel Rossi, the archbishop of Córdoba, one of Leo's planned stops. Leaders across Argentina's deep ideological divide, from right-wing President Javier Milei to his left-wing rival, Buenos Aires Gov. Axel Kicillof, joined in wishing the pope a speedy recovery. READ MORE: Pope Leo is eating and recovering after cancer surgery, doctors say "All of Argentina stands with His Holiness in affection and prayer," said Milei, who was raised Catholic but has more recently explored conversion to Judaism. In neighboring Uruguay, where Leo's visit is expected to energize the Catholic minority in a country that officially celebrates Christmas as Family Day, Cardinal Daniel Sturla, the archbishop of Montevideo, tempered hopes for the historic visit. "First, let us pray that he comes. We run the risk of being told in the coming days that he won't be able to come," Sturla told local media Tuesday, adding that the decision will ultimately rest with the pope's doctors. Peru eagerly awaits Leo's homecoming In Chiclayo, one of Peru's largest cities, excitement over Leo's anticipated homecoming turned to apprehension after his diagnosis. "Because of the affection that we feel for the Holy Father, who is also our bishop, we're worried about his health and about what will come next," said the Rev. Elmer Uchofen, who recalled how the future pope helped secure oxygen production plants during the COVID-19 pandemic, waded through mud in rubber boots to aid flood victims and celebrated Mass with prisoners in Chiclayo. Betania Marina Rodríguez, who leads a local association for Venezuelan migrants in Chiclayo and also worked closely with Leo, said she felt a collision of conflicting emotions. "We all want him to be healthy and strong," she said. "But we also long to see him, hear him and receive his blessing." WATCH: 'American Pope' traces Leo's journey from Chicago to the Vatican In Lima, Peruvians crossed themselves and recited the rosary before a life-size silicone statue of the pontiff outside a church. Others gathered at the centuries-old Las Nazarenas Monastery, home to a revered image of the crucified Jesus that draws vast religious processions each October. Teresa Ramírez, 73, clutched red, white and yellow roses — the combined colors of the Peruvian and Vatican flags — at the monastery as she offered her blessings to the man she called "the most beloved Peruvian in the world." "There's still time for him to come to Peru," she said. "May our heavenly Father's will be done." Leo, born Robert Prevost in Chicago, became a Peruvian citizen in 2015 and renewed his national identity document last year after becoming pope. At a nursing home in the Peruvian port city of Callao, another stop on Leo's planned itinerary, Mayela Medina, 52, expressed hope that the prayers of millions of Peruvians would bring comfort to the convalescing pope. "I went through dark days and long nights when I struggled to breathe," she said, recalling her own battle with respiratory illness. "I pray to God with all my soul that he does not feel abandoned." DeBre reported from Buenos Aires, Argentina. Associated Press writer Luis Andres Henao contributed to this report from Princeton, New Jersey. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. BIRMINGHAM, Ala.—It’s hard to forget Uncle Bobo.
And on this humid October day, his nephew says it’s hard to remember him, too.
Devolin “Bobo” Webster, 66, died unexpectedly in his home Saturday morning as the remnants of Hurricane Isaias passed through the Magic City, more than 200 miles from where the category 2 storm made landfall around 8:30 the night before.
A tree struck Webster’s home just after 5 a.m., according to the local coroner’s office, crashing through the roof and killing him.
Climate Central, a nonprofit that researches and reports on climate change’s effects on people’s lives, said exceptionally warm sea surface temperatures in the western and central Gulf of Mexico, where the storm formed, were up to 600 times more likely due to human-caused atmospheric warming.
Webster is one of eight people whose deaths officials have attributed to Isaias and its aftermath: two in Alabama and six in Florida.
Webster was a truck driver who loved his family, football and fishing, his loved ones said.
Webster’s nephew Paul Evans said that as a child, he would visit his uncle every summer, memories he still cherishes. Through the years, Evans began to look up to his Uncle Bobo, who helped him to see that it was possible to have a stable job, own a home and still help others.
“He was my favorite uncle,” Evans said. “He always had a smile on his face.”
Last Christmas, Evans said Webster called him over to his home, gave him an envelope and told him “Merry Christmas.” Evans opened it: $400.
“It was out of the blue,” he said. “But that’s just who he was.”
That’s what made Webster special, Evans said.
“He would do such nice things for people and never tell a soul,” Evans said. “He would just do it from the heart.”
Both Webster and another of Evans’ uncles were at home when what remained of Hurricane Isaias passed through Birmingham overnight Friday, bringing about 3 inches of rain and wind gusts of around 50 miles per hour.
Both men were asleep when the tree fell on the home, Evans said.
“Uncle Bobo was crushed by the tree,” Evans said. “And my other uncle tried to get to him.”
But the fallen tree had knocked a hole in the floor between the two bedrooms, Evans explained.
“He fell from his room all the way down to the garage floor,” Evans said. “And debris started falling on him. He’s covered in cuts and bruises.”
While Evans’ other uncle survived, first responders found Webster dead on the scene.
“We’re devastated,” Evans said of his family. “Uncle Bobo was special to a lot of people.”
Because of Birmingham’s location hundreds of miles from the Gulf Coast, Evans said his uncles likely hadn’t done much to prepare for the weather event.
That’s not uncommon.

Research shows that those living in inland areas are less likely to prepare for events like hurricanes they believe are unlikely to impact them.
One researcher also found that authorities in inland areas were less likely to issue evacuation orders. When they do, the research showed, inland residents were half as likely to evacuate as people living on the coast.
Climate change is likely to compound the risks caused by these dynamics. As hurricanes continue to intensify, so too will impacts farther inland.
In September 2024, Hurricane Helene made landfall in Florida’s Big Bend region as a Category 4 storm with 140 mph winds before quickly moving far inland, heavily damaging communities in Georgia and the southern Appalachians, with Western North Carolina hardest hit.
Helene killed roughly 250 people in the U.S., including more than 100 in North Carolina. Damage from the hurricane was estimated at about $80 billion.
In September 2021, Hurricane Ida made landfall at Port Fourchon, Louisiana, and, several days later, merged with a frontal system over the mid-Atlantic and Northeast before swamping parts of Philadelphia, and killing 30 people in flash floods in New Jersey and 13 in New York City, most of whom drowned in basement apartments swamped by flooding.
For Webster’s family in Birmingham, his death has been a way for them to reconnect, even in the wake of tragedy. Webster had recently returned from a fishing trip, his family said, and he’d given them some of his catch. They haven’t had the heart to eat it just yet.
But soon, Evans said, they’ll do what they can to heal from their unexpected loss, cleaning Uncle Bobo’s fish, scale by scale. They’ll fry them up in the Alabama sun and make a day of it.
It’s what Uncle Bobo would’ve wanted.

The News
President Donald Trump is pushing ahead with his deal to import Russian diesel, blowing past his partyâs growing complaints about taking help from Vladimir Putin.
âThe presidentâs main priority and commitment is to the American people and to help lower costs for the American people, and heâs doing that,â a White House official said after days of withering complaints by Republicans. âThe president has not shifted his stance on it.â
The Trump administration caused an intraparty furor earlier this month by announcing that the US will import roughly 2.2 million tons of Russian diesel in an effort to ease fuel price spikes that have hurt Republican candidates on the midterm campaign trail.
Itâs unclear exactly when the imports will officially arrive, but the economic boost from Moscow is sparking discontent as Republicans in tight races scramble to message around the surprise announcement.
Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, who is running for the Senate, said on Tuesday in a debate that she vastly preferred other options to bring down fuel prices â among them, suspending the gas tax, creating a diesel rebate program, and using more biofuels.
âWe need to lower diesel prices, but I donât think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it,â Hinson said.
The Russia deal completes a trio of Trump economic moves that are politically toxic to swing-state Republicans, joining his bid to encourage beef imports and his Canadian trade war. All three are unpopular enough among members of Trumpâs own party to create significant discord about the GOP plan to tackle rising prices.
Republicans are signing onto letters bashing the Russia diesel agreement and distancing themselves on the campaign trail: Former New Hampshire Sen. John Sununu, seeking the Senate again, said this week that the move would do little to lower prices in the US and âprovides an advantage to Russiaâ In Michigan, former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers similarly broke with Trump.
But other Republicans defended Trumpâs policy change.
âThe presidentâs got energy security and economic security front of mind right now. Heâs focused on Americans first,â Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., a top Trump ally, said this week.
Hagerty dismissed the prospect that US diesel purchases would unfairly aid Russia in its war against Ukraine: âWeâve got a number of sanctions in place and a number of efforts to bring Putin into alignment.â
For the White House, the argument is simple: Diesel prices are too high, and even a smaller-scale import plan helps ease the burden.
Others in the administration privately acknowledge, however, that thereâs a clear reason for the recent rise in prices: Trumpâs ongoing war with Iran. His administration also has long entertained ways to unwind certain sanctions on Russia in a bid to secure a peace deal with Ukraine â one that would also help ease inflation.
âHaving to do this is yet another inevitable consequence of the Iran war,â said a second Trump administration official, who added a hope that the diesel deal becomes part of âa broader diplomatic strategy.â
Know More
Already, two bipartisan groups of senators have pushed back on the decision, including seven Republicans. One House Republican has said heâll introduce legislation to block it.
âTrump and his team have misread the room on the Republican caucuses in the House and the Senate on this issue,â Bloomberg economist Chris Kennedy told Semafor. âTheyâre trying to respond to concerns from congressional Republicans in farm states about diesel prices â¦ and it doesnât seem to be landing very well.â
Fueling that discontent is Republicansâ dimming faith that Trump will choose to impose recently enacted Russian sanctions that were passed in honor of his longtime ally, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said earlier this month that the administration planned to âname namesâ â but whether to use that sanctions power would be âfor the president to decide.â
Asked this week about GOP skeptics of his diesel purchases from Russia, Trump dismissed them as âRepublicans that canât really be serious,â adding that itâs âa deal for the rest of the world.â White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers praised Trumpâs âgreat deal to supply the global market with massive amounts of diesel.â
âLowering prices for Americaâs great farmers, truckers, and families remains a top priority as the President simultaneously urges both sides of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to stop strikes against refineries, which are driving up costs and hurting American consumers,â Rogers said in a statement.
âWe didnât think [the bill] would change anything on the sanctions front â¦ and I think that this decision just reinforces that view,â said Kennedy, who served on the National Security Council during the Trump and Biden administrations.
Room for Disagreement
A handful of GOP lawmakers, including Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker of Mississippi, are taking a different tack by predicting the diesel imports never materialize.Some Republicans posit that Trumpâs new import deal violates a 2022 law that bans the US from purchasing Russian energy products. Others point to hurdles like European sanctions and Russian shortages.
Even if it does become real, it wonât do much to lower prices. Investors are already pricing in âlittle near-term impact,â Kennedy said, since the world uses far more diesel than Russia will export.
Wicker said heâs pitched the administration on alternative ideas. Itâs unclear what those could be.
Shelby, Eleanor, and Burgessâ View
Whether itâs red-dye diesel or Russian diesel, the Trump administration is pulling out all the stops to convince voters that itâs bringing prices down â¦ even as it maintains an Iran war that is driving costs up.
So far, the presidentâs advisers have little to show for it beyond making life harder for the rest of their party.

7e46d4fbd232.text: By — Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/lawyers-for-federal-reserves-lisa-cook-say-white-house-hearing-set-up-by-trump-is-biased Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Lawyers for Federal Reserve's Lisa Cook say White House hearing set up by Trump is 'biased' Politics Oct 14, 2026 5:46 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook's lawyers say that a committee set up by the White House last week to investigate an accusation against her is "demonstrably biased," though they did not close the door on the possibility that she would appear before the panel. Lawyer Abbe Lowell also said in a letter Tuesday that Cook would not be able to participate in a hearing Nov. 5 because she "will be executing her official duties as Governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The earliest that Cook could appear before a "committee of inquiry" that the White House set up last Friday would be after the Fed's policy meeting Dec. 8-9, the letter said. The letter was sent to William Scharf, a counsel to President Donald Trump. Lowell's comments are the latest turn in the Trump administration's extended efforts to fire Cook from her position as one of seven members of the Fed's board of governors. Trump has accused Cook of committing mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the board, a claim she has denied. No criminal charges have been filed. READ MORE: Trump establishes committee to investigate Federal Reserve's Lisa Cook in latest effort to fire her No president has fired a Fed governor before, a reflection of the Fed's traditional independence from politics. Yet Trump, who has repeatedly demanded that the central bank lower its key interest rate, has taken numerous steps that economists say have threatened that independence. The Justice Department earlier this year sought to investigate then-Chair Jerome Powell over brief testimony he had given about an extensive building renovation, though a judge threw out subpoenas in the case and it was later dropped. Cook was appointed by former President Joe Biden and is the first Black woman on the Fed's board. Trump first tried to fire Cook in August 2025, but the Supreme Court ruled earlier this year she could remain in her position while litigation continued. The court also suggested, in a footnote to the ruling, that Trump could try again to fire her if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee of inquiry announced by the White House last Friday is an effort to meet those conditions. WATCH: Supreme Court ruling proves Federal Reserve is unique agency, Lisa Cook's lawyer says Under the law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a Fed governor "for cause," but the Supreme Court didn't address whether Cook's actions met that standard. The committee of inquiry will ultimately recommend whether there is cause to fire Cook, a White House memo last week said. Lowell also said in the Tuesday letter that "we have significant concerns regarding the objectivity and fitness of the committee for its assigned purpose." One of its three members, Kevin Hassett, a top economic adviser to Trump, has already said the president has "cause" to fire Cook, the letter noted. The other two members — Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling and chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Andrea Rich — are also Trump appointees. "A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence – with no explanation for why it was not previously produced – is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence," Lowell's letter said. Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to SpaceX's Starlink internet network.
Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said unexpected new speed limits were disrupting its battlefield missions.
An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believed the restrictions were not a coincidence and were related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.
Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".
Musk - writing on X - had been responding to pleas from Ukrainian officials to restore connectivity, including from Zelensky who told UK media: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe [a] huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to... switch [it] on."
Starlink, which is owned by Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.
It had been partially restored by Wednesday evening, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said.
"Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support".
About an hour later, Musk replied to that post, defending his company's involvement.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.
Musk added that Starlink is for "civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".
The US government has not commented.
While both companies are owned by Musk's SpaceX, Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas, while Starshield is designed for government and military use.
The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that killed several people in Kyiv, officials said, and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.
President Zelensky said it was "one of the largest attacks" from Russia, and while "a significant part of the drones were shot down" there were "also hits".
At least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity, and residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit.
"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.
US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated towards Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities.
Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire, but on Tuesday, Trump denied this.
Speaking during a visit to London on Wednesday, President Zelensky agreed that he had felt betrayed after the US made a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its diesel.
"Really yes... but it's a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings," Zelensky said, when asked by UK journalist Piers Morgan if he felt betrayed.
During his one-day visit, Zelensky was greeted with a hug by UK PM Andy Burnham at Downing Street and held an audience with King Charles.
Ahead of the president's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones.
"We are behind you and that will not change," Burnham told Zelensky.

470ff0eac0b9.text: By — Heather Hollingsworth, Associated Press Heather Hollingsworth, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/a-gang-rape-allegation-at-cornell-highlights-how-title-ix-guides-campus-sex-assault-cases Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A gang rape allegation at Cornell highlights how Title IX guides campus sex assault cases Nation Oct 14, 2026 4:52 PM EDT Cornell University's handling of an alleged fraternity house gang rape is raising questions about how a decades-old federal civil rights law shapes colleges' treatment of campus sexual assault. The focus on Title IX, which prohibits sexual discrimination in education, comes after a woman identified only as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month against Cornell and seven fraternity members. She said she was assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024 after being pressured into snorting the fast-acting sedative ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol. The accused men have all denied her allegations, either saying the sexual activity was consensual or they weren't involved. WHAT: What the Cornell case reveals about how sexual assault allegations are handled Title IX was best known for most of its 54 years for opening doors for female athletes. But guidance issued in 2011 under President Barack Obama's administration made clear it also protects people who say they were sexually assaulted or harassed. The rules have changed with new presidential administrations, but Title IX proceedings are intended to help colleges decide how to discipline the people involved, regardless of whether they face criminal or other legal repercussions. Dual systems sow confusion A sexual assault case can be handled in criminal court and through the campus-run Title IX disciplinary process at the same time. In theory, the criminal proceeding could lead to prison time and the Title IX case to expulsion. In reality, serious consequences are rare in either system, said Megan Greeson, a professor of community psychology at DePaul University. She was among the authors of a review of studies involving 288,066 cases that found around 20% of those reported to police are prosecuted and 8% lead to convictions. WATCH: New details intensify scrutiny of Cornell's handling of gang rape allegations Jane Doe was no exception. Days after she gave her first substantial interviews to campus police, the county district attorney in upstate New York decided not to prosecute. Long after that, Jane Doe believed the criminal investigation was ongoing. Her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, said she was "misled." Her case illustrates a common complaint with the dual-track system. Greeson said she often hears: "What do you mean there's two different investigations?" How does the Title IX process work? On the surface, Title IX investigations look a lot like police investigations. Witnesses are interviewed, and the accused often hire attorneys. The process is so demanding that many victims drop their case or choose to go an informal route, in which the accused might be asked not to take classes with the accuser, or to switch universities — often with no mark on their record. WATCH: News Wrap: Cornell students protest handling of alleged rape When cases proceed to a hearing, schools have a lower bar for determining culpability than the justice system's standard of beyond a reasonable doubt. Title IX requires schools to find an accused student responsible if the evidence shows the allegations are more likely true than not. Beyond expulsions, consequences can include suspensions, loss of scholarships or withholding of a degree. A culpability finding can be noted on transcripts, which can make it difficult to get into graduate school or to obtain a state license in certain fields. The process ping-pongs between presidential administrations At some universities, including Cornell, Title IX offices handled fewer complaints after regulations narrowed the definition of sexual harassment during President Donald Trump's first term. Critics argued the rules discouraged students from coming forward with abuse allegations. Those who did faced a live hearing and cross-examination by a person of their alleged attacker's choosing. Former President Joe Biden's administration overhauled the rules to expand the type of behavior that's considered sexual harassment. Rules finalized in 2024 also provided recognition that Title IX protects LGBTQ+ students and made live hearings optional. WATCH: Appointing Cornell sex assault special prosector, Hochul says she won't let anyone 'sweep this case under the rug' A federal judge in Kentucky overturned Biden's changes in early January 2025. Trump's current administration subsequently reverted to the 2020 rules in a change that became official last month. Cornell's Title IX complaints fluctuated as the regulations changed, falling from 205 in 2019 to 98 in 2020, when COVID-19 also shut down campuses, before rising to 166 in 2024. Additionally, the Education Department 's Office for Civil Rights used to serve as a powerful enforcer in cases of campus sexual violence. Under Obama and Biden, it brought the weight of the government against schools that mishandled sexual assault complaints involving students. But investigations have dwindled since Trump returned to office. "There's become fewer and fewer avenues for accountability and support that students are able to access with the way the current administration is enforcing or really choosing not to enforce Title IX," said Emma Grasso Levine, the manager of Know Your IX, which works to address campus sexual violence. What do we know about how the Cornell Title IX case was handled? It started about three weeks after the alleged assault, when Jane Doe went to campus police. That same day, the head of Cornell's fraternities contacted the school's Title IX office. The Chi Phi fraternity house was immediately suspended and later closed for good.

Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham matters
Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed President Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday, as the Ukrainian leader looks to shore up his European allies five years into Russia's war on Ukraine.
Burnham told Zelensky that Britain "would forever stand by you" and that he was accelerating the delivery of air defences to Ukraine.

Thousands of students have taken to the streets in the Albanian capital of Tirana, attacking several government buildings on the second day of violent anti-government protests.
The demonstration began outside the ministry of education on Tuesday, as students called for better university conditions and job prospects.
Wednesday saw part of the education ministry's building set on fire, while the prime minister's office, finance and interior ministry, and several surrounding businesses were also attacked.
Albania's Deputy Prime Minister âAlbana KoÃ§iu has called for "calmness, self-restraint and maturity" and said "Albania does not need to burn to change".
Riot police have clashed with the protesters, using tear gas and water cannons to disperse them.
One demonstrator, Enida Bimi, told Reuters news agency that the protest is not just for the students, but "for all the people of Albania".
"The people are very angry at the system. They need to change everything. With this corruption all around, the crime and everything else is happening. And the people now are angry. They need to change the system," Bimi said.
Another protester, Arber Leshi, said people are angry at "the most corrupt government our country has ever seen".
Education Mirela Kumbaro said that while she respects the right to protest, "civic student protest and violence against public buildings and property are two different things".
Officials have criticised the behaviour of some protesters.
"Setting fire to an institution is not a peaceful protest. It is an act that endanger's peoples lives", said economy minister Delina Ibrahimaj, responding to a video appearing to show protesters throwing rocks at the finance ministry building.
Sixteen people were arrested "in connection with violent acts" during Tuesday's protest, Albania's state-run news agency said.
Sali Berisha, the leader of the opposition - the Democratic Party of Albania - has praised the protesters.
"The streets and squares of Tirana have never seen lions like these students," he said during an evening meeting on Wednesday, Albania's state-run news agency Ata reported.
This student-led protest comes after months of anti-government protests, known as the Flamingo Revolution, which is calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The protests were sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, which fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency from Rama's government.

f964ec80d2f1.text: By — Leah Willingham, Associated Press Leah Willingham, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/cornell-president-admits-he-never-followed-up-on-gang-rape-allegation-ahead-of-no-confidence-debate Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Cornell president admits he never followed up on gang rape allegation ahead of no-confidence debate Nation Oct 14, 2026 4:23 PM EDT Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff knew in 2024 that a student had reported being gang raped at a fraternity house, but never followed up to learn what had happened to her or whether any of the accused students had been punished. In an interview with The New York Times published Tuesday, a day before Cornell's Faculty Senate was set to begin debating a no-confidence resolution in his administration, Kotlikoff acknowledged that he did not know until recently that the woman had dropped out of Cornell or that students had been expelled or suspended over the incident. READ MORE: Cornell president calls alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' pledges greater transparency Kotlikoff publicly addressed what he called "deeply disturbing" allegations involving drug use and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house in a November 2024 message to the Cornell community, saying criminal and university investigations were underway. He subsequently convened a presidential task force to examine how Cornell handles sexual assault, but said this week that he never followed up to learn the outcomes of the criminal or Title IX investigations into the woman's allegations. Case has drawn national attention, roiled campus The case has drawn national attention since the woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit alleging that seven Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. On Tuesday, Kotlikoff announced a ban on fraternity parties through the end of the academic year and plans to give state police a role in investigating sexual assault reports. WATCH: New details intensify scrutiny of Cornell's handling of gang rape allegations Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten initially declined to pursue charges after reviewing a summary prepared by Cornell University Police, but later said it omitted key details. He reopened the investigation after the lawsuit was filed. Gov. Kathy Hochul subsequently removed him from the case, appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor and ordered an independent review of Cornell's handling of the allegations. The Cornell Faculty Senate's proposed resolution, declaring no confidence in the administration's ability to handle reports of sexual assault on campus, reflects growing concerns among some faculty members that people who report sexual misconduct face institutional barriers and fear retaliation. Some have called for Kotlikoff's resignation, while others have urged patience as independent investigations proceed. Kotlikoff was scheduled to address the Faculty Senate on Wednesday before members begin debating the resolution. Debate was expected to continue Oct. 28, followed by electronic voting by the Faculty Senate, which has approximately 130 voting members. A simple majority is required for passage. Professor who reported harassment says it nearly cost her career For Ariana Kim, an associate music professor at Cornell and co-sponsor of the resolution, Kotlikoff's acknowledgment that he had not followed up on the woman's case was deeply troubling. "I mean, that's appalling in and of itself, right?" Kim said. "That you don't know about a student who faced an alleged horrific crime, that you don't think to check in." Kim, a Grammy-nominated violinist, said she was motivated to take action after being struck by Jane Doe's story, as well as her own personal experiences on campus since she started at Cornell a decade ago as a young academic in her 20s. She said when she experienced bullying and sexual harassment by senior colleagues, Cornell failed to properly document her complaints and that she was never clearly informed what disciplinary action, if any, had been taken. "I was asked what I had done to provoke the situation," she said. WATCH: What the Cornell case reveals about how sexual assault allegations are handled Kim said she continued to be expected to work alongside colleagues involved in the dispute. She believes reporting the misconduct later affected her tenure review. She spent 18 months appealing an adverse tenure decision, a process during which she lost 20 pounds (9 kilograms) and struggled to eat or sleep. A university appeals board ultimately overturned the original decision, and she secured tenure. Now seeking promotion to full professor, Kim said she recognizes that publicly criticizing university leaders could again jeopardize her career. "I'm speaking out publicly against this administration that may very well deny my promotion," she said. Kim said she has considered leaving Cornell many times over the years but is determined to stay and make the university safer for those who come after her. "If by me fighting, it helps move the needle a little bit so that my female students aren't going through this in 10 years or my female colleagues aren't going through this in five years, then maybe it's worth it." Faculty members question whether Cornell can investigate itself Anne Marie Brady, a senior extension associate at Cornell's School of Industrial and Labor Relations and another co-sponsor of the resolution, questioned whether Cornell University Police can independently investigate serious allegations of sexual misconduct. "There doesn't seem to be independence between the administration and the Cornell Police Department," Brady said. She pointed to its handling of campus protests as one reason for her concerns and said serious criminal allegations should be investigated by outside

d49c0f37a64c.text: The rupture between President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over last week's diesel deal deepened Wednesday after an Elon Musk -owned satellite system used by Ukraine unexpectedly restricted service — undercutting Ukraine's fight against Russia. Why it matters: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When it doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Service was partially restored on Wednesday, but Ukrainian officials were still searching for answers about why the service was throttled and who was responsible. The limitations came days after a new crisis erupted between the U.S. and Ukraine over Trump's agreement to lift sanctions on Russian oil sales. Zelensky criticized the move, then Trump called for Ukraine to elect a new president. A senior U.S. official said the Trump administration had nothing to do with the alleged Starlink service constraints. But Ukrainian officials remain suspicious. Driving the news: Ukrainian officials said SpaceX imposed the restrictions Tuesday night. The system turned off, they said, when a drone exceeded 160 kph. In some cases, it disconnected when the speed went over 80 kph. The Starlink restrictions came several hours after the Ukrainian military did not receive an early warning about a Russian ballistic missile attack. Ukrainian officials said the U.S. has provided such alerts over the last several years as part of intelligence sharing between the countries. U.S. officials pointed to a technical malfunction in the system, but Ukrainian officials suspect that it was a warning shot from the Trump administration. "We had massive [Russian] attacks today and it's a pity that we also had difficulties ... about Starlink and about intelligence and a lot of different surprises," Zelensky said at the top of a meeting in London with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. "We count on the partnership with the U.S. but we just want to be very honest and very clear and be a strong partner." The latest: The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense said SpaceX continues to restrict Starlink to 160 kph — significantly higher than earlier but still well below its normal speeds. The ministry said it remains in communication "with partners and SpaceX regarding stable service conditions and the prevention of sudden restrictions." "The situation is better than it was this morning, but 160 kph is not enough for intercepting" some Russian jet drones, a Ukrainian official added. The intrigue: Ukrainian officials think the restrictions were imposed intentionally by SpaceX to press Ukraine to accept Trump's demand not to attack Russian oil refineries. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski wrote to Musk on X on Wednesday: "Hey, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you." Between the lines: Ukraine relies on two satellite systems. One is SpaceX's Starlink, which is used for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes. Both systems were restricted, according to Ukraine. What they're saying: In a post on X , Musk did not directly address the throttling of Starlink, but he did indirectly comment on which entity would have been responsible for the limitations imposed on Ukraine. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote. "Starlink," he added, "is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company." Behind the scenes: Zelensky's top advisers spoke with their White House counterparts Wednesday and asked whether there'd been a decision to shut down Starlink services and what could be done to fix the situation, two sources said. Ukrainian officials made similar calls to the CIA and the Pentagon. White House officials told the Ukrainians they don't have control over SpaceX, the sources said. One of the sources said the Trump administration is going to reach out to SpaceX to figure out what happened. The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Incumbent New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman clashed over high energy costs in the state’s only gubernatorial debate, offering sharply different visions for how to keep electricity affordable as demand rises.
Average residential electricity bills in New York rose 10 percent from 2024 to 2025, outpacing the national average. The state has the eighth-highest residential electricity prices in the country, which has made affordability a central issue in the governor’s race.
With less than three weeks until Election Day, recent polling data suggests Hochul leads Blakeman by around 12 percentage points. Blakeman has served as Nassau County executive since 2022.
During the debate, Hochul touted her “all of the above” energy strategy, which includes developing renewable energy and expanding nuclear power. Blakeman blamed the state’s high utility bills in part on clean energy programs, calling them a “slush fund” for “science projects,” such as offshore wind farms and solar panels that he claimed were “ruining agriculture.”
But state data shows that decarbonization programs account for only a portion of residential electricity costs. A 2025 Public Service Commission report found that measures mandated by New York’s Climate Act made up between 5 and 9.5 percent of a typical monthly residential electric bill in 2024.
Most of the bill reflects the cost of buying and delivering electricity. Rate increases in the state are often linked to surging electricity demand, which raises prices, as well as an over-reliance on gas-fired power generation, which in turn is tied to the natural gas market.
Utilities are also investing more in expanding electrical infrastructure to accommodate new power generators—and new customers.
The candidates also shared different visions of how to generate more power. Wind and solar projects, paired with battery storage, can typically be built at cheaper costs than fossil fuel infrastructure, potentially helping to meet rising electricity demand while supporting the state’s climate goals.
Hochul emphasized her push to build more nuclear power in the state, though she did not say whether she would reopen Indian Point, a nuclear plant north of New York City that closed in 2021.
Nuclear power remains a controversial topic in New York, with activists and critics raising concerns about costs, public health and possible environmental impacts linked to the long-term storage of “spent fuel,” which is extremely radioactive.
Blakeman has offered few details about his energy policy beyond attacking renewable energy initiatives. To lower energy bills, he has pledged to bring fracking back to New York, though the practice was banned statewide more than a decade ago over public health concerns.
The statewide debate over energy costs comes as New York faces growing electricity demand, driven partly by data centers, building electrification and manufacturing. The state’s grid operator faces a growing backlog of applications from proposed data centers, which could put even more pressure on the power supply.
Hochul touted her executive order for a yearlong statewide moratorium on data centers and pledged to require new facilities to “bring their own power.” In other states, meeting data centers’ rising electricity demands has led to plans for a buildout of polluting natural gas plants. Environmental advocates have called for greater public input on the state’s proposed data center policy.
Hochul also described herself as “laser-focused on affordability” and pointed to her administration’s energy rebate policy, which will send checks of up to $200 to 8.2 million households to offset rising costs. She did not answer a question about whether the rebates would become an annual benefit.
Blakeman has aligned himself with President Donald Trump, recently praising him at a rally in Syracuse. During the debate, Hochul challenged Blakeman over Trump administration policies, including tariffs and the Iran war, which have contributed to higher prices. In response, Blakeman said he and Trump have “significant policy differences.”
Hochul became governor in 2021 after Andrew Cuomo resigned amid a sexual harassment scandal. In 2022, she defeated current Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin, a former congressman from Long Island.

The Scoop
The White House played a central role in the Justice Departmentâs antitrust investigation into major TV networksâ temporary suspension of pooled coverage of the president, three people familiar with the matter told Semafor.
While the probe is progressing, some inside the DOJ are concerned about its legal merits. Two former DOJ officials said that the networks suspending their pool participation after three news outlets got barred from the White House are likely protected by the First Amendment â one cited a 1982 Supreme Court ruling that afforded those constitutional protections to group boycotts for political purposes.
Two of the people familiar with the matter suggested that the idea of an antitrust inquiry was first discussed inside the White House, which ultimately pushed for it from the DOJ. A third described the White House-DOJ interplay as a âdistinction [without] a difference,â given how closely the two are intertwined under President Donald Trumpâs administration.
A DOJ official disputed that the White House first raised the idea of a probe, saying that âseasoned attorneys within the Justice Department, including the antitrust division, first discussed this.â The official added that any requests for information from networks which may have been sent were written âbecause there is sound legal footing to investigate.â
In addition to the longstanding Trump-era blur between the DOJ and White House, the departmentâs antitrust division has close ties to presidential priorities. Sara Matar, formerly the divisionâs chief of staff, joined the White House counselâs office in August as an associate.
Notably, Laura Loomer â a staunch MAGA ally whose outside influence has occasionally resulted in changes within the White House â tweeted last month wondering why the DOJ hadnât âfiled an antitrust lawsuitâ against outlets that âcolluded to refuse to coverâ Trump.
Loomer attacked Woodward in her post; the following week, she traveled with Trump to Alabama, though itâs unclear whether she raised the issue with the president personally during that trip.
The White House referred Semafor to the DOJ in response to a request for comment.
Know More
The Trump administration has long argued that the Justice Department is not wholly separate from the White House, counter to the norms that took root after the Nixon era. At Semaforâs World Economy Summit in April, Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated that it is Trumpâs ârightâ to suggest targets for investigation â a stance he has echoed repeatedly since settling into his role at the top of the department.
âCertainly if the leader of the Free World learns about something or hears about something or wants us to focus on something, a certain area, that is, of course, what every Department of Justice has done,â Blanche told Semafor at the time.
âThis idea that President Trump has some sort of outsized control because of things that he says, that thatâs absolutely his right and his duty to do that,â Blanche added.

0c7fba5f803a.text: By — Mike Stobbe, Associated Press Mike Stobbe, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/how-proposed-cuts-to-this-major-national-health-survey-could-disadvantage-americans-with-disabilities Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter How proposed cuts to this major national health survey could disadvantage Americans with disabilities Health Oct 14, 2026 3:55 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — The federal government is planning to dramatically shrink its most influential health survey, and some researchers worry that the changes will underestimate how many Americans are disabled. At least half the survey questions could be axed. The cost-saving change is part of an ongoing effort to slim down the 69-year-old National Health Interview Survey, which for years has been suffering from declining response rates. READ MORE: Civil rights enforcement cuts mean fewer staff, closed offices, longer waits for students with disabilities As many as a quarter of wheelchair users and more than a third of people who are blind or deaf could be miscategorized as not disabled because of the shorter survey, according to some advocates and researchers. That could leave the government unable to recognize the health needs of many disabled Americans, or the damage caused by changes to Medicaid or other health insurance programs, they say. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The cuts are being ironed out and officials predict the whittling won't be as severe as what's been suggested in earlier proposals. Questions that have been proposed for removal deal with memory, fatigue, arthritis, difficulty walking and climbing stairs, as well as others about the use of hearing aids, canes, wheelchairs and scooters. READ MORE: Trump's actions signal a move toward institutionalizing people with disabilities, advocates warn "We just won't know any of that anymore," said Scott Landes, a Syracuse University sociology professor who researches people with disabilities. Officials are still determining exactly how much cutting will take place. Currently, the survey has 490 health questions for adults. U.S. officials expect that the 2028 questionnaire will have about 200 to 225 questions, said the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Stephen Blumberg, who oversees the survey. U.S. Census Bureau workers conduct the survey every year on behalf of the CDC. It's a $40 million annual project, and around 30,000 households answer the questions each year. Their answers have shaped the public's understanding of topics including how common chronic fatigue syndrome is, how many people get X-rays, what proportion of U.S. children suffer seizures, and how many Americans have health insurance. The survey's responses also are the foundation of how we measure the nation's progress — or backsliding — on problems such as obesity and smoking. Fewer people are interested in participating in such surveys. And the National Health Interview Survey is particularly daunting, as it can take an hour or more and has traditionally involved an in-person interviewer asking the questions. The planned redesign should cut it to about a half hour, Blumberg said. "People are busy. They're more protective of their privacy, and some don't trust the government to protect their data and use it only for statistical purposes," he said. "Fewer people see sharing information with the government as their civic duty." The survey was first conducted in 1957, and has been updated every 15 to 20 years. The latest update was put into the field seven years ago, prompting some advocates to ask why it was being changed so quickly. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the White House Office of Management and Budget were behind dramatic staff reductions, research funding overhauls and other federal health agency changes under the current Trump administration. But neither ordered this redesign, Blumberg said. Rather, the factors driving the current redesign include tightening budgets and difficulties fielding enough workers to do so many in-person interviews — which was affected last year by a federal hiring freeze. Another factor: The Census Bureau is reconfiguring its data collection platforms for the 2030 census in a way that affected the health survey, he said. Related to all that is a proposed change in how the health survey is conducted. Instead of starting with in-person or telephone interviews, people will receive an invitation to fill out the survey online or to fill out a paper questionnaire. That's because in-person interviews have proven difficult with the proliferation of gated communities, locked buildings without door attendants and doorbell cameras, according to officials. However, Census Bureau staff will visit homes for a smaller second round of surveying, Blumberg said. A notice about the survey redesign appeared in the Federal Register in August, opening a public comment period that runs through Oct. 20. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
