The News
Heidi Overton, President Donald Trumpâs nominee to run the Food and Drug Administration, played a larger role in driving the process to reduce the number of vaccines the government recommends to children than emerged during her Senate confirmation last month, when Republican senators asked her whether sheâd stand up to anti-vaccine voices in the administration.
An aide on the presidentâs Domestic Policy Council, Overton helped edit and craft a scientific justification that was used to underpin cutting the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommendations from 17 to 11 vaccines in January, according to a senior administration official and three people familiar with the process.
âIt was Heidi driving this whole thing,â said a former senior administration official, noting that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. supported the policy push.
The Senate health committee did not vote on whether to advance Overton to the Senate floor before departing earlier this month, leaving the decision for the lame duck session. If Republicans ultimately support her, Overton will lead the agency responsible for vaccine policy after making a bigger contribution to the Trump administrationâs effort to reverse decades of American policy on childhood vaccines than was widely understood.
âEvery vaccine on the US market right now are safe and effective according to the FDA,â Overton told Senate Health Committee Chair Bill Cassidy, R-La, during the hearing.
But throughout the fall of 2025, Overton built consensus across health agencies around narrowing the list of recommended universal childhood vaccines, meeting with Trump administration officials including Kennedy; then-FDA Commissioner Marty Makary; Mehmet Oz, who oversees Medicare and Medicaid; Jay Bhattacharya, the director of the National Institutes of Health; and Stefanie Spear, a senior HHS official and close confidant to Kennedy.
Others in the administration say that Overtonâs work is a reflection of the nature of a White House policy job, not her own priorities.
âI think there is a misperception that because Heidi is the point of contact for the White House on a lot of issues, that she personally is doing something because of her personal views or or motivations,â a separate administration official said, noting the White House is âtop-down.â
The Atlantic reported in July that Overton had been part of a team that created an initial draft of childhood vaccine recommendations.
Kennedy was prepared to endorse Denmarkâs vaccine schedule, which recommends vaccinations against 10 diseases for all children, as an option for American parents based on the memo. But Kennedyâs December press conference was canceled at the last minute, according to three people familiar with the discussions.
Before the scheduled event, HHS lawyers raised concerns to senior health officials that it lacked evidence and would be susceptible to legal challenges, two of the people said.
On Jan. 5, former Health Deputy Secretary and then-acting CDC Director Jim OâNeill signed a decision memo that adopted a revised childhood immunization schedule based on the assessment conducted by HÃ¸eg, the acting director of the FDAâs Center for Drug Evaluation and Research at the time, and Martin Kulldorff, an HHS aide.
The American Academy of Pediatrics challenged the revised schedule in court, and a federal judge put it on hold in March.
Know More
When Trump nominated Overton in August to lead the FDA, prominent Make America Healthy Again activists objected, saying she would be too friendly toward drugmakers if confirmed.
âThis narrative took hold that Heidi was not aligned with Kennedy on this, was more aligned with pharma [on] vaccine stuff, and was in favor of a more maximal vaccine schedule,â the former senior administration official said. âAnd thatâs just not the case, not what happened.â
An HHS official said Overton was tasked with putting Trumpâs policy priority into a document that was âsuitable for distribution throughout the White House.â
âSomeone needed to sort of pull the different strands together and make sure they came together into a quilt that was at least representative of what the different folks were trying to do,â the HHS official said. âThe president had already expressed, and has continued to express a very strong desire to revisit vaccines, in part because heâs concerned about complications. This is not something that she would have personally desired. I am quite confident.â
At her Senate confirmation hearing in September, Cassidy pressed Overton on her commitment to defending the safety and efficacy of vaccines, and asked whether sheâd stand up to Trump under pressure.
âIf he asks you to do something which goes against the guarantee youâve made to the American people through us, what will you do?â Cassidy asked.
âI would give him my best advice,â Overton replied.
Cassidy is a trained gastroenterologist and liver specialist who is leaving office this year after losing a primary election where Trump endorsed his challenger and has said Kennedyâs vaccine approach broke commitments made during his own confirmation process. His office declined to comment when asked about Overtonâs involvement in drafting the scientific justification document.
When Trump nominated Overton, Cassidy posted that her involvement in Trumpâs ânonsensical vaccine executive orderâ in August, which aimed to break up the established measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into multiple doses, was âalmost disqualifying.â
Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, D-Del., pressed Overton at the confirmation hearing about whether she thought splitting the MMR vaccine into multiple shots or reducing the number of childhood vaccines were âgood options.â
âMy job in my current role is to take the presidentâs directive, provide options to him for him to make the decision,â Overton responded.
Notable
- Overton was quiet on her own opinions during her confirmation hearing, STAT reported.

The Scoop
Perplexity is giving away the software it has been using to combat rogue AI agents, the company told Semafor Thursday.
Its âAI sandbox,â which it calls SPACE, is now an open source project, allowing outside developers to use the tool, which it says can keep AI agents contained. Perplexity said itâs lined up partners, including CoreWeave, Akamai and Crusoe, which have agreed to offer SPACE to customers.
Sandboxes, or isolated environments for testing and running AI models, have become a hot topic in the tech industry in the wake of reports from AI labs of models escaping their constraints, finding their way onto the open web and hacking unsuspecting victims like Hugging Face and the Australian government.
While AI companies focus on âalignment,â or training models to behave themselves, the security industry has been increasingly advocating erecting strict guardrails around AI models.
âA lot of companies are thinking about how to build secure AI agents, and in many cases they hit a wall,â said Zibi Braniecki, a member of the technical staff at Perplexity, in an interview with Semafor. âWe have a solution.â
Perplexity said it tested SPACE by giving nine frontier models instructions to try to break out. In 118 tries, none of them did, while Perplexity found they were able to break out of other sandboxes that were not open sourced.
Know More
Braniecki likened the effort to make SPACE open source to what happened with web browsers as the internet developed â companies came together to build guardrails that allowed secure browsing and online commerce. âRight now, weâre thinking too small,â he said.
Other companies like Nvidia have also released open-source security tools, such as Nvidia OpenShell, which runs AI agents in a sandbox and limits what they can reach.
Perplexity said SPACE also helps reduce wasted compute, which can be a byproduct of strict sandboxing.

167fa4d89967.text: Apple and Meta, whose leaders have spent years trading barbs over privacy and the future of computing, are joining forces to bring one of America's most powerful open-weight AI models to Apple's high-end Macs. Why it matters: The collaboration marks a striking détente between two longtime Silicon Valley rivals, underscoring how the AI race is reshaping relationships across the technology industry. The companies still compete over devices and the next generation of computing, but both see an opportunity in bringing powerful AI capabilities to personal computers. "We're excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again," Meta's AI chief Alexandr Wang told Axios. Driving the news: Meta is releasing Muse Spark Open, a model similar to Muse Spark 1.3, that it says is the most powerful U.S.-developed open-weight AI model available. Meta joins a host of Western AI companies that have released powerful open-weight systems that promise to slash AI costs, provide companies with more control and offer an alternative to the Chinese AI ecosystem. Nvidia on Tuesday released updated versions of its Nemotron family of models, and U.S.-based Reflection AI and France's Mistral both released new open source models last week. As proof of Muse Spark Open's capabilities, Meta worked with Apple to make the model run locally across two or four connected Mac Studios powered by Apple's M5 Ultra chips, using Apple's MLX framework. Zoom in : The prospect of a powerful model — it has 816 billion parameters — running on Apple hardware offers a proof of concept about just how much companies will be able to build their own AI systems. That could give companies more alternatives to Nvidia GPUs and proprietary models from leading AI labs, potentially shifting some of the economics of AI. Meta's model will be free to download, with a license allowing commercial use, and will also be available through cloud providers and developer tools. What they're saying: Wang said the companies have been working together for several months, with Daniel Gross, a former Apple executive now at Meta, playing a key role in bringing the two sides together. "I think he played a really big role in kind of getting the two companies to work nicely together," Wang said in a telephone interview. Flashback: Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg have repeatedly clashed over privacy and their competing business models. In 2018, amid Facebook's Cambridge Analytica scandal, Cook was asked what he would do if he were Zuckerberg. "I wouldn't be in this situation," Cook replied. Zuckerberg called Cook's comments "extremely glib." The rivalry intensified in 2021, when Apple introduced new privacy protections that struck at the heart of Facebook's ad business. Zuckerberg reportedly told employees that Facebook needed to "inflict pain" on Apple over the dispute, according to the Wall Street Journal. The big picture: The AI race is making for some strange bedfellows, scrambling longstanding Silicon Valley rivalries and even bringing together political adversaries. Anthropic is leasing up to $15 billion per year of computing capacity from Elon Musk's SpaceX, even as it competes with his AI company. Microsoft, OpenAI's longtime partner, is investing billions in rival Anthropic and incorporating its Claude models into its own products. And in Washington, progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders and MAGA strategist Steve Bannon have found common ground in calling for tougher AI safeguards and challenging the power of Big Tech. Between the lines: The Apple-Meta collaboration doesn't mean the companies have resolved their differences, but it suggests those disagreements no longer prevent them from working together when their interests align. Meta benefits from making its AI models widely available, while Apple can showcase the capabilities of its most powerful computers. And because the model runs locally, Meta doesn't receive users' prompts or other information — sidestepping the privacy concerns that have long divided the companies. "Meta has no control or visibility to any of that," Wang said of how developers use the model. Yes, but: Making powerful AI models openly available raises concerns that bad actors could remove safeguards and use the technology for cyberattacks or biological threats. What we're watching: Whether the collaboration marks the beginning of a broader relationship between Apple and Meta. For now, Apple is helping demonstrate that Meta's AI models can run locally on its computers. A more significant step would be Apple incorporating Meta's models into Apple Intelligence, giving the Facebook parent a role in powering Apple's own AI features. The bottom line: Wang acknowledged that Apple and Meta will continue to compete in some areas, but said that doesn't have to prevent them from working together. "Where it makes sense to collaborate and partner, we want to be able to do so," he said.

Grocery store shelves are bursting with fancy salts: Himalayan, kosher, sea salt and more. Considering these choices, it can be easy to forget about the public health victory found in basic, iodized table salt.
The nutrient iodine is a crucial component of thyroid hormones, necessary for fetal and early childhood brain development and health throughout life. At the start of the last century, iodine deficiency was a rampant and visible public health problem in the United States, with the telltale sign of enlarged thyroid glands, called goiters, especially prevalent in much of the north. A series of steps taken by a medical society in Michigan and U.S. salt producers brought iodized salt to tables across the country, and by the 1950s, occurrences of goiters had dropped precipitously.
But more recently, the United States appears to be backsliding on iodine nutrition. In 2017 and 2018, 24 percent of women and 30 percent of men, aged 14 and older, weren’t getting an adequate amount of the nutrient. That’s about twice as many as in 2001 and 2002, researchers reported in the Journal of Nutrition in 2025. Breaking the data down further, nearly half of pregnant women haven’t been getting enough iodine. The study reflects an estimated, short-term look at population iodine levels.
Long-term, a consistent dearth of iodine robs the body of the ability to produce sufficient amounts of thyroid hormones. If iodine levels in the population continue to trend down, that could eventually result in more goiters and harm brain development in children.
“The group that has the most severe potential consequences of iodine deficiency is pregnant women,” says Elizabeth Pearce, an endocrinologist at Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine. “Even mild degrees of iodine deficiency in pregnancy may be associated with measurably lower IQ in children.”
Yet women of reproductive age, at the U.S. population level, are on the cusp of mild iodine deficiency, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention stated in its 2026 Nutrition Report.
With all of the ways that diets, salt intake and noniodized options have changed over time, the importance of iodine nutrition may not be top-of-mind for the general public like it was a century ago. “Iodine deficiency is the leading cause worldwide of preventable developmental delay,” says Monica Serrano-Gonzalez, a pediatric endocrinologist at Hasbro Children’s and Brown University’s Warren Alpert Medical School in Providence, R.I. “People have kind of forgotten this is a risk.”
The “goiter belt”
When iodine deficiency keeps the thyroid gland from making enough hormones, the body calls for more, which stimulates and enlarges the gland. That supersized gland, called a goiter, bulges at the neck. In the United States, goiters were extremely common a century ago in the Northwest, Great Lakes and Appalachians; together, the area became known as the “goiter belt.” Iodine naturally occurs in seawater and soil. But in the noncoastal northern part of the country, soils and water sources have little iodine, so the crops produced in these inland areas lack the nutrient.
An examining physician for the World War I draft reported in 1918 that 30 percent of almost 600 men from a northern Michigan county had goiters, some large enough to be disqualifying. A 1922 Michigan Department of Health study of schoolchildren in four counties revealed that close to 50 percent had goiters. “It would have been a really visible public health problem at that time,” Pearce says.
In response to the state’s iodine issues, the Michigan State Medical Society recommended the addition of the nutrient to table salt. The minimal expense for iodization meant this common kitchen staple would remain affordable. Companies introduced iodized salt in Michigan in the spring of 1924. By the fall, the Morton Salt Company, a major producer, was selling iodized salt nationwide. Over time, the goiters of the “belt” dwindled.
Salt iodization has been linked to rising IQ in the United States. For example, for men born in areas without natural sources of iodine, there was a significant jump in World War II Air Force acceptances, based on a qualifying exam, after widespread salt iodization. The increase did not occur among men born in areas with adequate natural sources of the nutrient, researchers reported in the Journal of the European Economic Association in 2017.
Adding iodine to salt was never mandated by the U.S. government. But for a long time, the voluntary approach — combined with how most people consumed salt and other dietary habits — did the trick to get people enough iodine. Today, different meal practices and available food options are tearing holes in the iodine safety net. “Iodized salt is important, but it may not be reaching everybody anymore,” Pearce says.
There are many more noniodized salt options today, with one analysis reporting that only 53 percent of table salt sold in U.S. stores is iodized. People get much of their salt from prepared, processed and packaged foods, which generally are made with noniodized salt. Milk can provide iodine, due to iodine-supplemented feed and the use of an iodine cleanser on cows’ udders. But the amount of iodine in milk can vary greatly, a recent analysis found, probably because industry practices can differ. Diets that restrict dairy may also put people at risk of consuming too little iodine.
The U.S. recommended dietary allowance for iodine for adults is 150 micrograms per day, which rises to 220 mcg for pregnant people and 290 mcg for those breastfeeding. The amount of the nutrient that iodized salt contains can vary, but will be listed on the container’s label. Based on a 2023 federal report on food iodine content, one teaspoon of salt has around 300 mcg of added iodine. (The American Heart Association recommends a limit of 2,300 milligrams of sodium per day; one teaspoon of salt has 2,400 mg of sodium.)
The American Thyroid Association and the American Academy

US government officials raided the home of Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar this week as part of what's being called a "federal criminal investigation".
The search warrant was approved by a court, the justice department said. The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear.
The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya.
Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has said the raid is "the latest escalation" in President Donald Trump's "campaign of political intimidation". He has denied being involved.
What is Omar being investigated for?
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents searched Omar's home in Washington DC on 12 October, while she was there with her husband.
The Wall Street Journal reported that her cellphone, notebooks, personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized.
"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the justice department said in a statement at the time.
Since then, investigators have issued more than a dozen subpoenas to Omar's family members, Fox News reports.
Multiple US media outlets have reported that the investigation is tied to Omar's US citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.
Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.
Her marriages have also come under suspicion. Trump is among those who have accused her of marrying her brother to get US citizenship.
Omar's finances have been scrutinised in relation to her current marriage to former Democratic political consultant Timothy Mynett. She has denied any allegations of wrongdoing and has called the investigations into her "complete shams".
US Attorney Jeanine Pirro has said her office is investigating Omar's financial disclosures.
Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans and, earlier this year, fellow congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully sought a subpoena for her records.
How did Omar obtain her citizenship?
Mynett told Fox News that Omar came to the US when she was 12 as a war refugee. He said he has "no concerns" about her citizenship.
Omar was born in Somalia before fleeing with her family to a refugee camp in Kenya. She arrived in the US with her father and others in 1995 before becoming a naturalised US citizen in 2000.
According to US media, the crux of the investigation is whether her father lied about her age on the application, writing she was 17 rather than 18.
If Omar was 18 at the time her father applied for citizenship, she would have needed to pursue her own immigration process separately.
Who is Omar's father?
After arriving from Kenya, Nur Omar Mohamed initially settled with his family in Washington before later moving to Minnesota. He worked as a cabdriver and postal worker.
Omar described him as an educator and said he died in 2020 from Covid-19 complications.
According to the New York Post, which cited an Oxford University doctoral researcher, Mohamed "misrepresented himself as a refugee".
The Post said he had a decades-long military career, including a leadership position under former Somali President Siad Barre's military dictatorship.
Barre seized power in Somalia in a bloodless coup in 1969. While his supporters saw him as a pan-Africanist who supported causes such as the campaign against South Africa's racist system of apartheid, his critics viewed him as a dictator who oversaw numerous human rights abuses until he was driven from power in 1991.
"[Nur Omar Mohamed] was a full colonel in Siad Barre's military regime," historian and researcher Mohamed Haji Ingiriis told The Post. "Ilhan's father was never an educator."
The BBC has reached out to Omar for comment.
Can Omar be deported?
The Trump administration has made a concerted effort to detain and deport immigrants suspected of being in the US illegally. Permanent residents and green card holders have also been affected.
According to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, a nonpartisan data research company, there has also been a surge in denaturalisation lawsuits filed by the Trump administration.
Denaturalisation is where the US citizenship of a person who was not granted it by birth is taken away. The justice department must file a lawsuit proving the person lied in a material way during their application process.
This appears to be where the groundwork is being laid in the current investigation into Omar.
What has Omar said?
Trump has repeatedly suggested Omar be deported, calling for her to "go back" to Somalia.
At a rally in Ohio on Monday, Trump referred to the search of Omar's home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."
Trump went on to denigrate Somalis in the US more generally, which was greeted with chants of "deport" in the crowd.
After her home was searched, Omar wrote on X: "I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.
"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," she continued. "I will not be silenced."
Trump has said the investigation into her has "nothing to do with me".
The timing of the federal probe has defied justice department precedent of not taking action against officials running for office this close to an election.
The raid happened with the November midterm elections only weeks away, drawing condemnation from some of Omar's Democratic colleagues, who said she had been subject to relentless "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations".

Venezuela's former leader NicolÃ¡s Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in court on Thursday to plead not guilty to new charges of conspiracy to commit torture.
The US government initially accused Maduro of narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons-related offenses, before adding new charges against him and Flores last week.
Maduro and Flores were captured in January during a US military raid, after which they were taken to New York, where they remain in jail.
The couple has pleaded not guilty to the allegations and both have argued to have the case thrown out on the grounds that they qualify for sovereign immunity. Their trial is scheduled for June 2027.
In a new indictment last week, government prosecutors alleged Maduro and Flores "created and maintained a violent system of repression" that saw "thousands of Venezuelans" killed, harassed, and tortured.
Nicolas Maduro denied the new charges brought against him by the US government, telling a court on Thursday he denied the "false accusations and false testimony behind him."
"I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in Spanish through a translator.
Judge Alvin Hellerstein interrupted Maduro, and declared the court would enter a plea of not guilty for Maduro.
"I am completely innocent. I am not guilty," Flores said through a translator.
Maduro and Flores wore beige jail uniforms and both appear to have lost weight during their detention in Brooklyn.
The alleged torture methods included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture", the indictment states.
The US also accused Maduro of authorising the use of torture "against specific individuals" and alleges US citizens were tortured under this system.
Prosecutors already have accused Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices of engaging in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnering with cartels designated as terrorist groups.
Maduro previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.
He and his wife's lawyers have argued that Maduro is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal.
Flores unsuccessfully petitioned a judge to allow her to be released on bond while she awaited trial, arguing she had heart problems and other health issues while detained at the notorious Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.

52ad503c4fa6.text: By — Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/authorities-investigate-letters-with-suspicious-substances-sent-to-congressional-election-offices Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Authorities investigate letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to congressional, election offices Politics Oct 15, 2026 12:27 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal authorities are investigating letters with "suspicious substances" that have been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and are urging recipients to treat the mailings as "potentially hazardous." The investigation by the FBI, U.S. Postal Inspection Service and U.S. Capitol Police was first disclosed in a message from the Senate Sergeant at Arms obtained Thursday by The Associated Press. The notice, sent to Senate offices, said that law enforcement officials were working to intercept any additional letters, but "it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations." In Congress, the threat appeared limited to the Senate, though the House was monitoring the situation, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to discuss the investigation publicly. An FBI statement said the bureau and the Postal Inspection Service were "investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices." "Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident," the statement read. "We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters." Mailed packages containing a powdery substance led to the evacuation this week of election offices in at least two states, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The Ohio secretary of state said the Postal Service intercepted a package containing a white powder intended for its office and noted that similar mailings had been sent to election officials in multiple states. News of the letters comes just three weeks before Election Day and is reminiscent of a similar threat in 2023, when election offices in six states received mailings that contained a white powder. In some cases, the incidents disrupted work around local elections. Some of those letters contained threats and traces of the powerful opioid fentanyl, leading some election offices to stock up on the overdose reversal medication naloxone. The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors issued a joint statement condemning what they said were threats against election staff. "Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties," they said in their statement. Deputy Postal Inspector Brendan Donahue told reporters Thursday that "any threat or attack on election officials is unacceptable" and that "we are also working with our partners on identifying the individual or individuals responsible for the letters." Associated Press writer Nicholas Riccardi in Denver contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. b36cec555154.text: Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Data this week has all told the same story: This is a rip-roaring U.S. economy with all the inflationary pressures that might imply. The big picture: It puts Warsh and the Fed in a difficult jam. Top officials have signaled patience in further interest rate hikes in recent weeks, but the latest data implies broader inflationary pressures than previously thought, testing that conviction. There is scant evidence that price pressures are receding on their own and growing reason to fear that they are becoming more entrenched, which could compel a more aggressive rate-hiking response. Driving the news: On Thursday the government said the Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September, the highest since 2022 and far above the 0.6% analysts expected. It came on the heels of a too-hot-for-comfort reading on consumer prices Wednesday. Also Thursday, September retail sales notched a 0.8% rise, versus the 0.4% analysts had expected. And the August number was revised higher. There were only 199,000 initial claims for unemployment benefits last week, remaining near historic lows. Between the lines: The U.S. growth juggernaut shows no sign of diminishing — but neither do the price pressures that have bedeviled the economy for nearly five consecutive years. If anything, the PPI and CPI data released this week suggest inflation is broadening, showing up in sectors well beyond energy. State of play: In his appearance at the International Monetary Fund's meetings in Thailand Friday (11:30pm ET Thursday), Warsh has a final opportunity to comment before the Fed enters its customary quiet period in advance of a policy meeting that concludes Oct. 28. Colleagues including New York Fed president John Williams and vice chair Philip Jefferson gave rather clear signaling in the last couple of weeks that they see little urgency to raise rates at a second consecutive meeting this month. Warsh faces a dilemma. If he affirms that stance in spite of the hot price data, it could raise doubts about his determination to bring inflation under control. If he seems inclined to raise rates, he could seem overly reactive to a couple of economic releases, contrary to his stated goal of making the Fed less "data-point dependent." The intrigue: Surprisingly, bond yields are down Thursday despite the hot PPI number — and a surge in yields following the CPI number Wednesday mostly reversed later in the trading session. It seems to reflect a flight to quality among traders as optimism around the AI buildout fades. With semiconductor and related stocks down, money looks to be flowing into safer Treasury securities. The policy-sensitive two-year Treasury yield briefly touched 4.95% after the CPI number Wednesday, implying significant Fed rate hikes ahead. It was down to 4.72% Thursday morning — an astonishing move for any 24-hour period, let alone one that included hotter-than-expected inflation data. What they're saying: "Today's September PPI report reinforces Wednesday's CPI message that inflation is turning higher and moving in the wrong direction for the Fed," Nationwide financial market economist Oren Klachkin wrote in a note. "AI continues to lend upside pressure from categories directly and indirectly tied to the buildout. Businesses seem to be passing higher costs onto customers as the proxy for margins rose heftily in September."

"You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school.
The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?"
Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad.
Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people.
Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that.
President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail.
Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally.
But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni.
The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order".
The rules, approved on 21 September, ban clothing which contradict "the principle of secularism in education" in state schools. They do not mention the hijab. Similar guidelines were extended to teachers on 6 October.
In one video, pupils outside School No. 69 in Balakhany, outside Baku, hold a banner reading: "The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education."
Shahiza Huseynova, a mother who was protesting outside a school in the Mashtaga district of the capital, was detained on Tuesday.
In an interview with Meydan TV, an independent Azerbaijani-language channel based in Germany, Huseynova's husband Agha said she had been given a warning: "Either you take off your child's hijab and send them to school, or you go to prison."
Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class.
According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since.
The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed.
Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN).
Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran.
The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself.
On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites.
A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility.
Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families.
"A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said.
The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh.
The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states".
President Recep Tayyip ErdoÄan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation".
His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake".
"A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X.
Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in.
Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by KÃ¶klÃ¼ DeÄiÅim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group ÃzgÃ¼r-Der.
President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.
Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life".
Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil.
Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries.
That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall.

05ccb9951fb2.text: By — Matthew Perrone, Associated Press Matthew Perrone, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/a-new-sunscreen-type-for-americans-hits-store-shelves Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A new sunscreen type for Americans hits store shelves Health Oct 15, 2026 11:53 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — For the first time in more than a quarter-century, Americans have a new option when shopping for sunscreen: a skin-protecting chemical that's long been a go-to option in Europe and other parts of the world. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved bemotrizinol — sometimes called BEMT — in June. The first sunscreens containing it are now hitting U.S. store shelves, including formulas from Neutrogena and other manufacturers. WATCH: Dermatologist explains benefits of newly approved sunscreen ingredient Dermatologists say the chemical fills an important market gap by offering broad protection, like the most well-established sunscreen ingredients, but without their cosmetic downsides, including white streaking. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. BEMT has decades of safety data behind it, including studies showing it has minimal absorption into the skin. That's been a concern with some older sun-blocking chemicals. WATCH: Why sunscreen in the United States is behind the rest of the world "It's not a brand-new ingredient that you're going to be the first person to try," said Dr. Jennifer Stein, a dermatologist at NYU Langone Health. Here's what to know. New ingredient offers broad protection without streaks To be effective, sunscreens must protect against both forms of ultraviolet light that can damage the skin — UVB rays, which cause most sunburn, and UVA rays that pose the greatest risk of skin cancer and wrinkles. Sunscreens that block both forms are labeled "broad spectrum protection." Those that don't must carry an FDA warning label. READ MORE: Do you need SPF 30, 50 or 100? Dermatologists answer your burning sunscreen questions BEMT is the first chemical-based sunscreen in the U.S. that offers this dual protection. Previously, manufacturers had to mix multiple ingredients to protect against both UVA and UVB light. "This ingredient provides a solution for what is currently a big gap with respect to providing strong UVA protection," said David Andrews, chief science officer of the Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit that advocates for higher sunscreen standards. A different class of sunscreens, using minerals such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, has long been shown to offer strong protection against both forms of ultraviolet light. These mineral-based formulas work by physically blocking harmful rays from the skin. READ MORE: Why it's important everyone wears sunscreen — even if you have a darker skin tone But some people — particularly those with darker complexions — tend to avoid them because they cause white streaking and discoloration. In other cases, people don't like their texture or consistency. "Those are good sunscreens," Stein said. "But for people who aren't so inclined to use them — maybe they don't like how it feels on their skin — this is a nice option." There's less skin penetration with the new formula The fact that chemical-based sunscreens are absorbed into the skin means they have to be carefully studied to make sure they aren't building up in the body at unsafe levels. Last month, the FDA revoked approval of an older chemical ingredient, oxybenzone, after determining it was "absorbed through the skin to a greater extent than previously understood." READ MORE: How these ingredients make your sunscreen work That's not a problem with BEMT. "It's a molecule that's too big to really penetrate through the skin and get absorbed into the bloodstream," Stein said. "The older chemical sunscreens had small molecules." As part of its safety review, the FDA reviewed studies of BEMT in more than 500 patients conducted by Dutch manufacturer DSM Nutritional Products. Levels of the chemical absorbed into the skin were nearly undetectable, the studies found. Agency reviewers said research in people who used the sunscreen daily for up to three weeks showed that BEMT "did not cause irritation" or allergic reactions. As a result, the FDA designated the ingredient as "generally recognized as safe and effective," alongside the older mineral ingredients zinc oxide and titanium dioxide. More than a dozen other ingredients are currently used in U.S. sunscreens, but the FDA has said they will require additional evidence to support their safety and effectiveness. The FDA review is part of an ongoing effort to overhaul U.S. sunscreen ingredients that kicked off in 2019. More evidence is needed about the impact on coral reefs Scientists have shown that some sunscreen ingredients can trigger bleaching and damage coral reefs. That's led to bans on two chemical ingredients — oxybenzone, the ingredient recently targeted by the FDA, and octinoxate — in Hawaii and parts of Florida. It's estimated about 25% of the sunscreen people apply to their skin washes off while swimming or wading in the ocean. The U.S. government doesn't classify the environmental impact of sunscreens, and marketing claims like "reef safe" or "reef friendly" have no standard definition or requirements. The European Union's environmental agency has found "limited evidence of environmental toxicity" with BEMT, but longer-term research is needed. Mineral ingredients like zinc oxide are generally considered safer for the environment, although some experts recommend staying away from so-called nano formulations. Severe drought has been declared in parts of southern England after months of dry weather drove some reservoirs to exceptionally low levels.
Most of England and all of Wales were already under drought conditions after both nations' hottest summers on record, which has taken its toll on rivers, crops and nature.
Roughly 30 million people across parts of England and Wales are covered by hosepipe bans, as part of water companies' efforts to manage supplies.
So how is your area doing and are you in a drought?
First 'severe drought' declared
"Severe drought" - the highest category - has now been declared for parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex.
It means environmental authorities will ramp up monitoring of reservoir levels, river flows and water quality, as well as carry out extra checks on businesses withdrawing water from natural sources.
The "severe drought" classification was introduced following the 2012 drought and this is the first time it has been implemented.
The UK government says two previous events would have met the "severe drought" classification, had it been in place. They are:
- August 1976, for Devon and Yorkshire in England, and Gwent, Monmouthshire and Glamorgan in Wales
- November 1995, for Yorkshire only
Most of England and all of Wales were already in drought, following earlier announcements by the Environment Agency (EA) and Natural Resources Wales.
Parts of north-east and north-west England are in the category below drought, called "prolonged dry weather".
There are no official droughts currently in Northern Ireland.
There is no single definition of drought, but it is characterised by a period of low rainfall. As the ground dries out, crops and vegetation can begin to struggle.
If dry conditions persist, rivers, reservoirs and groundwater levels can also fall, putting pressure on water supplies.
The EA says that south-east and south-west England have experienced their driest April to September in more than a century.
Scotland does not declare droughts but monitors "water scarcity" - when there is not enough water of sufficient quality to meet demands of people and the environment.
While conditions have improved in parts of Scotland following recent rainfall, some south-eastern areas remain in the most extreme categories of "moderate" or "significant" scarcity, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.
Hosepipe bans for millions
Both drought and water scarcity can lead to hosepipe bans - officially called "temporary use bans" - if they are not already in place.
So far, 11 UK water companies have announced hosepipe bans in 2026. This means hosepipes cannot be used for watering gardens, washing vehicles and windows, and filling pools.
Ten companies are spread across central, southern and eastern parts of England, and one is in Wales.
Rivers, reservoirs and groundwater - how are supplies?
Our three main sources of water are reservoirs, rivers and from deep underground.
A key reason why parts of southern England have entered "severe drought" is low reservoir levels.
At this time of year, the Environment Agency says it would expect England's reservoirs to be about three-quarters full, but they are just over half full on average.
Ardingly Reservoir in West Sussex and Wimbleball Reservoir in Somerset are among those at "exceptionally low" levels.
DÅµr Cymru Welsh Water says most reservoir levels in Wales are normal for the time of year.
And reservoir levels in Northern Ireland and Scotland are close to average, according to the latest available data.
Many of the UK's rivers have also been affected by the low rainfall.
Most monitored river flows in England were classed as "below normal", "notably low" or "exceptionally low" in July, according to the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH).
South-east England relies more heavily on groundwater than reservoirs. Groundwater originates as rainfall and is naturally stored beneath the surface in the pore spaces and fractures in rocks.
Groundwater levels are generally declining following the prolonged dry weather. In September, about half of monitored sites across the UK recorded levels considered "below normal" or lower, with southern England and Wales typically faring worst.
Water can flow more slowly through some rock types than others, sometimes taking years to fully respond to current conditions.
These groundwater stores "respond more slowly to changes in the climate than rivers, which is why they provide a useful buffer during periods of drought", said Prof Alan MacDonald of the British Geological Survey.
It is why groundwater droughts in the south of England generally take a longer time to develop but can be longer-lasting if they do occur.
Is climate change to blame?
Droughts are complex phenomena, driven by a mix of natural and human causes.
The Met Office expects the UK to experience drier summers on average in future as the world warms, though there has been no clear trend so far.
But rising temperatures can play a more direct role by drawing extra moisture from the soil via evaporation.
"A warmer atmosphere is thirstier for moisture and this can mean water in the soil, rivers and reservoirs are depleted more effectively, leading to more rapidly onsetting droughts, heatwaves and wildfires," said Richard Allan, professor of climate science at the University of Reading.
But there are other factors that determine whether dry conditions lead to water shortages, including how we use water.
In a landmark review into the water sector of England and Wales, water companies were criticised for historic underinvestment in water infrastructure.
And while spring and summer were relatively dry for much of the UK, winter was much wetter than usual, raising questions about how effectively water is being managed.

Here's what to know about Pope Leo XIV's form of lung cancer Health Oct 15, 2026 11:18 AM EDT Pope Leo XIV had the lower section of his right lung removed after doctors diagnosed him with the most common form of lung cancer. While lung cancer is a leading killer, survival rates can be high if it's caught early, as the pope's tumor appears to have been. Here are some things to know. What is lung adenocarcinoma? The Vatican announced the pope's diagnosis as lung adenocarcinoma, which is one of many forms of lung cancer. WATCH: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer and prognosis There are two main groups, small cell and non-small cell lung cancers. The non-small cell kind make up the vast majority of the world's cases and adenocarcinoma is its most common subtype. Even it comes in varieties that can grow faster or slower. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "While it's still very dangerous, it has slightly higher cure rates than other types of lung cancer," said Dr. John Heymach of the MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston. Smoking is the leading cause of lung cancer. But as many as 1 in 5 lung cancers occur in people who have never smoked and it's not clear why, maybe in some cases just random chance, Heymach said. READ MORE: Doctors say Pope Leo's lung has recovered well from surgery and say his post-operative tests normal Other risks include exposure to radon gas, asbestos, radiation, secondhand smoke and air pollution, according to the American Cancer Society. How is lung cancer detected? Lung cancer symptoms don't usually appear until the cancer is advanced, according to the cancer society. They can include a persistent cough, chest pain, a hoarse voice, shortness of breath, and recurrent pneumonia or bronchitis — symptoms important to get checked. Sometimes, lung cancer can be found early when someone has an X-ray or other scan that shows a spot in a lung that needs further investigation. That's called an incidental finding, leading doctors to investigate well before symptoms and possibly early enough that the cancer remains small and hasn't spread. In the pope's case, a nodule in his lung was spotted during another exam. READ MORE: South Americans pray for Pope Leo's recovery as uncertainty hangs over his visit In the U.S., yearly screening with a low-dose CT scan, a type of X-ray, is recommended for certain people at high risk because of heavy smoking. How is it treated? Surgery is a mainstay when lung cancer is detected early, and increasingly is used even in more advanced stages. The pope had the lower section, or lobe, of his right lung removed to try to ensure that all of the cancer was removed. The right lung has three sections or lobes while the left has two. Each lobe has its own airway branch and dedicated blood vessels and when one is removed, "the other lobes actually pick up some of the work," said Dr. Ben Zhang, a thoracic surgeon at Allina Health in Minneapolis. The lungs gradually compensate over several months until most people, especially those who already were physically active, notice little to no difference with exertion, he said. The pope is known to engage in weekly tennis games and swimming. In the U.S., the average hospital stay after lung cancer surgery is two nights, Zhang said. It depends in part on how quickly the patient can get up and walk around, as well as pain and how long a tube that can drain air and fluid from the chest is needed. The pope was walking the next day, which Heymach called "typically a harbinger of a quicker recovery." Whether additional treatment is needed depends on the tumor's stage, based on factors such as its size and whether it shows signs of spreading via the lymph nodes, and if markers on its cells suggest it may be aggressive. Additional treatment can be chemotherapy, used before surgery to shrink a tumor or afterward to attack any lingering cells. Other options include radiation, immunotherapy or what are called targeted drugs aimed at specific molecular drivers of a tumor. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 70907431e33d.text: Data: AP-NORC; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios A quartet of polls out this week carry a stark message: Americans feel disgruntled, dizzy and down on the man in the White House. Why it matters: The vibes going into the midterms are bleak, with a large majority of voters wanting significant change. But the question remains whether those sentiments will drive them to the polls. Driving the news: Nearly two-thirds of Americans rate the economy negatively, per a Fox News poll out Wednesday. Seven in ten voters say they feel like things in the country are out of control, per a The Economist/YouGov survey conducted October 10-12. And eight in ten, new AP/NORC polling found, want to see either "substantial change" or "complete and total upheaval" in how the country is run. Among Republicans, 58% share those sentiments. Zoom out: That national angst appears to be dragging down the president's approval. Fox News found that Trump's approval rating on inflation, which picked up last month, is at a new low: 22%. His overall job approval rating has also fallen to a new floor in Fox News surveys for either term: 36%. Fox says that drop is largely driven by voters under 45, those with household incomes below $50,000, non-white voters and those without a college degree. The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Yes, but: Polling suggests that disgruntlement doesn't necessarily translate into a wellspring of positive energy toward Democrats. Far more voters say they're somewhat or very pessimistic about the Democratic Party's future (47%) than those who say they're optimistic (21%), per AP/NORC. About half say they're pessimistic about Republicans' future, while around 23% say they're optimistic. Still, Fox found that if the election were held today, 54% of voters would back the Democrat in their House district, while 45% would support the Republican — a wider lead for Dems than the prior month. Plus, Fox found that Republicans have lost ground to Democrats in earning voters' trust on key issues like inflation and foreign policy. Between the lines: Republicans know that they're playing defense in an uphill midterm battle . They have flooded the airwaves in once-safe states and are pulling ads in those that look like a lost cause, Axios' Hans Nichols reports. But it's not smooth sailing for Democratic leadership — they are still navigating tough races and risk welcoming a new, rebellious caucus to Washington that says it's willing to buck the party. The bottom line: Pollsters don't have crystal balls — and whether Americans' discontent translates into a midterm upheaval will only be clear after votes are cast. Go deeper: Americans are losing faith in their fellow voters Methodology: The AP/NORC poll was conducted October 8-12, 2026. Online and telephone interviews using landlines and cell phones were conducted with 1,119 adults. The overall margin of sampling error is +/-3.9 percentage points. The Econmist/YouGov poll was conducted October 10-12, 2026, with 1,403 U.S. registered voters surveyed via web-based interviews. The overall margin of sampling error is +/-3.5 percentage points. The Fox News poll was conducted October 9-12, 2026 under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), with 1,202 registered voters nationwide. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (114) and cellphones (786) or completed the survey online by following a link received via text message (302). The overall margin of sampling error is +/-2.5 percentage points.

A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.
They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon.
From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole.
The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought.
Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens.
The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found.
A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology.
"The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News.
Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s.
The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy.
"It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone."
But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident.
But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation.
"The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said.
This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear.
We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival. But they join a small but growing body of evidence which point to the possibility that human-on-human violence was more common and goes back further than the current scientific consensus would suggest.
"I unfortunately see the growing body of evidence as an indication that interpersonal violence goes deep into human prehistory," Stringer told BBC News.
A key piece of that evidence is a study published in 2022 of very early Neanderthal skulls from northern Spain at an archaeological site called "the Pit of Bones". It suggests that deadly violence was taking place about 430,000 years ago.
Researchers found 57 healed head injuries among 20 individuals. Nine individuals had potentially fatal skull fractures. Six had similar puncture wounds at the back-left of the head. Because the wounds repeatedly occurred in almost the same place, the researchers concluded that deliberate blows were more likely than accidental damage. One skull had two wounds that had probably been inflicted with the same object.
The Pit of Bones findings do not show that everyone in this population was habitually violent, but they provide strong evidence that repeated killing occurred among these people hundreds of thousands of years ago.
For decades, many archaeologists linked the beginnings of organised warfare to farming, when people began living in permanent settlements and competing over land, livestock and food stores.
But evidence from earlier hunter-gatherers and still older human relatives has since shown that individual killings pre-date farming by a very long way.
The live scientific debate is over how common such violence was, and when sporadic attacks became organised conflict and wars between groups.
The research has been published in the journal Scientific Reports.

A new set of remains found in modern-day Iraq suggests that one Neandertal probably suffered a devastating blow to the face before dying at the point of a spear many years later.
The size and structure of a puncture wound in a shoulder blade suggest that it was made by a wooden spear shortly before or after death, researchers write October 15 in Scientific Reports. But violence isn’t all this Neandertal may have known. A shattered tooth found with the remains hints that the deceased suffered a facial injury at some point in their life. Surviving this injury indicates that Neandertals may have helped each other in times of need, the study authors speculate.
These remains with visible trauma are “super cool,” because “there’s a lot of ways to die that leave absolutely no mark on your skeleton,” says Libby Cowgill, a biological anthropologist at the University of Missouri in Columbia who wasn’t involved with the study.
Neandertals were often injured throughout their lives, probably from hunting. But archaeologists have also uncovered occasional signs that Neandertals and other hominids — modern humans and their extinct cousins — were stabbing and pummeling each other, maybe even intentionally, as far back as 430,000 years ago. Signs of injuries caused by other hominids have included another Neandertal at the same Iraq site whose rib was probably stabbed.
During an excavation that began in 2019 at Shanidar, the famous Neandertal burial site in Iraqi Kurdistan, researchers uncovered remains from at least three previously unknown individuals. The set included ribs, hand bones, teeth and a perforated shoulder bone that probably belonged to a single individual who lived around 75,000 years ago.
At first, the team had no idea what caused the hole, says Emma Pomeroy, a biological anthropologist at the University of Cambridge. “It’s so round, it’s like, what is it?” she recalls thinking at the time.
The team removed the shoulder blade with the surrounding sediment and tested for evidence that roots or insects had damaged the fossil. But that didn’t fit the nature of the damage.
Instead, they found fragments of bone from the shoulder blade in the dirt that suggested it had been pierced when the individual, which the team named Shanidar A, was alive. The team also didn’t see any signs of healing around the puncture wound when they analyzed the bone under the microscope and using X-rays — suggesting that the injury had occurred around the time of death.
The next task was to find out what instrument might have caused the injury. The team compared the puncture with the fossilized remains of butchered animals found alongside human tools, as well as wounds created by archaeologists stabbing animal corpses with re-created Paleolithic weapons. Stone-tipped spears usually create a diamond-shaped hole. Wooden spears, on the other hand, tend to leave round puncture wounds.
The wound was “absolutely, without any question,” made by a wooden spear, says Bruno Maureille, an anthropologist at the University of Bordeaux in France who wasn’t on the study team.
The team also found a broken incisor alongside the rest of the remains. The tooth was so shattered that Shanidar A probably experienced a serious injury to their face. Tartar buildup suggests that the tooth splintered in half years before Shanidar A died, meaning they lived with their disability for a long time.
“Given it would have affected their ability to eat, to drink — they’d have been in massive amount of pain at first — it’s likely [to] have needed some care,” Pomeroy says. That one set of remains suggest both violence and care show that Neandertal “behavior is complex,” Pomeroy says. “Like us.”

Belfast Harbour is to become a live environment for testing zero-emission transport and energy systems.
It comes after a Â£15m investment from UK Research and Innovation's Local Innovation Partnerships Fund.
The cluster led by Artemis Technologies, will connect electric vessels, high-power marine charging, autonomous transport and energy systems through secure digital twin technology.
Testing these technologies in an operational port will show how they work as an integrated system and help reduce barriers to commercial adoption.
Artemis Technologies CEO Dr Iain Percy said they are creating a digital network that will allow them to "optimise" both transport and energy use.
"What does that mean for most people? It means your bus turns up at the right time in terms of transport.
"But in terms of energy it means, more significantly that when the wind is blowing too hard, the network tells our boat 'take the power' and ultimately as we build up, it tells Belfast Harbour which uses a huge amount of energy 'take that energy'.
"Equally when the wind doesn't blow, it says 'don't use that energy' and what does that mean?
"It means we don't have to shut down windfarms and ultimately lower energy prices," he added.
This is the second project announced from the Â£30m allocation to the Belfast-Derry Innovation Corridor.
Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said: "It will be developing to try and match up the energy supply with the demands of the harbour, which is a really big user.
"We are really world leading in terms of this so it is a really good investment," she added.
It's hoped what is learned in this project could have wider applications across Northern Ireland.
Dr Percy said: "Where the real accelerator value add comes in here, what can be done on that network can be rinse and repeat anywhere else."
"We already have real buy in from Foyle Port and other regions within Northern Ireland," he added.

For four generations, Neil Heseltine's family have worked on Hill Top Farm, perched on the hillside of Malhamdale amid the dramatic landscape of the Yorkshire Dales. And for most of that time, sheep were the mainstay of the business.
But, Neil says, over the past 20 years there has been "a complete turnaround" and he has shifted away from sheep farming to stay afloat. In that time the 1,500-acre farm has gone from a peak of over 800 lambing sheep to just 45 this spring.
"I dread to think where the farm would have been financially had we not started to make those changes," he tells me. "I either continued along the sheep-farming route because of sentimentality or made bold decisions."
While most upland farmers still keep sheep on their land, the changes here have been mirrored across not just the Dales but the entire British farming industry. The shepherd's life has never been an easy one, but for many it's getting tougher and more difficult than ever to make a profit.
The average British farmer is 60 years old, according to the National Farmers' Union (NFU), and prices for everything from fuel to fodder have risen hugely for them in recent years. Meanwhile, many farmers are facing significantly reduced income from subsidies and there are worries that recent trade deals will mean increased competition from overseas.
The UK's recent trade deals with New Zealand and Australia, struck since Brexit, eliminate tariffs and give producers in both countries large quotas on the amount of lamb they can export into the UK.
There are now 14.7 million breeding ewes in the UK - the lowest figure in living memory according to Phil Stocker, chief executive of the National Sheep Association.
Overall the national flock is also falling, down to 30.4 million sheep in 2025 - numbers last seen in the mid-20th Century, when the UK population was smaller and thus the potential market for lamb and mutton reared here was much lower.
And over the last 50 years there has been a significant fall in lamb and mutton consumption according to Becky Smith, a senior analyst at the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), which represents farmers.
In 1980 the average UK household purchased 128g of sheep meat (lamb and mutton) per person, per week. In 2024 that same measure was down to 23g per person, per week.
Sheep farming has shaped the image many of us have when we picture somewhere like the Dales with drystone walls to keep livestock enclosed and green, rolling hills kept short by seasonal grazing.
But any desire to protect the heritage of one of the UK's oldest agricultural industries is rubbing up against not just a diminishing appetite for sheep meat but also the question of whether some of our uplands might be better used to promote nature recovery and biodiversity.
All this raises the question of whether we have passed "peak sheep" in the UK - and, in turn, what that might mean for consumers. Will my children still be eating our lamb for their Sunday roast or in their baltis and bhunas in 25 years time?
And, what will happen to some of our most revered and beloved landscapes like the Lake District, Yorkshire Dales, Scottish Highlands and Welsh mountains, and the people who live and work there?
Why sheep farming has become so tough
At Craven Cattle Mart on the outskirts of Skipton, North Yorkshire, the auction ring is buzzing as farmers from across the Yorkshire Dales and Pennine Moors come to buy and sell livestock.
To an outsider, business might look brisk - but general manager Jeremy Eaton says it's nowhere near as busy as when he started in the industry 47 years ago.
"We'd have some sales at this market where we'd regularly be selling 19,000 store lambs," he says. "Now we're fortunate if we get to 8,000 or 9,000."
People who work sheep know that it's some of the hardest farming there is. A former shepherd once told me that sheep are only ever trying to do one of three things: "Escape, or die, or escape and then immediately die."
Globally, lamb consumption is expected to grow by 15% between now and 2032, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and the Food and Agriculture Organization.
But changing tastes in the UK mean mutton, made from mature sheep, is no longer eaten in the same volume it was by previous generations and lamb has seemingly gone from a weekly staple to a meat more often eaten on special occasions, with "white meat" like chicken being increasingly chosen over lamb and beef.
The drop in the national flock has actually led to robust growth in the price paid for lamb according to Becky Smith from the AHDB, with the sheep price hitting record highs in 2024.
But despite the higher price for their sheep, upland farmers with tight margins feel the pinch more than many when diesel and oil costs go up. And on top of that, the cost of feeding sheep has also rocketed - the average cost of a bale of hay is Â£155 a tonne this spring compared to Â£75 a tonne this time last year.
Farmers and groups such as Compassion in World Farming have also raised concerns that new trade deals could undermine UK agriculture because farms here must meet high welfare standards that may not be not required in several partner countries.
Extremely tight margins mean growing numbers of younger people can't see a future in farming.
This is immediately apparent as you wander around Craven Cattle Marts. "You can see here today, most of the generation of farmers are over 60," says Hayley Baines, a 39-year-old sheep farmer from Gisburn in the Ribble Valley. "There [aren't] many young ones because there's better options."
And some welcome the decline in sheep farming.
"Fewer sheep means less suffering [â¦] a sheep's life in the wool and mutton industries belies our reputation as a nation of animal lovers," says Mimi Bekhechi, senior vice president at the UK's People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta).
