The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe.
Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.
For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.
This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.
Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.
France's prime minister, SÃ©bastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
JÃ©rÃ´me Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.
The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.
"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.
So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy?
Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.
Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?
"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.
She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.
"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."
"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.
"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."
"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.
Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.
But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.
France's national motto is libertÃ©, Ã©galitÃ©, fraternitÃ© (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.
I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.
They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.
"France likes to speak of Ã©galitÃ©," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."
None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.
The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.
They are part of a defiant French tradition.
Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les MisÃ©rables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'Ãªtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas."
("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")
Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."
Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.
Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.
This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.
France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.
Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said.
At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity.

Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem.
For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill.
"When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump.
While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day".
Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology.
The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells.
Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts."
The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality.
Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory.
When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells.
In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue.
Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance.
This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks.
"You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processesâ¦ as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world.
The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away.
Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells.
But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers.
Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner.
Bad smells from waste sites â a common cause of complaints â are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says.
In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city.
A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits.
"Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume."
The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (Â£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus.
The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns.
This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?"
Meanwhile, some of the sites that have been blamed for causing unpleasant smells in Des Moines have spent millions of dollars to upgrade their own odour control systems.
Smithfield Foods, which operates a meat processing in Des Moines, says it has invested $2m to install a regenerative thermal oxidiser that destroys the chemicals associated with bad smells. Even so, the company says it does not believe it is the source of odour complaints.
Before installing the monitors â which some local companies help pay for â officials in Des Moines would drive out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air.
Relying on the human nose to sniff out industrial smells is still commonplace. Claudia Barrios ObregÃ³n from Kunak, the company behind the monitors in Des Moines, says: "Right now, the way that cities control or measure odours is olfactometry: a human panel measures and gives an opinion of what the odour is like. But that's not that realistic."
The Spanish company's monitors are an example of so-called electronic noses that make it easier to detect smells.

26055e1c283b.text: By — Victoria Eastwood, Associated Press Victoria Eastwood, Associated Press By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/saudi-diplomat-says-iran-is-encouraging-houthi-escalation-of-attacks-on-the-kingdom Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Saudi diplomat says Iran is encouraging Houthi escalation of attacks on the kingdom World Oct 15, 2026 7:16 PM EDT CAIRO (AP) — Iran's government is encouraging the latest escalation in attacks by the Tehran-backed Houthi rebels and doesn't seem ready to make the needed concessions in the wider war with the United States, one of Saudi Arabia's top diplomats said Thursday. Rayed Krimly, deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry, spoke to journalists in a rare briefing following more than a week of Houthi attacks targeting the Riyadh international airport, the headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco and other aviation, oil and military facilities across the kingdom. READ MORE: Iran-backed Houthis strike Saudi oil company Aramco's headquarters, officials say At least 19 people, including foreigners, have been killed in what Krimly called war crimes. King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital alone has been targeted 20 times by the Houthis this month, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the rebels said Thursday. The escalation between the Saudis and the rebels in neighboring Yemen has exposed the kingdom's challenges in intercepting the attacks in the latest front in the Iran war, while further rattling global markets. It also has reinforced Saudi appeals to allies including the United States for more military help. Saudi Arabia says the Houthis had turned down a meeting Krimly said the Saudis had reached out and called for a meeting in Oman with the Houthis in July "to resolve outstanding differences and bring an end to this escalation," but he said the rebels refused to participate. Days later, the Houthis made one of their most significant territorial grabs yet, racing down Yemen's Red Sea coast to seize land on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier this month, the Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive in Yemen to retake those areas. That caused new friction between Mideast rivals Saudi Arabia and Iran. "We think the escalation by the Houthis at this later stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," Krimly said, adding that Iran "continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of relevant U.N. Security Council resolutions and in violation of its commitments in the Beijing agreement." That deal saw Saudi Arabia and Iran restore diplomatic ties after a seven-year rift. While Iran's government has said it is open to dialogue on helping to find an end to the fighting, Krimly said Saudi Arabia has not requested any Iranian mediation. "We maintain direct channels of communication with the Houthis, and Oman serves as a facilitator of these talks and not as a mediator," he said. Saudi Arabia still has direct communications with Iran, he added. In the middle of the series of attacks on the Riyadh airport, the Saudi and Iranian foreign ministers spoke at least once by phone. At the same time, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi as recently as Thursday called the Saudi blockade on the Houthis unjust and illegal. Iran takes a 'long, long time' to respond to mediators On the wider Iran war, Krimly said the kingdom continues to support the mediation efforts of Qatar and Pakistan in trying to maintain talks between Washington and Tehran. Mediators are trying to work out two issues, he said. One is a solution that would ensure safe passage for ships through the Strait of Hormuz in return for ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, which is aimed at bottling up Iran's oil exports and applying economic pain. The other issue is a "clearer commitment" on how negotiations over Iran's nuclear program will take place and what they will include. "In both fronts, the Iranians take a long, long time to come back to the mediators with any new proposal, and what they come with is insufficient," Krimly said. "And then they begin to talk about a temporary arrangement in (the Strait of) Hormuz, and a temporary arrangement to this and that, and then we spend sometimes weeks and months discussing this, back and forth. "They don't seem to be able to reach consensus on the needed solutions that will pave the way for a peaceful solution of the conflict," he said. Iranian officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment. China and Russia are thought to be helping Iran and the rebels Krimly also said the kingdom believes that China and Russia are involved in supporting both Iran and the Houthis, but he gave few details. "Of course, some of the capabilities of Iran, and of the Houthis, do come -- or the intelligence -- do come from at least elements in Russia or China, even commercial elements sometimes, but we do discuss these matters regularly with China and Russia, and we will continue to do so," he said. A new report this week said the Houthis are attempting to build a new advanced medium-range ballistic missile system with the help of Chinese parts. Krimly said Saudi Arabia continues to have direct communications with members of the Gulf Coordination Council including the United Arab Emirates, which had been a key member of the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis until friction led the UAE to withdraw its support months ago. As for the mutual defense agreement the kingdom recently signed with Pakistan and Turkey, Krimly offered no new details on what assistance the two partners might offer as the Houthis keep attacking. It’s not unusual for Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin to be on the road touting the Trump administration’s agenda, but his travel itinerary in the weeks before the midterm election looks like a trail of political hot spots.
On Thursday, Zeldin traveled to an auto repair shop and a construction firm in central Pennsylvania with Rep. Scott Perry, one of the most endangered Republicans in Congress. Earlier in the week, Zeldin was in Iowa with Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is in a neck-and-neck race for the state’s open Senate seat. Zeldin later headed to a family farm in Wisconsin with Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden, who is fighting to keep his seat representing the state’s 3rd Congressional District.
Zeldin’s slew of stops with candidates—all promoted with press releases from EPA headquarters—generates concern, in the view of the political watchdog group that is taking on a $20 million taxpayer-funded advertising campaign praising Trump and his administration.
“It does raise questions on whether the EPA administrator is engaged in political activity in a way that violates the Hatch Act,” said Kedric Payne, senior director of ethics for the Campaign Legal Center, referring to the 87-year-old law that limits the political activities of federal employees. Although cabinet officials like Zeldin get more leeway under that law than most civil servants to attend campaign events and the like, they are not permitted to use taxpayer resources to do so.
“With the use of the EPA and its press and communications shop to put a spotlight on this travel, an investigator truly needs to know what is being said at these gatherings,” Payne said.
Federal employees whose travel is supported by taxpayers can violate the Hatch Act even if they don’t explicitly urge people to vote for a candidate, he said. The series of taxpayer-funded ads the Campaign Legal Center and others sued over did not call for support of any political candidate, but a federal judge blocked the TV spots until after the election.
Payne said there is often “a fine line” between permissible and impermissible activities under the Hatch Act. The determination hinges on whether there could be any other explanation for the cabinet official’s activity, other than promoting a candidate.
An EPA spokesperson said Zeldin’s visits are fact-finding ventures and part of his job as the nation’s top environmental regulator.
“Administrator Zeldin’s travels are driven by one thing: his commitment to getting regulators out of Washington to meet with the regulated,” the spokesperson said. “Every day of each of these trips, Administrator Zeldin has asked for feedback from Americans on what the Trump EPA can do better, and he’s taking that feedback back to D.C. to make decisions.
“His main message to people wherever he goes is that EPA is back to its core mission, protecting human health and the environment, and we want to know how we can do that better,” the spokesperson said.
One environmental aide in a past administration who spoke on background said it was not unusual for cabinet members to fan out across the country to sell their accomplishments.
For example, during President Joe Biden’s administration, EPA Administrator Michael Regan made one visit with a member of Congress in the month prior to the 2022 midterm elections. Regan traveled with Rep. Pat Ryan of New York, a Democrat, who was then in a fight to keep his seat, to see an EPA-managed asbestos removal site in Ulster County. In 2024, none of the visits Regan made with members of Congress were in contested districts. In one case he traveled with Republicans, Sen. Thom Tillis and Rep. Chuck Edwards of North Carolina, to see the impacts of Hurricane Helene.
But under Trump, who held the 2020 Republican National Convention on the grounds of the White House, the lines between federal activity and political activity often have blurred.
The Atlantic reported last month that the Trump White House had launched an unofficial competition encouraging cabinet secretaries to travel the country to promote the administration agenda in advance of the midterm elections, with officials getting points for visits to politically competitive districts or states and getting docked for visits to solidly blue areas. By The Atlantic’s count, seven other cabinet members had eclipsed Zeldin’s visits to political hot spots during the summer.
But in recent weeks, in addition to his trips to Iowa, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, Zeldin made what an EPA press release called a “three-day swing” across Michigan with two Republicans whose races will be crucial to deciding congressional control: Rep. Bill Huizenga and Rep. Tom Barrett. Zeldin also traveled to Maricopa County, Arizona, which has a close congressional race and two states with key Senate races—Maine and New Hampshire—although he did not travel with any candidates on those trips.
According to EPA press releases, Zeldin’s October visits to battleground districts resembled other stops he has made in a tenure that took him to all 50 states within his first nine months in office, touting the Trump agenda. In Iowa with Hinson, Zeldin unveiled an “American Farmer First” policy including support for corn ethanol demand. In Pennsylvania, four days later, Zeldin appeared with Perry, who in a debate with his challenger the previous night said that he wanted federal support for ethanol ended. Zeldin and Perry focused on Trump’s deregulatory agenda and how they say it has helped small business. And in Wisconsin, Zeldin talked about how the Trump administration had lifted a requirement for anti-pollution sensors on diesel engines that were blamed for engine failures and shutdowns.
The message that the Trump administration is putting American farmers first and lowering costs comes when Republicans are facing headwinds from the pain Trump’s tariffs and the Iran War run-up in energy prices, especially diesel fuel, has inflicted on consumers.

After days of bitter back-and-forth between the two leaders, Ukraine has resumed strikes on Russian energy targets following three days of Ukrainian cease-fire. The president had demanded an energy cease-fire this past Sunday between the two. Russia never stopped its attacks. Lisa Desjardins begins our coverage. Lisa Desjardins: In Ukraine's capital city today, Russian strikes reverberate in broad daylight, that after Ukrainian officials say Russia launched a large-scale overnight attack, more than 850 drones. But Russia too is burning. The Associated Press reports Ukraine hit this oil refinery. Volodymyr Zelenkskyy, Ukrainian President: Three days, we didn't attack any energy, diesel and et cetera systems of Russia, and three days they attack us. Lisa Desjardins: Late yesterday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenkskyy told The Financial Times that Russia never abided by the cease-fire announced by Trump. Zelenskyy criticized the U.S. for limiting intelligence resources like Starlink. He was blunt. His patience is gone. Question: If they keep doing this, how much longer will you maintain the stoppage of attacks on Russian refineries? Volodymyr Zelenkskyy: That's it. Block is out. Lisa Desjardins: His candor continued when asked about Trump's relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin and their deal on diesel. Volodymyr Zelenkskyy: He speaks about it, I mean, openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people, because, for him, I don't know, people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it's means they're very strong because they -- you can, I mean, hold the power. How it can be when some people are surviving, fighting, dying, you make some business with the guys with such aggression? Lisa Desjardins: For his part, Putin accused Ukraine of violating the truce. Vladimir Putin, Russian President (through interpreter): They made a first step. We started to respond by striking at energy facilities, which they are now squealing about. It was them who started it. They should have thought properly about consequences. Lisa Desjardins: And Russia's foreign minister said Zelenskyy's comments point to a deepening rift between Kyiv and Washington. Sergey Lavrov, Russian Foreign Minister (through interpreter): The fact that this is such a direct and indeed crude challenge to President Trump is, in my view, something everyone already understands. Lisa Desjardins: Zelenskyy spent his day at an E.U. summit in Brussels focused on support from his European allies. Kaja Kallas, High Representative, European Union: We definitely have different approach to this war. We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender. Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach. Lisa Desjardins: The talks come as the entire region grows more war-weary. Two cargo ships were set ablaze today in Romanian waters in the Black Sea. Seven crew members are missing. Nicusor Dan, President of Romania (through interpreter): There are attempts by Russia to destabilize societies and to reduce support for Ukraine. And our response is, we continue to support Ukraine. Lisa Desjardins: European leaders also rejected Trump's push to control and release frozen Russian assets, he said, as a bargaining ship. Friedrich Merz, German Chancellor (through interpreter): These are assets that are frozen in Europe. And they should remain frozen in Europe. This is our business. And we decide on it. Lisa Desjardins: And, as world leaders talk, the war grinds on, on the ground. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Lisa Desjardins.

1c81e86f4ab7.text: For perspective on the tensions between President Trump and Ukrainian President Zelenskyy, Amna Nawaz spoke with former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine William Taylor. He’s now a distinguished fellow at the Atlantic Council. Amna Nawaz: For perspective now on the tensions between President Trump and President Zelenskyy, we turn to former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine William Taylor. He's now a distinguished fellow at the Atlantic Council. Ambassador Taylor, let's begin with Ukrainian President Zelenskyy's decision to resume strikes on Russian energy targets after complying with President Trump's demand to stop those for a few days. Is that the right call for Ukraine right now? William Taylor, Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine: Amna, it's absolutely the right call. As you say, the president held off for three days. He had agreed to this cease-fire, energy cease-fire, that President Trump suggested or demanded without consultation. But, nonetheless, President Zelenskyy said, yes, good idea. He suggested this before. He made this proposal before. And the Russians have always said no before, but maybe President Trump had had a conversation with President Putin and was going to get President Putin to agree this time. So President Zelenskyy stopped firing at the refineries for three days while the Russians continued to batter the Ukrainians, energy, civilian targets, killing civilians. He couldn't -- he couldn't stop. President Zelenskyy had to resume the attacks when the Russians had never stopped. Amna Nawaz: Ambassador Taylor, you heard there the remarkable public expression of frustration, of anger from President Zelenskyy. Is that a risky move for a nation that is still so dependent on support from the U.S.? William Taylor: Amna, less support from -- less dependent on support from the U.S. at this point than it was, say, a year-and-a-half ago, because the United States doesn't provide any weapons. We don't provide any financial support. We don't provide any political leadership. We don't lead the Ramstein process, by which we coordinate the assistance going, the military assistance going. We don't do any of that. So we're -- the Ukrainians are not so dependent on us as they were. Now, it is true that military intelligence is important to the Ukrainians coming from the United States, but they also get that from other places as well. But in answer to your question, I guess I would not have gone the ad hominem with that. I wouldn't have made comments about President Trump and why he wants to stay in power. You know, you don't need any of that. You just stick to the results that he's after, which is pressure on Putin to stop the war. And the pressure point on Putin to stop the war is attacks on refineries. Amna Nawaz: You heard Russia's Sergey Lavrov there point to the rift between the U.S. and Ukraine. At this moment, does this deterioration in relations between the U.S. and Ukraine, does that further embolden Putin? Could we see a ramping up of Russian attacks? William Taylor: They're already at the top of the ramping up of Russian attacks. And, Amna, what Lavrov says, what Putin says, they would love to have this dispute, this rift, as you say. This is what their goal has been, is to cut off support for Ukraine. The United States has indicated, the Senate, the House has indicated strong support. When you ask Americans if they support Ukraine, they do, and they oppose Russia. The United States will continue to have a strong relationship with Ukraine, and I believe this administration will as well. Amna Nawaz: You have heard President Trump recently strongly criticize President Zelenskyy very directly, saying Ukraine needs a new president. We should point out Zelenskyy's term did expire back in 2024. He's operating under a constitutional wartime extension in Ukraine. What about people on the ground in Ukraine? Do they want elections? Do they want a new president? William Taylor: They don't, Amna. They don't. I have been there many times. I have been there 15 times since the big war started in 2022. And I have talked to the people about -- I have talked to opposition parties, who you would think would want to have elections so they can get -- no. The opposition parties, the people, civil society, the election experts, democracy experts are all united at this point in Ukraine. They don't think elections are appropriate now. They can't have elections now. They don't want it. They support their president for now. They're eager to have elections, Amna. They're really eager to have elections when the cease-fire comes, when the war is over. They are eager. They're going to be -- there's going to be real competition, but not now. Right now, they support their president. Amna Nawaz: In the 30 seconds or so I have left, I have to ask, do you see this as a new all-time low in relations between the U.S. and Ukraine? William Taylor: An all-time low. Again, the Ukrainians are in better shape now than they have been before because they're less dependent on us. They have seen that they can't really depend on one thing to the next day, one commitment to the day, a withdrawal of that commitment the next. So, they're in better shape now. They have got strong support from the Europeans. That's going to keep them going, and maybe the Americans will come back as well. Amna Nawaz: That is former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine William Taylor joining us tonight. Ambassador Taylor, always good to speak with you. Thank you. William Taylor: Thank you, Amna.

b023eb3ef735.text: In our news wrap Thursday, President Trump canceled plans to livestream the December execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan, federal law enforcement agencies are investigating a series of letters containing what they're calling "suspicious substances" that were sent to congressional and state election officials and police report multiple victims in a shooting at a school in Bend, Oregon. Amna Nawaz: We start the day's other headlines with a late-breaking story out of Bend, Oregon, where police say there are multiple victims following a shooting this afternoon at an elementary school. Officials say children are among the victims. Their status is unclear, but at least two people were hospitalized. Officials also say the shooter was shot and killed at Silver Rail Elementary School possibly by a bystander, though that is not yet confirmed. Federal law enforcement agencies are investigating a series of letters containing what they're calling suspicious substances that were sent to congressional and state election officials. In a statement provided to the "News Hour," the FBI says it's investigating each incident and -- quote -- "working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters." Elections officials in at least six states have reported receiving such mail, including Ohio, South Dakota, and Maryland. It comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections. President Trump has canceled plans to livestream the December execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan amid growing bipartisan backlash. The president posted online that he still believes -- quote -- "Streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent," but he added -- quote -- "Many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die." Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the livestream plan last week. But a growing number of Republicans, including Vice President J.D. Vance, said they would not watch. In Texas, voting rights groups are suing the state's Department of Public Safety and the secretary of state over the delay of nearly 600,000 online voter registrations. Officials say a software glitch in their online portal caused the backlog. The lawsuit claims that Texas failed to provide a reliable online registration system. Local election staff are working overtime to process the registrations before early voting starts on Monday. In Northwest Pakistan, the roof of a private school collapsed during morning classes today, killing at least 34 children and a teacher. Authorities in the city of Peshawar said rescue workers arrived within minutes, and that rapid response saved dozens of lives. Crews cleared debris, with officials saying everyone trapped beneath the rubble was eventually pulled out. Hospital officials say more than 50 other people were injured, some in critical condition. The local police chief says the school's owner has been arrested. Mian Saeed, Peshawar Police Chief (through translator): This is a truly tragic incident, and we will certainly investigate and file a report against the owners. Holding classes for children in such a fragile building located within such narrow streets, this clearly represents a grave instance of negligence. Amna Nawaz: Thousands of mourners attended a mass funeral later in the day. The children killed or injured were all between the ages of 6 and 14 and all lived in the same neighborhood as the school. In Albania, violent clashes erupted in the capital of Tirana today as anti-government protests stretched into a third day. Alarms sounded as protesters attacked this bank. Riot police retaliated with water cannons and tear gas. The nation's Health Ministry says more than 80 people were injured, most of them police officers. The student-led demonstration started amid anger over a major development project backed by President Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. They're also demanding better school conditions and for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. He has refused to do so. In New York City today, ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, pleaded not guilty to new charges of torture. He's accused of overseeing a violent campaign against opponents and others, including three Americans. The allegations were added to an earlier drug trafficking indictment against the couple. Maduro told the court today the indictment contains what he called false accusations and false testimony. The couple were seized from their Caracas home by the U.S. military in January, and their trial is set for next June. President Trump's new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, is facing questions about her legal credentials. Multiple news outlets report she has not passed the bar exam in any state. Zacharia holds a law degree from Pepperdine's Caruso School of Law. She's referred to herself online as general counsel in past roles, and Mr. Trump has called her an attorney. But legal experts say neither of those titles should be used unless someone has passed the bar. Zacharia held her first briefing as press secretary this week, taking questions from three outlets in a 15-minute appearance. On Wall Street today, stocks managed to end higher despite ongoing worries about AI. The Dow Jones industrial average jumped more than 550 points. The Nasdaq added just 20 points, so a small gain there. The S&P 500 rose a third of 1 percent. And we cover news big and small here at the "News Hour," and in this case, very small. The London Zoo announced the birth of 15 Afia Birago puddle frogs, one of the world's smallest and rarest amphibians. The frog is about a fifth of an inch in size, no larger than the tip of a pencil. These are the first to be born in captivity. Researchers are racing to save the species, which was only identified in its native Ghana eight years ago. Now there are a few more.

4bda74177fc1.text: The CDC has confirmed more than 4,000 cases of measles this year as the country grapples with the largest outbreak of the highly infectious virus in 35 years. Nearly a fifth of cases comprise children under the age of five, and 95% are among unvaccinated people. Amna Nawaz spoke with Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease doctor based in Pennsylvania. Amna Nawaz: The CDC has now confirmed more than 4,000 cases of measles this year as the country grapples with the largest outbreak of the highly infectious virus in 35 years. Nearly a fifth of cases comprise children under the age of 5, and more than 90 percent are among people who are unvaccinated. Pennsylvania is the epicenter of the outbreak with more than 1, 100 cases. That includes five measles-related deaths and potentially a sixth still being investigated. For more on what we're seeing and its impact, we're joined now by Dr. Evan Shirey. He's a pediatric infectious disease doctor based in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Dr. Shirey, welcome and thanks for joining us. Dr. Evan Shirey, Penn State Health: Thank you for having me. Amna Nawaz: So you're in Hershey in Central Pennsylvania, the middle of your state's measles epicenter. Just tell us what you're seeing at your hospital right now. Dr. Evan Shirey: Yes, unfortunately, I have been seeing a lot of children and a lot of babies who have been admitted to our hospital and have been very sick. I am seeing the severe consequences that can come from this virus. Amna Nawaz: Tell us about those consequences. What are the measles like in those young children you're seeing? How does it present? Dr. Evan Shirey: So there are a number of complications that can come about from measles. One that we really worry about is encephalitis, and that's when the virus causes infection of the brain. Children with encephalitis from measles in some cases may be unresponsive. In other cases, they may be awake and aware, but confused. They don't know where they are. They're scared, in some cases, not even able to recognize their own parents. These cases are really, really tragic to see. We see infections where the virus infects the lungs or the airways, and we call that a bronchopneumonia. These children might come in breathing really fast, breathing really heavily, gasping for air, in some cases needing different forms of respiratory support and oxygen, and in some of the extreme cases we have seen have even need to be put on a ventilator. We have seen babies who have come in who are unable to nurse or unable to take bottles, and just all forms of various different kinds of suffering from the manifestations of these infections. Amna Nawaz: And, Dr. Shirey, do we know what's driving this outbreak, how it's gotten so severe in Pennsylvania? Dr. Evan Shirey: So we know that, historically, the measles virus caused a lot of infections. We had three or four million infections every single year in this country, and that also resulted in 50,000 hospitalizations, around 500 deaths every year. So we know this is really bad virus. We know the measles virus can spread like wildfire. It is famous for how infectious it is. One person with measles can infect up to 18 others. The reason that we have not been seeing measles cases up until now is because we had a very safe and a very effective vaccine that we had been using for decades that actually resulted in elimination of the virus from this country. The virus is back because of a failure to vaccinate. Amna Nawaz: Given that we thought measles was eliminated about 25 years ago, is this something you ever thought you would be seeing during your time practicing as a doctor? Dr. Evan Shirey: Absolutely not. I spent a lot of time learning about measles as a medical student and as a resident and as an infectious diseases fellow going through all of my training. I always expected that measles was going to stay in the textbooks, and I did not expect that I would live in a world where I was in an ICU taking care of patients in real life. Amna Nawaz: Can I ask you about the rhetoric we're hearing from some of the nation's leaders? I mean, famously, the HHS secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has had some anti-vaccine views and vaccine skepticism he's expressed. How does that complicate your job on the ground? Dr. Evan Shirey: I think it's a real shame. I think that this outbreak just really highlights how important it is that, when we communicate about these important health issues, that we lead with honesty and the truth. I think it's -- overall has been a shame that the anti-vaccine movement has gained the power that they have and that they have gained the influence in reaching ordinary Pennsylvanians. I see in my clinic when I talk to people about vaccines that the types of fears that people have over these last five, 10 years are really just a different dynamic from the way things used to be. And I think that is largely -- unfortunately, it's related to the success of the anti-vaccine movement as a whole. Amna Nawaz: Whenever we cover these kinds of stories, I should mention to you we hear from people who say, look, if you or your children are vaccinated, you will be fine, so there's not much to worry about. What do you make of that argument? Dr. Evan Shirey: So, first and foremost, I want to be very clear that the vaccine is extremely safe and extremely effective. We have been using the MMR vaccine really in the same form since the late 1960s. So we have decades of experience with this. Billions of people have received this vaccine. So I lead with reiterating the truth that the vaccine is very safe and very effective. For people who are vaccinated, I do want to give reassurance, if you are vaccinated, the vaccine is protective. The unfortunate thing that I think people need to understand is that not everyone can receive the vaccine. And so the vulnerable among our communities have been relying for decades on the rest of us to be vaccinated at a high enough rate to achieve herd

The UK said Thursday it was prepared to align its tariffs on Chinese EVs with those of the EU, delivering a boost to Brussels as it negotiates with Beijing to narrow the trade gap.
European leaders have adopted a more aggressive stance to shield native businesses from a tidal wave of Chinese imports, which policymakers have blamed for deep job losses among European automakers and other sectors.
So far, counter-efforts have involved both protectionist and industrial policies, including âMade in Europeâ rules that have stoked discord among some of Europeâs largest economies.
Having won Beijingâs agreement to halve hybrid vehicle imports, Brussels is now eyeing checks on Chinese chemicals and machinery, Politico reported.

de9e899f5801.text: President Trump is cutting checks to Americans and promising more with less than three weeks left in a midterm cycle largely focused on affordability. Trump argues they’re refunds for excessive healthcare costs and promised economic dividends that only his party can deliver. Democrats contend he’s trying to bribe citizens to vote for Republicans. Liz Landers has an accounting of the payouts. Amna Nawaz: President Trump is cutting checks to Americans and promising more with less than three weeks left in a midterm cycle largely focused on affordability. Trump argues they're refunds for high health care costs and economic dividends that only his party can deliver. Democrats contend he's trying to bribe citizens to vote for Republicans. Our White House correspondent, Liz Landers, is here with an accounting of those payouts. Good to see you, Liz. Liz Landers: Yes. Nice to see you. Amna Nawaz: So let's start with those checks some Americans have already started to receive in the last week or so for Affordable Care Act fees. How much are people getting and what's the president's rationale for those? Liz Landers: People are starting to get these $500 checks really in the last week or so. It's gone out to about a million Americans so far across 30 different states. And this is for people that don't get premium assistance. With these checks was a personal letter that the president wrote. And it says in part: "I'm proud to return your money to you, and I will never stop fighting to put the American people first, restore affordability, protect your hard-earned money, and lower the cost of health care." Now I spoke with Cynthia Cox about this. She's the director of the Affordable Care Act Program at KFF. And she said that this move from the administration is unprecedented. But she also explained how this can help Americans and how these checks will factor into overall rising health care costs. Cynthia Cox, Program on the ACA Director, KFF: For people who get ACA coverage, in particular, the people who lost subsidy this year, they're probably paying a couple thousand dollars more in their premiums this year than they were last year. So the $500 checks are probably going to help. I mean, $500 is nothing to sneeze at, but they're still having a much higher cost beyond that $500 this year than they were last year. Liz Landers: Cox says that the timing of this is political. She said she first heard about this idea floated out there last year, but, of course, now it's being implemented just a few weeks before a midterm election. The White House fact sheet that they put out claimed that the Biden administration -- quote -- "accumulated a significant surplus of funds that were not used to benefit the Americans who paid these higher premiums." But I asked Cox about this, and she says that the different administrations between the Biden and Trump administration have collected different user fees, and that the Trump administration inherited this surplus from the Biden administration, and now they're sending it out as checks. Amna Nawaz: Meanwhile, that's not the only check the administration is sending out. There's more than 20 million Medicare enrollees who could receive a payment as well. What's the reasoning behind those payouts? Liz Landers: These are $90 checks, so much less money, only one-time payments. And this is going to Medicare Part B participants. But Medicare Advantage enrollees and other people with disabilities and some low-income Medicare recipients are not eligible for this. Of course, Medicare Part B covers things like ambulance services, doctor visits, lab tests. So this is helpful, of course; $90 is not nothing. And this will go out to about 21 million Americans. This payment is coming through the Medicare Improvement Fund created by Congress in 2008. And it's not the first time that the fund has been used. The Obama administration and Congress redirected money to expand coverage, but it's the first time that it's been used for direct payments like this. Amna Nawaz: Liz, meanwhile, there's this other promise the president made you reported on that he first made from the midterm convention stage in Dallas that he would send $5,000 to all American adults. Let's just start with what that would cost. Liz Landers: It would cost about a trillion dollars and add that much money to the national debt, which is why you have seen people raise immediate questions about this. This, of course, made big news when the president announced this from the stage during the midterm convention about a month ago. And he has been repeating this and promising this over and over to Americans throughout just about every midterm rally that I have watched and covered. And, yesterday, he talked about this yet again. President Donald Trump: If Republicans can win the House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate, I am going to give all adult citizens in the United States of America $5,000. (CHEERING) President Donald Trump: Think of it. Liz Landers: President Trump was asked in September, sort of right after this announcement, why are you doing this if your economic policies are working? And he said that this is not to turn out voters. He said instead it is a -- quote -- "reward" for voters having to put up with Biden's economic policies. There are, of course, lingering questions about congressional approval of this. Just a reminder, Amna, we're hearing the president make all these promises. He also promised in November of last year, almost a year ago now, that a $2,000 dividend check would be going out to every American for a tariff revenue refund. That has yet to materialize.

The US is sending hundreds of soldiers to Latin America as the Pentagon widens its campaign against drug traffickers, The New York Times reported.
A 600-strong battalion is reportedly being deployed to Panama; the head of a research group that tracks such deployments said he could not recall one âthat ever came close to 600 except for contingencies like invasions or natural disasters.â

cee9de1b6aa0.text: President Trump will travel to Georgia on Friday to stump for Republican Senate candidate Mike Collins. Collins is in an uphill battle against incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. Liz Landers visited Georgia for a closer look at that race. Amna Nawaz: So we just heard some of the president speaking in Montana this week. We know he's been out on the road. Where is he heading next? Liz Landers: Yes, Amna, he is traveling to Dalton, Georgia, tomorrow to stump for the Senate candidate there, Mike Collins. I was in Georgia recently for a closer look at that race, where Collins is in an uphill battle against the incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff. On his vineyard in Southern Georgia, Gary Paulk feels the impacts of many of President Trump's policies firsthand. Gary Paulk, Paulk Vineyards: The fuel today is twice as high as it would have been this time last year. Liz Landers: Polk is a fifth-generation muscadine grape farmer in rural Ray, Georgia. Gary Paulk: Pick them up and eat them, yes. Liz Landers: Mmm. Gary Paulk: Sweet. Liz Landers: Really sweet. He says fuel prices, tariffs that have raised his costs, and an immigration crackdown that has made it harder to find workers have all taken a toll. The president says all the time that he is doing these mass deportations because noncitizens, people who are here illegally in some cases are taking jobs from Americans. Is that the case? Gary Paulk: That's just -- that's not true. They're not taking -- they're not taking jobs from Americans, and, actually, a lot of times that they are filling jobs that Americans don't want, more ag jobs and more remedial -- you know, labor-intensive jobs, construction jobs. Liz Landers: Paulk also worries about access to health care in rural areas after his 36-year-old daughter, Amy, suffered serious strokes that nearly took her life. Gary Paulk: Amy has come a long way. She still can't speak very well. She's just now starting to eat some soft foods, but she's a fighter. Liz Landers: After weighing all these factors, Paulk has decided for the first time in his life to cast a ballot for a Democrat, incumbent Senator Jon Ossoff. He doesn't agree with the Democrat on all issues, notably abortion, but it is Ossoff's help in getting federal aid after Hurricane Helene wreaked havoc on Paulk's grape crop that won his vote. Gary Paulk: He's done a lot of things and proposed a lot of things. And he's crossed party lines to do it, especially with the hurricane disaster. They got $531 million appropriated for the hurricane disaster for farmers in this area. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA): The country needs us to work. Liz Landers: At 39, Ossoff is the youngest sitting U.S. senator and the only Democrat running for reelection in a state Trump won in 2024. A hotly contested swing state in recent elections, Georgia was expected to be a tight contest again. But Ossoff has built a comfortable lead, in part by relentlessly focusing on affordability. Sen. Jon Ossoff: Millions are just one medical bill, short paycheck, or bad alternator from disaster. You work harder and harder, but the treadmill gets faster and steeper and the bills get higher and higher. Liz Landers: Ossoff's opponent is Congressman Mike Collins, whose campaign has been plagued with troubles from the beginning, from a campaign kickoff ad that misspelled Georgia to lackluster fund-raising and a series of scandalous headlines that two former aides and even Collins' son-in-law have promoted antisemitism and white nationalist views. Sen. Jon Ossoff: If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club. His office has been in cahoots with some of the most notorious white supremacists around the country. Liz Landers: Collins strongly denies the allegations. Rep. Mike Collins (R-GA), Senatorial Candidate: I have condemned racism, antisemitism, hate. I don't care where the source is. And I tell him that too. It's wrong. We have no place in this world for that. Liz Landers: A lifelong Georgian whose father was a congressman for 12 years, Collins attacks Ossoff as left-leaning and out of touch with Georgia values. Rep. Mike Collins: I am unapologetically pro-God, pro-Trump, pro-Second Amendment. I believe in a strong military. Peace through strength works. If it's not good for Georgia and it's not good for this country, I will never support it. Liz Landers: Collins has made crime and illegal immigration his major campaign issues, touting his bill, the Laken Riley Act, that requires federal authorities to detain undocumented immigrants who commit theft or violent crimes. Rep. Mike Collins: Every life taken by an illegal immigrant is preventable. But it can only be stopped when we have leaders that will prioritize American lives. Liz Landers: Collins supporters like his message. Woman: Absolutely, I'm supporting Mike Collins. Man: He gets results, and that's what I want from any candidate that I vote for. Liz Landers: They also worry the national conversation is hurting him. Man: There is the worry with what's going on nationally and internationally with the president that I think is really hurting Mike Collins. And so I don't know if it's necessarily his fault. Liz Landers: President Trump has endorsed Collins. For his part, Ossoff has kept President Trump front and center in his attacks, making viral headlines with this aside: Sen. Jon Ossoff: So, he doesn't want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar. (CHEERING) Liz Landers: That brief mention of Trump aide Natalie Harp ricocheted around the Internet for days and prompted this response: Question: What is your response? President Donald Trump: Who said that? Question: Jon Ossoff. President Donald Trump: You mean Pee-wee Herman? Pee-wee Herman look-alike. Liz Landers: Ossoff's campaign style has made him a social media star and even sparked talk of a future presidential run.

75301ab41989.text:
Civilian airports are increasingly becoming military targets, as nations at war seek new ways to inflict economic and psychological damage.
Ukraine, under US pressure to stop striking Russian refineries, has expanded its targets â bombing data centers and clogging air space â while considering more aggressive tactics like directly hitting Russian airports, The Atlantic reported. Kyiv said Thursday it only responds in kind âto specific Russian strikes.â
Such a shift would intensify threats to global aviation safety: The Houthis have reportedly struck Riyadhâs airport 20 times this month, clouding Saudi Arabiaâs investment outlook; Germany accused Russia of attempting to bomb Leipzigâs airport in August; and an Iran-linked threat prompted the US to remove bombers from a UK airfield earlier this month.

US President Donald Trump canceled his defense secretaryâs plan to livestream the execution of a former military officer after widespread backlash.
More than 70 retired military leaders condemned the âbarbaricâ order. The last known US public execution was in 1936, and only Iran and Afghanistan still regularly perform them. 680993da8d47.text: By — Steve Peoples, Associated Press Steve Peoples, Associated Press By — Linley Sanders, Associated Press Linley Sanders, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/frustrated-with-trump-voters-overwhelmingly-want-change-ap-norc-poll-finds Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Frustrated with Trump, voters overwhelmingly want change, AP-NORC poll finds Politics Oct 15, 2026 6:27 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — A strong majority of voters believe that President Donald Trump is falling short at home and abroad, and they want major change in the upcoming midterm elections, according to a new AP-NORC poll that raises serious warning signs for the Republican Party at a critical moment. The survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, conducted less than four weeks before Election Day, finds that registered voters who identify as Democrats are more enthusiastic than Republican voters about casting a ballot. More voters want Democrats to win control of Congress and have a more negative view of Republicans. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Democratic advantage is small in some cases, but, taken together, the findings paint a challenging picture for Republicans, who are clinging to control of Congress under the weight of an unpopular war with Iran and surging prices at home. READ MORE: Retail sales saw 0.8% bump in September, but big chunk of spending went to paying for gas About 8 in 10 voters overall say the economy or the cost of living is among their top issues for the upcoming election, while about two-thirds say this about healthcare and the war in Iran. Other issues that are stronger for Trump — like immigration or crime — are lower priorities. "The world is going backwards. We can barely afford anything," said Diana Walker, a 65-year-old Democrat from Decatur, Georgia. "Everybody's down. I don't care if you're a Democrat or Republican, we're all catching hell." Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting than Republicans Less than a month before the final midterm votes are cast, the poll finds that Democratic voters are more motivated to vote. Overall, about two-thirds of registered voters say it's "extremely" important to vote in the upcoming election, while about 2 in 10 say it's "very" important. But about three-quarters of Democratic voters say that voting in this November's midterm elections is "extremely" important, compared with roughly 6 in 10 Republicans. READ MORE: Democrats see voter enthusiasm in fundraising haul from small-dollar donors before the midterms Ryan Longbrake, a 52-year-old Democrat from Columbus, Ohio who works in technology marketing, said he's especially excited about casting his ballot, and he's already taken steps to ensure that his wife and two college-age daughters will vote as well. "I believe that there is change on the horizon and there is an excitement within our party," he said, pointing to Democrats' momentum in Ohio's elections for governor and U.S. Senate. The party is also investing resources in Republican-leaning states, like Iowa and Kansas, where the political environment has put Democratic candidates on friendlier footing. Republicans have controlled Congress for the past two years, but about half of registered voters now say they'd prefer to see the Democratic Party control the House or the Senate. A smaller percentage, roughly 4 in 10, say they want the Republican Party to control each chamber, while 15% are undecided. The vast majority of voters want change One thing is crystal clear on the eve of the 2026 midterms: Voters want change. About half of voters say they want "substantial change," and roughly 3 in 10 want "complete and total upheaval" in the way the country is run. Democrats and independents are much likelier than Republicans to want a full overhaul of the country's direction. But even Republican voters are still looking for something different. Slightly fewer than half, 45%, want substantial change, while 13% want upheaval. "I'm kind of tired of sending people there and nothing gets done," said Krista Kohles, a 70-year-old Republican from near Davey, Nebraska. "Nothing's changing." Trump's numbers on key issues are weak Voters are deeply frustrated with Trump and his leadership on the issues they say matter most. Only about one-third of registered voters overall have a "very" or "somewhat" favorable view of the Republican president, and a similar share approve of his performance as president. Voters continue to be frustrated by the high cost of living, an issue that Trump vowed to address before winning a second term in the White House. Nearly two years after his successful election, about 8 in 10 registered voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living, in line with a September AP-NORC poll. About three-quarters disapprove of his performance on the economy. READ MORE: Most Americans blame Trump for high prices as his economic approval hits new low, AP-NORC poll shows Even among Republican voters, only 44% approve of Trump's performance on the cost of living, while 54% approve of his leadership on the economy. That's a sharp contrast with other issues, like crime, on which Republican approval is much higher. There are cracks in Trump's Republican base on other issues, too. Just 69% of Republican voters support Trump on foreign policy as the war in Iran stretches into its eighth month, despite his promises that it would only last four or five weeks. DonnaJean Weber, a 72-year-old Republican from Manistee, Michigan, says she will continue to support Republican candidates this fall, but she's not happy with the state of the economy under Trump's leadership. As each school shutters, students, faculty, and the surrounding community struggle to find a way forward. Paul Solman reports on one such school and the effects of its demise. It's part of our higher education series, Rethinking College, and produced in collaboration with the Hechinger Report. Amna Nawaz: Across the nation, scores of small private colleges and universities are either closing or under threat. With each shuttering, students, faculty, and the surrounding community struggle to find a way forward. Tonight, Paul Solman reports on one such school. This story was reported in collaboration with The Hechinger Report and is part of our higher education series Rethinking College. Tommy Lee Jones, Actor: The answer you're looking for lies right here. Paul Solman: Box office sensations. Lupita Nyong'o, Actress: I would make a great queen because I am so stubborn. Paul Solman: Award-winning actors. Narrator: We have shared the incommunicable experience of war. Paul Solman: PBS' most celebrated documentarian. The common thread, all grads of a little liberal arts school in Massachusetts, Hampshire College, founded in 1965 as an experiment, no grades, no required classes, students designing their own curriculum. Ken Burns, Documentary Filmmaker: I don't recognize the person who entered Hampshire College in the fall of 1971 and the person who graduated in the spring of 1975. Paul Solman: Filmmaker Ken Burns. Ken Burns: It just rearranged all my molecules. I don't think I would be talking to you as a documentary filmmaker and so many other things if Hampshire hadn't provided the kind of preparation that it had. Jim Wald, Former Hampshire College Professor: We would teach people to be thinkers about profound issues of knowledge and society, and that way they would be adaptive learners who could carry on this process of individual thinking as they pursued careers and so forth. Paul Solman: History professor Jim Wald taught at Hampshire for nearly 40 years. Jim Wald: When it opened, it was the hot place, I'm told, more selective than Harvard or equally selective as Harvard. Hampshire was always way up there in really making students do a lot of work, because the idea was to show people how to be scholars. This is what it means to be a historian or a biologist. Paul Solman: Or become a filmmaker like Barry Sonnenfeld or writer like Jon Krakauer. Jim Wald: Our students were challenged much more than others in a lot of other schools. The college has a Latin motto, non satis scire, to know is not enough, embodying this idea of wisdom and critical thinking. Paul Solman: An ethos that persisted for actors like Lupita Nyong'o of the "Black Panther" and "The Odyssey" and Liev Schreiber. Liev Schreiber, Actor: Hampshire was interested in radical questions. The faculty and the other kids were interested in things that were different. Challenging the world in which you live in, in a positive and constructive way was certainly the ethos. Paul Solman: And students like Chloe De Lisle today, finishing her thesis in ethnomusicology. Chloe De Lisle, Hampshire College Student: I'm looking at the process of when sound in film becomes part of the music and how that represents a protagonist's trauma. Paul Solman: What would be an example? Chloe De Lisle: "Apocalypse Now" and how the signature helicopter sound that really permeates the film is part of the protagonist's experience and trauma, and then a collective cultural trauma. Paul Solman: Ken Burns' final thesis 51 years ago? Ken Burns: My half-an-hour film called "Working in Rural New England" for Old Sturbridge Village, which is a living history museum. Paul Solman: So you mean you literally began your career doing what you have been doing ever since at Hampshire? Ken Burns: It's even worse than that, Paul, which is the last shot of the film for Old Sturbridge Village was a pan across a painting from an agrarian to a kind of industrial or preindustrial sequence. Paul Solman: Just like so many pans in his PBS films, and thus Hampshire's hallmark from then to now, focused exploration. Chloe De Lisle: Here has allowed me to really do whatever I want and really create my own major, and that's meant everything. And I have just gotten to pull all my interests together and create something really cool. Paul Solman: A result of deep connection with the school. Mars Richman, Former Hampshire College Student: With the class structure, without those prerequisites, able to do what you want, chart your own course, I feel that I was able to be focused faster than most people would at a traditional college. Paul Solman: First year student Jupiter Brady-McCullough feels the same. Jupiter Brady-McCullough, Former Hampshire College Student: I made some great friends. I had some really amazing classes with some really amazing professors, and I learned a lot about myself. So I think I'm not alone in feeling kind of hopeless, in that we see a lot of these small schools closing right now. Paul Solman: And this barren scene on Hampshire's campus could become a reality for scores of schools across the country. One analysis finds that, in the next decade, of the nation's 1700 nonprofit private colleges and universities, more than 400 are on the brink, meaning the nearly 700,000 students projected to go to them are at risk. In fact, when Hampshire announced last April that it would be closing at the end of this year... Mars Richman: I cried all day. Everyone cried all day. We were... Paul Solman: Really? Everybody? Mars Richman: Everybody cried all day long. Paul Solman: But you knew that school had been in trouble? Mars Richman: We all -- I mean, we all knew, but it kept not dying. Logically, we all knew someday it would, but it kept kind of escaping death. Madeline Keating, Hampshire College Student: Hampshire means everything to me. Paul Solman: Madeline Keating is finishing up

9aae638bb1c4.text: Why do great ideas and works of art sometimes get forgotten? And why do some get revived? These are among the questions explored by musician, writer and visual artist David Byrne in his new book, "Sleeping Beauties." Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown recently joined him in Brooklyn for our arts and culture series, CANVAS. Amna Nawaz: Why are some great ideas and works of art forgotten, and why are others revived? These are among the questions explored by musician, writer, and visual artist David Byrne. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown joined him recently in Brooklyn for our arts and culture series, Canvas. (MUSIC) Jeffrey Brown: Questions and more questions. David Byrne is a man with a curious and quirky mind, including when it comes to writing songs. David Byrne, Musician and Author, "Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up": Sometimes, I will start with the title of a song. I did a song called "I Met the Buddha at a Downtown." And I go, all right, what happens? What's he like? What's he doing? Jeffrey Brown: What's this Buddha guy doing at the party? David Byrne: What does he say to you? What do you say to him? What does he say to you? Jeffrey Brown: He's a man of many turns, front man for the rock band Talking Heads, musical experimenter and collaborator with artists around the globe, Oscar winner for co-writing the score for "The Last Emperor," Broadway star in "American Utopia," and a lot more, including cycling man about town, a regular sight on New York streets, and the subject of his 2009 book, "Bicycle Diaries." Now he's asking new questions stemming from the fairy tale of Sleeping Beauty, the princess cursed to sleep 100 years, who can be awakened only by the kiss of a prince. Byrne came across an article in a science journal that applied the term to studies that for various reasons have been ignored or forgotten, only to be later recognized and given renewed prominence. David Byrne: I immediately thought, I know this phenomena. I know it from musicians that I might like, but I feel like didn't get their deserved appreciation. I know of we're always reading about this or that or the other, and they're suddenly rediscovered, and it's like now we understand it. Now what they did makes perfect sense. Jeffrey Brown: Something's lost and then found. David Byrne: Found again, yes. And it's -- I just love these stories, the stories of kind of a resurrection or that kind of thing, of somebody -- somebody or some work kind of coming back to life and being re-appreciated. Jeffrey Brown: The result is the book "Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up." David Byrne: This kind of clocklike device will kind of keep the telescope always pointed at the object you're observing. Jeffrey Brown: It's a mix of art, science, and technology that reflects his own interests. He asked to meet us at Pioneer Works, an artist- and scientist-led cultural center in Brooklyn that he loves for its focus on creativity in its many forms. His book offers many examples of world-famous artists lost to history for a time, sometimes centuries, thankfully rescued. Perhaps you know this image by Italian early renaissance painter Sandro Botticelli. David Byrne: Botticelli is really well-known. Jeffrey Brown: Very well-known today. David Byrne: Very well-known. He's on tea towels. You can get a watch with Venus on it. You can get you name it, and those images that are on there, Birth of Venus and all that stuff. Jeffrey Brown: Yes. David Byrne: So when you tell people, no, this guy went way out of favor for hundreds of years... Jeffrey Brown: Byrne tells the story of Botticelli's artistic death at the hands of the crusading religious zealot Savonarola and his much later rebirth in the late 19th century. David Byrne: Gradually, he gets re-appreciated, until, by the beginning of the 20th century, there were more books written about Botticelli than any other artist. Jeffrey Brown: There are as many or more examples in the fields of science and technology, such as Gregor Mendel, today known as the father of genetics, whose initial paper in 1866 went largely unrecognized. David Byrne: For various reasons, it didn't click until, later on, two scientists were doing a very similar kind of research, and they thought, before we publish this, let's take a look and see if maybe someone else has done something similar before we take all the credit. Yes, they found Mendel's paper. And they go, oh, my God, he kind of did it all. Jeffrey Brown: And then there's something you might not expect in a book like this, concrete. David Byrne: This is one of my favorite ones. When people ask me, what's your book about, and I go, concrete. Jeffrey Brown: Concrete. David Byrne: Yes, concrete. And they go, what? What? Concrete's everywhere, yes, highways, buildings, everything. Jeffrey Brown: Yes. David Byrne: And I go, yes. The Roman concrete, the Pantheon, for example, the dome of that is unreinforced, and it's lasted 2,000 years and doesn't have a crack in it. The companies that make concrete now rate their concrete as guaranteed to last 50 years. Jeffrey Brown: Fifty years. David Byrne: Five-zero. Jeffrey Brown: Yes. David Byrne: That's a little bit of a difference. So you go, what happened? Who lost the recipe? Jeffrey Brown: Not so much lost, Byrne shows, as not understanding or ignoring Roman materials and building practices, a bias thinking we know better than people of the past. The key for Byrne, the rediscovery to benefit us today. David Byrne: Let's focus on how these things got rediscovered, because that's really what we want to know. We want to know if there's other ones out there and how can we find them? The question is, what are we suppressing, or what have we forgotten that's out there? Because we do the same things. Jeffrey Brown: Byrne himself is still very much producing his own art. He just finished a long tour for his most recent album titled "Who Is the Sky?" A
