81005b278cd6.text: Geothermal — power drawn from the Earth's natural heat — is pulling off something remarkable in today's hyper-polarized America: Winning fans across the political spectrum. Why it matters: The bipartisan appeal, combined with surging electricity demand from AI , is helping fuel investment in a niche energy source yet to prove it can compete at scale. Driving the news: Geothermal received unusually extensive attention in a bipartisan Senate bill introduced late last month to expedite infrastructure permitting . The House this summer passed a package containing several of the same geothermal provisions, including measures sponsored by lawmakers as ideologically distant as Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Mike Kennedy (R-Utah) . The rising cachet of geothermal is the product of three trends converging: Technologies adapted from the oil and gas industry, including fracking, are making it possible to tap heat in more places than just far-flung hot springs and volcanoes. Tech companies, on the hunt for reliable electricity, are willing to pay a premium for next-generation geothermal to power data centers. Investment is surging as companies race to scale a renewable energy source that can generate power around the clock. Catch up quick: The geothermal-specific provisions in the Senate bill go further than the broader permitting reforms offered to other renewable energy sources, including wind and solar. The bill would make it easier for geothermal developers to explore and lease federal land, speed up drilling permits and exempt certain activities from environmental reviews. Geothermal retained federal clean-energy tax credits in Republicans' sweeping tax law last year, even as wind and solar faced an accelerated phaseout. State of play: Fervo Energy, an advanced geothermal company that went public earlier this year, is at the leading edge of this convergence. It was founded nearly a decade ago by Tim Latimer, a former drilling engineer in the oil and gas industry. "I don't think any of us saw in 2017 that a few years later we would be in the biggest demand power boom for electricity that we had ever experienced," said Latimer during a recent on-stage interview with Axios in an event aptly titled "The energy source nobody argues about." The AI boom has "accelerated our business tremendously." Chart: Amy Harder/Axios; Note: Other includes project finance and debt. Fervo's IPO proceeds reflect capital raised at the time of its listing, not its current market value; Data: Currence The intrigue: Geothermal's appeal crosses traditional political divisions precisely because it doesn't fit neatly into Washington's usual energy-policy boxes. Its renewable characteristics appeal to Democrats. Its reliance on drilling expertise and overlap with the oil and gas industry appeals to Republicans. Its ability to provide stable, carbon-free electricity makes it attractive to utilities and tech companies. By the numbers: The average winning bid for federal geothermal leases has surged, reflecting growing commercial interest. The average winning bid in 2023 was $10 an acre, and so far this year, the average is $182, according to Guy Cohen, a geothermal analyst at the market intelligence firm Currence. A record $1,207-an-acre bid was placed for a single parcel in Utah this summer . Reality check: Geothermal's political popularity and investment boom are running ahead of its commercial reality. The technology remains expensive, and questions persist about whether it can reliably generate electricity over decades. Geothermal currently generates less than 1% of U.S. electricity, and those eye-popping leases are for the right to explore for geothermal, not for active geothermal wells. Fervo's stock has fallen nearly 70% from its first-day closing price following its IPO earlier this year, amid what Axios Pro calls a broader slowdown among energy startups. Tom Erb, Fervo's government affairs and policy manager, says the construction costs at its flagship project in Utah are about half those of new nuclear plants. He acknowledged that underground heat can diminish over time, requiring additional drilling, but said those costs are factored into company projections. What they're saying: Jigar Shah, a former Energy Department official under President Biden, says geothermal's current momentum still depends on state policies encouraging clean electricity and tech companies willing to pay a premium. "I don't think this moment would work without above market mandates from states or the data centers," Shah said. Friction point: Geothermal has also encountered local opposition, particularly over water. Traditional geothermal projects can disrupt hot springs and wetlands critical to wildlife, said Patrick Donnelly of the Center for Biological Diversity. Newer technologies like Fervo's avoid some of those risks, he said, but questions remain about their water consumption. What we're watching: Geothermal has found something rare in Washington: Political consensus. The test now is whether that consensus survives the industry's growth.

d9912477397a.text: Wall Street appears to be hitting its limit on AI, and financiers are starting to say the quiet part out loud: All of this AI spending doesn't look like it can pay off, at least not for everyone. Why it matters: The gap between what it costs to build AI infrastructure and what companies are actually paying to use it is widening. Wall Street's anxiety is surging as the debt piling up to fund data centers and chips looks increasingly disconnected from economic reality. Driving the news: A massive gap is opening up between AI infrastructure spending and expected returns. While AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, research from Gartner forecasts they will generate no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over that same period. More than $4 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of write-downs by the end of 2032 if companies maintain their current investment pace. Gartner also predicts that more than 80% of specialized AI cloud providers, known as neoclouds, will cease operating independently by 2030. Case in point: CoreWeave, one of the largest neoclouds with among the closest ties to Nvidia — the AI boom's financial and spiritual foundation — has faced a multi-day selloff of its stock and debt. Yields pushed above 15% and its stock tumbled 15.5% before rebounding after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spoke up on the company's behalf. Follow the money: Sources on Wall Street used to tell Axios that as long as the AI buildout was paid for in cash, there was nothing to worry about. But today, a third of the capex being spent on AI is coming from debt, and capital markets are showing signs of severe fatigue. It's getting harder to secure financing. Global AI-related debt issuance plunged to $23 billion in September 2026, down sharply from $113 billion in June, per the Financial Times . Banks are actively pulling back to avoid concentration risk, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon confirming his bank is tightening up on credit. Infrastructure projects and providers are struggling: approximately $18 billion in bank loans for an Oracle data center campus recently slid into stressed territory, while Nvidia-backed AI cloud provider Firmus shelved an IPO that sought a valuation north of $30 billion. Zoom in: The constant spending relies on the belief that compute demand will never falter — a belief that has structural cracks. Reflection AI co-founder Ioannis Antonoglou told Semafor that businesses may need "a decade or two decades" to fundamentally redesign their operations around AI. That's 10 to 20 years of companies slowly adopting the technology that's being built (expensively) today. Between the lines: This creates a mismatch: Data centers and chips require enormous investment today, but the returns that could justify that spend will take years to materialize. Put bluntly, there is a massive gap between AI spending and AI revenue, one that won't close for many, many years. At the same time, companies that are adopting AI quickly are getting smarter about using tools more efficiently, turning to open-weight models that are less compute-intensive to cut costs. Reality check: Look at Anthropic's latest financials for a counterpoint to the bears. The company is raking in cash, turning free cash flow positive in the third quarter and growing revenue nearly 50% compared to the April-to-June period. But even Anthropic's staggering growth has slowed, albeit expectedly because trees can't grow to the sky. The bottom line: The debt-fueled AI buildout is not an isolated problem for tech investors alone to worry about. The stock market and economy have become increasingly tied up with the AI boom. If the AI bet doesn't work, markets and the economy could falter as well.

37a079dab129.text: MAGA activists are pushing for President Trump to resort to extraordinary measures — including martial law — if they believe the midterm elections are "rigged." Why it matters: Some of the proposals go far beyond Trump's legal authority — and there's no evidence that the elections will be rigged. But people in this orbit have close access to the president. Prominent MAGA election activist Tina Peters met with Trump this month. Convicted in 2024 of crimes tied to a breach of election equipment, Peters was released this year after Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) commuted her sentence. Peters and her attorney, Peter Ticktin, also visited Trump at the White House in late June . Peters did not respond to attempts to contact her for comment. Zoom in: On a September 30 video call for MAGA election activists streamed on Rumble, speakers warned of widespread election security breaches they believe will occur in November — and urgently pushed for remedies. Ticktin, Trump's childhood friend, said on the call "there would have to be martial law in the event... [of] another rigged election." "They'll probably need to be commandeering of ballots and election equipment to make sure that we can get to the bottom of it before anything further occurs," he later told Axios. Gregory Stenstrom, who testified about alleged voting irregularities in Pennsylvania in 2020, said he most wanted the election paused over security concerns. Alternatively, he proposed Trump invoke the National Emergencies Act to force states to change how they run elections. Stenstrom could not be reached for comment. Peters was also on the call. She's been promoting her own plan online since August, which calls for switching to hand-marked paper ballots and a manual recount of all votes where feasible. "Her plan is secure the paper ballots and recount by hand," Ticktin said. In an interview with Colorado Public Radio, he further explained this "would eliminate whatever effect the machines have." State of play: The streamed call is a regular feature in this activist community, drawing voices from across the country. Steve Stern, the host, directs his viewers to sign up through the Republican Party to become poll workers and observers for November. Stern declined an interview request. Reality check: "Emergency powers are not just a blank check for the president to go do whatever they want. The president still has to act within the Constitution and within statutes set by Congress," said Derek Tisler, counsel for the Brennan Center's elections and government program. He said those legal limits include : Election timing: Congress sets the date of federal elections. Trump cannot unilaterally delay the midterms. Counting and voting systems: States choose their voting systems and determine how votes are counted, subject to federal law. Trump cannot mandate a nationwide hand recount or order machines replaced. Emergency and martial law authority: Emergency powers do not allow Trump to override state election laws or constitutional restrictions. Martial law would not give Trump authority to seize control of election materials or override federal and state election laws. The big picture: Skepticism about the 2020 election extends into Trump's administration, including officials now involved in election integrity. Heather Honey, most known for denying the results of the 2020 election in Pennsylvania and Arizona, is now the Homeland Security Department's deputy assistant secretary for election integrity and senior advisor to the ICE Director. White House adviser Peter Navarro continues to promote his own report of mass election fraud and irregularities around the 2020 election. Between the lines: "This election did not sneak up on the administration. They've been in office for 21 months. We're 20 days away from this election, and they haven't done any of this stuff," said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Axios in a statement: "Americans deserves elections that are safe, secure, and transparent to ensure full confidence in the results. President Trump believes every legal vote must count, every election must be protected, and Americans must have complete confidence in the integrity of our elections."

After Booting 760K People From ACA Plans, Trump Administration Has Added Some Back
Late last month, the Trump administration announced that it had cut 760,000 people from the Affordable Care Act rolls, claiming fraud and improper enrollments and touting billions in potential taxpayer savings.
Not all of those kicked off were fraudulently enrolled, KFF Health News has learned. Insurance industry sources said the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has reinstated a small number of people whose coverage should not have been canceled. More could follow in the coming weeks if enrollees discover they are uninsured when they go to use their coverage.
Still, the sweep was long overdue, say supporters such as Brian Blase, whose Paragon Health Institute has supplied many of the sometimes controversial findings cited by those who allege widespread enrollment fraud in the ACA. But other policy experts question how many legitimate consumers were caught in the dragnet, perhaps because they failed to open a letter from their insurer or answer a phone call.
Questions continue to swirl, even as a second phase of the anti-fraud effort is underway. An additional 419,000 sign-ups are being scrutinized. Insurers must let CMS know how many of those enrollees don’t respond to outreach efforts by “around mid-to-late November, after the midterm elections,” said David Merritt, senior vice president of external affairs at the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association.
He confirmed that some BCBS members are among those who have been reinstated. He also said that CMS has an expedited review process for those who discover they have been improperly disenrolled.
Overall, however, the administration is providing few details about the cancellations, such as how robust the outreach was to those it targeted, how long it takes for people to get reinstated after discovering their coverage was wrongly canceled, and how many such cancellations have been reversed.
“It may be true that some of those enrollments were not authorized, but it can be equally true that people got lost in the shuffle and have a valid enrollment. Without more information, it’s almost impossible to tell,” said Katie Keith, a director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at Georgetown Law. “That they are not being very transparent is telling too,” she said of the administration.
The enrollment cut comes as part of a larger Republican strategy to focus on fraud in government programs, including Medicaid and hospice care, which polls show resonates with GOP voters.
At an Oct. 14 press conference, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz touted the removal this year of subsidies for about 189,000 ACA enrollees with duplicate Medicare, Medicaid, or Children’s Health Insurance Program coverage, citing not fraud but a failure to look for concurrent enrollments or continued coverage for dead people. They credited an effort begun last year by the Trump administration to restore more frequent data matching checks than were done under the prior administration.
Unauthorized sign-ups by rogue insurance agents seeking commissions and other potential impropriety in the ACA marketplace — applicants’ providing incorrect income estimates, for example — has been a concern for several years, with much debate over the magnitude of the problem.
Even so, how the recent move to cancel the 760,000 enrollments will play out politically is uncertain. Healthcare costs are tied with gas prices as a top concern for voters. It is likely that many removed from the ACA are in red states, such as Texas, Florida, Louisiana, and Mississippi. Those areas saw rapid growth in ACA enrollment from 2020 to 2025, driven in part by now-expired enhanced subsidies put in place during Joe Biden’s presidency. Additionally, the cancellations target only enrollees in states that use healthcare.gov, the federal ACA marketplace. The 21 states fully running their own marketplaces generally have more robust fraud prevention programs, such as multifactor authentication, and have reported few or none of the kinds of unauthorized sign-ups plaguing the federal marketplace.
“To the extent there is a reaction depends on whether the government got it wrong, whether people try to get care and then find out their coverage is no longer active,” said Adrianna McIntyre, assistant professor of health policy and politics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.
How It Played Out
According to information the agency provided to KFF Health News, CMS in June selected for further review nearly 1.2 million enrollments that had all of what it deemed four warning signs for fraud:
- The application included no Social Security number or immigration document number.
- A broker was involved in the sign-up process.
- The plan had no monthly premium payment.
- The enrollee had had no contact with their insurer and no claims filed.
Then, as first reported by KFF Health News, CMS sent lists of those ACA accounts to specific insurers, instructing the carriers to review them and use at least two methods of contact — such as a phone call and a letter — to try to reach the enrollees. Policyholders were given 30 days to respond to the insurers’ outreach and provide the missing information. CMS disenrolled those who didn’t respond.
Johnny Wallin, chief operating officer of Texas-based Marketplace Insurance Exchange, which helps clients in about 35 states enroll in coverage, said insurers reached out to his organization for help contacting people on the CMS lists, prompting “an all-hands-on-deck” effort by agents to reach clients, some of whom were vacationing overseas.
“Getting them to answer the phone isn’t easy,” he noted, although he suspects his agents had a better chance of getting a reply than an insurer because their clients are familiar with their phone numbers. Still, they could not reach about 60 of them.

The nation’s uninsured rate hit a historic low when Xavier Becerra was health secretary. Now he wants to be California’s next governor as states stare down the biggest rise in the uninsured rate in a generation.
Next Governor To Face Thorny Choices After California’s Rapid Medicaid Expansion
In March 2025, when California ran out of Medicaid funds to pay doctors and hospitals, the state borrowed $3.4 billion to keep the program afloat. It was, as a spokesperson for Gov. Gavin Newsom insisted, nothing new. Indeed, a handful of times over the years, the state had taken out internal, short-term loans to sustain its healthcare program for the poor and disabled.
The unprecedented move came a few months later, when Newsom and Democratic state lawmakers agreed to pay down the loan — which grew to $4.4 billion — over 10 years instead of later in the year. California’s healthcare safety net, it seemed, was buckling.
Rising healthcare costs systemwide were partly to blame. But so were several state-led expansions that made California’s Medicaid program, known as Medi-Cal, one of the nation’s most generous.
Now, with congressional Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act expected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over 10 years, California and dozens of other states must contemplate the limits of their generosity. The problem is particularly acute in the nation’s most populous state, which spends more on Medicaid than New York and Texas combined.
“We know we can’t afford to serve everybody we want to serve in the model that we have today,” said Mark Ghaly, the former top Newsom health official who now co-chairs the Future of Medi-Cal Commission, a 29-person panel with the goal of modernizing and sustaining California’s Medicaid program for those who need it. “What can we do differently? What can we do smarter?”
The 2025 law that Newsom, a Democrat, has dubbed President Donald Trump’s “Big Ugly Bill” is expected to leave millions more Americans without health insurance, mostly because of new work requirements. It also curbs the use of healthcare provider taxes and other strategies states have deployed to maximize federal funds. Some state lawmakers and consumer advocates have argued the federal cuts, along with rising costs, present an opportunity for the next governor to overhaul a program plagued by long appointment wait times, low reimbursement rates for healthcare providers, and volatile financing.
“If we continue to just give millions and millions into the same system and expect something different — I’m sick and tired of that,” said Caroline Menjivar, a Democratic state senator representing a Los Angeles-area district where roughly half of constituents rely on Medi-Cal.
Democratic lawmakers, who have often clashed with Newsom on Medi-Cal rollbacks, succeeded in getting him to delay a number of painful cuts until 2027 in hopes that a new governor might reverse them.
So far, neither of the candidates running in the November election to replace Newsom have offered substantive proposals for weathering the upheaval health policy experts say is on the horizon for a program that covers 1 in 3 Californians — roughly 13.6 million people.
Republican Steve Hilton, a former Fox News commentator, wants to pare back Medi-Cal eligibility and has promised to end coverage for immigrants without legal status, citing that benefit as an example of “wildly unsustainable” state spending. Democrat Xavier Becerra, who has spent decades trying to expand government-funded healthcare, has promised to protect Californians from the massive federal cuts.
Expanding Coverage
President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the law that established Medicaid and Medicare in 1965 to cover certain low-income groups, such as families with children, older people, and those with disabilities. Over the past six decades, states have substantially widened that pool, most notably under the Affordable Care Act’s Medicaid expansion to childless adults.
Starting in 2024, California offered healthcare coverage to all low-income residents, regardless of age or immigration status, although lawmakers scaled that back this year. At the same time, the state opted to cover a slew of non-mandated benefits such as physical therapy, hospice care, and housing assistance.
“California has always struggled with wanting to have as broad a program as possible but then having to figure out a way to pay,” said Jennifer Kent, who oversaw Medi-Cal under Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat. “There is no population that we have met that we don’t want to offer coverage to, and we’ve never met a benefit that we don’t like.”
Since 2010, California’s Medi-Cal enrollment has nearly doubled while spending has ballooned from $50 billion a year to $222 billion. It now makes up more than 40% of overall state spending, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Conservatives argue the program is bloated and rife with fraud. They say the federal changes will force states to refocus resources on the neediest.
“The role of the safety net programs was just that — to be a safety net,” Hilton said in an interview. “I don’t think it’s a particularly positive boast to say 40% of Californians should be on a program that was designed for people living in poverty.”
Becerra declined an interview request.
Nelly, a 59-year-old from Los Angeles County, was one of millions who have benefited from the state’s Medi-Cal expansion, but she was initially reluctant to sign up.
For years after she left her corporate job to care for her ailing mother, Nelly said, she didn’t consider applying. She remained uninsured until three years ago, when she woke up and couldn’t see out of her left eye.
She enrolled in Medi-Cal in the emergency room. It now covers her appointments with specialists and transportation to and from. While her condition may exempt her from the new Medicaid work requirements, Nelly said, she’s still worried about losing coverage after experiencing numerous

On a misty and breezy morning last fall, Marc Hamric, a North Carolina Division of Marine Fisheries veteran, and two other technicians were conducting field work in Turnagain Bay, a remote area near Cedar Island.
They had brought their boat ashore, but because the water was so rough, it came loose and floated away.
One DMF technician swam after it and had trouble hoisting himself aboard. Hamric swam to rescue him. Meanwhile, the technician managed to get on the boat and steer back to shore, but didn’t know Hamric had followed him into the bay.
As the two technicians searched the water for Hamric, one was on speaker phone with the team’s supervisors, sobbing as he explained what happened. The technicians eventually found Hamric in the water. They tried to resuscitate him. Shortly after an ambulance arrived, medics pronounced him dead.
Chloe Dorin, then a biologist with DMF and one of the supervisors, was on the call. “I heard the whole thing,” Dorin said in an interview. “It has been a little over a year now, and I still think about him every day.”
The Carteret County sheriff ruled Hamric’s death an accident. Yet current and former employees say DMF routinely requires technicians to work while sleep-deprived and in dangerous conditions: in rain, wind and fog as dense as fresh concrete.
Interviews and government documents depict DMF as a floundering bureaucracy that jeopardizes the safety of its technicians who work on the water. The division has also failed its state-mandated duty to protect aquatic life and coastal habitats, in part because of incomplete and incorrect scientific data, according to court records, state reports and employees.
Some current and former employees who shared their experiences asked not to be named for fear of retaliation. Inside Climate News also relied on internal emails, legislative and federal documents, a confidential whistleblower report filed with the state auditor’s office and a recent superior court ruling against the division.
DMF, which is housed under the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality, is responsible for the stewardship of the state’s fish, clams, oysters and crabs in all coastal waters up to three miles offshore.
It must comply with federal requirements, legislative mandates and rules passed by the state Marine Fisheries Commission, itself mired in internecine politics between commercial fishermen whose livelihoods depend on their catches and recreational anglers who fish out of tradition or need.
DMF did not answer questions from Inside Climate News about the allegations but provided a statement:
“The Division of Marine Fisheries is aware of claims made by former employees who recently left the agency. An initial review by the Division has found these claims to be unsubstantiated, misinformed or lacking proper context. The Division takes its role to provide science-based guidance to the Marine Fisheries Commission very seriously.
“There are policies in place to maintain a safe working environment for employees and ensure that fisheries data is reliable. DMF is always looking for ways to improve and is evaluating the feedback from these former employees to determine if there are additional steps we can take to improve safety and transparency.”
After two years, Dorin said the workplace culture at DMF eventually became too much to bear. Not only was she concerned about worker safety, but she came to doubt some of the science that underpinned DMF decisions. She said she had uncovered several years’ worth of incorrect data regarding hard clams and poor scientific sampling protocols for bay scallops. She saw technicians break down under pressure.
“There are extraordinarily capable, hardworking people at DMF. In many ways, they are exactly why I feel compelled to write this,” she said in her Sept. 10 resignation letter to DEQ leadership, several state lawmakers and Gov. Josh Stein.
“I have watched good people be ground down by a dysfunctional system,” Dorin wrote. “I believe serious consideration should be given to dissolving the division in its current form and rebuilding it from the ground up.”
Stein’s office did not respond to a request for comment on Dorin’s letter.
In 1997, the state legislature passed the Fisheries Reform Act to address overfishing and plummeting fish stocks. Yet over the past 29 years, DMF has failed to manage fisheries and protect aquatic life and coastal habitats, according to court documents.
Of the 13 species under DMF’s care, seven have collapsed, two are depressed and the status of three others are unknown, court documents show. Only one, red drum, is recovering. None shows signs of long-term viability.
DMF’s challenges—not only politics but also coastal development, degraded water quality and climate change—are legitimate, former and current employees say, but they don’t explain all of its missteps.
“We’re so impressed with short-term economic gain that we don’t take the long-term viability of the resource”—the fish and their habitats—“into consideration,” said Louis Daniel, a marine scientist and a DMF employee for 21 years, including nine as its director. He left the division in 2016, after he was demoted by then-DEQ Secretary Donald van der Vaart, an appointee of Republican Gov. Pat McCrory.
“What’s in the best interest of the resource is in the best interest of everybody, and that’s where we have failed miserably as a state,” Daniel said.
Hamric had been with DMF for 28 years. He was beloved by his colleagues, employees said, and he won a DEQ Distinguished Employee Award in 2024. In her resignation letter, Dorin addressed his death. “There have understandably been many discussions about safety since then,” she wrote. “But there is a question I believe has received far too little attention: Why were staff operating on the water under poor conditions in the ﬁrst place?”

The News
Prediction market Kalshi is in no rush for the Supreme Court to wade into its battle with states.
The company agrees with skeptics like the NFL that justices must eventually opine on whether states and tribes should regulate its sports event contracts as sports bets, a Supreme Court litigator working with Kalshi told Semafor. But it also believes that pending rehearing petitions and forthcoming Commodity Futures Trading Commission rules are currently muddying the waters, the litigator said.
Kalshi, represented by the attorney who convinced justices to strike down Trumpâs tariffs, recently requested a month-long extension from the court. That extension, coupled with Kalshiâs rehearing petitions, has led the gaming industry to believe the company lacks confidence in its case.
âItâs fitting that as Halloween approaches, Kalshi seems spooked by the idea of the Supreme Court taking up the case next year,â American Gaming Association spokesperson Rob Lockwood told Semafor. âBecause they donât want to risk losing sports gambling â which is roughly 85% of their total volume!â
The litigator disputed that characterization, calling the extension request a common move that was necessary for Kalshi to respond to the amicus briefs due the same day. Nevada, they noted, recently requested a similar extension in a related case.
Know More
The Supreme Court has until January to decide which cases it wants to hear in its current term, which began earlier this month. A clash between federal appeals courts has made the prediction markets litigation a likely pick: The Third Circuit has sided with Kalshi, while the Sixth and Ninth Circuits have sided with the states.
Kalshi has filed rehearing petitions asking the Sixth and Ninth Circuits to review their latest rulings, citing the forthcoming CFTC rules. Nevada has already pushed back on the Ninth Circuit request, arguing that the pending regulation âwould not change the outcome here.â
CFTC Chair Mike Selig, whoâs defended prediction markets in courts across the country, told Semafor earlier this year that he would âwelcomeâ a Supreme Court ruling. That âwould really settle the matter,â he said.

The group is chaired by Amy Kremer, a longtime Tea Party activist who argues Republicans are missing an opportunity to lead on AI policy that doesnât cater to big companies. Sheâs been leading a bus tour across the country dubbed the âAI Data Center Revolt.â
The frameworkâs priorities go beyond what some Republicans who are interested in regulating AI on Capitol Hill have proposed, and significantly further than the Trump administrationâs current light touch on AI.
Still, this vocal group may have more sway going forward if Republicans perform poorly in the midterms and AI anxiety is a factor.

This story is part of an investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project. Read the other stories here.
In August 2022, dozens of protesters spilled into the streets of Kayar, a fishing town on Senegal’s Atlantic coast, demanding the closure of a nearby fishmeal plant, Touba Protein Marine.
Marching from the fishing wharf to the factory, they carried signs reading “Kayar is sick” and chanted, “Time to respect our Kayar.” The factory, they said, had been built less than a third of a mile from residential homes, triggering local health problems.
That same year in Vietnam, hundreds of residents on the country’s northeastern coast surrounded another plant and, for days, blasted loudspeakers at it in protest.
In India, in 2024, the odor from fishmeal factories spurred protests that lasted more than 100 days, ending in a boycott of local elections and in villagers convening parallel meetings to pass resolutions against the plants.
These uprisings were not set off by the kind of industrial disaster that usually commands global attention. What brought people onto the streets was the foul smell of fishmeal: the protein-rich powder manufactured in poorer coastal communities by unloading, cooking, pressing, drying and grinding up fish.
Today, two-thirds of global aquaculture—a $313 billion industry and the fastest-growing food sector in the world—grows species that are fed fishmeal and fish oil.
“We don’t invite family or friends here because we are embarrassed that we live in a place that smells like it’s rotting,” a man in Songkla, Thailand explained. Those living near plants describe nausea, headaches, eye irritation, dizziness, coughing fits and loss of appetite. They recount laundry brought in early, doors kept shut in coastal heat, sleep interrupted at night and a low-grade sense of agitation that comes from never being able to trust the next gust of wind.
A global investigation of this product’s hidden costs by The Outlaw Ocean Project revealed that the industry’s rancid odor was among the least tracked, most personally intimate and widely suffered impacts of aquaculture.
The investigation documented complaints about stench made relating to at least 60 plants in 15 countries. And we found that globally, more than 9.5 million people live within a mile of fishmeal plants—including nearly 1.7 million under the age of 15.
Farmed seafood sold at Walmart, Kroger and Costco was fed fishmeal tied to stench complaints at plants in India, Vietnam and Peru, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool created by the Outlaw Ocean to track the aquaculture industry.
For some communities, the stink corroded the local economy by undercutting tourism and scaring away restaurant patrons and beach visitors. In Mar del Plata, Argentina, the smell from fishmeal plants was so bad that tourists visiting a local hotel sometimes had to step into the courtyard to vomit, while in Huaquillas, Ecuador, residents told a daily newspaper that the smell was “unbearable” and “impossible to be around.”
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
The foul smell was more than just a nuisance, it was also an indicator of the release of noxious chemicals like ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, cyanide and methane, which have been known to cause serious health problems, including pulmonary edema. The worst part of the odor comes from trimethylamine, or TMA, a colorless “fishy” gas identified as “strongly toxic and carcinogenic,” by the Society of Chemical Industry.
Yet emitting bad smells is typically seen as more of an inconvenience than an actual environmental or health hazard, even if it results in sickness.
“The technology for detecting and characterizing complex odors has not developed to the level of a reliable surveillance method, which has hindered regulatory frameworks,” stated a group of environmental engineers at Florida Atlantic University.
While many studies focus on the health and environmental impact of specific chemicals emitted by sewage plants, livestock operations, composting facilities, landfills, paper mills or petrochemical industries, little research has concentrated on the impact of smell, according to a study in the journal Environmental Health.
Fishmeal stench is not an unsolvable problem. When factory owners have tried to reduce it, they have usually succeeded. In 2008 in the U.S., in 2021 in South Africa and in 2022 in Yemen, plant owners installed various types of devices, some of them called scrubbers, that researchers later concluded had drastically reduced the foulest-smelling chemicals. Scrubbers, however, are not more common partly because they can cost upwards of a million dollars.
Costs notwithstanding, there are deeper reasons that stench stays far away from consumers. In wealthier nations, plant neighbors more often successfully pressure their governments to require odor controls.
In North Carolina, for example, multiple juries found in favor of plaintiffs suing the largest pork producer in the world. One appeals court judge wrote that the medical risks and stench of spraying untreated hog waste high into the air “violated homeowners’ rights to the healthful enjoyment of their property.”
But in poorer nations, where the vast majority of fishmeal plants are located, people living in the industrial areas where these plants are built usually lack political clout. Their governments are also more desperate for revenue and more reluctant to put up regulatory burdens that may scare away foreign investment. As a result, there is little incentive or pressure for foreign fishmeal producers to fix a problem that does not directly impact their bottom line.

The Signal Interview
Nobuhiro âNobuâ Toriiâs appointment as CEO of Suntory last September returned the leadership of the group behind Yamazaki whisky to its founding family, 126 years after his great-grandfather, Shinjiro Torii, set up shop as a wine importer in Osaka. But the younger Toriiâs succession was an abrupt and unplanned one.
Takeshi âTakâ Niinami, Suntoryâs first non-family CEO, quit after police searched his home for suspected illegal supplements. They found none, and the high-profile executive denied having broken the law. But the board decided that Niinamiâs resignation was necessary, and elevated Torii from his role as president, which heâd assumed just a few months earlier.
It was a rare upset in a family business that prizes stability, and Toriiâs message in his first interview with a Western news outlet since becoming CEO is that he brings a steady hand and a long-term focus. But he also displays an ambition to turn an increasingly tough market for the alcoholic drinks with which Suntory is synonymous to its advantage.
Niinami was a dynamic, âhands-onâ leader, integrating deals like the 2014 acquisition of Jim Beam bourbon while family chairman Nobutada Saji âkept our corporate culture,â Torii says. Toriiâs own role combines those two imperatives, he implies: âI donât have any aggressive strategy, but I really want to keep our corporate culture,â he says. â[The] culture is very important for the further growth of the company.â
The onetime bankerâs challenge is that he took the reins as the groupâs growth had faltered, with operating income falling last year on almost flat revenues of about $22 billion. Most notably, spirits consumption in Suntoryâs largest markets has been in decline after peaking during the pandemic. Companies across the industry have been idling facilities, with Suntory pausing production at one of Jim Beamâs three Kentucky distilleries to upgrade the site while demand is low.
Toriiâs task is to find growth in new countries and categories while showing that he can find opportunities again in the core liquor business. The group has predicted a rebound in its profits this year, and its new CEO is projecting optimism.
His familyâs willingness to think across generations will be central to Suntoryâs ability to achieve its goal of becoming the world leader in whiskies and ready-to-drink spirits, he suggests. âIt takes at least five to 10 years to have a good whisky, so the strategy must be long-term-oriented.â
A private company looks for long-term opportunity
Suntoryâs history informs Toriiâs reticence about making sudden strategic turns. The spirits industry is not a fast-moving consumer goods business but a slow-moving one, he says, recalling how the company misread demand for one of its brands more than 40 years ago. âWe believed Suntory Old Whisky would continue to sell more, more, more, more, more, and that was a mistake,â he says. âOnce we change the strategy in the whisky business, it will take many, many years to recover.â
Toriiâs group has a Tokyo-listed subsidiary, Suntory Beverage & Food, but the holding company itself is private, he notes, allowing it to take a longer-term view of the market. âWe donât have any stock price. So now itâs a good chance for us to strengthen our brands,â he says. Shares in publicly listed spirits companies such as Diageo and Pernod Ricard have been falling for several years, he notes, so âthey have to control their stock price by cutting some costs.â
âWe are still investing in our brands while our competitors seem not to invest a lot,â he says, describing his rivalsâ market behavior as âdefensive.â
Toriiâs belief in private companiesâ superior ability to invest through cyclical downturns echoes that of Sazerac, the US drinks company whose unsolicited bid for Brown-Forman was rejected by the Jack Danielâs maker this year. But he suggests that Suntory is unlikely to be so ambitious about acquisitions.
More than a decade on from the balance sheet-stretching Jim Beam purchase, Suntoryâs financial capacity is ârelatively strong,â Torii says, but he notes that interest rates have increased, which would make any purchase more expensive to finance.
âOur first priority now is [to] invest in our brands,â he stresses.
Asked whether he expects further consolidation in the liquor industry, Torii replies with a joke. âWell, itâs already consolidated, and if some spirits company [should have] an interest to acquire us, I would consider [it],â he laughs. But he quickly confirms that the familyâs controlling stake would let it block any unwanted transaction.
How demographics and diversification shape Suntoryâs strategy
Investors have grown concerned that young consumers are more abstemious than their parents were at the same age. In a speech in New York earlier this month, Torii said people were becoming âmore intentional in their alcohol consumptionâ but also more focused on the quality of the drinks they chose, which he believes will favor his products. âAt Suntory, quality is not a department; quality is a philosophy,â he told his audience.
âThe biggest difference between my generation and the younger generation is probably this one,â he says, gesturing to an iPhone. His point is not just that more people are socializing virtually rather than in bars and restaurants; it is that the high cost of their electronic devices has made them more selective about other spending.
âWe have to educate younger generations to understand the attractiveness of whiskies or other spirits,â Torii says. Still, he sees little evidence that recent inflation gains are making them sharply more cost-conscious about their drinking.
Instead, he thinks that consumers may be acclimatizing to higher prices. Twice in the past six years, Japanese customers raced to stock up on Suntoryâs products before the government raised liquor taxes, he says. The third such increase went into effect this month, but this time there was no such rush.

The Signal Insight
When Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni moved to trademark her voice last week, she highlighted growing fears about AI deepfakes sounding ever more convincingly like the people they impersonate, from politicians to CEOs. But she also shone a spotlight on the fast-developing business of helping prominent individuals secure rights to their voice likenesses â and on the companies that say âvoice AIâ will soon become how many people handle customer service and corporate sales calls or interact with devices from cars to robots.
ElevenLabs established itself as one of the most highly valued of those startups this month with a $300 million employee tender, at a $22 billion price tag.
The London-based company has worked with celebrities from Matthew McConaughey to Sir Michael Caine to trademark their voices, and created a custom voice for Yahoo based on its co-founder, Jerry Yang. It says it has developed comprehensive safeguards to detect and prevent unauthorized voice cloning or other abuses.
Most of ElevenLabsâ revenues come from corporate customers like Deutsche Telekom and Revolut, and co-founder Mateusz âMatiâ Staniszewski says businesses should prepare for a world in which customers increasingly expect to speak to AI agents rather than type with chatbots.
âVoice will be one of the key interfaces in the future; for a lot of use cases, the primary interface,â he predicts. âVoice is easier, it conveys a lot more information than text would, and it allows the technology to be present but not overwhelming.â
This conversation has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson: Give us an example of the benefits you see in voice AI.
Mati Staniszewski: We have an AI interviewer for [sales and development representative job candidates]. Usually you go to the website and fill in a form. We added [the option] to speak with an agent, and a lot of people started engaging through conversation, and two things happened. One, the ease of making it quicker for you to speak than to type resulted in us having a lot more people [applying]. Two, people started leaving a lot more information than they usually would. Weâve had more than 3,000 leads come through this so far, and more than 500 were qualified, so they were good leads.
What should CEOs do to make sure their human employees are getting the most out of their AI agents?
If you donât get this right, the other parts wonât matter. Ultimately, for an agent to work, it needs the right knowledge. It needs the right set of steps and workflow. It needs to understand what itâs doing. Like a human, it needs a lot of coaching in the early phases to make sure it works. And it needs the right guardrails and safeguards, so it doesnât go off-script.
You donât want competition between [humans and agents.] You want to find a way to bring people to manage the agents and be rewarded fairly for doing that well. And itâs not a one-and-done process. You keep improving, you keep iterating, and sometimes [you] need to jump in. You want to make sure that there is a loop: agent to human to agent. The key thing across all those efforts is that the AI agent needs to know when to bring in a human agent.
Are you looking to go public anytime soon?
We would love to go public one day. We would like to be ready â ready, but not necessarily go public â in the next 18-24 months. And then decide based on the wider side of triggers.
Whatâs the advantage, do you think, of going public when thereâs been plenty of capital to power your growth so far?
We would love for [our users] to have the ability to be part of the journey, and the later you do it, the lower ability they will have. We see a lot of people building with ElevenLabs, and weâd love for them to have an ability to be part of that. There are other [advantages], but we are building a company to stand the test of time, and the companies we work with are looking for partners that are planning to be here in 50 years, in 100 years, and we want to be that company.
Sir Michael Caineâs voice is a big part of his identity as an actor. Why did he decide to work with you rather than against you?
We created, effectively, a marketplace where people can [record] their voice, we authenticate it, they can share it, and they earn compensation as a result. So weâre trying to bring the industry on board, and [people like Michael Caine] want to be part of that future too, assuming you find a way to respect their work and give them the ability to earn compensation [from it].
CEO impersonation scams seem to be very prevalent. Have you ever had that problem with your technology?
With our technology, you always have transparency into how [an AI voice] was generated. You can take action. So, if somebody [was scammed], we could assist. Iâm not familiar with any CEO that was impersonated, but we have guardrails. So if you try to ask about money, that gets either blocked or detected and flagged for human review, so we can proactively take action. And then, if you want to clone a voice to a high [quality], you need to go through an additional authentication mechanism. So you cannot just clone a voice that easily.
Notable
- Staniszewski sees his companyâs European roots â it was born in Poland and is based in London â as âa huge advantage.â London has plentiful talent which wants to âbuild something ambitious on a global scale,â he says. And because ElevenLabs focused from the start on the polyglot European marketplace, creating a model that could work equally well in many different languages âwas never an afterthought.â

Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi has told Israel to stop its "forced establishment" of settlements in the West Bank and reverse its actions, his office said.
The "Palestinian question" is "the greatest historical injustice of this century", Wang told Israeli President Isaac Herzog in a face-to-face meeting on the sidelines of a conference in Azerbaijan on Thursday.
Beijing has been a longstanding supporter of the Palestinian cause and has maintained that a "two-state solution" is the "correct direction".
It has also been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East.
In 2023 Beijing brokered a deal to restore diplomatic ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility. Earlier this year, it was part of efforts, along with Pakistan, to propose a ceasefire in the US-Israel war against Iran.
Beijing's efforts to tackle the war in Gaza have focused on Palestinian unity.
In 2024 Beijing got rival Palestinian factions to agree to form an interim "national reconciliation government" for the occupied West Bank and Gaza after the war with Israel, although it was never implemented.
Now, Wang says the "immediate priority" is to fully open access to Gaza and stop the continued spread of a "humanitarian catastrophe".
China is willing to work with the international community to get the parties to return to dialogue and "seek a political solution to the conflict", Wang said.
In a post on X, Herzog said he was "pleased" to meet Wang and their talk "focused on the relations between our countries and the situation in the Middle East".
"I emphasised Israel's desire for peace in the region, alongside the strategic threats to our security, first and foremost from Iran and its terror proxies," he wrote.
China maintains close ties with Iran and is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which had previously come under US sanctions because of Tehran's nuclear programme.
One year into the ceasefire, people in Gaza continue to live under the regular threat of Israeli strikes, displacement and food security challenges.
Although large-scale bombardment has stopped, Israel has continued strikes in Gaza almost every day. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes there in the year since the ceasefire started in October 2025.
The US-brokered ceasefire was the first phase of a deal to end the war in Gaza, which had been triggered by a deadly Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
But progress into the deal's next phase has been stalled, with both Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violating the terms of their agreement.

This coming holiday season, brands will have a new type of shopper to court: AI agents.
Cheq, a cybersecurity company that verifies AI shopping agents, says it recorded a 100x surge in agentic traffic over a 45-day period following the release of consumer AI agents like Instinct and Metaâs Muse. While agents still make up a small fraction of online shoppers, theyâre growing quickly, especially among a constant drumbeat of consumer agent releases, Cheq CEO Guy Tytunovich said.
But not everyone is on board: Amazon and eBay have blocked agents to reinforce control over their ads businesses and checkout experiences.
Consumers are hesitant, too. Shoppers are now as likely to be swayed by an agentâs recommendation as by an influencer, Morning Consult finds, but few are comfortable letting AI make purchases on their behalf. This holiday season will be the first true test of which brands are best at displaying their wares in ways that agents find irresistible.

Reedâs view
Fear is rising that the AI bubble is about to burst under the weight of mounting debt, as my colleague Liz Hoffman detailed yesterday, including this great quote from an unnamed data-center financier: âWeâre not an ATM for your dystopian future.â
Perhaps lenders have grown tired of funding the data center buildout, but money is not going to be the thing that finally causes the AI train to go off the rails. Everything is bottlenecked. Itâs not just chips, memory, and EUV machines. Itâs refrigeration units that cool the GPUs and the raw materials needed to make components, like glass.
If it werenât for this bottlenecked supply chain, itâs likely AI revenues and user numbers would be growing much faster. Every time companies reach a new level of token efficiency, some new use case for AI is born that burns through ever more compute, proving Jevons Paradox. My favorite example of late: Decompiling video games to create mashups, something that used to take people years to do manually can now be done by AI in a weekend. It may be the thing that finally turns Gen-Zers into fans of AI.
The total addressable market of AI is roughly 100% of the earthâs population, and demand for it will continue to soar. The enterprise market has only dipped its toes into AI, and the consumer hasnât even begun to dive in. Anthropic told investors this week that itâs making 85% gross margins. Even if that number is a gross exaggeration, this is a cash cow business. Theyâll service their debt obligations, in other words.
I agree with the lender who lamented being an ATM for the AI industry, but probably for a different reason. Why would you want to lend money for measly interest payments when you could invest and get a massive return? Thereâs a reason hyperscalers and neoclouds reached for debt: Itâs relatively cheap.

The Scoop
Investors are pouring cash into a hot new sector of the AI economy: model routing â a practice allowing developers and companies to easily switch between different AI models.
Startup TrustedRouter, which launched publicly six weeks ago, is among a growing crop of model-routing firms looking to cut AI costs and reduce businessesâ dependence on any single model maker. The company this week closed a $6 million seed round, led by Sierra Ventures, it told Semafor.
The biggest player in the routing space is OpenRouter, which started with a $12.5 million seed round in February 2025 and has since agreed to sell to payments provider Stripe in a $7.5 billion deal.
TrustedRouter, CEO Joseph Perla said, aims to differentiate itself by offering end-to-end encryption and verifiable confidential computing for some open-weight models, meaning neither TrustedRouter nor the data center running the model can read a customerâs prompts or outputs, unlike with closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic, which donât currently offer the same guarantees.
OpenRouter also doesnât offer those protections, according to Perla: âSecurity is just a pure baseline. It just has to be secure.â
Know More
Perla, a former Facebook engineer and early Lyft hire who has founded and sold several startups, hopes to win over businesses that are seeing their AI spending balloon, but also putting a premium on keeping their data private.
âIf we all encrypt our AI chats,â Perla said, âwe can slow downâ the cycle in which frontier labs absorb user data to train future models.
He said Chinese AI models, including those from DeepSeek, Zhipu, and Moonshot, are among the most popular on his platform, but he wants to also see a more vibrant American open-source ecosystem. Thereâs been a flurry of Western open-weight releases in recent weeks, including from Reflection AI and Mistral; on Thursday, Meta released what it called âthe most capable US open-weight model to date.â
Eventually, Perla said he wants to launch the âNew York Token Exchange,â a marketplace for AI models in which thousands of models from thousands of hosting providers â any data center willing to run an open model â would compete to serve each request, turning AI tokens into a commodity that could be traded with futures, hedges, and price indices, like oil or electricity. He hopes to stage âmodel IPOsâ for new open-weight releases.
J.D.âs view
Thereâs clear demand from developers for routing services, and TrustedRouter could fill a void for the most privacy-obsessed among them. Whether it goes from niche to mass market could depend on how competitive open-weight models get. If they keep lagging behind their closed competitors at OpenAI and Anthropic, some enterprises and developers will put up with the higher cost and lack of encryption to get a better output for their most advanced tasks.
A project I oversaw last week, in which we analyzed thousands of cable news segments about data centers using AI, cost about $140, because we used advanced closed models. Running that through TrustedRouter on encrypted, confidential infrastructure with less advanced Chinese models would have cost under $20, though the output likely wouldnât have been as good. These kinds of tradeoffs will keep confronting tech leaders as long as that disparity persists.

The lack of a shared lexicon is undermining responsible AI-military integration
We need a common way to talk about military AI—across services, agencies, and indeed, the world.
Today’s headlines are full of killer robots and doomsayers, but the most urgent risk in military AI is more mundane: the people shaping it share neither a common lexicon nor common data.
The problem is not a lack of discussion. The authors have taken part in many global deliberations, both as conveners and as private-sector representatives, and we can report: If the world is to forge responsible governance of AI in the military domain, it will need shared definitions and a way to fuse relevant developments and decisions into something approximating “ground truth.”
The players in AI-military integration come from every realm: governments, militaries, the private sector, academia, the legal system, civil society, human rights, technology, journalism, and more. In multilateral negotiations and colloquial parlance, they speak varied languages—literally and topically. They are guided by varied incentives: some are eagerly pursuing AI-military integration, while others are trying to regulate it. A word like “autonomy” means something different to a general, an engineer, a lawyer, and a human rights advocate, not to mention the nuances born of the 200 or so countries they call home.
The staggering breadth of these players, combined with the wide range of AI applications, means that data about their actions is scattered. It can be found in government contract announcements, legislation, news coverage, court documents, patent applications, and beyond, in nearly every global language. This has made it impossible to track and compare developments within and across countries.
Without common language and common data, humanitarian organizations often talk past supply-chain experts. Tech executives fail to communicate effectively with academic researchers. Efforts to develop responsible AI-military integration cannot move ahead.
This is not a new concern. In 2024, the Responsible AI in the Military Domain Summit, or REAIM—the preeminent forum for global discussions of the topic—urged stakeholders to begin “fostering a common understanding of…capabilities and limitations [of AI-military integration], and a shared understanding of the possible applications…and their potential impacts, including both benefits and risks.” The same year, the United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research Roundtable for AI, Security, and Ethics identified six priority areas for governance, including: “Building a shared and solid knowledge base on AI in the military domain, developed through cross-regional, inter-disciplinary and multi-stakeholder input.” And last year’s report by the Global Commission REAIM urged states to “maintain international repositories of best practices, including AI concepts and definitions, AI capabilities in specific contexts of application…and military AI policies” to support national and international regulatory efforts.
One effort to bridge the data gap is the AI-Military Integration Database, operated by AIMID, a private company whose CEO is one of the authors. The database does a daily scan for news and information about AI-military integration in more than 20 languages—news reports, company announcements, academic articles, legislation, contracts, think tank reports, and more. The result is an ever-growing knowledge graph: a structured, footnoted map of actors, technologies, events and the relationships between them. This makes it possible to see which countries are doing what, with what technologies, from what companies, and for what use cases. In short, AIMID aims to deliver a single, verifiable picture of global AI-military integration, a data-driven “ground truth.”
Among other benefits, the database aims to help allies and partners pool knowledge about testing, evaluation, verification, and validation—supporting innovation and interoperability while avoiding the costly duplication of technical efforts. It might also help reduce tension between global rivals by providing empirical reference points, reducing dangerous interstate misperceptions, and ensuring that states’ security policies are anchored in evidence rather than ambiguity. For anyone concerned with responsible AI-military development—governments, businesses, NGOs, academics, or average citizens—AIMID serves as a unique resource,
But more than merely recognizing that data fragmentation is hindering responsible military-AI progress, defense leaders around the world should next fund and adopt the tools necessary to fully understand the data and intelligence-gathering side of this new ecosystem. Indeed, while organizations like AIMID cannot fully solve the fundamental problem of data fragmentation, they represent some of the best resources available.
This commentary is published in coordination with the 2026 Global Security Forum, of which Defense One is a media partner.
Dr. Jason Warner is the CEO of the AI-Military Integration Database (AIMID). He holds a Ph.D. from Harvard University.
Sofia Romansky is a Strategic Analyst at The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies (HCSS) and Subject Matter Expert for the NATO Defence Education Enhancement Program (DEEP). She previously served as the Project Coordinator of the Global Commission on Responsible Artificial Intelligence in the Military Domain (GC REAIM).

A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.
Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.
This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.
The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.
While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September â and suffered few casualties in return.
The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".
Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.
He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.
This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.
Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.
Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.
Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.
Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.
Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.
The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.
An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."
He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.
Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".
"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."
Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.
In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.
"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."
"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".
That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.
"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.
"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvresâ¦ each of these actions is a building block towards victory."
All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.

803ac97aef4c.text: It was an economy bursting at the seams: robust growth powered by a tech boom, low unemployment, elevated inflation and Fed rate hikes to try to cool things down. The big picture: That was the situation in the year 2000, and it reminds us a great deal of the conditions in 2026. The worrying part, however, is this: Then, as now, there were early warning signs that the technological boom powering the good times may not last forever. And indeed, the cracks that appeared in the tech sector in 2000 would spill over into a broader bear market and mild recession in 2001. We're not predicting that this time. History only rhymes; it doesn't repeat. But it is a historical episode worth weighing when thinking about the range of possibilities for how things may go in 2027 and beyond — particularly this week, as the debt markets funding the AI build-out have wobbled. Flashback: While 2001 was a nasty year for the U.S. economy — a full-fledged tech bust exacerbated by the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks — the year before was pretty great by nearly every measure. The unemployment rate reached a multi-decade low of 3.8% in April 2000 and closed the year at a mere 3.9%. GDP rose 4.1% for the full year, powered by stunning rates of productivity growth. It coincided, however, with high inflation, driven particularly by surging energy costs. The Consumer Price Index was up 3.4% over the course of the year. Zoom in: Against that backdrop, the Alan Greenspan-led Fed felt compelled to try to cool things down, lest that inflation become more entrenched. The central bank increased rates three times that year, including a super-sized half-point in May. But here's where the parallels to today get even more interesting: Greenspan's justification for rate hikes could be lifted from today's Fedspeak about the AI boom — or would be if today's central bankers shared his penchant for circumlocution. What they're saying: The "profoundly beneficial forces driving the American economy to competitive excellence are also engendering a set of imbalances that, unless contained, threaten our continuing prosperity," Greenspan told Congress in February 2000. "The problem is that the pickup in productivity tends to create even greater increases in aggregate demand than in potential aggregate supply," he said. "This occurs principally because a rise in structural productivity growth has its counterpart in higher expectations for long-term corporate earnings." "This, in turn, not only spurs business investment but also increases stock prices and the market value of assets held by households, creating additional purchasing power for which no additional goods or services have yet been produced." Between the lines: He was talking about the productivity boom driven by the internet and related IT innovations of that era, but it is very much applicable to the AI boom today. Yes, AI-fueled productivity could create a boost to the economy's supply potential in the future, with corresponding noninflationary growth and higher incomes. But that's in the future. Right now, that potential is causing surging asset prices and rising demand for inputs to the build-out, pushing inflation higher. Reality check: The stock market peaked in March 2000. By 2001, an all-out tech rout was underway, as much of the investment in fiber-optic cable and other internet infrastructure was ahead of its time. That reversed the playing field for the Fed, as the wealth effects and an investment boom that appeared to be overheating the economy in 2000 instead dragged it down. The Fed enacted a surprise half-point rate cut on Jan. 3, 2001, and would ultimately cut rates 11 times (!) in 2001. Yes, but: Interestingly, while the tech bust hammered Americans' wealth, employment prospects and capital spending, the turn-of-the-century productivity gains continued throughout that recession and the ensuing jobless recovery. The bottom line: Even if the AI boom drives the kinds of long-term productivity surges its proponents anticipate, there is a risk of a bumpy path ahead — and policymakers would do well to study the parallels from 26 years ago.

Triceratops’ massive skulls were built for horn-to-horn grappling. The rhino-like Centrosaurus could withstand stabbing its nose horn up and down. And the parrot-faced Psittacosaurus would have been wise to avoid a fight: Its head was ill-suited to handle blows.
New simulations using 3-D models of the heads of five different horned dinosaurs reveal what forces the skulls could withstand in battle. The results provide insight into how these dinosaurs evolved to use their face-based armory in combat, researchers report September 24 in PeerJ.
Ceratopsians — horned dinosaurs like Triceratops — have been hypothesized to use their imposing headgear as armaments for battling with other members of the species.
Fossilized facial injuries consistent with head-to-head violence have provided physical clues. “We know from many fossils that ceratopsian skulls tended to get banged up a little bit … in very particular spots on the frill or on the cheek,” says Andrew Farke, a paleontologist at Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology in Claremont, California. But little else was known about how ceratopsians actually used their horns in battle.
Studying the biomechanics of the animals’ weaponized skulls could provide information on what movements and forces the dinosaurs evolved to tolerate. Such biomechanics research had previously been done on the bite stresses of theropod dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus and on the forces felt by the club tails of armored dinosaurs, says vertebrate paleontologist Eric Austin Ames Jr.
Ames and his colleagues at the University of Bristol in England developed digital 3-D models of six skulls across five ceratopsian species spread across the group’s evolutionary tree. They simulated the combat stress experienced across the skull, varying the direction of attack and how the weaponry was used. Higher stresses in the skull meant a greater risk of mechanical failure, Ames says. The dinosaurs are more likely to have evolved to fight in a way that was well-tolerated by the skull’s mechanics.
The team found that early members of the group from about 125 million years ago — like the hornless, husky-sized Psittacosaurus — didn’t have skulls well-suited for combat of any type. The pig-sized Protoceratops had a skull that tolerated ramming fairly well. Larger, later-diverging species like Centrosaurus and the three-horned Triceratops and Spiclypeus appeared adapted to a wider range of combat styles.
Centrosaurus may have been a specialized stabber, lunging its head to jab at opponents. “When we tested [the skull] with vertical forces, it actually handled the stresses really well,” Ames says. “But when we tried side-to-side, it did not perform very well.”In contrast, Triceratops and Spiclypeus had skulls that tolerate the forces generated by interlocking horns and wrestling.
Ames thinks ceratopsians’ horns and frills probably first evolved for social and sexual display, but were soon used for full contact purposes. “Throughout their evolutionary history, their [horns’ traits] started to really explode in diversity and that coincided with different intraspecific combat styles,” he says. “This is something we see in modern herbivores.”
Much like with the antlers and horns of modern deer, buffalo or antelope, these weapons could have easily been turned on predators as well. “These adaptations are kind of like a Swiss Army knife,” Ames says. “They can be used for multiple things.”
The team created its 3-D models from surface scans of fossilized skulls. More detailed models that better simulate the complicated internal structure of these dinosaurs’ immense, bizarre skulls could provide even more insight to this prehistoric fight club, Farke says.
