A pastor and his wife have been arrested in South Africa after 200 people, some in chains, were found held at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centre in the north-eastern part of the country.
The facility, operated from a church in Mpumalanga province, was discovered during an operation by officials in the area on Thursday.
Authorities said they uncovered "gross inhumane conditions" when they raided the facility, with some patients found with "sores all over their bodies" and "others chained to each other".
Police have since charged the couple, who were running the facility, with kidnapping but could add more charges. They have not yet commented.
Illegal rehabilitation centres have mushroomed in South Africa in recent years as drug use spirals in the country.
Last year, the department of social development said it had uncovered over 100 unlawful facilities operating across the country, mostly in Gauteng province, home to the country's largest city, Johannesburg.
A girl of 16 and a boy of 11 were found being kept in the same room as adults in the Mpumalanga centre.
The couple running it told officials they were housing 60 people, but upon inspection, more than three times that number were found, including more than 30 women.
The group, mostly believed to be drug addicts, were found in crowded rooms and without access to functioning bathrooms or running water.
"Some [of them had] been at the alleged illegal centre for a while," the department said.
Gift Skhosana, one of those held at the facility, told local broadcaster Newzroom Afrika it was "common practice" for patients to be chained.
"They chain us as punishment [and] when you gain entry," he said.
Despite this, Skhosana, who was a drug user, said the facility helped him get clean and overcome his addiction.
Another person, who was not named, said his experience with the facility left him needing help mentally.
The couple charged a monthly fee of 3,000 rand ($182; Â£137) to house the patients, of which almost a half would go to the church.
Fourteen of those found at the centre have since been taken to hospital for further medical treatment, police said.
Officials said 132 have been reunited with their families.
The couple is expected to appear in a local court on Monday.

0c1a14d530b7.text: By — Bill Barrow, Associated Press Bill Barrow, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-will-rally-georgia-republicans-despite-party-divisions-in-battleground-state Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump will rally Georgia Republicans despite party divisions in battleground state Politics Oct 16, 2026 10:57 AM EDT ATLANTA (AP) — Donald Trump's midterm campaign blitz arrives in Georgia on Friday for a rally with top Republican candidates in a state that has long been the epicenter of the president's false claims about election fraud. In Dalton, the population center of conservative northwest Georgia, Trump will appear with Senate candidate Mike Collins and gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson as part of the White House effort to boost Republican enthusiasm in an election that could reshape the final years of Trump's second presidency. WATCH: Inside Georgia's Senate race and Collins's uphill battle against Ossoff "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party," said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Yet unlike some of Trump's recent trips to solidly Republican states — Alabama, Montana, Tennessee — Georgia is a critical battleground. That means Jackson, a billionaire businessman, and Collins, a two-term congressman, need more than Trump stalwarts to defeat their respective Democratic opponents, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms and Sen. Jon Ossoff. "I'm surprised Georgia Republicans want the president here," Ossoff said. "The president coming to town reminds Georgians that Donald Trump and Mike Collins" have pushed policies that have "driven the cost of groceries, fuel and healthcare to their all-time highs." READ MORE: Talarico compares his campaign to David and Goliath after GOP invests over $158M against him Collins spokesperson Meyer Siegfried said the congressman welcomes the president's attention. But he also stressed that Collins is a "bipartisan workhorse who will work with anybody," while adding that "Ossoff hates Trump more than he loves our state." Bottoms also seemed thrilled with Trump's visit. "When Donald Trump says he wants people to imagine that he is on the ballot, I am asking the people of Georgia to do just that," she said, pointing to Jackson's promise to be Trump's "favorite governor." WATCH: Georgia's Ossoff and Collins face off in Senate debate The risks have been evident even in the heavily Republican corner of Georgia where the president will visit. Voters there sent erstwhile Trump ally Marjorie Taylor Greene to Congress before she broke with the president and resigned. Trump won the district by about 37 points in 2024 and Greene won by 29. In the April special election to replace Greene, Republican Rep. Clay Fuller won by 12 points. Republican candidates have run separately The Dalton event will be the first time this fall that Jackson and Collins have appeared at the same venue. That contrasts with Ossoff and Bottoms holding joint rallies across Georgia, with the next scheduled for Saturday in Cobb County outside Atlanta. Collins has been dogged by anemic fundraising and controversies that leave even Republicans questioning his viability against Ossoff. Jackson has focused on sharing the stage with other statewide Republican nominees and party leaders, and none mention Collins. "That was not a neglect," Trump's former agriculture secretary and onetime Georgia Gov. Sonny Perdue said after one rally. "I think it was really respecting a Rick Jackson event and focusing on his election as governor." Asked about the joint rally, a Jackson spokesman said only, "Rick will be in Dalton and looks forward to reminding Georgia voters that bad mayors do not make good governors." Trump was last in Dalton on Jan. 4, 2021, the day before Ossoff and Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock won concurrent Senate runoffs. He had already lost the presidential campaign to Joe Biden but was unwilling to accept it. "There is no way we lost Georgia. There's no way," Trump said that day. "That was a rigged election but we're still fighting it." Election denial lingers in Georgia Collins was elected to Congress in 2022, and he's echoed Trump's lies about 2020. He declined to recant those views this week when Ossoff pressed him during a debate. "There was a lot of doubt in that election. Yes, Joe Biden was the president," Collins said, without saying Biden was duly elected. Trump endorsed Collins days before his June runoff victory over former football coach Derek Dooley. When announcing his decision, Trump complained that Dooley had conceded that Biden was elected legitimately. Gov. Brian Kemp did not endorse Collins until September, and he warned voters during the primary that the congressman could not win in November. Trump did not endorse Jackson until after he'd won a Republican primary runoff over the president's original pick, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, who had been part of Trump's effort to overturn Biden's victory. The president cited Jones' loyalty in his endorsement. Jackson doesn't regularly mention Trump like he did during the primary campaign, when the first-time candidate compared his business background to Trump. He's more likely in recent weeks to compare himself to Kemp. But the governor won't be with his fellow Republicans on Friday, according to his top political adviser. "He has a family obligation that day," said Cody Hall. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 25c4dff1172f.text: By — Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/talarico-compares-his-campaign-to-david-and-goliath-after-gop-invests-over-158m-against-him Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Talarico compares his campaign to David and Goliath after GOP invests over $158M against him Politics Oct 16, 2026 10:44 AM EDT At a packed rally in Texas on Thursday, James Talarico compared his U.S. Senate campaign to David — who fought Goliath — as the Democrat faces more than $158 million in outside spending by Republican leadership and the world's richest man, Elon Musk. Talarico told rallygoers under bright lights that David may not have had Goliath's strength, but he had a slingshot. READ MORE: Frustrated with Trump, voters overwhelmingly want change, AP-NORC poll finds "You are my slingshot," he continued, without mentioning Musk or the other spending against him. "We are going up against our own Goliaths." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The description falls in line with Talarico's past rhetoric painting politics not as right versus left, but the ultrawealthy versus everyone else, as he tries to become the first Democrat to win statewide in over 30 years. Talarico's own campaign has raised record amounts of money in one of the nation's more expensive and competitive Senate races. The national conversation around Talarico's campaign has evolved over the past months. Initially, the state lawmaker was considered just the latest of several Democratic candidates over the past years who gave the party a hope of flipping Texas, only for that hope to deflate come Election Day. WATCH: An accounting of Trump's promised payouts and questions they raise Now, Talarico is seen as a real contender to win the seat against Republican candidate Ken Paxton. Talarico's success so far can partly be chalked up to voters' apprehensions toward Paxton, who faced questions in his past over corruption, including being impeached by his own party in the Texas legislature. He was later acquitted. Texas will help decide control of the U.S. Senate While outside spending in support of Paxton has flooded the Texas airwaves with ads, Talarico's campaign itself has outpaced Paxton's in fundraising from donors eager for Texas to forgo its solidly Republican title. The prospect of a flagship GOP state turning blue doesn't just fill Democrats with glee and Republicans with alarm. Whoever wins will help determine which party controls the Senate in President Donald Trump's final two years in office, making it either smooth sailing for Trump or a bog of investigations and opposition. WATCH: Inside Georgia's Senate race and Collins's uphill battle against Ossoff Talarico, a seminarian and state representative, has also tread a very careful path — as nonpartisan as he can — from the major metros that already tilt Democratic, along the border towns that flipped from blue to red last election, and to the rural Republican high plains and desert. The candidate has distanced himself from former President Joe Biden's administration and his own party, and while progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders is coming to Texas this month, he won't be sharing a stage with Talarico. Talarico's talk of affordability resonated at rally Talarico's strategy is to take direct aim at what voters say they are most concerned about: the costs that have inexorably grown for years. That unaffordability, Talarico argued at the nighttime rally in Texas that was packed with younger voters, is because billionaires and corrupt politicians have rigged the system. It resonated. "They think that they can buy us, and that they can essentially be the kings of the country," said Kaitlyn Johnson, a 29-year-old bartender who attended the rally. WATCH: Democratic and GOP strategists on how Trump's unpopularity is shaping the midterms Johnson felt that Talarico put words to that feeling she'd held for a while, and the high costs keep nagging at her, too. "I make decent money," she said, "but there's no way in hell that I'm going to be able to buy a house anytime soon." Paxton has backing from Musk, Trump Trump and Republicans are well aware of Talarico's ability to connect with voters, and of Paxton's struggles to find purchase in what would otherwise be a relatively easy race for a Republican. The president has made several trips to Texas to rally for Paxton. Paxton has received significant financial support from Musk, who last year headed Trump's Department of Government Efficiency. Musk contributed $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, federal campaign spending filings showed Thursday. The Senate Leadership Fund gave $158 million to Texas PAC, the largest contributor to Paxton's campaign. Musk also provided $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group that supports Paxton. The rally Thursday in the small city of San Marcos south of Austin follows nine days earlier this month when Talarico was out of the public eye due to the flu. His absence sparked a swirl of conspiracies online, including the false claim that he was at a mental health treatment center in Ohio. Shared by conservative social media influencers, the claim quickly fell apart at closer inspection. Associated Press reporters Thomas Beaumont and Joey Cappelletti contributed. Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.
The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.
Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.
On Friday, the Pope's doctors said tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his procedure.
His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.

754c09d9a8c4.text: By — Stephen McGrath, Associated Press Stephen McGrath, Associated Press By — Veselin Toshkov, Associated Press Veselin Toshkov, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/drone-strikes-in-the-black-sea-raise-fears-of-russian-escalation-to-test-natos-response Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Drone strikes in the Black Sea raise fears of Russian escalation to test NATO's response World Oct 16, 2026 10:35 AM EDT SOFIA, Bulgaria (AP) — A string of drone attacks on at least seven cargo vessels in the Black Sea this month, off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, has some members of the alliance wondering if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking escalation to test their support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow's full-scale invasion. The attacks in the two countries' exclusive economic zones threaten a global shipping route and have left two people dead, with at least 25 still missing. They also run the risk of drawing other countries directly into the war for Ukraine. READ MORE: Drone strike on ship in Romanian waters raises fear that war in Ukraine is spreading Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukraine's Black Sea and Danube river ports, leaving Kyiv increasingly reliant on alternative routes to get its grain exports to markets in Africa and the Middle East. Russian drones have repeatedly violated Romanian airspace near some of Ukraine's Danube ports. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. In the latest incidents, fires broke out on two ships struck by drones Wednesday and Thursday, one in Romania's territorial waters. Romanian President Nicusor Dan said Thursday in Brussels that "two drones" had hit the vessels but did not say whose drones they were. "There will be a reaction from the Romanian state," he warned. READ MORE: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries as relations with Trump sour Increasingly, the suspicion falls on Russia. "There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favors Russia — and indeed, the logic points in that direction," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told his country's Parliament. "The problem is that we cannot prove it." Multiple vessels struck by drones in October The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader, a chemical tanker traveling from Tunisia to Romania, was struck by a drone Thursday and caught fire. Five crew members were rescued but another seven are missing. On Wednesday, a drone strike and fire were reported on the Comoros-flagged Yara J, a chemical and oil tanker traveling from Turkey to Romania. Romania's acting Defense Minister Radu Miruta said an investigation was underway. WATCH: Ukraine resumes strikes on energy targets, saying Russia never stopped its attacks On Tuesday, two ships were struck by drones off Bulgaria's coast. Rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members from the Ukraine-operated Chelsea 3, sailing under a Maltese flag, but 11 crew from the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity are still missing. The crew of the Chelsea 3 reported the ship's deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones. Earlier this month, sea and aerial drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. A Togo-flagged ship sank with no sign of the 12 sailors reported on board, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated 18 crew members from a Palau-flagged vessel that was damaged. A day earlier, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank off the coast of Romania. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as "a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel" in neutral waters. Russia's ambassador in Sofia, Bulgaria, said she didn't have any information from the Russian defense ministry. NATO's defense clause under scrutiny NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on X on Thursday that he met Radev and Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and "the latest attacks on commercial shipping." "NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities," he said. "NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed." WATCH: Ukraine less reliant on U.S. as Trump-Zelenskyy rift deepens, former ambassador says Article 5 of the NATO charter has a mutual defense guarantee — an attack on one is an attack on all — but Romanian defense analyst Radu Tudor said it was uncertain as to whether it covers many of the Black Sea drone strikes because they occurred in the alliance members' exclusive economic zones. "It's a matter of discussion whether the exclusive economic zone is included in the Article 5-type reaction or not," he said. "And it seems that until now, it isn't — which raised a lot of questions." NATO has been too slow to respond in the Black Sea, he argued. "Tens of incidents are happening and Russia is getting closer to NATO borders. … Words are not enough," Tudor said. A growing threat The Black Sea drone incidents in October are just the latest in a long string of drone airspace incursions to rock Romania and other NATO members since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. While most have come from Russia, Ukrainian drones have also crossed borders. In August, Romania deployed two F-16 fighter jets to destroy a naval drone that was reportedly carrying explosives and was spotted near a major Black Sea gas project, a decision that Acting Defense Minister Miruta said was made to "protect the lives of the several hundred people" working on the gas platform. Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for decades.
Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too.
So what is happening?
How big and unusual are these protests?
Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of DurrÃ«s, ShkodÃ«r, LezhÃ« and Vlora in the west, GjirokastÃ«r in the south and KorÃ§Ã« in the east.
The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living.
Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers.
Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons.
Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony.
Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation.
A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too.
Every evening, throughout the summer for some 135 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign.
The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead.
The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder.
One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue.
So has the Flamingo movement radicalised?
The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.
They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night.
But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.
The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.
Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.
Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."
Another called Brunela told the BBC's What in the World programme she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."
An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.
After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system.
How is the government handling the unrest?
Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos.
"All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday.
The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward".
Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama.
But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance.
So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it.
On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved.
Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU.
Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday.
"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence."
Is Albania safe to visit?
Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being.
The UK government has urged visitors to check media, external for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local authorities.
Albania is a popular tourist destination, and the government in Tirana has warned that violence tarnishes the country's image, affecting both tourism and its European path.

52faa1649351.text:
- Published
Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.
A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt.
Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence: a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby.
The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car.
"We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys â¦ started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck â look, I am bleeding!"
Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured.
Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars â including one of his own.
"As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him.
Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports.
"Weâ¯condemn criminalâ¯violenceâ¯by any partyâ¯in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions,â¯of those responsible," the spokesperson said.
Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me.
The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year.
Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack.
In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could â one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below.
Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts.
All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts â small encampments on hilltops â are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support.
"This is a hotspot â there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today."
But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees.
There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave.
But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return.
As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back.
American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene.
"I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes."
In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined.
As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing.
Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation â a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts.
The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank.
Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves.
What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase.
The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers

Alexisâs view
The Iran war is shaping up to be the catalyst of a seismic shift in Africaâs energy sector. And, in the case of the continentâs richest man Aliko Dangote, the conflict has proven the old adage that luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity.
Dangoteâs mega-refinery on the outskirts of Lagos State has revealed the scale of a West African market underserved by locally refined fuel, while upending conventional thinking by showing African refineries can supply markets in Europe and Asia. At the same time, disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has exposed the vulnerability of nations that are heavily dependent on fuel imports: South Africa and Kenya have hiked prices, which runs the risk of driving inflation. Meanwhile, President Bola Tinubuâs removal of Nigeriaâs subsidy three years ago has allowed prices to skyrocket, turning the cost of fuel into a key campaign issue ahead of Januaryâs election.
Policymakers have been quick to react to the altered energy dynamics. South Africa announced plans to increase its strategic oil reserves for the first time since the end of apartheid to mitigate supply shocks, Angola wants to implement faster exploration concessions while urging southern African governments to help finance a new refinery, and plans to build refineries in Uganda and Tanzania have gathered pace.
Fola Fagbule, who heads the Kenya regional office of multilateral lender Africa Finance Corporation, which helped to finance Dangoteâs Lagos refinery, called the impact of the Nigerian billionaireâs project a âBig Bangâ moment. He told me various projects are being developed across the continent âas a result of the new realities in the energy market.â
The shift has potential pitfalls. Daniel Evans, global head of fuels and refining research at S&P Global Energy, acknowledged the increased appetite for downstream investment across Africa, but warned difficulties remain around projects that require high levels of capital expenditure.
But a new generation of refineries has the potential to transform economies, not only protecting countries from future energy shocks but providing the baseload power needed to ramp up manufacturing. As Fagbule put it, the legacy of this paradigm shift could be how it triggered âmassive, large-scale industrialization in Africa that nobody expected.â

11f413faa10f.text:
AI experts are coming â and the pretenders too. âAnybody who knows anything about AIâ is in high demand from investors trying to play the AI trade, said Gemma Postlethwaite, CEO of expert network GLG. And there are plenty of deepfakes and people using AI chatbots willing to play the part.
âWe have to be able to deliver experts that not only are who they say they are, but know what they say they know,â Postlethwaite tells Semafor. To test for authenticity, GLG is doing additional screening and ID verification â increasingly on camera with questions designed to trip up AI avatars. Itâs also parsing transcripts to find âsituations where somebodyâs expertise is going off-piste,â she said. âThink of it like a digital fingerprint of knowledge.â Verify, then trust.
GLG is also connecting frontier AI labs with subject-matter experts to help train models in sensitive subjects, such as child psychiatrists who can craft responses to kids in crisis and nuclear or bioweapon experts to respond to bad actors looking for instruction manuals.

Forest clearing in the Congo Basin nearly matched losses in the Amazon for the first time in a decade of monitoring, even as deforestation slowed worldwide, a new study found.
The destruction releases vast stores of carbon, adding to climate change that is already contributing to drought and forest fires across the tropics.
Expanding farming, timber, and mining activities are driving the clearances in the basin, which is home to the worldâs second-largest tropical rainforest, the Forest Declaration Assessment group said.
In DR Congo, where most of the forest is situated, decades of conflict â along with poor oversight â have fueled uncontrolled logging, driving up the rate of tree loss in central Africa this decade. Meanwhile, there has been a steep decline in deforestation in Latin America and the Caribbean, leaving the two regions almost on a par.

The founder of 777 Partners, the poster child for the underbelly of Wall Streetâs insurance push, pleaded guilty to fraud Thursday.
A Semafor investigation in 2023 found that 777, which announced itself with a bold bid to buy UK soccer club Everton, had been funneling insurance policyholdersâ money into risky bets that it ginned up itself. The collapse of 777, and the spotlight on exactly what it had been doing with policyholdersâ life-insurance money, threatened to bring new scrutiny to what has become Wall Streetâs favorite trade.
It turns out the party pooper, as we wrote a few weeks ago, wasnât 777 founder Joshua Wander, a hotshot outsider, but rather a consummate insider: Mark Walter, who did as much as anyone to invent the private equity-insurance trade and is now embroiled in a DOJ investigation that has generated scrutiny of the entire industry.

He was then shot by a person at the scene who followed him inside, authorities said. The suspect was found dead inside the school minutes after the shooting was first reported, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said. The three children killed were aged 5, 8 and 11. Another child, 7, and a teacher, 54, were injured and taken to the hospital in critical condition, he said. The first 911 call came just before 1 p.m. from a person in a vehicle outside Silver Rail Elementary who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, Krantz told reporters. Further 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived on scene within minutes, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said. The attacker, who police identified as a Bend resident, was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said. Parents hugged, kissed and held their kids' hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favorite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home. The school in Bend, which is about 125 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Portland, had 459 enrolled students as of last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education. The school serves students in kindergarten through fifth grade. The high-desert city has ballooned in population over the past three decades and is a tourism and outdoor recreation hub near Mount Bachelor. Classes, sports and extracurriculars were canceled Friday for all 32 schools in the Bend-La Pine district. The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University. The attacker used a pump-action shotgun that was purchased by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation. At a news conference, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek said her heart was "absolutely broken" and thanked the civilian who pursued the shooter. "To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she said. South Africa is planning to tighten the rules around pharmacies making their own compound versions of medicines, including the popular weight-loss and diabetes treatments Ozempic and Mounjaro, Reuters reports.
The move is likely to be welcomed by pharmaceutical giants such as Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly as they seek to curb the pharmacy-made products competing with their blockbuster GLP-1 drugs.
South African Pharmacy Council CEO Vincent Tlala said his organization was working with the industry regulator to update standards governing the compounding of medicines because they are worried that some pharmacies have become, in effect, âsmall-scale manufacturers,â producing large quantities of treatments in advance, rather than for specific patients.
The discussion on new guidelines, expected to be published around March next year, follows Juneâs court victory for Novo Nordisk against local compounding pharmacies making unauthorized copies. With the highest adult obesity rate in Africa, at 30%, the drugs are in high demand in South Africa, but the cost of the trademarked version puts them out of reach for most people.

8232418c4183.text:
South African Black-owned businesses face a funding shortfall of $45 billion, a new report shows, citing âexplicit investor biasâ alongside barriers such as limited collateral and governance concerns.
The findings come three decades after the democratic government introduced a raft of measures â known as Black Economic Empowerment (BEE) â aimed at reversing the dispossession suffered by Black people under apartheid and colonialism. Despite the efforts to redress the problem, South Africa remains one of the worldâs most unequal societies.
The study, published by British International Investment and Swedenâs Swedfund, both state-owned development finance entities, lands as Washington steps up pressure on Pretoria to dismantle BEE. US Ambassador Leo Brent Bozell III has put scrapping the policy on a list of demands tied to improving the investment climate. Pretoria has refused, despite disagreements within the coalition government. Instead the policy conversation has moved to creating a $60 billion fund to help scale up small Black-owned businesses.

7ec8f7847bc7.text:
Nigerian investment firm Cascador and lender Sterling Bank launched a $200 million fund for small and medium enterprises, in a bid to close a credit access gap that constrains the growth potential of a vital pillar of African commerce.
More than 90% of African businesses are categorized as SMEs, accounting for more than half of GDP in most countries and the majority of employment. But a $331 billion SME financing gap means that, despite being the backbone of the continentâs economies, many African entrepreneurs lack capital to invest in production and generate growth revenue.
Cascador recently published a paper that found only 22% of sub-Saharan Africa businesses hold a bank loan or line of credit, compared with 36% globally. The firmâs new facility with Sterling Bank will offer loans of up to $1 million per business in an attempt to help the enterprises secure larger and longer-tenor capital.

3d856785c778.text:
Africaâs largest initial public offering is set to take a more pan-African shape with the Dangote Refineryâs push to extend the sale of its shares to Egypt.
The sale will involve the use of depositary receipts, the same instruments that will be used to offer ownership in the continentâs largest refinery to prospective shareholders in Botswana and Kenya.
The IPO aims to raise $1.6 billion through the sale that started mid-September in Nigeria. The company has imposed a hard cap of $2.1 billion, but has âreceived subscriptions amounting to more than three or four timesâ the target, billionaire owner Aliko Dangote said this week. A two-week extension on the subscription period to Oct. 27 is designed to accommodate efforts to add more African bourses to the process, he said.
Dangote set a minimum entry price of 40 cents per share to attract potential retail investors. Policymakers around Africa see in the IPO a sign that capital markets can be deepened by broad-based participation, but the process of creating sale instruments in individual stock exchanges has highlighted a need to simplify regulations to allow more cross-border investment on the continent.

Six months after the Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the moon, the value of their closeup view is coming into focus. The first science results, released on October 7, reveal details of the moon’s array of colors, how often it gets hit by tiny rocks and lessons for squeezing as much science as possible out of future human lunar missions.
“We worked extremely hard to make sure we were able to maximize lunar science return from wherever we could in this mission,” said Artemis II flight science operations lead Kelsey Young at a virtual Lunar Surface Science Workshop meeting on October 7. “This is creating yet another tool in our toolbox as planetary scientists to understand our moon, our solar system, even our own planet.”
NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon in April — the first time humans had been anywhere near our natural satellite in more than 50 years. Astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen spent about seven hours in close proximity to the moon taking scientific observations, describing the moon’s surprising colors and textures and witnessing a solar eclipse from space.
Almost all of that event was livestreamed. But the astronauts took thousands of photos, notes and audio recordings that weren’t immediately made public. Part of the science team’s job was to digest those observations and release the data to anyone who wants to study them within six months of splashdown on April 10.
With three days to spare, the team released three reports and a massive data archive on October 7, the 67th anniversary of when the Soviet Luna 3 spacecraft took the first photograph of the farside of the moon. The results offer a rare test of what trained human observers can add to lunar research and what NASA can learn for future missions to the lunar surface.
“We’re really excited to release all of this data,” earth scientist Sara Schmidt of NASA Johnson Space flight Cener in Houston said during the meeting. After six months of hard work, “this is enabling science to happen for the next, I don’t know, 60 years, if not more.”
How astronauts learn to observe the moon
Surprisingly, the most valuable data from the mission were not the mind-blowingly gorgeous photos, but the astronauts’ verbal and written descriptions of what they were seeing.
Before launch, the astronauts had extensive training in lunar geology and science observations. They were an extension of the science team, said field geologist Cindy Evans also of NASA Johnson Space Flight Center, one of the astronauts’ instructors.
“You could hear it in their voices. They understood the language of geology,” she said.
That training was meant to help answer a question Young hears often: What can humans add that a camera can’t?
During the flyby, the astronauts worked in pairs. Two of them spoke to mission control on the ground, giving periodic updates to the science team on what they were seeing. The other two recorded themselves describing their observations and reactions and used a stylus to annotate specially made maps of the moon that had been uploaded to their tablets during flight. Those notes, doodles and recordings were not made public until now.
The idea was to give the crew high tech field notebooks, Young says.
“If you have any field experience, you know your field notebook is your best friend,” she said in the meeting. On Earth, geologists capture nuance and context in written and spoken words, as well as sketches, she said. “We wanted to provide the ability to capture that nuanced information from the crew.”
One example of this was when Koch sketched her view of the Orientale basin, detailing differences in texture and layers around the crater.
“Sketches can be so powerful,” Young says. “They’re quick and dirty and that’s exactly the right thing to do. You’re capturing that nuance really quickly before it leaves your brain.”
Some of the most unique observations came during the 54 minutes when the moon eclipsed the sun, giving the astronauts a view of the solar corona, interplanetary dust and other stars and planets. That was a favorite moment for planetary scientist Jennifer Heldmann of NASA’s Ames Research Center in California.
“That audio showed their sheer joy and amazement in what they were seeing and where they were,” Heldmann says. “They were so blown away by what they were seeing, while also taking very relevant science observations.”
But some of the most affecting moments were when words failed. When Glover and Koch saw the Earth emerge from behind the moon, for a while all they could say was “Oh my gosh!”
“I guess I should be trying to describe it, but I mean, good grief,” Glover’s tablet recorded him saying.
“No, I tried, but it’s impossible,” Koch agreed. “You might be able to fly a spaceship and talk, but if you can see that and talk, you just ain’t right.”
Astronauts spotted tiny impacts on the moon
Another thing the astronauts were able to see during the eclipse were impact flashes — tiny blips of light marking where bits of rock hit the moon.
“It’s a pinpoint of light,” Hansen said in his recorded observations. “It’s not like a meteor, you didn’t see anything else, it’s just like a bloop.”
Before launch, the science team identified and prioritized observations they hoped the crew would be able to make during the flyby. Impact flashes were at the top of the list. Seeing the flashes would give scientists a way to estimate how often the moon is struck by incoming rocks, and how large those rocks are. That’s an important thing to know for protecting future missions where astronauts will walk on the surface or build a long-term moon base.
Scientists didn’t know whether the astronauts would see any flashes at all. They saw five. The flashes were “pinpricks of light lasting less than a second, with no color associated with the flash,” Heldmann said at the meeting.

Saudi social media looks different this week. Throughout the first six months of the war, the widespread response to Iranian attacks was posting images of the flag, the crown prince, and a prayer for the country. Now, following Houthi strikes on the kingdom, my social feeds (algo: female, Gen Z, relatively liberal) are full of soldiers saluting the flag, or reading the Quran beside missile racks.
Nationalist language has sharpened too: One viral post tells Saudis to defend their homeland and warns against âtraitorsâ who would âcast doubt on their loyalty.â Many are repeating the official mantra that âthere is no fear in the Saudi dictionary.â The framing of the war has also shifted, from a US conflict to the kingdomâs.

46963c10d759.text:
Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding and Zambiaâs state miner ZCCM-IH say they have patched up their financing dispute over Mopani Copper Mines. The statement skirted the charges in ZCCM-IHâs September letter, which accused IRH â part of Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayedâs International Holding Company â of failing to provide equity funding and taking on unapproved debt. Instead, the partners pointed to new joint-exploration projects, saying they âremain aligned on the long-term developmentâ of the mine, but left funding questions open.
The truce followed a meeting in Abu Dhabi between Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema and IRHâs CEO on the day the letter became public. IRH paid $620 million in 2024 for a 51% stake in Mopani as part of a deal worth more than $1 billion. Neither side can afford a fight: Zambia needs Gulf capital for its bid to more than triple copper output to 3 million tons a year, and IRH aims to lift Mopaniâs production from 66,369 tons in 2025 to 300,000 tons by 2029.

a839f9f7992c.text:
The sheer volume of properties selling in Dubai for $5 million-plus â even during wartime â has lured one of Los Angelesâ top luxury real estate agencies. Whether they will bring their Netflix reality show cameras is another question, but The Oppenheim Group, known for Selling Sunset, pressed ahead with opening a new office in September. Despite signs the premium segment is stalling, some brokers and developers say this is a much-needed correction in one of the worldâs hottest real estate markets that is helping to avert a market crash.
Jason Oppenheim, president of The Oppenheim Group, is among them. âNow you just have a slow burn, and thatâs exactly what you want in every real estate market,â he told the Financial Times. Another sign of confidence: A $1.4 billion extension of Dubaiâs financial hub is going ahead, selling units at the under-construction Four Seasons, Bloomberg reported.

37155f9f214f.text:
The deadliest week for civilians in the Gulf marks a turning point in the US-Iran war that has engulfed the Middle East from Beirut to Aden, and from Irbil to Salalah. Saudi Arabia stepped up strikes on Yemenâs Houthis after the group hit Riyadhâs airport 20 times this month, killing 17 people and injuring 333. Despite Riyadhâs considerable air defenses and vast military spending, the militants have been able to outsmart the systems using relatively cheap drones and missiles.
Iranian attacks on the Gulf have brought the region closer together, and the latest strikes by Tehranâs allies in Yemen have galvanized support for Saudi Arabia. Authorities in the region are reinforcing this message of unity: In todayâs Friday prayer sermons in Kuwait, imams were instructed to praise the kingdomâs support during Iraqâs 1990 invasion and condemn the Houthis. Similar expressions of support were also voiced in Bahrain, Qatar, and the UAE.
While security is by far the most pressing priority, new projections from the IMF have revealed the warâs deepening economic toll. Jihad Azour, the fundâs regional director, told Asharq Bloomberg that the Gulfâs financial reserves, diversified export routes, and government interventions have cushioned the shock. But the IMF now predicts a deeper contraction than previously expected, with GDP trailing pre-war forecasts even after energy production and trade recover.

b43a6b8e80eb.text:
Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?
A new version of Tesla's Roadster electric sports car, equipped with thrusters which apparently allow it to hover and turn in mid-air, has been unveiled in Texas.
"You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," the car firm's CEO Elon Musk said as he presented the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.
Musk said an audience was needed to prove the car "is not AI", before showing a demonstration of the Roadster driving up and off a steep ramp, spinning in the air, and landing using air jets.
But there are several reasons we're unlikely to see a flying car on our roads anytime soon, as the BBC's technology editor Zoe Kleinman explains.
Video editor: Serene Khalifeh

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of India's "cockroach" movement, and a few others were detained in Delhi as police tried to stop a protest demanding the resignation of the country's election chief.
Hundreds had gathered in Connaught Place, one of the capital's busiest commercial districts, waving Indian flags and shouting slogans despite a heavy security presence.
Police sealed off Central Park, the planned site of the protest, and deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel to prevent the gathering.
The Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) accuses India's Election Commission of manipulating voter lists to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling BJP. Both deny the allegation.
The group has held a series of protests in Delhi in recent weeks, with police repeatedly detaining its leaders and supporters. Friday's demonstration unfolded under similarly heavy security presence, though the police response was more restrained than during last weekend's sweeping crackdown.
Hours before the protest, police went to the house where Dipke was staying. In an exchange broadcast live on Instagram, he challenged officers who had come to caution him against holding the march, asking whether waving the Indian flag was against the law.
Hours later, the BBC saw officers surround Dipke as he approached his car and force him into a police vehicle. Some supporters tried to stop it from leaving.
It was Dipke's second detention in less than a week. Last Saturday, police had boarded his plane shortly after it landed in Delhi to prevent him from reaching another demonstration. He was released the following day.
The movement's two other main leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were also detained last weekend and later released. But on Wednesday, they were sent to jail for five days after returning to Jantar Mantar, a protest site near parliament that police had recently declared off-limits. Friday's march was partly intended to demand the release of Das and Ranka.
Dipke's detention means the movement's three main leaders are once again in custody.
The CJP said it had lost contact with him and accused police of taking him to an undisclosed location and denying him access to lawyers.
But they insist the arrests and detentions will not stop them. "They may detain three people, but how will they stop 30 tomorrow? How will they stop 300 leaders?" CJP spokesperson Mehr Pasricha told the BBC.
Police have not publicly confirmed the grounds for Dipke's detention or responded to the CJP's latest allegations.
Anish Gawande, the opposition politician who had been hosting Dipke, also questioned the police action.
"Detaining a lone man walking with the national flag in his hand is a bit of a joke," he said.
At Connaught Place, the police presence dwarfed the protest itself.
Around 200-300 people initially gathered outside Central Park, which authorities had closed. Unable to enter, they walked around its perimeter, waving Indian flags and shouting slogans. More protesters arrived as the evening progressed.
Officers kept emerging from buses parked around the district. Journalists crowded the streets too, and together with police, they far outnumbered the demonstrators.
For much of the evening, police largely held back, with the BBC witnessing only a handful of detentions. But as darkness fell, officers began using force against some protesters.
The BBC saw some young demonstrators being pushed into a bus where women were already being held. Inside were around 50 female officers, far more than the number of detainees.
The BBC also saw two people being injured during the police action. One protester fell to the ground and appeared to have hurt their leg.
Among those detained was Neha Bora, a prominent leader of the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) who has emerged as one of the faces of the recent protests. She had also been detained during last weekend's crackdown.
Barely five months old, the CJP began as an online campaign in May after India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches. Dipke embraced the insult and turned it into a rallying cry.
By July, the group had become a formidable force, drawing thousands of young people into protests over leaked exam papers. A march towards parliament in July descended into clashes with police, bringing the movement wider attention and intensifying pressure on the government. The unrest eventually forced the resignation of India's education minister.
The CJP has since turned its attention to India's electoral system, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a sweeping revision of voter lists known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
Critics say the exercise risks removing legitimate voters from the rolls, potentially depriving them of the right to vote. The Election Commission says it is targeting ineligible, dead and duplicate voters and denies allegations that it is favouring the ruling BJP.
Last weekend, authorities imposed severe restrictions to stop CJP supporters from reaching a planned rally, sealing off roads, shutting metro stations and deploying thousands of security personnel across Delhi.
The BBC witnessed, external dozens of protesters being detained across the capital, including students and journalists.
The action drew criticism but police defended it as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings.
Dipke, Das and Ranka were released the following day after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour. But the dispute over where they could protest was only beginning.
Police removed Jantar Mantar from Delhi's list of approved protest sites, naming three alternative venues.
Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory stands close to Parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent. The CJP accused authorities of trying to push demonstrations away from the seat of power.

eea31f97e4c6.text: Iran-backed militias in the region have been sending money back to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to relieve the economic pressure it's under after nine months of war , U.S. CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said Friday. Why it matters: While the U.S. military has been preparing for a possible resumption of major combat operations against Iran, the Trump administration continues to put immense pressure on the regime with its naval blockade and severe sanctions. U.S. officials say the economic chokehold is causing serious difficulties for Iran and its security forces, while making the regime frustrated and aggressive. The White House hopes the pressure will induce Iran to make a deal that includes nuclear concessions. But so far, that hasn't happened. Driving the news: Cooper said the naval blockade has cost Iran $25 billion in lost oil revenue. Additionally, CENTCOM and the Treasury Department have managed in recent weeks to freeze $350 million that Iran had in cryptocurrency. Behind the scenes: In a video message released Friday, Cooper revealed that Iran-backed groups such as Hezbollah, Hamas and Shia militias in Iraq — which have been funded by the IRGC for years — now have to give the money back. "The financial strain on Iran's military has become so significant that there are reports about Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments for their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also isn't paying its troops," he said. Cooper said the Iranian government is withholding salaries, pensions and benefits from public sector workers, including the internal security forces and the IRGC. State of play: Cooper attributed the significant increase in Iranian attacks against ships in the Strait of Hormuz to "desperation" within the IRGC. Despite those attacks, he said that the Strait of Hormuz is still open — with 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil moving through it over the last week. Yes, but: In recent weeks, CENTCOM has almost completely stopped conducting strikes against Iranian anti-ship missiles and attack drone launchers in the area of the strait. The pause in strikes, which was ordered by the White House to avoid escalating the war ahead of the midterm elections, made Iran more confident about launching attacks, a U.S. official said. Consequently, CENTCOM is concerned that the increase in ship attacks will cause shipping companies to think twice about transiting the strait — resulting in less oil coming out and a spike in oil prices. U.S. officials say Iran is also attacking more ships to try to raise oil prices and ratchet up pressure on Trump ahead of the midterms. What to watch: The White House and Qatari mediators are still waiting to hear back from Iran about a U.S. counterproposal to end the war. "It's still in internal deliberations in Tehran," a U.S. official said. Regional mediators told Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in recent days that Iran shouldn't wait until after the midterms to give its response, a regional source with direct knowledge said. The regional mediators told Iran there's no guarantee that Trump will be more conciliatory after the midterms — on the contrary, he might be more aggressive.

The News
John Thune took criticism from President Donald Trump, agitated online conservatives, and occasionally frustrated some of his own members this year.
Yet his next leadership election is looking smooth compared with the past couple of bouts to lead the Senate GOP. In fact, Thune may actually run unopposed this year, regardless of how the midterms go.
âIâm not aware of anyone who wants the job. I certainly donât,â Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., told Semafor. âI donât envy the leaderâs task.â Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who challenged Thune in 2024 and Mitch McConnell in 2022, told Semafor thereâs âno wiggle room; I am not running for leaderâ this cycle. He said Thune is âprobably the only person thatâs going to run. But I always want to say if other people run and someone comes up with better ideas, youâve got to listen to them. But Iâm not running.â
Know More
The biggest headache for Thune was the Save America Act, a voter ID bill that lacked a strategy to become law in the Senate. Trump repeatedly leaned on Thune to kill the filibuster in order to pass it, and other senators wanted Thune to try to force Democrats to pull off a talking filibuster to block the bill.
Eventually, though, the effort and outrage over its stalled status faded away. With Democrats favored to win the House and potentially even take the Senate, the fight over killing the filibuster is back on ice.
Thatâs all good news for Thune, who says heâll likely run for another term regardless of whether Republicans lose the Senate. If no one challenges him, it would be the first unanimous GOP leadership election since 2020. Notably, Johnson had backed Scott in previous leadership races.
Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, told reporters on Thursday that Thune âwill get elected pretty resoundingly.â
âDo I think heâs got broad support? Yes. I donât think thereâs an insurgent movement thatâs against him,â Moreno said. âThereâs not a single Republican running nationally thatâs saying, âHey, if you elect me, Iâll vote against John Thune as leader.ââ
Several Democratic candidates say they wonât support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for another term as leader of their caucus. But no one is indicating they are looking to challenge Schumer, either, which means those could just be protest votes. Former Democratic leader Harry Reid received a handful of ânoâ votes in his leadership race after losing control of the Senate in 2014.
Republicans will have their leadership election on Nov. 10; Senate Democrats are likely to have theirs in early December, although the date isnât set yet. The midterm results remain an X factor for both Thune and Schumerâs futures.

President Donald Trump faces a deadline Sunday to decide whether to impose certain penalties on other countries under a bipartisan sanctions law he signed last month.
Any move by him to waive sanctions on Russian individuals or entities will be met with criticism, as would a decision not to impose tariffs on China for buying Russian gas. But Washington is hoping heâll spare at least one country: India.
âBoth the United States and India should not buy Russian oil and gas, but I donât think simply imposing big tariffs on India is the way to get them toâ reduce their purchases, said Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security.
Punishing India for its reliance on Russian energy âwould deal a body blow to the US-India relationship,â argued Sadanand Dhume, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.
The US and India are currently locked in trade negotiations, which more tariffs would surely disrupt. Fontaine said it is â100%â possible that the Trump administration uses the sanctions law to pressure India to give in to its demands in those discussions. Trump had previously hiked tariffs on India over its Russian energy purchases, but later removed them as trade talks progressed.
Asked whether Trump had made a decision on which sanctions, if any, to impose at the deadline, a White House official said that he âsigned the act and the administration will comply with the actâs requirements.â The bill gives the president broad power to waive penalties if he deems it in the US interest.

b7876ef2b2d8.text: By — Deepa Bharath, Associated Press Deepa Bharath, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/community-leaders-say-foiled-hindu-temple-attack-was-result-of-surge-in-online-hate Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Community leaders say foiled Hindu temple attack was result of surge in online hate Nation Oct 16, 2026 4:02 PM EDT A thwarted mass shooting targeting a large Hindu temple in suburban Chicago was fueled by years of hateful rhetoric on social media against Hindus and Indians, community leaders say. WATCH: Social media's role in fueling extremism and misinformation in a divided political climate Authorities on Wednesday arrested Alexandros Paporakis, 19, who they said drove to the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, Illinois, on Sunday afternoon, armed with a rifle and body armor. Officials said he remained in the parking lot for several minutes, but left after his weapon jammed. Paporakis was arrested later that day near his home in Palatine, Illinois, after a co-worker at a Taco Bell alerted authorities to his plan to "kill Indian people." The temple, the largest in Aurora, was crowded Sunday with thousands observing the first day of Navaratri, a nine-night celebration of Shakti -- the divine feminine energy believed to be foundational to all creation. U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who represents Illinois' 8th congressional district, said he and his parents were inside the temple Sunday afternoon. "Little did we know there was an attacker outside with sinister intent," he said Thursday. "This has really shaken us." During a news conference Friday morning in Chicago, Krishnamoorthi stood with several other faith and civic leaders calling for the attempted mass shooting to be investigated as a hate crime. Speakers also called for an organized community response to prevent hate and extremism targeting all communities. Hindus face online hate and real-world threats Pushpita Prasad, a spokesperson for the Coalition of Hindus of North America, said attacks against Hindus and Indians have been escalating in recent years. She said the racial slurs are increasingly visible online. "You see vitriolic posts associating Indians with dirt and creating disgust about their appearance, food and cultural practices," she said. "Sooner or later, all that online hate is going to migrate to the real world." Over the past two years, the rising wave of anti-Hindu hate has included a rash of vandalism and attacks across the country. Most recently, on Oct. 3, vandals hurled bricks at a Hindu temple in Richmond Heights, Ohio, shattering several windows while devotees were praying inside. In June 2025, a gunman fired bullets into the Sri Sri Radha Krishna Temple in Spanish Fork, Utah, causing thousands of dollars in damage. In Sugar Land, Texas, a 90-foot statue of the deity Hanuman, consecrated in 2024 at a temple complex, continues to draw disparaging comments, including one YouTube personality who recently urged its demolition. In Frisco, Texas, where people of Indian origin make up about one-third of the population, speakers have used public comment periods during city council meetings to label the Indian community as "invaders," characterize Hindu temples as a threat and accuse H-1B work visa holders of stealing American jobs or committing fraud. Leaders call for resources to combat hate and extremism Temple administrators in Aurora issued a statement Thursday assuring the community that they value the safety of devotees, employees and volunteers, and have implemented additional security measures including an "armed security presence." Krishnamoorthi said the temple, situated on 20 acres, is a cultural hub for the community in the Chicago area. It has been his family's home away from home for about 40 years, he said. "For people who were newly immigrated, this became their connection to the homeland," Krishnamoorthi said. The temple serves as a venue for concerts, dance performances, birthdays and weddings, and the cafeteria that serves South Indian cuisine is popular, he said. Krishnamoorthi called for the FBI to prosecute this incident as a hate crime, and for social media companies to end the hateful rhetoric online. "The FBI also needs to redirect resources to combat domestic violent extremism," he said. "Election fraud and immigration are not the biggest threats facing our country." Joel Finkelstein with the New Jersey-based Network Contagion Research Institute, which tracks cyber-social threats, said in 2025, anti-Indian content on X tripled in weekly volume. The administration's changes in immigration policies, particularly relating to the H1-B visa, corresponded with measurable surges in racial slurs and deportation rhetoric targeting Indians, he said. Amid the increase in online hate, Finkelstein said the South Asian community in the U.S., despite significant resources, lacks the ability to advocate for itself with strength and unity. "There is nothing to stop it from getting worse," he said. Advocates say xenophobia has fueled hate Sravya Tadepalli, executive director of Hindus for Human Rights, says her organization has formed strong coalitions with Muslim, Sikh and other organizations whose members also face hate. "It's important to understand that rhetoric is not just rhetoric," she said. "It is harmful and can result in violence." Manjusha P. Kulkarni, co-founder of Stop AAPI Hate, said her organization's research showed that online slurs targeting South Asians rose 109% from 2023 to 2025. Statistics aside, Kulkarni said she was personally shaken by the threat in Illinois. "It hits all of us who are temple goers," she said. "Seeing how going to my house of worship can put me and my children at risk is very scary." AAPI Hate pointed to "xenophobic policies and rhetoric" that depict Indian people as a demographic threat — including Vice President JD Vance calling H1-B workers "indentured servants" an

Marines fielding new tech for prolonged medical care on the battlefield
Mobile blood refrigeration, ultrasounds, and power generation will keep troops alive beyond the “golden hour.”
The Marine Corps is preparing for a future battlefield on which the injuries are the same but the ability to quickly fly troops to a trauma hospital is very limited. To close that gap, the service is fielding new tech like mobile blood banks and ultrasounds, with a self-contained power source to keep them running.
The Expeditionary Medical Refrigeration Unit and Mobile and the MEQU mobile blood warmer were deployed to U.S. Central Command this year, where a unit set up a continuous mobile blood bank and sent their notes back to the Marine Corps on how to make it better, officials told reporters Friday during a media round table.
“We were told that the EMRU was instrumental to their ability to maintain a revolving blood bank to ensure that they had what they needed to be ready to care for injured service members,” said Navy Cmdr. Kyleigh Hupfl, clinic for Expeditionary Medical Systems.
The concept of the “golden hour,” the critical time period after a casualty that made all the difference in getting a wounded service member from the battlefield to hospital triage during the Global War on Terror, will be much more complicated in a near-peer fight.
While ground fighters could sometimes shoot down a medevac helicopter in Iraq or Afghanistan, an enemy with more sophisticated surveillance and missile technology will mean commanders have to wait to call in evacuations and work to stabilize casualties on site for much longer than in more recent conflicts.
“We're leaving the golden hour behind, and we're moving toward those longer patient-care hold times,” said Col. Paul Gillikin, program manager for Combat Support systems. “Again, fully recognizing the future fight against a peer competitor, over those great distances in the Pacific—we know that we're not going to have the developed [forward operating bases], the full mobility, the Iron Mountain.”
The No. 1 cause of battlefield death is severe bleeding, so being able to not only slow bleeding but give transfusions on site will be crucial.
“We need to be able to bring cold-chain distribution forward without relying on heavy generators, and we need to be able to do that in a sustainable way. We need to be able to warm that blood so that we don't get that patient in a worse-off situation,” Hupfl said. “We need to be able to see, after that, whether they have continued bleeding, so that the commander can make a risk decision on putting an evacuation asset at risk to get that patient out.”
That’s where the battery-powered EMRU and the associated blood warmer come in, as a mobile system that keeps blood products refrigerated, then heats them to body temp for quick transfusions. The Corps is also fielding the KOSMOS point-of-care ultrasound to assess internal bleeding, and the Marine Corps Squad Power Manager medical kit variant to keep them all running.
“We expect in the Marine Corps to be in distributed environments, where the evacuation will be delayed or contested,” said Brig. Gen. Tamara Campbell, deputy commander of Portfolio Acquisition Executive Marine Corps. “And so the equipment that we're looking at is to take that into account, regardless of the time it takes to apply that care. We need to do that at any time so that any of our soldiers, sailors, Marines—anybody that's within our operating environment needs that level of care.”
