The State Department is updating its travel advisory for mainland China to include an increased risk level for wrongful detention, according to a new plan seen by Semafor.
The State Departmentâs move comes after two US citizens were labeled as wrongfully detained earlier this year, and at a complex moment in the relationships between the two most powerful countries in the world. Despite a personally warm relationship between the presidents, the countriesâ deep differences from the Taiwan Strait to trade to artificial intelligence remain.
A person familiar with the situation told Semafor the departmentâs change is connected to the continued detentions of the two Americans, Min Zin and Youlin Chen. Zin is a Myanmar scholar who was detained in June and accused of endangering Chinaâs national security. Chen is a seismologist detained in 2024 and charged with espionage. Both are US citizens.
The travel advisory as a whole remains at a Level 2, which urges Americans to âExercise Increased Cautionâ when traveling to China, but the department is adding a âDâ risk indicator for wrongful detention. Previously, the travel advisory for mainland China had an âOâ risk indicator, which meant that there were âother potential risks not coveredâ by the departmentâs specific risk categories.
âThe U.S. Department of State has determined that Americans are at serious risk of wrongful detention in China,â a State Department spokesman said in a statement to Semafor. âThe D risk indicator means the State Department has determined Americans are at risk of wrongful detention by the government of the country.â
A group of bipartisan senators introduced a resolution last month pushing the department to add the wrongful detention indicator to its travel advisory, citing the two detained citizens.
The spokesman added that wrongful detention is determined by a variety of factors, including having US citizenship or a connection to the US. This is the latest update to the State Departmentâs China travel advisory â in early September, the department added stronger warnings about wrongful detention, the âarbitrary enforcement of local laws,â and the usage of exit bans.
Asked why the travel advisory remains at a Level 2 given the new wrongful detention label, the spokesman said it âidentifies a specific risk of wrongful detentionâ and that âthe overall Travel Advisory level reflects a broader assessment of safety and security conditions.â

ab741c1a3f7c.text: Have some sympathy for Capitol Hill's leaders next year, no matter who wins in November. 😩 Why it matters: The next Congress promises a thousand different ways to be miserable. And three of the big four leaders are expected to receive a two-year contract extension, with guaranteed long nights, bad days and short tempers. The fate of the fourth — Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) — rests on the outcome of the election. 🤕 The best (and worst) news for Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is that the job as party leader is likely his if he wants it, even if Republicans lose the majority. Like his first two years as leader, Thune's next two will be marked by constant second-guessing , or worse, from a president who commands his party, crushes his opponents and questions Thune's courage . Then there's the GOP base. MAGA influencers are seething over Thune's reluctance to try to nuke the filibuster and jam through a voter-ID bill . Between the lines: Four of Thune's confidants — DHS Secretary (and former senator) Markwayne Mullin and Sens. Steve Daines (R-Mont.), Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas) — have left or are leaving the building. A fresh class of House conservatives will arrive in the Senate. They're likely to want to move fast and break things. The intrigue: Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) has not announced a third attempt to lead his party, but plenty of Republicans on the Hill suspect he will. Scott notably backtracked on his support for Thune in September. But Thune doesn't have to worry about his number two. Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) — who would be the top contender if Thune stepped down — has doubled down on his support. ⚠️ Thune's relationship with Speaker Johnson has been rocky throughout the year . If Republicans lose the House majority, Thune could find himself coordinating and strategizing with a new House leader. Most of Johnson's colleagues don't expect him to stay if the House flips. However, in the campaign's final weeks, Johnson has been playing Hamlet , publicly entertaining his next moves. With or without Johnson on stage, Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) are widely viewed as top contenders. 😎 Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) appears secure in his job as Democratic leader. His longevity in the role — or the Senate — is not. He's up for reelection in 2028 and could face a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). Many Democrats expect him to retire. One possible result: YOLO Chuck , a 76-year-old majority leader with an angry base and ambitious colleagues, but nothing to lose. 🤬 One urgent task for Schumer is to get on the same page as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), whose progressive members have some strong feelings about Schumer and the Senate. Jeffries and Schumer took dramatically different approaches to funding the government in March 2025. These differences would be harder to manage in the majority, especially if Jeffries struggles to maintain discipline within his ranks. However, Jeffries — like Schumer and Thune — doesn't appear to have any formidable challengers for party leader. Jeffries could face many of the same headaches Johnson did — a wing of his party that ran on anti-establishment principles and whose votes cannot be counted on . What we're watching: Trump and Schumer have a complicated relationship . But the president has indicated he sees Jeffries as someone he could work with.

6eb0247622ef.text: By — Gabriela Aoun Angueira, Associated Press Gabriela Aoun Angueira, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/la-fire-survivors-set-to-lose-case-managers-as-california-and-femas-standoff-drags-on Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter LA fire survivors set to lose case managers as California and FEMA's standoff drags on Politics Oct 16, 2026 3:43 PM EDT ALTADENA, Calif. (AP) — Throughout the arduous process to rebuild the Altadena home where she lived for nearly 50 years, Mary Landau has sometimes felt like giving up. Much of what has sustained her is the encouragement she receives from her disaster case manager. "She said, 'You can do this,'" said Landau, a 78-year-old retired teacher who enjoys studying Altadena history and cannot imagine living anywhere else, even after the Eaton Fire destroyed her house. "She gave me hope and strength." WATCH: A year after the devastating LA wildfires, communities struggle with rebuilding Landau meets weekly with Veda Ashby Romero, a trained recovery expert who helps her navigate insurance, complete online forms and qualify for financial assistance. Now Landau is one of roughly 1,400 households affected by the 2025 Los Angeles fires who are set to lose their disaster case managers by the end of October, as a standoff between California and the Federal Emergency Management Agency over the program's funding drags on. The news has rattled Landau. "The safety net has been pulled out from under me, and the hope is not as strong as it was," she said. The program's early termination is the latest setback for LA communities in the middle of recovery and awaiting billions of additional federal dollars. It also highlights how some disaster-impacted communities still face issues like delayed FEMA payments and inconsistent communication, despite President Donald Trump's administration pledging to streamline processes after long criticizing the agency's bureaucracy. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. FEMA did not respond to a request for comment but has previously touted the assistance it has provided for the program. The White House says California has mismanaged the crisis. Case managers simplify a notoriously opaque recovery process Landau kept her insurance policy up to date for the 1938 two-bedroom, one-bathroom ranch home where she raised her three children and tended a wildflower garden. She still faced a shortfall of at least $200,000 to rebuild the modest home and owed $225,000 on her mortgage. Ashby Romero supports her through the insurance process — a tedious one that has involved multiple adjusters and required creating an inventory of the half-century's worth of possessions she lost. She also found Landau a grant to cover a year's worth of mortgage payments. "I would never have gotten it without her," Landau said. "I'm very bad with paperwork." Trained disaster case managers help people find rental assistance, new employment and money to close the gap between what insurance pays and the actual cost to rebuild. They guide survivors on how to avoid scams, challenge insurance payouts and appeal FEMA decisions. "The recovery process is very complicated, and a lot of the systems are not designed to make it easy for people," said Matt Gsell, disaster recovery manager at CORE, the nonprofit managing Landau's case and one of five participating in LA's case management program. Late reimbursements and insufficient funds led California to end the program After the January 2025 fires, California requested $28 million for case management. FEMA instead awarded $13.2 million for 24 months, to be paid in four equal installments. FEMA can fund disaster case management for presidentially declared major disasters. The money is reimbursed to the state, which usually contracts with one or more nonprofits to administer the program. In the case of an exceptional disaster, states can request extensions for up to 36 months. By August, FEMA had made only one of the four payments, leaving the state to front the rest despite "numerous requests" for reimbursement, according to the California Department of Social Services. FEMA also had not answered a March request for an additional $6.5 million to sustain the program the full 24 months, in light of high demand. Seven hundred households remain on a waitlist for services. California then announced it could no longer float the costs and would shutter the program at the end of October. FEMA eventually reimbursed the outstanding payments but did not give an answer about the additional money. Rep. Judy Chu, a Democrat whose district includes Altadena, told The Associated Press that FEMA also had not responded to questions from her office about the additional money. US President Donald Trump has denied limiting Ukraine's access to Starlink's sister internet network Starshield after it restricted drone speed, hampering Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.
"It wasn't me and I don't think it was [Starlink owner] Elon [Musk]," Trump said, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said speed had yet to be restored.
Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions, while Reuters news agency reported on Thursday that the order had come from inside the White House.
Ukraine was hit by several deadly strikes on Tuesday after the network slowdown.
Starlink is a civilian-use high-speed internet network operated by Musk's SpaceX. Starshield - which relies on Starlink- is its military-grade sister service that was designed for the Pentagon.
The US had previously warned it could withhold sharing intelligence, crucial for Kyiv's defences, if Ukraine did not stop hitting Russian oil refineries.
Tension has been brewing between Washington and Kyiv for days over a recent controversial diesel deal between Russia and the US.
Zelensky - angered by the deal - resumed targeting Russian oil refineries this week in a move criticised by Trump three days after he announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Kyiv said it would stop the strikes if Russia did the same but Moscow never confirmed the ceasefire and continued its attacks.
"If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" Zelensky asked EU leaders at a summit on Friday.
Trump had also said that Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".
But speaking to reporters as he left the White House on Friday, the US president said he had a good relationship with his Ukrainian counterpart.
Asked about Starshield, he said he was "not sure" it "ever came down".
Musk earlier explained that Starshield was managed by the US government, and that the Pentagon could have been responsible.
In its report about the alleged order regarding Starshield, Reuters quoted two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.
The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.
On Tuesday night, Starlink restricted speed limits to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.
Some 600,000 in Ukraine were left without power as communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military were also hit in the deadly attacks.
A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an investigation into the disruptions to the network.
"Restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure," the letter read.
On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron vowed that EU states would not abandon Ukraine.
Speaking at the end of the two-day summit in Brussels attended by Zelensky, Macron said it was Europe's job to hold the line in the face of some people's "ambiguities". That was apparently a reference to signs of wavering US support for Ukraine.
Funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another freezing winter - its fifth since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - topped the summit's agenda.
The war will cost â¬155bn (Â£131bn; $174bn) next year, Zelensky told the European Council, with at least â¬70bn needed to come from the EU for defence and weapons.
Macron said Europe was working to help Ukraine with its satellite and early warning systems, and Ukraine's friends would look at its request for further aid.

3d6fb390e610.text: An October shooting by federal immigration officers in New York City has led to a head-turning show of unity from House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Why it matters: This unlikely collaboration between leaders of Democrats' competing establishment and progressive wings shows how opposing Trump-era immigration enforcement has become an area of party consensus. Democrats "are definitely unified across the spectrum re ICE," Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the chair of the Queens Democratic Party and a close ally of Jeffries, told Axios. He added that "the Mayor has also reached out ... to me in regards to local issues and I believe Leader Jeffries is also indicating he wants to work with the NY Congressional delegation." Driving the news: Mamdani led a letter dated Oct. 16 with over 100 other Democratic elected officials in New York City, including every Democratic member of the city's congressional delegation, to parking lot and garage owners. "In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent, lend, or otherwise make your property available to ICE as a staging area for its enforcement operations," the letter reads. The officials argued that the shooting of 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in New York's Marble Hill neighborhood in early October was "not an isolated case," pointing to past instances in Queens and Manhattan . "Owners who refuse to take part in these federal civil immigration enforcement operations advance public safety by protecting their own staff and customers, as well as fellow New Yorkers beyond their lots and garages." Between the lines: Jeffries and Mamdani have walked a careful line as two of the most prominent national figures within their respective Democratic Party factions. Jeffries rankled the left, including some members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, by waiting until 11 days before last year's election to endorse Mamdani for mayor. The two came into conflict this summer when Jeffries supported Democratic Reps. Dan Goldman and Adriano Espaillat while Mamdani campaigned hard for their primary challengers, though the Democratic leader notably downplayed the clash . Yes, but: The two have also had other notable moments of accord, such as when Mamdani opposed City Councilmember Chi Ossé 's ultimately aborted plan to try to primary Jeffries from the left. They also appeared together at a ribbon-cutting for a housing development in Brooklyn on Thursday. Zoom out: The letter's signers also include Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who accused then-candidate Mamdani last year of making "references to global jihad," for which she later apologized . Goldman and Espaillat, who were ultimately unseated by their Mamdani-backed challengers, signed on as well. So did retiring Rep. Nydia Velázquez, who was burned by Mamdani endorsing Claire Valdez over her chosen successor, according to the New York Times . What we're hearing: "It's significant to see Mayor Mamdani lead a letter like this that includes both U.S. Senators and the full NYC Democratic House delegation (including the two he opposed in this spring's primaries)," a prominent Mamdani ally said in a text message to Axios. The person added: "It reflects both how universally hated ICE is by Democrats — and how much work the mayor has done to build bridges." The Mamdani ally spoke on the condition of anonymity to offer candid analysis of the delicate relationship between the mayor and the party establishment. The bottom line: Others argued that Democratic unity around opposing ICE was the overriding factor. One Democratic elected official from New York told Axios: "The fact that everyone signed on has more to do with the power of the issue than the power of the Mayor." A person in Jeffries' orbit similarly argued that immigration is simply "a unifying issue for Dems," but acknowledged that Mamdani "is consistently reaching out to the delegation to build ties and smooth things since the elections, which is smart."

77aab25361a9.text: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was ousted Friday after just five days on the job, according to two senior Trump administration officials. Why it matters: Zacharia will be the shortest-tenured press secretary in modern history, with her first and only week in the White House marked by speculation about her legal credentials and criticism of her first press briefing. Trump told reporters Friday that he had urged Zacharia to "reconsider" the job, saying: "The news has been so nasty to her. I've never seen anything like it actually. And I said to her, 'honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider." "POTUS is a big fan of Katie's, and what POTUS said to the reporters is exactly what he said in private," a senior White House official said. Her five-day beats out Anthony Scaramucci's 11 days during Trump's first term. That led to his last name becoming synonymous with a unit of measurement known as "A Scaramucci." Driving the news: Zacharia was seen as a surprise pick when Trump announced her hiring on Oct. 9. She started work the following Monday, Oct. 12, and gave her first — and likely only — press briefing the following day. In that press conference, she was visibly shaky and nervous and left the president unimpressed, a White House official told Axios. Trump was also "blindsided" when he learned she wasn't an "attorney" as he had posted on Truth Social when he announced her hire. Zacharia tried to do damage control after a Wall Street Journal report that she wasn't licensed to practice law in any U.S. state. She told Fox News that she failed the exam and never retook it, since she was moving to China But her interview explanations weren't seen as up to snuff by Trump, the source said. Background: Zacharia's hiring was solely a Trump decision, one furthered along with the strong input of his personal assistant Natalie Harp. Zacharia flew out Thursday to Washington, slipped quietly into the White House without seeing any friends in the media or administration and had a good meeting with Trump. On Friday, Trump offered her the job on the spot. Contrary to other reports, Trump told Chief of Staff Susie Wiles his decision. Wiles, who did not know Zacharia before, raised no objections because she knew the press secretary job is a personal one for the president, another administration source said. Before hiring Zacharia , Trump wanted to hire former Fox News host Maria Bartiromo, two administration sources said, but she signaled she was not going to take the job. Conservative commentator Scott Jennings was in contention but wasn't offered the job. Behind the scenes: Zacharia's arrival concerned some staffers who feared she wanted to replace them. Zacharia denied this and tried to put their minds at ease. A White House official told Axios that Zacharia and her family are having dinner tonight with Vice President Vance and Vance's family at the VP's residence at the Naval Observatory. "The warmth for Katie goes well beyond the president," the official said. What we're watching: Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy said he spoke with Trump on Friday and that the president is in "no rush" to name a replacement for the press secretary. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout. Go deeper: Trump press secretary explains failed bar exam Barak Ravid contributed to this story.

The real job of the Army’s new ‘robotics technicians’ is constant adaptation
The age of battlefield autonomy demands more than just drone pilots and mechanics, Special Forces’ training chief says.
You likely have a picture of the future of drone-assisted warfare: a soldier in a trench or a bunker, eyes enveloped in a virtual reality headset, hands clasping a controller, attention on targets below the drone he steers. But the reality of robot-assisted soldiering has already moved elsewhere, according to the military leaders who are training elite forces for future conflict.
On Oct. 2, 10 warrant officers became the Army’s first robotics technicians under the new 390A military occupational specialty. On Tuesday, Maj. Gen. Jason Slider, who commands the U.S. Army John F. Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School at Fort Bragg, described how their jobs will go far beyond remotely piloting or maintaining a drone or ground robot.
“It's important that it's not a pilot. We're not building a pilot. What we're building is a soldier that can adapt a piece of robotic kit to the mission, to the enemy, to the terrain,” Slider said at a Defense One event on the sidelines of the AUSA annual conference.
He described this as one of the most important lessons to emerge from Ukraine in terms of designing doctrine and training for the age of battlefield autonomy.
“We looked at the Nagorno-Karabakh, at Ukraine, and we're studying the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East,” he said. Militaries that “solely focus on pilots quickly lose the advantage to an adversary or an enemy force that can adapt that piece of tech to the mission.”
Adaptation was key to Azerbaijan's 2020 victory over Armenia in Nagorno-Karabakh. A 2021 report from the Center for Army Lessons Learned describes an Azerbaijani tactic in which “remotely piloted Soviet-era AN-2 biplanes flew at low altitudes as decoys to force the Armenians to respond against the perceived threat,” a use of robotics to surprise and confuse the enemy, not just drop bombs on them.
The United States used a similar tactic in the Middle East at the outset of Operation Epic Fury earlier this year, swarming Iranian forces with cheap drones modeled after the Shahed drones that Iran was using against U.S. forces. Both cases show the importance of deploying robotics, autonomy, and semiautonomy in ways the enemy had not yet predicted.
Chief Warrant Officer 5 Michael Updike, one of the architects of the 390A program, said at the Defense One event that the robotics technician military specialty will include aspects of intelligence analysis, command and control, communications, software development under extremely difficult and disconnected conditions, and even acquisition.
“What it encompasses is different pillars of not only software engineering and mechanical engineering but your data science, understanding research and development,” Updike said. “They have to do all that innovation in the field without…large-language models that are connected to the internet.”
The job will also entail rapidly inventing new capabilities on the ground, much as Ukrainian forces have done, and working with contractors who can do so as well.
During the first phase of the 19-week 390A training course, a group of students improved hardware and software to allow drones under electromagnetic attack to communicate with one another in a mesh network.
“They took a high-definition, $1,000 camera, put it on this quadcopter. They were being jammed in frequencies but they were using a mesh network. So, even though one node was taken out, they had multiple nodes where they could still have communications with the quadcopter or the unmanned drone to be able to still accomplish that mission,” Updike said.
To teach the skills of constant adaptation, Slider said, much of the course is designed to “drive failure” and force reconsideration. That’s something that the course architects themselves had to do when f, the students began, in Slider’s words, “outpacing the curriculum” four weeks in. They were too good at drone warfare, which meant that the course wasn’t hard enough. So Slider worked with academics, sources, and international partners to make the course more difficult, adding additional weeks of training.
“The problems that they were able to solve during the culminating exercise were much closer to the need that the operational force was communicating to us,” the general said.
The 390A program won’t be limited to Fort Bragg. This week, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said, “Traditionally, historically, those types of [military occupational specialty] might live at — with the special forces and never be proliferated throughout the Army.”
Telle said that his office was working with the office responsible for special operations and low-intensity conflict to expand the specialty but did not provide further details.

Candidates running for the US Senate in next month's midterm elections have taken to the debate stage over the past few weeks - with some heated exchanges and stinging personal attacks.
As the 3 November election approaches and parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged, particularly within some of the hotly-contested Senate races.
Here's what you need to know.
1. Not all Republicans are standing behind Trump
Republicans running for office are facing the same question they have been asked in elections since 2016: how aligned are they with President Donald Trump?
Conservatives who have bucked the president in the past have generally not fared well with voters.
The president has seen low approval ratings in recent months, with polls suggesting voters are largely concerned with the cost of living and high fuel prices.
While some Republican candidates have remained in lockstep with Trump, a Reuters analysis indicated, external that two-thirds of candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this election cycle.
Susan Collins, a Maine Republican running for her sixth term in the Senate who has repeatedly broken with Trump, is again putting clear distance between herself and the president.
"I voted with President Biden 91% of the time," Collins said during a debate last week.
"The fact is, this year alone, this Congress alone, I voted against President Trump 137 times," she said.
Collins is fighting a tighter Senate race than she expected against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. A New York Times/Siena University poll from mid-September suggests Collins could be ahead in that race by 3%, while others indicate Jackson is in the lead.
Elsewhere, some Republican candidates are choosing to separate themselves from the Trump administration's specific policy decisions, while expressing loyalty to Trump himself.
In Iowa, traditionally a Republican stronghold, Congresswoman Ashley Hinson is facing a tougher-than-expected challenge in her Senate race.
She is taking on Democrat Josh Turek, and some polls suggest he has a narrow lead.
Hinson has not gone as far as Maine's Collins in separating herself from Trump, but she has broken with the president on some policy points.
During a 13 October debate with Turek, Hinson was asked about the Trump administration striking a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes to the US, followed by several other shipments.
The Republican candidate did not mince her words: "We need to lower gas prices in this country, we need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it."
2. Personal attacks are a common theme
As they have debated in recent weeks, the candidates haven't held back on deploying pointed personal attacks against their opponents.
The race for the vacant Michigan Senate seat - between rivals Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, and Mike Rogers, a Republican - has seen its fair share.
Rogers, a Trump-backed former congressman, questioned during a debate whether anyone in his Muslim opponent's family might be on a "watchlist".
El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, pushed back strongly.
He called the Republican "a sock puppet for the Trump administration" and said he was "weak, cowardly [and] won't stand up until his poll numbers drop".
On Thursday, as a protester interrupted a Maine debate between Jackson and Collins, who suggested that the person interrupting the debate was associated with her opponent.
Jackson then said to Collins: "Oh shut up, I don't even know that kid."
Further south in Georgia, more personal attacks were exchanged between incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Representative Mike Collins, a Trump-backed Republican.
What started as an exchange where Ossoff accused Collins of taking money out of Georgians' hands to give to data centre developers, quickly turned into a hurling of insults that included Ossoff calling Collins a "bigot" who has "hired half the Third Reich".
Incendiary posts on social media from Collins' son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, have become a point of contention in the race.
In one post, Scheer blamed "Israel and Zionist Jews" for policies he said were intended to "undermine the white, Christian nature of America".
Collins defended himself by accusing Ossoff of "spewing" "craziness".
"I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don't care where the source is," the Republican said.
3. Some candidates are skipping debates entirely
There are 35 Senate seats up for grabs this November, but in 21 there are no debates scheduled among the main candidates, an ABC News analysis found.
One race's lack of debates has surprised many observers: the Texas contest between James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, and Ken Paxton, a Republican and former state attorney general.
Polls in the typically Republican state suggest that Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win. Should he succeed, he could help give Democrats control of the US Senate by flipping one of the four seats they need to create a majority.
Talarico has accepted four debate invitations from different news networks. Paxton, meanwhile, has not accepted any of those invitations.
In July, Paxton's campaign spokesperson told media outlets that he would debate Talarico. But since then, the campaign, and Paxton, have said little on the matter. Trump, who backed Paxton in the Republican primaries, has even urged the candidates to debate.
"One thing about not showing up is you lose the opportunity to make the case for yourself, and instead, what you do is you give your opponent the ability and the opportunity to make your case as negative as possible," Peter Trumbore, a political science professor at Oakland University, told the BBC's US partner CBS News last month.

42a8120d018d.text: By — Haven Daley, Associated Press Haven Daley, Associated Press By — Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/man-who-stopped-the-oregon-elementary-school-shooter-has-2-daughters-at-the-school-his-mom-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Man who stopped the Oregon elementary school shooter has 2 daughters at the school, his mom says Nation Oct 16, 2026 3:01 PM EDT BEND, Ore. (AP) — The man who stopped a deadly elementary school attack in Oregon by shooting the teenage gunman inside the building is the father of two girls at the school, his mother said Friday. In a statement read to reporters Friday, Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, intervened in Thursday's attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend and shot the teenage shooter. Three students and a teacher were killed in the attack, and a fourth student and another teacher were critically injured. READ MORE: Teen shooter kills 4 at Oregon elementary school before being shot by a witness "He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support," Freeman said, noting that her son is a lifelong resident of Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 in central Oregon that has grown quickly in recent decades. Police have not yet identified who shot the gunman, only saying that the suspect was found dead inside the school minutes after the shooting was first reported. They also haven't named the gunman. At a news conference hours after Thursday's attack, Gov. Tina Kotek — without naming him — praised Giamanco for following the gunman into the school, saying he helped end the rampage and likely saved lives as police began arriving on the scene. "To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," said Kotek. Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a densely packed neighborhood filled with newly built homes. Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartner at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that a member of the public pursued the shooter. "I think it's miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening," Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. "I'm feeling very grateful." The shooter used a gun bought by his mom A makeshift memorial at a sign marking the Silver Rail Elementary School near a cordoned-off area, following a shooting, in Bend, Oregon, on Oct. 16, 2026. Photo by David Ryder/Reuters The 16-year-old suspect, identified only as a Bend resident, was found dead inside the school minutes after the first calls for help, Police Chief Mike Krantz said. Police said he got into the school by shooting through locked doors. The children who were killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. Authorities didn't give details about the teacher who was killed. Another 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded in the attack and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, he said. The attacker used a pump-action shotgun that was purchased by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation. Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent's consent. Police said they didn't know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or if he had attended it. Police respond within minutes The first 911 call came early in the afternoon from someone outside the school who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, the police chief said. More 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived within minutes, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said. The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said. READ MORE: 3 students and a teacher killed in Oregon elementary school shooting, police say The school has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education. Children were taken by bus to a nearby church serving as a reunification center for families. Parents hugged, kissed and held their kids' hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favorite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home. A community grieves Shaken residents held a vigil Thursday night, where children drew hearts in chalk on the sidewalk and held candles side-by-side with adults. Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for the area's 32 schools. Bend, the biggest city in central Oregon, is about 125 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Portland. It has ballooned in population over the past three decades and is a tourism and outdoor recreation hub. The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University. Just four years ago in Bend, a grocery store employee who had served in the U.S. Army attacked a gunman who was spraying shots inside the supermarket. Both the employee, whom police hailed as a hero, and a customer were killed, and the gunman died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Durkin and Tucker reported from Washington. Associated Press reporters Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City, Gene Johnson in Seattle, Ed White in Detroit and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed. 7cc2f2cb2a26.text: President Trump said Friday that his administration did not disrupt an Elon Musk -owned satellite system used by Ukraine to wage war against Russia. Why it matters: The restrictions imposed earlier this week on the system hampered the Ukrainian military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones for 24 hours. It raised concerns that the Trump administration and possibly Musk were retaliating against Ukraine for its attacks on Russian oil refineries and President Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of Trump's diesel deal with Russia. What he is saying: "I just checked this morning — it wasn't us," Trump told reporters. "I don't know if it was anybody, because it wasn't me and I don't think it was Elon." He was responding to a question about a Reuters report that the order to slow the satellite system came from the White House. Trump said that from what he was briefed the system is currently fully working with no restrictions. do we need this? no one is saying otherwise The other side: Ukrainian officials remain highly skeptical of Trump's claims and believe someone in the U.S. government participated in throttling the systems. "Our guys who speak to SpaceX say the White House was involved in the decision," a Ukrainian official said. Catch up quick: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When Starlink doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Ukraine relies on two satellite systems: One is SpaceX's Starlink, which it uses for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes. Both systems were restricted, according to Ukraine. In a post on X on Wednesday, Musk hinted the U.S. government was involved in disrupting Starshield. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote. The big picture: The limitations came days after a new crisis erupted between the U.S. and Ukraine over Trump's agreement to lift sanctions on Russian oil sales. Zelensky criticized the move, then Trump called for Ukraine to elect a new president.

ESCANABA, Mich. âÂ Abdul El-Sayed and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are already thinking beyond 2026, even though heâs not a senator yet.
During three different stops Thursday on his Senate campaignâs bus tour through redder, rural areas of this swing state, El-Sayed and Ocasio-Cortez drew crowds that showed notable star power. While Republicans see Michigan as their strongest chance to pick up a Senate seat, the progressive pair are casting themselves as heirs to the broader movement that Bernie Sanders has commanded for a decade â a push they plan to expand beyond this state.
âOnce you elect one person like that, people will then catch on,â Ocasio-Cortez declared of El-Sayed in this paper-producing town, whose county last went Democratic in 2008. âAnd we will start electing more people like that.â
In a region walloped by the sort of deindustrialization that President Donald Trump had returned to office pledging to reverse, El-Sayed drew loud applause for vowing to move beyond him: âDonald Trump is just the worst symptom of the disease of our politics â the disease of the system of allowing billionaires, corporations, special interest, the bought and sold politicians, the way that the money brings the system against us.â
While Ocasio-Cortez has yet to make her decision on a 2028 presidential primary that sheâd enter as an automatic contender, her Michigan tour amounted to calling her shot. Sheâs betting on El-Sayed as proof of concept for her brand of populism, embracing his play for the left in a tight Senate race even as the strategy sparks internal Democratic worries about a possible drift of Black and Jewish voters towards Republicans.
If he defeats GOP nominee Mike Rogers in a remarkably anti-Trump cycle to become the first Muslim senator in US history, El-Sayed could spark his own presidential boomlet. But for the moment, in a state thatâs now among the Democratic nominating calendarâs earliest to vote, his campaign served as a vehicle for Ocasio-Cortez to spell out more ambitious policy than a single candidateâs platform.
When one attendee in Escanaba asked the duo about eliminating interest on student loans. El-Sayed said âyou shouldnât have to go into debt to get a higher educationâ and that Democrats should find creative ways around the Supreme Courtâs rejection of a Biden-era student loan forgiveness program.
Then Ocasio-Cortez went a step further, saying that student loans should be interest-free, public colleges should be tuition-free, and âwe have to really be asking ourselves what is the utility of putting people in indentured servitude their entire lives for seeking an education.â
The crowd cheered.
(At another point, the New Yorker laughed off cries from supporters asking her to run for president.)
Know More
Although Democrats have often fallen short in this part of Michigan come November, itâs been favorable territory for progressives during primaries. In this yearâs Senate primary, El-Sayed carried the three counties where he held events Thursday, as did Sanders during the Vermont independentâs 2016 Democratic presidential bid.
âI just want to have a conversation about gas, groceries, the ability to see a doctor. Want money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for all?â El-Sayed told reporters. âI think thatâs what Yoopers want, too.â
He knocked Rogers, who generally avoids the large gatherings favored by the El-Sayed campaign, for not appearing in the Upper Peninsula this fall.
âSo whenâs the last time he was in Iron Mountain? Whenâs the last time he was in Escanaba? Whenâs the last time he was in Marquette? I donât know. At least I show up,â said El-Sayed.
A Rogers spokesperson pointed to previous stops by his campaign in the Upper Peninsula towns over the last year, including in Marquette in June.
âAOC is the latest trick up the Democratsâ sleeve, but Michiganders know better than to fall for it,â said the Rogers spokesperson. âWhile Abdul El-Sayed tries to run from his own progressive policies, AOCâs visit reminds voters exactly who he is â a radical leftist who wants to defund the police, force EV mandates on Michiganders, and jack up our utility prices even higher.â

8a58f8d74a26.text: By — Russ Bynum, Associated Press Russ Bynum, Associated Press By — Sudhin Thanawala, Associated Press Sudhin Thanawala, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/more-roller-coasters-shut-down-as-authorities-investigate-fatal-fall-at-georgia-amusement-park Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter More roller coasters shut down as authorities investigate fatal fall at Georgia amusement park Nation Oct 16, 2026 2:41 PM EDT ATLANTA (AP) — A growing number of amusement parks have shut down roller coasters as police and state regulators investigate what caused a man to fall out of his seat and plummet to his death at a Georgia park. Sea World Orlando in Florida and La Ronde theme park in Montreal, Canada, confirmed on Thursday they had temporarily closed rides, bringing the total number of roller coasters halted to 11. READ MORE: Roller coaster rider's death puts spotlight on safety of ever more thrilling rides Police and a state regulatory agency are investigating what caused Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old school employee from Atlanta, to fall from the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. Witnesses described seeing him ejected from the coaster; some people who rode the Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints. Nine of the roller coasters taken out of service have the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system as the Goliath at Six Flags. Mom says her son's restraint didn't work properly Erica Billups said her son and daughter rode Goliath about an hour before Kariem's death and encountered a problem with the restraint on one seat. Her son initially sat in that seat and tried to lock it, but then moved when it repeatedly became unlocked. The roller coaster embarked with the seat empty and the harness up, she said in a post on X. She confirmed the post in a text message to The Associated Press on Thursday. She said staff did not tell her kids there was a problem. Summer Bates, who was at the Georgia park with her husband and three children and saw Kariem fall, told the AP previously that her older two children kept trying to push their restraints down tighter while on the ride. She understood why they were doing that later when she was on the coaster, she said, because the restraints didn't feel secure. Six Flags did not immediately respond to an email for comment on any issues with restraints. At least one of the other closures is for safety La Ronde in Montreal said one of its coasters — also named Goliath — is offline "while we conduct a thorough safety review in collaboration with the ride's manufacturer." Sea World Orlando said that it closed its Mako roller coaster with no set date to reopen. Neither La Ronde nor Sea World Orlando said why those specific rides were closed. Both were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard, which also built the Goliath ride in Georgia and eight of the other coasters that Six Flags closed. Bolliger & Mabillard declined Thursday to answer questions about the shutdowns. In an updated list of ride closures provided Thursday, Six Flags no longer included the Goliath coaster at its Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California. The coaster has a different manufacturer and restraint system from the others. Six Flags had listed it as closed earlier in the week. Online photos and videos of most of the closed coasters show each equipped with so-called "clamshell" restraints, mounted in front of each seat on a vertical bar that sits between the rider's knees. The bar locks the padded restraint into place over the rider's lap and upper legs. READ MORE: Man killed on a Six Flags roller coaster was thrown from the ride and hit other patrons, police say It's unclear from the images whether any of those coasters also have seat belts or other secondary restraints. Goliath in Georgia has no such backup restraints. Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, a trade group, said the similar restraint systems are almost certainly why most of the coasters were closed. Speigel said they're likely to remain shut down until investigators have determined what went wrong on the Georgia coaster, but he said that "obviously it was something with the restraint." Roller coaster manufacturers decide what type of restraints to use after considering speed, force and the track's transitions, said Brian D. Avery, a University of Florida professor and amusement ride safety expert. He advocates the use of a backup restraint for riders, but there is a long-running debate in the industry over whether that would increase wait times, Avery said. Bolliger & Mabillard says it is investigating The company said in an email it would have no further comment until it had a "better understanding of what transpired" on Monday. Kariem was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride. Goliath, one of Six Flags Over Georgia's headline attractions, towers above the park's entrance. It opened in 2006 and features a series of hills and turns. It doesn't take riders upside down, but its first hill rises to 200 feet (61 meters) and it has a top speed of 70 miles per hour (112 kilometers). Nick Mendenhall, who had just ridden Goliath with his son and was watching the coaster cars passing overhead, said it looked like Kariem was hovering because the car was moving underneath him. He fell headfirst back into the coaster, Mendenhall said, and then was ejected from the ride on its final turn. Six Flags has faced legal trouble before A class-action lawsuit filed by investors in 2025 alleges that Six Flags concealed the poor state of its amusement parks — including long-neglected maintenance — ahead of its merger with major amusement park operator Cedar Fair. Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder
Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.
Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.
Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.
"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.
"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."
Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.
It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.
The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.
It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.
Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws â which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services â will help Australians become happier and healthier.
But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.
The choice
Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.
Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.
It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.
He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.
"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.
"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."
The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.
Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."
Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.
Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see â and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.
Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.
But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.
Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms â often unsolicited â serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.
Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.
"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.
While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.
"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.
Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s â a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.
More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.
The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.
"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.
"If people want to doom scrollâ¦ that's fine, that's up to them."
The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services â social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more â to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".

a710d13eda99.text: By — Rob Gillies, Associated Press Rob Gillies, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/prime-minister-mark-carney-says-u-s-is-trying-to-break-canada-as-alberta-votes-on-separation-path Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Prime Minister Mark Carney says U.S. is trying to break Canada as Alberta votes on separation path World Oct 16, 2026 2:07 PM EDT CALGARY, Alberta (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned Thursday that the United States is trying to break Canada so it can "own us" as he urged oil-rich Alberta not to begin a process toward separation in Monday's referendum. The vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, which has the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. "This referendum comes at the worst possible time," Carney told a large pro-Canada rally in Calgary. "The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us." READ MORE: Carney and Macron deepen ties as Canada turns toward Europe and away from U.S. dependence He did not directly mention the U.S. or its President Donald Trump in that passage, but has done so in similar past speeches. Carney's warning came as U.S. President Donald Trump wages a trade war with Canada and after his repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state. Carney has argued that Canada needs to become more economically resilient and less dependent on the United States. Carney urged Albertans not to use the vote simply to send Ottawa a message, saying a decisive result could settle the separation question. "Don't be fooled by the idea you can 'send a message' with your vote," Carney said. "This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty." Carney makes the case for Canada Carney, who grew up in Alberta, spent Thursday campaigning in Calgary before addressing the Forever Canadian rally at the BMO Centre. His office estimated about 5,000 people attended, with some waiting more than two hours to get through security. Organizers were also holding a second rally with Carney in Edmonton on Friday. Earlier Thursday, he pointed to the many Albertans who were born or educated elsewhere in Canada and to firefighters who come from across the country to help Alberta during wildfires as examples of the ties binding the province to the rest of Canada. Attendees react during the Forever Canadian rally at the BMO Centre, ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty, in Calgary, Alberta, Canada, on Oct. 15, 2026. Photo by Todd Korol/Reuters At the rally, Carney also acknowledged the grievances that have fueled alienation in Alberta. "The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real," he said. Carney said that while growing up, Ottawa made Albertans feel "like our resources weren't our own" and that more recently the province was made to feel its energy contributions were "against the tides of history." A Liberal prime minister finds unlikely support The setting is striking for a Liberal prime minister. Alberta has spent decades feuding with Liberal governments in Ottawa, particularly over energy and federal power. But Carney has broken with some of the policies associated with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, fast-tracked a proposed new oil pipeline to the Pacific and called Canada an energy superpower. READ MORE: Carney says Canada can emerge from Trump's trade war with a stronger and independent economy Carney pointed to the Pacific Link pipeline as evidence of a changed relationship, saying it would create more than 140,000 jobs and generate revenue for social programs. His biggest cheer came when he said the pipeline would reduce Canada's dependence on the United States. "Careful, they might think that's election interference. A little touchy," Carney joked, drawing laughter. He was referring to U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra's warning to Canadian politicians not to interfere in the U.S. midterm elections. Tanya Clemens, co-chair of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, acknowledged Carney presents a challenge. "He's formidable for sure," Clemens told The Associated Press. Clemens argued, however, that Carney's agreements with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith amount to "pinky promises" that do not resolve long-standing grievances with Ottawa. Keith Wilson, another leader of Let Alberta Decide, rejected Carney's argument that global instability made this the wrong time for the vote. "The worst timing for this, why? I don't understand what's the logic," Wilson said. "Then it's the best time for him to get back to Ottawa." Wilson said Carney should ask Parliament to repeal federal measures that separatists say have hurt Alberta, including authority he says could be used to tax oil exports in retaliation against the United States. He predicted Carney would eventually impose such a tax despite Carney saying he sees no value in using Canadian energy exports as leverage against the U.S. "It's one cabinet meeting away," Wilson said. "He's gonna do it. He has to do it." READ MORE: Carney pitches Canada to global investors amid trade war with Trump Smith, who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, cast her ballot Wednesday and said she voted for Alberta to remain in Canada. She has said support for separation remains too high for her liking. "Canada can still work," Smith said after voting. "We just need to make some changes." Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University, called Carney's popularity in Alberta "highly unusual" for a Liberal prime minister. Price, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-casts-doubt-on-press-secretary-katie-zacharias-future Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter White House press secretary Katie Zacharia leaving the job after Trump casts doubt Politics Updated on Oct 16, 2026 4:09 PM EDT — Published on Oct 16, 2026 1:49 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Katie Zacharia is departing as White House press secretary, a person familiar with the matter said Friday, after a short and rocky tenure that was defined by questions about her professional background and lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists. The person, granted anonymity to discuss a personnel decision not yet made public, said Zacharia would be transitioning out of the role. The shift comes after President Donald Trump cast significant doubt on her future earlier Friday, telling reporters that he would have a discussion with her following his weekend travel — and that if he were her, he would reconsider the job. READ MORE: Katie Zacharia's debut shows the pitfalls and possibilities of White House press secretary's role Zacharia had come under immediate scrutiny when she appeared uncomfortable during her inaugural briefing on Tuesday, delivering halting remarks touting the president and his accomplishments. Her 14-minute briefing was followed by criticism that the conservative commentator had long called herself a lawyer when she had not passed a bar exam nor was otherwise credentialed to practice. Zacharia was a surprise choice when Trump announced her appointment on Oct. 9, as the successor to Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary who had been part of Trump's inner circle for years. The chaos surrounding her appointment was reminiscent of some of Trump's short-lived staff picks from his first term. Trump said he told Zacharia that she might want to change her mind about the job, and said he thought she had been treated unfairly by the press. "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy,'" Trump told reporters on the White House lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia. "I said, 'Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider.' I said, 'You think about it, but I would reconsider.'" Messages to Zacharia seeking comment were not returned on Friday, and the White House offered no immediate comment. In his own comments, Trump said he told his press secretary, "'Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this,'" and that he wanted "her to have a good life" and not be subjected to criticism, which he likened to being "brutalized by the media." The president said he'd make a final determination later, perhaps after his campaign travel on Friday and this weekend, adding, "When I get back, we're gonna talk." He was asked who might replace Zacharia, and said that there were a lot of people who wanted the job. Zacharia's first official day on the job was Monday Zacharia's short tenure has been defined by criticism for a lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists and questions about her professional background. In her briefing on Tuesday, she took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative-leaning or Trump-friendly outlets, and left after only about 14 minutes. Zacharia has said she wanted to keep her briefing short to ensure Trump had enough time later that morning for his own question-and-answer session with reporters, and that she had not been fully briefed by White House staff beforehand. READ MORE: Claim that Trump press secretary Katie Zacharia is a lawyer comes under scrutiny She later traveled with Trump when he held rallies on Wednesday and Thursday in Alaska, Arizona and Montana — but did not hold more press briefings. In an appearance on Fox News Channel earlier Friday, Zacharia was asked if she had the president's confidence and responded: "I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me." But she also wouldn't say when her next press briefing might be. Questions about why Zacharia called herself a lawyer Zacharia, a Pepperdine University law graduate, also faced criticism for describing herself as a lawyer when appearing as a commentator on conservative television outlets. Zacharia said the term was a proper one to use when she was offering legal analysis, and said she had worked as a lawyer in China. Zacharia said Friday on Fox News that she wasn't asked about passing the bar before becoming press secretary, and Trump noted in his subsequent comments that she was hired as a spokesperson for the White House, not as an attorney. Before joining the White House, Zacharia had been working in communications for Trump Media, the company that oversees the president's social media site, Truth Social. She also briefly worked at the Department of Homeland Security during the second Trump administration. Price reported from Dobbins Air Force Base, Georgia. Sean "Diddy" Combs has been transferred from a New Jersey correctional facility to a prison in Pennsylvania, the US Federal Bureau of Prisons says.
The rap mogul was moved to FCI Allenwood Low on Friday, a prison official said, but declined to discuss why he was moved, citing privacy, safety, and security reasons.
"His transfer from one low-security facility to another is an important distinction," Combs' spokesman told the BBC, adding that the move "is consistent with a decision made with safety and security in mind".
Combs, 56, who was sentenced to 50 months behind bars, has asked an appeals court to release him from prison and overturn his conviction on two prostitution-related crimes.
Combs' spokesman, Juda S Engelmayer, did not comment on an Associated Press report, external that Combs had been living a "luxury lifestyle" behind bars in New Jersey or on reports swirling about his health and treatment in lockup.
The move comes about two weeks after NBC News, external reported that the Bad Boy Records co-founder had access to mobile phones, liquor and other contraband at Fort Dix, as well as allegations that he had paid inmates to cook, clean and make his bed for him, and give him massages. He was also involved in two fights, according to NBC.
"It's because of the disruptive behaviour," Jose Rojas, union secretary for local federal prison employees, told NBC News of the move. "He's been causing too much trouble over there."
NBC reported Combs was stripped of 41 days for good conduct, pushing back his scheduled release date, which is now listed in the prison's online records as 2 March 2028. He was originally expected to be released in January 2028.
Engelmayer said he appreciates that the Federal Bureau of Prisons is "taking the safety and security of Sean and everyone involved seriously" and "we are grateful for the attention being given to his well-being and hope he can continue serving his time without unnecessary disruption".
The Federal Bureau of Prisons declined to comment on the reports.
"For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or disciplinary sanctions," spokesman Donald Murphy said.
FCI Allenwood Low is a low-security federal correctional institution for male offenders that is about 155 miles (250 km) west of New York City.
The facility houses about 1,044 inmates, according to its website, a significantly smaller population than the one at Combs' previous facility, Fort Dix, of more than 4,200 inmates across two campuses. Allenwood also has medium and maximum security facilities nearby.
Federal prosecutors in New York have accused Combs of using his money, power, and the threat of violence to coerce women into unwanted sexual encounters.
After a high-profile jury trial in New York last year, two of Combs' ex-girlfriends testified that he abused them and forced them to participate in so-called "freak-offs" with male escorts.
In July 2025, Combs was convicted on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution. They jury acquitted him of two more serious charges, sex trafficking and racketeering conspiracy, and he was sentenced to more than four years in prison that October.
Later that month, Combs was transferred to the federal correctional institution at Fort Dix in New Jersey, where he had been serving out his sentence until his transfer on Friday.
In April, a US appeals court heard arguments to overturn his prison sentence but has not yet issued a decision.

8e08e5e92f18.text: By — Elaine Kurtenbach, Associated Press Elaine Kurtenbach, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/imf-world-bank-meetings-focus-on-global-risks-and-potential-benefits-of-ai Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter IMF-World Bank meetings focus on global risks and potential benefits of AI World Oct 16, 2026 1:30 PM EDT BANGKOK (AP) — Guardrails are urgently needed to contain potential risks from the boom in artificial intelligence, the head of the International Monetary Fund said Friday, likening the technology to a Formula 1 race car that might go off the track and run people over. "We are racing, and the question is how do we put barriers? So if a car was to fly out it doesn't kill people," IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said. "I have high respect for the industry. I think what you're doing is incredibly important for humanity. You may give us the biggest gift, but if the car runs over people, that gift may not be so worthwhile," she said while speaking on a panel on the impact of AI on the world economy along with experts including Anthropic co-founder and head of policy Jack Clark. READ MORE: Fed chair Warsh says price stability is key but shies away from signals about rates Clark is among technology industry leaders pushing for faster action on regulating AI. In a blog post last month, the rival to OpenAI proposed that the world's top artificial intelligence companies come up with a coordinated way to pause development of advanced AI systems, warning the technology is improving so quickly there's a risk humans would lose control. "I think it's worse than you describe. I think it's Formula 1 at night without maybe brakes in the cars," Clark said. "And it's remarkable to me that the toys I buy for my children are regulated more than the literal superintelligence I work on at my day job." He added that the effort to build policy frameworks to regulate AI is underway. "The world is now taking this seriously, and I think if we take it seriously, we are going to be able to get our arms around it," Clark said. "But it cannot only be companies making these decisions. And if we're negligent about this, we're going to get some form of chaos." The impact of AI on jobs is yet to be fully understood, but an IMF study found three main trends. About 10% of jobs might be transformed or newly created, while work involving repetitive tasks will be gone, Georgieva said. The third category will be service sector jobs generated by people who benefit from the investment boom. "The net impact is positive," she said, though she added that "services don't pay a lot." "So you get young people who normally would have gone into professional routine jobs now serving coffee in Starbucks. And that is not what I think young people in the world aspire for," she said. READ MORE: IMF chief urges wealthy nations to rein in debt to ease global economic pressure Tiff Macklem, the governor of the Bank of Canada, compared that to the effects on employment from more open trade, which has generated great global wealth and raised millions out of poverty. But many millions also lost their livelihoods as manufacturers moved jobs to China and other developing countries. He said "in aggregate there is an overall benefit," but acknowledged that in both trade and technology "there will be winners and losers." "You have to find a way to help the losers," Macklem said. "Without a system to help them cope with the loss you get a backlash." Dozens of people marched in Bangkok on Thursday and Friday in peaceful protests, seeking to draw attention to growing inequality and other frustrations. Georgieva noted that to ensure that the benefits of AI can reach the maximum number of people, they have to have electricity and access to digital networks. Cybersecurity also is essential. During the wide ranging session, the speakers were also asked about how they used AI in their own lives. Georgieva said she'd used it to track calories and lose weight. The IMF chief, who has described her personal AI assistant as bossy, joked that she'd like AI agents to be more polite. "I mean, the agents we get, they can be really annoying," she said. "So can we work on, like, their manners?" Maybe, said Clark. "We have this dial between sycophantic and rude," he said. "So we'll spin it around the other way." AP journalists Haruka Nuga, Tian MacLeod Ji and Sakchai Lalit contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
