READ MORE: Trump administration sues California to block counting of alleged noncitizen mail ballots The letter Friday from a senior Justice Department official and obtained first by The Associated Press is the latest salvo in an ongoing tussle with heavily Democratic California, coming just a day after the Trump administration sued the state to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as "likely" noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. "The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful," warns the letter from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. It adds: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime." The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel's office and also is copied to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice. Neither office immediately returned a request for comment, nor did the state attorney general. It is unclear how many individuals the Justice Department might look to try to investigate and charge, though any federal criminal cases in the Los Angeles area would be handled by the office of Bill Essayli, the region's top federal prosecutor and one of the Justice Department officials who filed the federal complaint Thursday against California. The Trump administration has made the pursuit of noncitizen voters a priority Sent less than three weeks before the Nov. 3 election, the letter adds to simmering tensions over voter rolls between California and the Justice Department and reflects the Trump administration's aggressive hunt for noncitizen voters. It has made the issue a priority this year, including by demanding detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. READ MORE: Trump's focus on noncitizen voting has led to 160 arrests. That shows it's rare, experts say In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state. That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero. The letter follows a Justice Department lawsuit The Justice Department lawsuit was filed after California officials were given, and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. Rick Hasen, a UCLA law professor, said the letter "ups the ante by threatening election officials with potential criminal prosecution." Over 23 million people are registered statewide, and a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts could determine which party controls the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. An Oregon teacher threw her mobile phone before she tackled and tried to wrestle away a shotgun from the arms of a teen suspect who opened fire on a special educational needs class.
As she tussled with him on the floor of the class - where three children and a teacher were killed - a bystander ran inside. Armed with a .40-caliber pistol, he opened fire and killed the teen.
The bystander, a dad of two girls at the school, had been driving past Silver Rail Elementary in Bend when he saw the suspect firing in the car park then shooting through a window to enter.
The details of the Thursday attack were confirmed by police, who said the 16-year-old suspect was a prior student at the school.
Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.
"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday.
Police offered more information on the attack at at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.
Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.
Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives.
He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there.
A search warrant has been executed at the suspect's home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.
Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but police are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear.
Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.
But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.
The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside.
Police said he had a legally concealed .40 caliber in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him.
In a statement to the BBC's partner CBS News, Giamanco's family said he is a "lifelong resident of Bend" and that he "is not seeking recognition".
The family said Giamanco wants to express his "gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support". He and his family "respectfully ask for privacy".
US President Donald Trump praised the bystander's actions on Friday, calling him a "great hero".
Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been "much worse" with no intervention.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.
Without naming the bystander, Governor Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".
Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.

It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.
Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.
There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.
In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.
Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.
There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.
Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.
Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.
They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.
The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.
On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.
The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-WÃ¼rttemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.
Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.
Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.
All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.
The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.
Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.
In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.
A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.
In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.
He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.
She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.
She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.
The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.
Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."
The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.
Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.
However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers.
Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.
Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".
Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.
The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

This is the first documented instance of barn owls nesting in Manhattan in modern history, according to one expert, and the owls have attracted nightly crowds of people in the street eager to get a glimpse of the elusive birds. Word of the barn owl family didn't get around until last week, when Elisabeth Williams, an Upper West Side resident, notified a local news outlet on Oct. 6 that she and her husband saw multiple owls at the water tower atop a building on West 75th Street close to Central Park West. The couple had previously seen a single owl on an apartment windowsill a few days earlier and were shocked even then, Williams recalled. "In a place like Manhattan, you normally really have to go out of your way to encounter nature," she said. "And here it was, just sort of right outside our window." Barn owl sightings are rare in New York City It's not the first time that birds have captivated New Yorkers. Residents have fallen in love with American woodcocks, who are known to stop in Midtown Manhattan's Bryant Park every year as they migrate north in early spring. After Flaco the Eurasian eagle-owl died in 2024, dozens of mournful fans gathered to say goodbye to the beloved creature who flew around Manhattan and became a joy to many after someone let him out of his zoo enclosure the previous year. Then there was Pale Male, a red-tailed hawk who nested above Fifth Avenue for three decades before dying in 2023. But barn owl sightings in New York City parks are very rare, according to the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation. New York is at the northern fringe of the barn owl's range and the barn owl population has declined "at an alarming rate" over time, according to the state Department of Environmental Conservation. e565f536e217.text: There are many more questions to be answered about the deadly elementary school shooting in Bend, Oregon. To explore some of them, Amna Nawaz spoke with James Densley, professor and chair of criminology and criminal justice at Metro State University. He is best known for co-creating the Violence Prevention Project, a database of mass shooters in the United States. Amna Nawaz: There are many more questions to be answered in the days ahead. To explore some of them, we're joined now by James Densley. He's professor and chair of criminology and criminal justice at Metro State University in Minnesota. He's best known for co-creating The Violence Prevention Project. That is the largest, most comprehensive database of mass shootings in the United States. Welcome and thanks for being with us. So, some limited information about the shooter and the way this attack unfolded so far. But, from what we do know, what stands out to you about this shooting? James Densley, Co-Founder and President, The Violence Project: There are several things. We have 26 years of school homicides in our database, nearly 400 cases. And this is the first time a civilian shot and stopped the attacker. Usually, when school shootings are stopped before the police arrive, it's by a teacher, a coach, a custodian, or another student who tackles the shooter before they reload. So that's a very unique thing. You know, we have a father here with two daughters at the school. He ran toward the gunfire. It's incredible bravery. And I'm sure it'll be held up as proof of one argument to another, but we must not forget that this also began with a 16-year-old who got hold of a gun that they should not have had. And that's the best part of prevention that we have here for the next time. Even with a hero on the scene, in three minutes, four people were already dead. So, stopping a shooter is not the same as preventing a shooting. And so the real goal is to never need these heroes at all. Amna Nawaz: We should also point out the teacher who was involved in the altercation with the shooter apparently threw her cell phone at him and was fighting with him when that father entered the building and ultimately shot him. But I should also point out what officials shared about the fact that the shooter entered the building by forcing his way, shooting his way through locked doors. The superintendent today mentioned how much they have invested in security. How should we look at that, the front-end security that many schools have now put in place? James Densley: Yes, it's a great question. The doors were locked and he shot through them. The locks buy time and time saves lives usually. But a locked door is also the last line of defense. It's not the first. In our data, shooters force their way into schools in only a handful of cases. Most of those, though, do tend to be former students, because they know the building and they're prepared to break in. And by the time someone is shooting at your front door, prevention's already failed in many ways. The real work, I think, has to happen weeks and months earlier, when someone notices warning signs and can step in. Amna Nawaz: Officials also said today they don't yet know how the shooter got the weapon or the ammunition. It's been reported, however, that the shotgun belonged to his mother. Is that kind of situation consistent with what we have seen in the past where a minor gets access to a weapon from a parent or relative? James Densley: Yes, sadly, that's part of the story that's painfully familiar. In school mass shootings in our data, whenever a shooter is a teenager, and we know where the gun comes from, it usually comes from home every single time, actually. It's typically parents and grandparents. Children are too young to buy these guns, and so that's why they take them. But this is also the most preventable part of the problem. A lock safe at home costs a few hundred dollars. It's the cheapest school safety measure in America, and it's the one that's right in your house, not even at the school. So I would say, for every parent watching this tonight, ask yourself this question. Could my child access my gun today if he or she wanted to? And if the answer is yes, then you need to do something about this. Now, we have seen cases in Oxford, Michigan, and also the Apalachee High School in Georgia where parents have actually been charged and found negligent and guilty for these cases. So the law is starting to treat these unsecured guns as part of the crime. Amna Nawaz: Got a minute or so here left, but I have to ask you about what we heard from the school superintendent when he said how deeply impacted everyone in the community is and how this will stay with them for years to come. From the shootings you have looked at in the past, how does it stay with a community? James Densley: I mean, it's just -- it's every parent and every community's worst nightmare. I mean, the youngest child killed was just 5 years old in this case. In our data, no younger child has died in an attack on a school. And the shooter was 16. This is children killing children. It's a tragedy on so many levels, and it will have ripple effects throughout that community for generations. There's going to need to be a lot of care and compassion and aftercare and support for these families and for this community. And my heart goes out to them, and I'm sure everybody else who's watching this tonight as well. It's just devastating. Amna Nawaz: That is Professor James Densley from Metro State University joining us tonight. Thank you so much. James Densley: Thank you.

White House correspondent Liz Landers has a fact check on some of Trump's claims. Amna Nawaz: Ahead of the midterms, President Trump is on the campaign trail looking to rally his base in battleground races. His controversial comments at those rallies have drawn attention. To fact-check some of the president's claims, we're joined now by our White House correspondent, Liz Landers. Liz, let's just start off with something the president talks about frequently at these rallies, which is immigration. Here's what he had to say about Somali immigrants during a rally in Ohio earlier this week. President President Donald Trump: All they do is kill each other in the streets. Then they come into the United States of America and they tell us how to run our country. We're not going to stand for it. They drive up taxes. They drive up health care costs, insurance costs, childcare costs, and they cheat on everything. It's a disaster. And we're not going to stand for it. Amna Nawaz: Setting aside the comments about violence there, what do we know about what the president had to say about immigration driving up costs? Liz Landers: Yes, the Congressional Budget Office has analyzed this and looked at the immigration surge here in the United States starting in 2024 and projecting for 10 years and says that the immigration surge will actually add $1.2 trillion to federal revenue. And, by 2034, the annual increase in revenue will be up to $164 billion. So this surge is projected to boost economic activity and, in turn, tax revenues. And when it comes to what he was saying about insurance there, undocumented immigrants are not eligible for Medicaid coverage. There are certain circumstances where lawfully present immigrants may have some kind of qualified status, but they have to wait five years before they are eligible for it. And KFF has found that immigrants are not more likely than U.S.-born citizens to report using government assistance for food, housing, and health care, Amna. Amna Nawaz: There's another comment the president made that got a lot of attention at a rally in Arizona. He called for the death penalty for leakers. Take a listen. President Donald Trump: In my opinion, leakers should be shot. (CHEERING) President Donald Trump: They should be shot. In the old days, we used to shoot leakers when they leak what time you're going to attack a country? No, leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly. They're real -- to me, they're the scum of the earth. The leakers are the scum of the earth. Amna Nawaz: Liz, do people who leak information ever face capital punishment? Liz Landers: Well, in this instance, it sounds like the president is talking about recent leaks around the U.S. attacks on Iran. So, most government leaks are prosecuted under the Espionage Act of 1917, which penalizes the unauthorized retention or dissemination of national defense information. Those charges have a standard prison term sentence of either five to 10 years maximum in jail. Most federal crimes that qualify for the death penalty involve murder or death themselves. There is one exception with this. That is treason. But the last person to be tried with treason in the United States was Adam Gadahn in 2006 for providing aid to al-Qaida. And the last person to be sentenced to death for treason was in 1948. It was a Japanese American who'd been convicted of torturing Americans during World War II, but he was deported to Japan before that happened. Amna Nawaz: So, at that same rally, the president also questioned the results of the 2022 Arizona governor's race. Take a listen. President Donald Trump: The damn machines were broken in Republican areas. They were broken purposely, and you couldn't vote. (CHEERING) President Donald Trump: What a rigged election that was. And it's a shame. It's a shame and that they can allow that happen. Amna Nawaz: Liz, what do we know about that election and where this fits into the president's longstanding claims of election fraud? Liz Landers: He reiterates this and lies about this almost on a daily basis. This line that the machines were broken purposefully in Republican areas is false. I was on the ground in Maricopa County for that election in 2022. And what happened was, there was an issue with the printer in some, not all, vote centers throughout Maricopa County. The ballot ink was too light. It could not be read by tabulators. And what happened was, it created frustrations with the lines there. People were having to wait to have their ballots processed, but it did not disenfranchise any voters in Maricopa County or prohibit them from casting a ballot. There were some subsequent legal challenges that were brought by Kari Lake. Those were thoroughly reviewed and dismissed across multiple levels of the judiciary there. Amna Nawaz: So, speaking of election administration, we know the Trump administration continues to try to compel states to turn over voter information, try to restrict who can get a mail-in ballot. The Department of Justice filed a lawsuit just yesterday against California's secretary of state and also Los Angeles' top elections official. What are they alleging here? Liz Landers: We have been following how the federal government is trying to impact the midterm elections, even though states in the Constitution are the ones who are designated to set the time, place and manner of how their elections are conducted. The Department of Justice sent this letter on Wednesday to both the secretary of state there, the top elections official in L.A. The Arizona Department of Water Resources filed a motion Friday to join in a lawsuit against the federal government’s plan for Colorado River operations over the next 10 years.
“Arizona believes the federal government’s new operating framework ignores basic elements of the law of the river and could result in cuts to the state apportionment that would devastate Arizona’s economy,” said Tom Buschatzke, director of the Arizona Department of Water Resources, in a press conference announcing the legal action.
The state joins Nevada in suing the Department of the Interior and Bureau of Reclamation, alleging the federal government’s plan unfairly places the brunt of water cuts on Arizona and its Lower Basin peers, Nevada and California. The Colorado River Basin is split into lower and upper halves, and the Bureau of Reclamation’s reductions in water allocations over the next 10 years fall solely on the Lower Basin states.
“Arizona has always been willing to do our part to protect the Colorado River, but we will not accept a forced federal plan that solves this crisis on the backs of our families, farmers, and businesses,” said Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs in a statement. “We are drawing a line in the sand. I am taking this legal action alongside Nevada because the federal government refuses to hold the Upper Basin accountable for the water deliveries they owe Arizona, and is threatening to force draconian cuts that go well beyond the Lower Basin Agreement.”
In a joint statement, Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo and Southern Nevada Water Authority General Manager John Entsminger welcomed the news Arizona was joining its lawsuit.
“Arizona’s decision to join our lawsuit is an important step in challenging a federal plan that unfairly burdens the Lower Basin and fails to require the Upper Basin to make meaningful reductions,” Lombardo said. “Nevada will not accept a framework that puts our water supply and the future of our communities at risk.”
Arizona has long stood to lose the most in the tense negotiations over how to reduce the use of water from the Colorado River. One of the biggest users of Colorado River water, the state has some of the least senior water rights on the river, meaning it takes far larger cuts than other states in times of drought.
The Colorado River provides water to between 35 and 40 million people across seven Western states, 30 tribes and two Mexican states as it wends its way through the Southwest, home to some of the country’s most arid and drought-stricken landscapes. Dams on the river provide electricity to millions.
The 1922 compact between the river’s users assumed roughly 17.5 million acre feet of water was available to the two basins and Mexico, but the historical average of its natural flow has only been roughly 14.7 million acre feet. That number plummeted to an average of 11.2 million acre feet between 2020 and 2024 due to climate change, according to provisional data from Reclamation, with demand outpacing supply. The seven states that depend on the river have been in tense, deadlocked negotiations for years over how to distribute water cuts, and have missed their deadlines to come to an agreement, leading to the federal government’s decision.

In July, the federal government issued its record of decision for operations of federal infrastructure, like Glen Canyon Dam and Lake Powell, which dictates how much water is released to the Lower Basin. The plan outlines a 10-year management approach beginning in 2027 that could adjust to changing hydrological conditions that affect the river’s flow, with operations updatable every two years. The cuts imposed by the plan, however, are limited to the Lower Basin states, which consume the lion’s share of the river’s water. The Upper Basin states of Colorado, Wyoming, Utah and New Mexico, which have argued they don’t yet use their full allocation of water, face no mandatory cuts under the plan, a point of contention between the two sides.
The first two years of cuts are based on a plan submitted by Arizona, California and Nevada, and reduce Arizona’s allocation of water from the Colorado River by 760,000 acre feet, California’s by 440,000 acre feet and Nevada’s by 50,000 acre feet (one acre foot is roughly 326,000 gallons—enough water for two-to-four households a year).
Arizona and the Lower Basin states are still working to implement those cuts, and the lawsuit exists on a parallel track to address the state’s concerns with operations after the first two years, Buschatzke said. The federal plan has outlined future cuts to the Lower Basin totalling up to 3 million acre feet, more than twice what will be implemented in the initial two years of the plan.
The issues Arizona hopes to deal with in the lawsuit are twofold, Buschatzke said. First, the federal government’s plan fails to deliver what Arizona and the other Lower Basin states are owed under the rules and regulations that guide Colorado River use, known as the “Law of the River.” Second, he said, the federal plan “could effectively dry up the Central Arizona Project,” the canal system that delivers Colorado River water to Phoenix, Tucson and other communities.
Legal action, he said, is needed to protect Arizona’s water.
“The Lower Basin states have contributed millions of acre-feet of water towards stabilizing the river system, with more than 5.5 million acre-feet of Arizona water left in Lake Mead since 2014,” Buschatzke said. “No state has sacrificed more … but the United States decision puts the entire burden of sacrifice on the shoulders of three states, and we are joining Nevada in challenging that framework.”

818c5287bda4.text: By — Chan Ho-him, Associated Press Chan Ho-him, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/china-says-it-will-curb-tech-exports-including-ai-citing-national-security-risks Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter China says it will curb tech exports, including AI, citing national security risks World Oct 16, 2026 6:00 PM EDT HONG KONG (AP) — China on Friday said it plans to restrict or ban exports of 40 technologies that span artificial intelligence, chips and solar power as its technology race with countries including the United States intensifies. The Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology jointly published a draft document with the proposed updates for China's catalog of technologies subjected to export bans or restrictions. READ MORE: China and U.S. agree to establish AI safety channel and continue trade and military talks A spokesperson from the commerce ministry said in a statement that the move was "necessary" and cited national security as one of the reasons. The proposal came as China and the U.S. made progress in dialogues over AI safety and governance and on the setting up of a notification mechanism between the two superpowers for AI incidents that could threaten national security. Twenty-three AI technologies, from advanced large models to agents, are included on Friday's list, according to the Chinese ministries. U.S.-led restrictions have curbed the export of some advanced technologies to China over the past years, with the country blocked from accessing the world's most cutting-edge AI chips and the advanced chipmaking machines that make them. Exports of core technologies of AI large models trained using sensitive national data would be prohibited under the Chinese proposal, along with AI agents that are designed to be used in highly sensitive environments such as national defense and critical information infrastructure. "The Chinese government is implementing such necessary measures with the aims of reinforcing the security bottom line, preventing misuse and abuse, and ensuring that AI remains under human control," the commerce ministry's statement said. Meanwhile, exports of AI models with parameter counts of 2 trillion or above, or with certain world-leading capabilities, could be restricted. An AI model's parameter count is a key metric that reflects its learning capacity. Chinese AI models including Moonshot's Kimi K3 and Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-Max are among those with parameter counts exceeding 2 trillion, but Friday's proposal did not name specific models. Several chip design technologies, including for some AI processing chips and memory chips, are also included in the proposed export restrictions. Twelve solar power-related technologies are also included, including those related to the making of polysilicon, a core raw material for the solar supply chain, as well as five biomedicine technologies including those related to cell and gene therapy. The move "can be seen as a response to Western countries posting sovereignty requirements on AI, robotics, telecommunications, and other key technologies," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia. The aim would be to better regulate access to the Chinese technologies, he believes. The U.S. Commerce Department in June had asked Anthropic to bar foreign nationals from using some of its most powerful AI models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, citing national security concerns. The restrictions were later lifted. AI is increasingly strategic for both China and the U.S., added Gary Ng, a senior economist at French bank Natixis. "The world is getting more fragmented in trade and investment, but also in access to technologies," Ng said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 795c9bdc4e8c.text: By — Sam Metz, Associated Press Sam Metz, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/arab-led-parties-could-decide-the-israeli-election-if-anyone-would-partner-with-them Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Arab-led parties could decide the Israeli election, if anyone would partner with them World Oct 16, 2026 5:55 PM EDT BAQA AL-GHARBIYYE, Israel (AP) — Mansour Abbas has done nearly everything Israel asks of its Palestinian citizens. The leader of a small Arab political party condemned Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack. He rarely speaks about the war in Gaza or Israel's occupation of the West Bank, instead focusing on local issues like crime. He broke a taboo in 2021 by bringing an Arab party into an Israeli government, in which he served as a loyal partner. This time around, the second-ranked member of his party list is a mainstream Jewish candidate. But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his chief rivals have said they won't form a coalition with his or any other Arab-led party after the Oct. 27 election – even if that means months of gridlock and another round of voting. WATCH: Netanyahu's handling of Oct. 7 emerges as key issue in Israeli election It's a measure of where Israel's long-marginalized Arab minority finds itself three years after the Oct. 7 attack. Their speech is heavily policed, their leaders have been branded as traitors, and at one point their parties were outlawed before a court lifted the ban. Yet in a tight race, Abbas and other Arab politicians are poised to play a potentially decisive role in choosing the next prime minister — a rare opportunity to wield their influence. The stakes in the coming election are "existential," said Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List of Arab parties, which adopt a less conciliatory line than Abbas' Islamist Ra'am party. "We have to use our political power in order to basically block the deterioration of the situation," he said at a small campaign event in Tel Aviv, before slipping out the back to avoid a crowd of far-right protesters. A campaign billboard of Arab lawmaker Mansour Abbas is seen from a busy road in Haifa, Israel, Oct. 12, 2022. File photo by Ronen Zvulun/Reuters Activists say protests are heavily policed – crime less so Palestinians who remained within Israel after the 1948 war surrounding its creation, and their descendants, today make up about 20% of the population. They have citizenship, including the right to vote, but their close family ties and support for Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank lead many Jewish Israelis to view them with suspicion. They face discrimination and suffer from soaring crime rates, a problem that Arab activists blame on police negligence and the police say is rooted in the refusal of community leaders to work with them. The homicide rate among Palestinian citizens is more than 22 times higher than among Jewish Israelis, while arrest and indictment rates are far lower. The Abraham Initiatives, an Israeli organization that advocates for equal rights, has tallied 184 crime-related killings in Arab communities so far this year. The group said in July that only 12% reported in the first half of 2026 had been solved. Authorities have meanwhile aggressively curtailed freedom of expression, activists say. Police have routinely broken up anti-war protests, restricted displays of Palestinian flags, and arrested hundreds of people over social media posts, according to the Israel-based rights group Adalah. "They're not writing 'Kill the Jews.' Some of them are writing, 'We pray for Gaza,'" Hassan Jabareen, its general director, said. The Israeli government says it is a Jewish state in which minorities have equal rights, and that its crackdown on certain kinds of speech and protests is rooted in security concerns. Jabareen said the perceived over-policing of protests and under-policing of violent crime leaves Palestinians feeling less like citizens and more like threats to be contained. "We have to choose between the danger of being killed and being discriminated against," he said. A taboo was broken, and then Netanyahu returned Arab-led parties have long served in opposition to a system they believe is fundamentally unfair. Until 2021, none had joined a coalition government. Abbas' decision to do so five years ago marked a major shift. The 52-year-old dentist argued that Arab leaders needed a seat at the table. Critics accuse him of sidestepping the larger Israeli-Palestinian conflict to court potential coalition partners, while he argues that focusing on local issues is the best way to serve his constituents. "Crime and murder are issues linked to people's lives and there is no value higher than the value of human life. We're responsible, as representatives elected by the Arab public, to serve this public," he said at a campaign event in northern Israel last week. The government he joined lasted a little over a year, until new elections in 2022 returned Netanyahu to power at the head of the most nationalist and religious government in Israel's history. Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has described Palestinian citizens of Israel as an "internal front" in the war and "an existential threat to the state." With the far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir in charge of law enforcement, at least 200 Palestinian citizens indicted for speech-related offenses have been classified as security prisoners, according to Adalah. They've been subjected to brutal conditions, including overcrowding and severe restrictions on food, often in the same facilities as suspected militants from Gaza. In theory, they could be kingmakers Multiple parties compete for the 120 seats in Israel's national assembly, known as the Knesset. None is expected to win anywhere near 61 seats, so whoever succeeds in cobbling together a majority coalition will be the next prime minister. That can give small parties outsized influence. Netanya

52a24c8e5678.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrats-say-trump-increased-investments-in-drugmakers-that-were-given-medicare-exemptions Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Democrats say Trump increased investments in drugmakers that were given Medicare exemptions Politics Oct 16, 2026 5:32 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Investments in pharmaceutical companies made on behalf of President Donald Trump increased significantly after he returned to the White House last year, with his portfolio adding millions of dollars in stock in firms that benefited from a Republican-backed law that shields certain medications from Medicare price negotiations, according to a report from congressional Democrats. The report, released Friday by the Joint Economic Committee's minority arm, found that Trump's pharmaceutical stock holdings grew from a maximum reported value of $1.7 million in 2024 to as much as $56.2 million at the end of 2025. The report said that included up to $39.1 million worth of stock held in companies that benefited from exemptions to Medicare's drug price negotiation program, which came through a provision in Republicans' 2025 tax and spending law. READ MORE: Trump is taking credit for sharply declining drug prices. The reality is more complex Additional analysis of Trump's financial disclosures provided by committee Democrats showed that his investment portfolio bought as much as $2.55 million in shares of pharmaceutical companies benefiting from the exemptions on three dates before he signed the legislation in July 2025. That included up to $950,000 in purchases on July 1, 2025, the day the Senate passed the bill. His portfolio also bought as much as $1 million in AbbVie stock in August 2025, after the bill became law. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Republican president's wealth has grown since he took office last year through a web of business interests, many of which have benefited from the policy moves of his administration. The White House has repeatedly denied any ethics issues and accused Democrats of "attempts to fabricate conflicts of interest." WATCH: Tracking the Trump family's business deals and profits in his 2nd term The report also noted that the exemptions policy could leave some Medicare beneficiaries paying thousands of dollars more for certain cancer treatments and other medications than they would have if Medicare had been allowed to negotiate lower prices. The findings come as Trump has made lowering prescription drug costs a central part of his healthcare policy, striking deals with pharmaceutical companies that his administration says will make medications more affordable for Americans, although drug pricing is based on a complicated set of factors. Recent polling from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that most Americans think Trump is profiting off the presidency in unethical or illegal ways and is focused more on his wealth than on helping people like them. Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan, who leads the Joint Economic Committee's minority arm, called the report's findings "outrageous and yet typical from this president, who makes the American people foot the bill again and again for his own gains." Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. He denied any conflict of interest. "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold," Ingle said in a statement. A law from President Joe Biden's Democratic administration allowed Medicare for the first time to negotiate prices for some of the costliest prescription drugs. Republicans' 2025 tax and spending bill expanded an existing exemption for medications developed to treat rare diseases or conditions, delaying when certain costly drugs could become eligible for negotiations or excluding them entirely, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF. Also known as the orphan drug exclusion, the carveout allows drug companies to continue charging lucrative prices that might otherwise have been reduced through Medicare negotiations. Supporters of the change argued that a broader exemption would encourage drug companies to develop treatments for rare diseases. Critics say it allows makers of blockbuster medications to avoid negotiations that could lower costs for Medicare and its recipients. The report estimated that Medicare beneficiaries receiving the cancer drugs Keytruda, manufactured by Merck, and Opdivo, by Bristol Myers Squibb, could pay roughly $5,000 more annually than they would if Medicare negotiated prices for the medications. Trump's portfolio includes stock in both firms. The report also said that Trump's portfolio continued to buy and sell pharma company stocks throughout the first eight months of 2026, adding as much as $3.5 million in stock wealth in the sector. All recent U.S. presidents have dumped their stocks before assuming office, put their money in broadly diversified funds or set up a "blind" trust so they couldn't even know what they owned. Trump has put his broader business interests in a trust managed by his sons. But the arrangement rejects the conflict of interest protections that his recent predecessors in office had instituted. Associated Press writer Bernard Condon in New York contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. A Mexican judge has sentenced three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad to 158 years and nine months in jail each.
The Robinsons and Rhoad were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck on a secluded beach in Baja California in 2024 while they were on a surfing trip, the court heard during the trial.
The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico.
The guilty verdict was handed down last week. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them".
The convicted killers' full names could not be given for legal reasons, and they were only identified as JesÃºs Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ãngel JesÃºs.
In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, JesÃºs Gerardo (alias "El Kekas"), was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.
The court heard that the bodies of the victims were found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads.
At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in the beach town of Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.
Ensenada has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.
The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.
Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week, when their families were able to identify them.
Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.

US President Donald Trump has used his presidential authority to block numerous sanctions on Russia that were recently passed by the US Congress in an effort to punish the country for its war on Ukraine.
In an executive order on Friday night, Trump said that it is in the US "national interests" to withhold some of the sanctions. Trump signed the sanctions bill into law in September, and it was due to take effect on Sunday.
It comes days after Trump said the US would import Russian diesel in an effort to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections in November, which will decide which party controls Congress.
The plan shocked lawmakers, and has triggered a bipartisan backlash.
The US sanctions law is named for the late Republican South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, who was one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.
The law took aim at Russian's economy, and gave Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas â most significantly China and India.
Additionally, the law includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.
On Thursday, a bipartisan group of 20 US lawmakers issued a letter calling on Trump to respect the new law, which is due to take effect on 18 October.
The lawmakers thanked Trump for signing the sanctions bill, and urged his "full and faithful implementation" of the law.
The lawmakers said it would be "decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously" and called on the Trump administration "to apply the Graham law's sanctions to their fullest extent and without delay".
Last week, Trump announced that he had held a phone call with Putin, and had agreed to purchase diesel from Moscow.
US allies criticised the move, anxious that it could help Russia in its war effort.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".

Brazil's government says deforestation rates in the country's Amazon and savanna regions have fallen to record lows ahead of a presidential election run-off where the rainforest's future is a key issue.
Left-wing President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva, when he assumed office three years ago, pledged to end deforestation by 2030 in the Amazon. It had surged under his right-wing predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro.
On 25 October, Lula will face Bolsonaro's son Flavio in the run-off, with polls suggesting a neck-and-neck race. Flavio is expected to continue his father's policies if he wins, though he has pledged to fight organised crime in the Amazon.
Satellite data shows that in the year up to July 2026, the deforestation rate fell by 41.8% in the Amazon - the biggest drop since records began in 1988. The fall in the Cerrado, Brazil's savanna region, was 23.8%.
The Amazon rainforest - the world's largest - is a crucial buffer in the global fight against climate change and 60% of it is located in Brazil.
Jair Bolsonaro promoted mining in indigenous lands in the Amazon and forest clearances soared at the same time as resources to protect the forest were cut.
During Bolsonaro's presidency from 2019 to 2022, the Amazon lost nearly 60% more in forest lands compared to the previous four years, AFP news agency reported, citing official data.
Lula reversed Jair Bolsonaro's policies and saw deforestation rates drop to a six-year low during his first year in office. Lula tightened up environmental monitoring and penalties for illegal logging.
"Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," he said in a post on X on Friday.
Tropical rainforests like the Amazon are home to millions of species. In a healthy state they absorb vast quantities of planet-warming carbon dioxide, helping to keep the Earth cool.
But they have come under increasing pressure from decades of deliberate land clearance for agriculture and logging, as well as climate change, which scientists warn can create conditions for wildfires.
Brazil's Environment Minister, Joao Paulo Capobianco, described the decline in Amazon deforestation as "absolutely stratospheric".
It is a "historic achievement" for Brazil, said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.
It shows that "with political will, it is possible to curb deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions", Astrini said.

US actress Selma Blair has spoken out after being accused of assaulting multiple people on a flight travelling to New York.
A publicist for the Legally Blonde star said she "did not intend to harm anyone" and there was "much more to this story". Blair "experienced a medical emergency on the flight" and is still fighting âmultiple sclerosis (MS), the statement read.
The statement says that Blair, 54, has a neurological disorder that "bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her".
The star pleaded not guilty to charges that she assaulted an officer and a nurse after being removed from the flight. She was also accused of assulting two flight attendants on board.
In a statement to the BBC, Blair's team said the public account of what happened to her aboard a Delta Airlines flight to New York "has been built almost entirely on a police statement and a decade-old headline". They also denied media reports that she had attempted to open the door of the aircraft.
The publicist noted Blair's fight against multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic illness the actress revealed publicly in 2018. She announced in 2021 that she was in remission for the disease, but the statement notes that the Hellboy and Cruel Intentions star "still has bad days".
It adds that she also has pseudobulbar affect (PBA) - a disorder that develops in the context of a brain injury or underlying neurological dysfunction, according to the US National Institutes of Health.
The disorder affects emotional expression that can result in sudden involuntary, and out-of-control episodes of laughing, crying, or anger that do not match how a person actually feels.
She described Blair's physical achievements since her MS diagnosis as "nothing short of a miracle" and noted that she still lives with pain daily.
"Selma had never been arrested before Sunday night," the statement said. "There is much more to this story than has been reported, and we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgment, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion."
The incident happened on a flight travelling from Los Angeles to New York on Sunday evening. New York airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on a Delta Airlines flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.
A pilot asked for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to audio recorded on air traffic control obtained by CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
Blair was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons by the FBI for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US that relates to the on-board altercation.
The two additional charges of assault were filed in state court after she was taken off the plane. She has pleaded not guilty to those charges and was released on bail.
With additional reporting by Rebecka Pieder.

With November already on the horizon the UK is yet to see its first named storm of the season.
Deep Atlantic lows responsible for more turbulent conditions have been steered away by dominant areas of high pressure.
This year the headlines have been about worsening drought rather than the impact of gales.
However, could this be the calm before the storms as the Met Office predict a growing chance that late autumn and early winter will turn wetter and windier as El NiÃ±o strengthens in the Pacific.
Why has it been a quiet start to autumn?
As autumn sets in and the nights get longer temperatures around polar regions start to fall. This causes a greater contrast with the warmer tropics which can fire up a more potent jet stream - the fast moving, narrow band of fast winds high in the atmosphere.
The jet stream is largely responsible for developing and delivering our stormier pressure systems.
Typically in autumn the jet stream would be a regular visitor to the skies above the UK, steering wet and windy weather towards us.
However, so far this season it has often been sitting to the north or north-west of the UK. This has meant south or south-westerly winds bringing warmer than normal conditions and high pressure having more of an influence leading to reduced rainfall for many.
These weather patterns have therefore meant only occasional bouts of stronger winds across the north-west of the UK, with little disruption.
The heaviest of the rain has also been focused across Scotland and Northern Ireland while parts of England and Wales have continued to be much drier than normal.
Parts of Herefordshire for instance have only received a tenth of the rainfall they would normally have seen by mid-October so far this month.
Some of the biggest impacts of the dry weather have been across the southern England where exceptionally low reservoir levels have prompted the Environment Agency to declare "severe drought" in some areas.
The quiet before the storm?
A change in the position of that jet stream and its strength is expected through the coming week.
This will allow deeper low pressure systems to affect more parts of the UK marking a shift to a more widespread wetter and windier weather.
Forecasts will need to be monitored closely as there is potential later in the week that we could see our first spell of widely disruptive weather this season.
There are also longer term signals for increased rainfall and storminess later in autumn and early winter in the UK.
The Met Office's current three month outlook covering October, November and December forecasts a double the normal chance of wetter weather and 1.3 times the normal chance of windier weather which is consistent with the type of patterns seen with previous El NiÃ±o events.
When do we see the most named storms?
Storms are most often named when potentially damaging winds are forecast, but can also be named for flooding rain or disruptive snow.
They were first named to help bring public attention to episodes of severe weather, to help people prepare to avoid the worst impacts by planning ahead.
In Europe, there are five storm naming groups created from the meteorological agencies based in a similar geographic location.
The UK, Ireland, and the Netherlands form the western storm-naming group which started naming storms in 2015.
Weather systems are named by the the UK's Met Office, Ireland's Met Ãireann and Netherland's KNMI based on expected weather impacts as well as how likely those are.
Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer. The only month with no named storms in the eleven years that we've been naming storms in the UK, is May.
The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months. This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year.
It is not unusual to still be awaiting the arrival of the first storm at this time of year. In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November.

Evacuation orders in California are in effect due to a rapidly growing wildfire that has already burned six homes in the southern Los Angeles area.
The Norte Fire erupted on Friday in Orange County and quickly grew to 465 acres by the evening. One firefighter suffered heat exhaustion while battling the blaze.
Officials say the fierce Santa Ana winds will blow until Saturday, bringing further risk of more conflagrations.
The US National Weather Service (NWS) has issued a red flag warning for several California counties due to strong, gusty winds combined with low humidity and dry vegetation that create critical wildfire spread conditions.
The Norte Fire is one of 13 burning across the state, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection.
In an update on Friday evening, Division 3 Fire Chief Mark Backoff said that six homes had either been damaged or destroyed by the Norte Fire, and one firefighter had been injured from heat exhaustion.
"We continue to engage in the firefight, and have additional resources coming," he said.
Footage posted online showed blazes tearing through homes in the communities of San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano.
The Bryson Fire, burning in the affluent coastal city of Malibu in Los Angeles county, has also sparked evacuation orders throughout the Santa Monica mountains and has grown to 147 acres.
More than 400 firefighters have been fighting the blaze.
Further south, the Henderson Fire in San Diego country erupted on Thursday, and has grown to over 2,000 acres, including around Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton.
The size of the blaze has twice forced officials to close the I-5 highway, an important route that runs the length of the US West Coast.
The fires are being fanned by the Santa Ana winds, which normally begin during cooler months from late September to May.
Officials say the winds peaked on Friday, but will remain dangerous into early Saturday morning.
Winds topped 40mph (64km/h) in the Los Angeles area, the NWS said, adding that motorists should watch for debris blown into roadways.
Temperatures were far above average for this time of year in southern California, further driving up the fire danger.
The NWS has issued a heat advisory, saying that the danger of heat-related illness remained high.
Forecasts expect temperatures to reach 95F (35C) in southern California on Saturday.

Tofino approached each of his handlers in turn as they knelt in shallow water and stroked his sides.
Shortly after, a crane hoisted the more than 1,500kg beluga whale into a lorry to be shipped out of Canada to his new home, SeaWorld San Antonio - the last of 30 belugas and four dolphins to leave Marineland, a shuttered sea park near Niagara Falls.
Marineland needed to find a new home for its whales. But when the Canadian government rejected its plan to sell them to China over concerns about animal welfare, the park's operations said they would have to be euthanised.
That spurred an international rescue operation by several aquariums, leading to the largest ever transfer of captive whales this summer. But hopes that the animals were headed to a better life have been dampened by a number of deaths in the group.
Photographer Carlos Osorio documented the move, which involved whales being flown to Chicago, Atlanta, San Diego, San Antonio, and even Valencia, Spain.
Osorio recalls watching footage from a drone overhead as Tofino appeared to say his own goodbyes.
Tofino was the last captive whale in Canada. The country banned cetacean captivity and breeding seven years ago, and Osorio felt the weight of the moment.
"This is the last one to happen, and it's never going to happen again," he says.
Despite the rescue operation, tragically, five of the belugas have since died, as well as one dolphin.
Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has seen the most deaths. Peekachu, 23, Rain, 20, Orisis, 26, and Caspian, 27, were all transferred from Marineland, while longtime Shedd resident Beethoven, 34, also died after eight Marineland belugas were brought there over the summer.
Necropsies found chronic inflammatory disease in the gastrointestinal systems in Peekachu and Rain.
Foreign objects were also discovered in their stomachs, including feathers, large rocks and flecks that appear to be paint â objects Shedd believes were ingested before they were moved to Chicago.
Osiris's preliminary examination identified chronic liver disease.
Europe's largest aquarium, OceanogrÃ fic ValÃ¨ncia in Spain, recorded the death of one beluga, Jelly Bean, and one dolphin, Echo. The dolphin arrived with "serious vision problems" and other health issues, it said, and "began having difficulties swallowing and respiratory problems" in the hours before she died.
Experts say it is too early to judge the outcome of the transfers, especially considering the whales were facing euthanasia and had been living in an ageing facility. According to a tally by the Canadian Press, about 20 whales died at Marineland between 2019 and September 2025.
Once the country's most popular amusement park, Marineland closed in 2024 after years of animal welfare concerns and financial woes, and following the death of its longtime owner.
Public attitudes towards keeping whales in captivity have also changed drastically since Marineland opened in 1961. Like Canada, more countries are moving to ban or restrict the practice, including France and Mexico.
Melissa Matlow, a spokeswoman for World Animal Protection Canada, says that worldwide there are about 3,600 captive cetaceans â a group of marine mammals which includes whales, dolphins and porpoises.
But there are few alternatives for whales raised in captivity without the skills to survive in the wild.
Matlow says that leaves a "growing animal welfare crisis on our hands".
Still, her organisation had concerns about the relocation of the Marineland whales.
"If an animal was not healthy enough to withstand the stress of transport, it should not have been transported," she said in a statement.
In early October, Shedd said it knew some of the Marineland belugas "could have substantial, longstanding medical needs".
Assessments before the move "informed our planning but could not reveal every underlying condition or predict how each whale would respond to the transition. The rescue offered a path to continued, specialised care".
They said the remaining rescued belugas show positive signs, including eating well.
World Animal Protection Canada had suggested two alternatives: repurpose Marineland into a hospice-style facility for the remaining captive whales and dolphins, or fast-track development of a proposed seaside sanctuary in Nova Scotia, the Whale Sanctuary Project.
As they can't be released, "the next best thing we could do is provide sanctuary for them, where they can at least live in the ocean, and they can have back their autonomy", says Lori Marino, a neuroscientist behind the Whale Sanctuary Project, which she hopes could eventually house about 12 to 15 whales.
"I look at it as an exit ramp," she adds.
The project was initiated a decade ago, she said, but construction only began in the last two months. Fundraising is continuing and needs an additional C$6m ($4.2m; Â£3.1m).
But offshore sanctuaries have yet to be proven a successful solution for retiring performing whales.
One offshore facility for belugas is being created in Iceland, but in July organisers determined that more work was needed, and delayed the introduction of two whales until next summer.
"They are kind of more theoretical and aspirational at this point," says Michael Weiss, research director at the Center for Whale Research in Washington state, who adds that they would definitely "improve the welfare of the animals" compared to concrete tanks.
"It's a very old idea," he says, noting that net pens have been used to rehabilitate injured wild whales, or temporarily used while re-introducing captured orcas back into the wild.
