What is the point of a protest?
To raise your voice against injustice? To draw attention to a cause? Or to make those in power uncomfortable enough to listen?
For more than three decades, Indians have tried to do all three in a narrow, tree-lined road near Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century astronomical obervatory in Delhi.
But that may now be coming to an end.
This week, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar, located close to parliament, would no longer be a designated protest site.
The decision comes months after the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - not a political party but a collective which began as a joke - led a massive protest there demanding the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands turned up and Pradhan subsequently resigned.
Police barricaded Jantar Mantar soon afterwards, preventing further demonstrations. Last week, an attempt by CJP supporters to march there, this time demanding the resignation of India's election chief, ended in a police crackdown.
Protesters have now been directed to three other sites. Two are far from parliament, while the third, the sprawling Ramlila Ground, is often booked months in advance. Unlike Jantar Mantar, which is free, all three charge tens of thousands of rupees a day.
Delhi Police says, external it acted after the Supreme Court suggested identifying alternative sites with adequate infrastructure. But critics say the move could push protests beyond the reach of ordinary Indians, further from the seat of power and into venues many cannot afford.
Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed everything from mass movements that shook governments to small, lonely demonstrations by people desperate to be heard. Farmers, students, grieving parents and ex-soldiers have gathered under its trees, holding placards and shouting slogans. Not every protest made headlines, but for many, it was a place to turn to when other doors had closed.
This week, when the BBC visited, those scenes seemed a distant memory.
Yellow barricades blocked both ends of the road, with hundreds of paramilitary personnel standing guard, batons in hand.
In a nearby lane, uniformed men sat in shops drinking tea or scrolling through their phones. At one of the few shops without policemen, the shopkeeper folded his hands and said he did not want to answer any questions.
Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 1720s, Jantar Mantar was once better known as a tourist attraction than a place where a thousand revolutions were imagined.
Its story as a protest site began in 1993, when the then-Congress government stopped allowing demonstrations at the Boat Club lawns opposite the old parliament.
Historian Harleen Kaur has traced how, from the 1960s onwards, successive governments brought in new rules that shifted the site of protest in Delhi further away from parliament.
"Jantar Mantar, situated 3km (1.86 miles) from the Parliament House, [allowed the government] to contain protesting crowds at some distance from the Parliament House and PM's residence," she wrote in a 2023 paper, external.
Yet, the road saw countless spirited protests over the years.
Rachna Dhingra, an activist with the Bhopal Group for Information and Action, an advocacy group for survivors of a 1984 gas leak disaster, camped at Jantar Mantar with hundreds of others for around five months in 2008, trying to get the government to agree to demands including setting up a commission to allocate resources for rehabilitation schemes.
Through a scorching summer, they held press conferences, met politicians and even chained themselves to railings opposite then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's residence to draw attention to their cause.
It was also where she formed solidarities with others - Tibetans protesting against China, activists opposing the displacement of people over large dam projects and even just lone protesters who caught a train from their home towns with nothing but a placard and a grievance.
"It can be lonely to protest but that place became a home for so many of us. We shared each other's stories, struggles and victories," says Dhingra.
Dipa Sinha, an academic associated with the Right to Food campaign, has seen ground-breaking laws - a landmark rural jobs guarantee scheme, the National Food Safety Act and Forest Rights Act - take shape at Jantar Mantar.
"It was a place where you could discuss issues with people who came to Delhi from across the country," she says.
Protesters would demonstrate outside government offices, including the erstwhile Planning Commission and the agriculture ministry, where they were often detained by police, before returning to Jantar Mantar to "gather, discuss and strategise".
But sustaining a protest for months was not easy.
Dhingra says they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets when it rained, used public toilets near the site and went to nearby gurdwaras to freshen up.
In 2017, the National Green Tribunal cited the lack of infrastructure, along with complaints from locals, to have Jantar Mantar shut down for protests.
A year later, the Supreme Court overturned this, citing the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly guaranteed under the constitution.
When asked whether the proximity to parliament made a difference to their cause, Dhingra quoted the reactions of her co-protesters who had come to Delhi for the first time.
"That's the president's house? Does the prime minister live there? How can they not listen to us when we are at their gates?" she remembered them saying.
Sinha points out that Jantar Mantar was also near institutions like the Press Club and Constitution Club, making it easier to get media coverage, and for politicians to drop by and meet protesters.
It was a simpler time - sometimes they would ask for permission from police only on the morning of the protest.
Those rules have become much stricter, external now.
In recent years, when Dhingra tried to protest at Jantar Mantar, she was told no-one could stay the night.

0db634514f41.text: By — Michael Casey, Associated Press Michael Casey, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/fundraising-to-protect-key-natural-sites-falls-short-ahead-of-un-biodiversity-summit Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Fundraising to protect key natural sites falls short ahead of UN biodiversity summit World Oct 16, 2026 7:58 PM EDT Efforts to raise hundreds of billions of dollars to preserve the world's oceans, forests, rivers, lakes and other parts of the natural world have fallen short ahead of a key U.N. summit on biodiversity. The yawning gap between the stated ambition of nations to protect biodiversity and what money has been raised will be a central topic in Yerevan, Armenia, when the biodiversity conference, known as COP17, gets started on Monday. The nearly two-week event, scheduled to end Oct. 30, is a chance for nearly 200 countries that are part of the treaty to take stock of their progress on 23 global targets after agreeing to a historic deal crafted in Montreal in 2022. The United States is not a party to the treaty. Countries in Montreal committed to protect 30% of land and water considered important for biodiversity by 2030, a goal known as 30x30. READ MORE: UN biodiversity talks end with nations backing $200 billion per year plan to protect nature They also promised to raise $200 billion a year by 2030 for biodiversity and begin phasing out or reforming subsidies that could provide another $500 billion for nature. There were also commitments to increase to $20 billion annually by 2025 money that went to poor countries. That number would increase to $30 billion each year by 2030. "We're not moving fast enough," convention executive secretary Astrid Schomaker told The Associated Press, before a U.N. progress report released Thursday found fewer than half of parties' biodiversity targets are on track and that current commitments would only protect 26% of land and only 12% of sea by 2030. Data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development showed countries were raising between $75 billion and $92 billion each year from 2023 to 2025 — less than half the 2030 goal. Commitments to reduce $500 billion in harmful subsidies — government support and funding for sectors like fisheries and agriculture — have gained little traction, with few countries identifying which subsidies they would cut. Countries were on track to provide the $20 billion to poor countries by 2025. The latest data showed $19 billion had been raised in 2024. But a drop in foreign aid raises questions over whether the upward trend will continue. "Do we have enough money actually to finance the commitments that countries have made? And how do we get more finance to flow toward biodiversity positive outcomes?" Schomaker said. "That is the crucial question for the COP." Biodiversity has taken a beating worldwide The campaign to protect biodiversity, which first garnered global attention with the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, has often seemed like a losing battle. In a bid to grow their economies and support increasing populations, countries have converted forests into farm land, overfished their waters and reduced habitats of many plants and animals through unchecked development. Climate change, at the same time, has created the conditions for widespread wildfires and prolonged droughts that have decimated ecosystems. As a result, three-quarters of the world's land has been "severely altered" by humans and a million of the world's plants and animals are threatened with extinction, according to a 2019 U.N. report. Wildlife populations have also plummeted, according to the WWF's 2026 Living Planet Report released this month. They have declined on average by 73% between 1970 and 2022. "We are losing everything that matters for us as humans on this planet," Schomaker said. Meanwhile, there are some signs that countries are protecting more biodiversity. Countries have announced over 5,000 initiatives tied to the treaty. A report from the Campaign for Nature, a global initiative which has spearheaded the 30x30 effort, found that countries in Latin America have already committed to protecting 29% of their land while those in Oceania have promised to preserve 41% of their seas. Last year, the Philippines created a marine protected area where catching rays and sharks is prohibited, according to the Wildlife Conservation Society. In 2023, Cambodia set aside almost 100,000 acres (40,000 hectares) of flooded grassland habitat for protection while Argentina created a national park in 2024. At the conference on Friday, a 17-nation coalition was launched to accelerate species recovery. It also would support one of the Convention targets, which calls for halting extinction of threatened species and reducing extinction risk. Nine private organizations, including the Bezos Earth Fund, also announced plans to spend $500 million over the next five years to prevent extinctions and recover the world's most threatened species. "We have a shared responsibility to ensure that threatened species have a future," said Fabio Alberto Arjona Hincapié, Colombia's minister of environment and sustainable development, whose country is a coalition co-chair. Brian O'Donnell, director of the Campaign for Nature, said where and what we need to protect is clear, as are the methods to do so. "What is now needed is an upswing in political ambition and determination," said O'Donnell. O'Donnell said an international agreement reached last year to protect marine diversity on the high seas — the High Seas Treaty — would help but more was needed. Help for developing countries and subsidies will be central topics Many expected conference attendees are hoping countries, the private sector and philanthropies use the meeting next week to announce major biodiversity funding initiatives. Italy's defence minister has said it is a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.
In a BBC interview, Guido Crosetto warned that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace.
US officials have said Trump has not asked for the slowdown of internet speeds the US provides to Ukraine and which are vital for its war effort. Trump has also denied that the US has stopped sharing early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks with Ukraine.
Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice", and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine.
Trump agreed the deal with Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices.
Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table.
"Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome.
Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war.
"If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side â and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness â then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned.
"I think that is completely wrong."
Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid.
The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified.
In our interview, the defence minister vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached.
The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners.
That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.
At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".
Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".
But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia.
"When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.
But Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.
During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms, instead of education.
Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs."
In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.
Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the IxÃ¨ institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.
There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.
But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow â targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia".
"In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued.
"It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."
Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.
The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".
A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.
But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response.
"You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.
With additional reporting from Rome by Davide Ghiglione.

a05c4ee0eebf.text: By — Sam Metz, Associated Press Sam Metz, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israeli-settlers-attack-palestinians-during-west-bank-olive-harvest-and-beat-u-s-photojournalist Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israeli settlers attack Palestinians during West Bank olive harvest and beat U.S. photojournalist World Oct 16, 2026 7:46 PM EDT ABU FALAH, West Bank (AP) — Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian villages across the occupied West Bank on Friday, setting fire to cars and trees and beating residents and a foreign journalist, in the latest violence to disrupt the territory's annual olive harvest this month. Local officials and the Palestine Red Crescent Society reported attacks in at least eight villages in the northern West Bank, where most of the olive groves are concentrated and tens of thousands of Palestinian families depend on them for income. Settler violence against Palestinians has soared this year and spiked further in the weeks leading up to Israel's election on Oct. 27. The far-right government that has emboldened the settlers could soon be voted out of power — or win another term. Israeli authorities have done little to stop the attacks, according to residents and rights groups, who say the military has aided, protected or stood by as settlers lay siege to Palestinian villages. The violence has drawn accusations of " ethnic cleansing " — including from the British government, which has said Israel is turning a "blind eye" to the campaign underway. "If anything, they're sometimes assisting settlers in the attacks." Journalist attacked while covering harvest The West Bank has been under Israeli military rule since the 1967 Mideast war and today is home to around 3 million Palestinians and more than 500,000 Israeli settlers. The U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said last month that more than 1,600 attacks across the territory had been reported between January and August. Yesh Din and other rights groups say authorities rarely arrest or indict the perpetrators. Israel's military on Friday condemned the violence and acknowledged that a journalist was injured in Abu Falah. On Friday, settlers attacked the village as residents, accompanied by peace activists, set out early for the harvest. As the group of masked vigilantes approached, several members beat Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was hospitalized for her injuries. The perpetrators — armed with bottles and slingshots — "were kicking me for like 10 minutes and I was trying to hold onto my cameras and my bag," Levine said. Levine said her helmet and protective vest, which was marked "PRESS," likely saved her from more serious injuries. "This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities," the Foreign Press Association said. Israeli troops later arrived in Abu Falah and drove up to the village after dispersing the crowd in the olive groves. Residents said that soldiers later fired live ammunition at village council member Abdel Jaber Hassan, even though he was unarmed and far from the trees. The military said that soldiers had fired because an individual was running toward them with a sharp object. Nazem Saleh Shoman, another village council member, denied that account and said Hassan was shot at close range while carrying olive harvesting tools. Across the West Bank, the Palestine Red Crescent Society said that its medics had tended to 14 wounded people in six locations, while local officials reported at least four injuries in two additional villages. 'Nothing has been left intact' At least four Palestinians have been killed and more than 100 injured since harvest season began earlier this month, the Ramallah-based Palestinian Health Ministry said last week. Yesh Din said on Friday that it had already documented hundreds of incidents of settler violence directly related to this year's harvest. In Turmus Ayya, a village northeast of Ramallah, mayor Nawaf Zghoul said settlers early Friday had burned several cars in the hamlet's surrounding olive groves. "The settlers were lying in wait for farmers working on their land and attacked them," he said. "Nothing has been left intact." Israel's military said that suspects had fled the scene before troops arrived. Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, the BBC has confirmed, as the fallout from her shaky public debut appears to have reached its climax.
Speaking to reporters moments before news of her exit dropped on Friday, President Donald Trump said he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider".
Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing in the role on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters.
She spent the days after playing defence, answering tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job.
Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during a press gaggle outside Marine One.
"I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this," Trump said.
"You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media.
The BBC confirmed she was leaving the job a few hours later.
As the country draws closer to the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House.
"The White House Press Secretary is gone. MAGA extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X.
Zacharia's tumultuous week began on Tuesday, after she appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing that lasted 14 minutes, where she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions, and referred to her husband as the president.
During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practice law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam.
She replied: "When I was in China."
After intense scrutiny and digging by the press, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.
She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials".
Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity from conservative-leaning Fox News lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday.
When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'"
Zacharia also described for Hannity how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?"
When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning.
She told the show's hosts she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney, because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one.
Host Lawrence Jones, asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?"
She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me."
Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team.
In his first term, Anthony Scaramucci, left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days.
"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

Avian flu, cost-cutting and Brexit are among the reasons behind the transfer of captive birds from one of Northern Ireland's best-known wildlife sites, according to the charity that runs it.
Director of Operations at Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) Alex Lane said avian influenza, as well as difficulties in transporting birds since Brexit, has contributed to the decline in the number of captive birds at Castle Espie.
The closure of both the site's captive bird programme and guided school tour programme is part of wider WWT cost-cutting measures.
An Assembly member has described the changes to the education offering as "disappointing".
Alex Lane said the site used to have around 500 birds in its captive collection - but, a combination of Brexit and avian influenza means today, there are fewer than 100.
Both the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs and the UK's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs have been contacted for comment.
From November onwards, all captive birds at Castle Espie will be transferred to other WWT sites across the UK.
The centre, which is located in County Down, will also no longer offer guided school tours.
However, the centre have said they will "continue to welcome self-guided school visits".
Castle Espie, which is managed by the WWT, is located on the shores of Strangford Lough, just outside Comber.
The reserve is a safe haven for native and exotic birds, ducks and geese, and some of its collection including globally at-risk species.
It has different types of wetlands, including freshwater and sailing lagoons as well as seasonally flooded areas.
SDLP MLA Cara Hunter, who sits on the Stormont education committee, told BBC News NI that the "loss of guided educational visits is disappointing".
"Castle Espie has played an important role in introducing generations of young people to nature, conservation and the unique environment on their doorstep.
"I would be concerned that these changes could reduce opportunities for schools, particularly those with limited resources, to access high-quality environmental education."
The MLA added that "opportunities that educate, inspire and broaden horizons are quietly lost while Stormont remains distracted from the issues that matter most to families".
Alex Lane, Director of Operations at WWT, said rising costs and the challenge around income means charities like the WWT are facing "increasing pressure".
"We've got a sizeable deficit and obviously that's unsustainable in the long term," she told BBC News NI.
Lane said it is important the WWT have surplus income so that they can "do the conservation work that is part of their mission".
She said the site used to have over 500 birds in its captive collection - but, in part due to avian influenza, today there are less than 100.
Lane added that another factor in the decline in the number of captive birds is the increased difficulties in transporting birds since Brexit.
"There is no aligned system for bringing birds into Ireland from mainland UK.
"We've got a vastly reduced collection, and that's not by choice. That is the impact of avian influenza and the restrictions placed on bird movement as a result of Brexit."
It is thought that diverging post-Brexit bio-security checks has increased red tape for moving birds between Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
Under the strict mandates of the Windsor Framework, these regulatory shifts also mean heavy administrative and logistical costs.
According to the UK Government's official website, external, the movement of captive birds from Britain to Northern Ireland requires an export health certificate.
There is also a requirement for captive birds to be checked at the point of entry when transported to Northern Ireland, to protect animal health and welfare and public health.
However, Lane said there will be benefits to the decommissioning of the captive bird collection.
"The intent with the site is to reset it as this hub for wetland nature conservation.
"We're effectively opening up more space for wild birds."
Lane said the site "needs to stop" its formal education offering in part due to financial pressures WWT faces.
She added that there is also an insufficient number of schools booking guided tours at the site to cover costs.
Lane said the low number of school visits may be partly be caused by the cost of transport.

Pope Leo XIV's health should not be taken "for granted", a British senior Vatican official told the BBC.
Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican's foreign minister since 2014, said the news of the Pope's ill health was "a bit of a game changer", adding "it's going to make things a bit different".
The Pope was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma following surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung.
Speaking on Tuesday after the Pope's operation was announced, but before his cancer diagnosis, Archbishop Gallagher said: "I think we were maybe taking him a little bit for granted."
The 71-year-old had surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
Speaking to Radio 4's the Sunday Programme, due to air this weekend, the Archbishop said: "It's in some ways I think going to be a bit of a game changer after having the latter years of Pope Francis when he was in the wheelchair.
"And Pope Leo comes along and he's sporty and he seems to be in excellent health, and now we're told that he's not in excellent health and things have got to be sorted out."
Asked how it will make things different going forward, the Archbishop said church figures might have assumed "that he was not quite like the rest of us who are very aware of our vulnerabilities and the ageing process".
He went on: "But lots of us have been through similar experiences at different times in our lives, and we've got through them, and so we hope it's going to be the same case with Pope Leo.
"I am concerned. I think we've got to ask the question: how was it discovered? What happened?"
The Vatican has said the Pope is showing steady improvement in hospital, and he was expected to lead Sunday prayers.
They had stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.
The Angelus prayer is traditionally recited at the Vatican, overlooking crowds in St Peter's Square but has sometimes been given from a hospital window by previous popes when necessary.
No date has been given for Pope Leo's hospital discharge, but recovery was expected to take around a week.
Leo himself announced the news of his operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said.
Archbishop Gallagher, who is from Liverpool, also said he expected the Pope to visit the UK at some point.
"We have exchanged a little bit," he said. "He's just beginning to think about what he might do in 2027, but it's still very much at the examining the possibilities (stage)".
He would "bring a spirit of renewed hope", said the Archbishop, after the Pope received a rapturous welcome in France and Spain earlier this year.
"But these things do take quite a lot of planning, and so you don't just do it overnight."
You can hear more of Archbishop Gallagher's interview on The Sunday Programme on Radio 4 at 0710

A judge in the US state of New Mexico has thrown out charges against Emmy-winning actor Timothy Busfield on Friday, saying there were issues with how prosecutors presented the case.
The West Wing and Field of Dreams actor was indicted in February on four counts of criminal sexual contact of a child. Busfield has denied all allegations.
The charges stemmed from accusations brought by child actors he worked with on the Fox series The Cleaning Lady, which he directed and produced.
The judge said on Friday that the prosecutor "failed to act in a fair and impartial manner". The district attorney's office said it is evaluating options on how to move forward.
State District Judge Joseph Montano granted the defence's motion to dismiss the indictment on Friday, citing mistakes that undermined the grand jury process.
"Our office has received the order and is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed," a spokesperson for the Office of the Second Judicial District Attorney in Bernalillo County told the BBC on Friday.
The BBC has contacted a legal representative for Busfield.
The actor surrendered to state authorities in January when a warrant was issued for his arrest. A judge later ordered his release pending trial.
Busfield had originally been taken into custody in Albuquerque on two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and one count of child abuse.
The indictment against him, reviewed by the BBC, said that on or between 19 October 2022 and 10 September 2023, Busfield "touched or applied force to the intimate parts" of one of the unnamed boys when he was under the age of 13.
The Thirtysomething actor's defence team submitted more than 70 letters from people vouching for his character and said that he underwent and passed a polygraph test pertaining to the allegations against him.
In a warrant for Busfield's arrest, prosecutors had said the parents of the boys alleged that he groomed and sexually abused the youngsters while working on The Cleaning Lady.
Authorities claimed the boys referred to Busfield as "Uncle Tim" and alleged that he "would tickle them on the stomach and legs". Both boys told authorities they were touched inappropriately for years, his arrest affidavit stated.
Busfield's lawyers had said the actor was being accused as an act of revenge after the children were fired from the series, which angered their mother.
The BBC's Nardine Saad contributed to this report.

75c837003997.text: Pope Leo XIV was discharged from the hospital on Saturday after having surgery to remove a cancerous nodule in his lungs. Why it matters: His discharge clears the way for his rigorous upcoming travel schedule and may alleviate fears of a leadership vacuum at the Vatican. What they're saying: " In light of the blood tests and chest X-ray performed this morning, and following an assessment of his clinical condition, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge ," The Holy See Press Office said in a Saturday statement attributed to Leo's doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora. Catch up quick: The Vatican announced Leo would be having surgery to remove a nodule from his lung on Oct. 11, and later said the surgery removed the lower lobe of his right lung. The Vatican confirmed the surgery was successful on Tuesday, and later said that Leo was walking around, eating normally, and that his blood tests and chest X-rays were normal. Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer, per the Cancer Center, and if caught early, survival rates are very high. Zoom out: His hospitalization and subsequent cancer diagnosis struck fear into Catholics across the world, who offered him prayers and well-wishes as he recovered. For example, a group in Chicago, the first American Pontiff's hometown, created a care package for Leo featuring get-well cards and a Chicago White Sox blanket. The Vatican has not yet said if any additional treatment is needed. Go deeper: Chicago Catholics pray for Pope Leo XIV after lung cancer diagnosis

842254457f55.text:
US withdrawal won’t end the region’s ISIS dilemma
Iraq, Syria, and their regional partners must cooperate to replace what U.S. troops once provided.
The U.S. military recently completed its withdrawals from Iraq and Syria, ending a decade of leadership in the counterterrorism fight against the Islamic State in the Levant. The gradual drawdown was meant to avoid a sudden vacuum that proxy militias, malign regional actors, terrorist organizations, and great-power rivals could fill, as happened in Iraq and Afghanistan. Yet ISIS, while greatly reduced, persists in Iraq and Syria, which must now build a sustained regional counterterrorism effort to prevent the group’s resurgence.
The absence of an American footprint in the two countries reduces cost and risks to personnel, but it also diminishes visibility into ISIS networks, undermines security relationships, and eliminates a forward position from which Washington could detect and disrupt terrorist threats before they affect U.S. interests and foreign partners.
While ISIS has mounted fewer attacks in Iraq and Syria since 2025, this is evidence not of diminished capacity but of strategic recalibration. In Syria, ISIS has been busy diversifying its targets and methods. In June alone, ISIS attacked oil tankers, commercial trucks, security checkpoints, military regional headquarters, political figures, judges, and buses ferrying personnel from the Ministry of Defense. In July, a bomb killed 10 people at a Damascus café frequented by officials working in the Justice Palace. Two more bombs exploded during President Macron of France’s first state visit, killing 10 and 18 people near the Four Seasons Hotel and Ministry of Tourism respectively.
Counterterrorism infrastructure, never perfect to begin with, can erode quickly after American forces leave. This has been seen in the dissolution of the Counter-ISIS mission and the emptying of ISIS detention camps like Al Hol and Al Roj. It has also been seen in the region’s prisons. As ISIS has lost operational capacity and territory, the group has turned to prison breaks as a strategic imperative, undertaking campaigns like the “Breaking the Walls” Campaign of 2012-13 in Iraq to replenish its ranks.
The threat is acute in Iraq, which took in 5,700 ISIS-affiliated prisoners—not only Iraqis and Syrians, but residents of 61 other countries—after the SDF’s January collapse in northeast Syria. It put them in prisons that were already overcrowded and under-resourced, and accepted responsibility for their detention, interrogation, and trial. The U.S. presence had helped encourage the humane treatment of prisoners and fair trials for those charged with terror crimes, reducing ISIS’ ability to use the prisons for recruiting, networking and organizing. Now, the troops have departed amid real concerns about backsliding.
In Syria, concerns remain about whether Syrian forces can integrate effectively and quickly to sustain ISIS’ defeat, in the face of recent incidents like ISIS infiltration into the Syrian Army and recent high-profile plots and attacks beyond ISIS’ traditional area of operations. Syrian prisons have also been targeted for breakouts, including ISIS’ 2022 attack on Al Sinaa prison and a January attempt at the Shaddadi detention facility.
Throughout the fight against terrorist organizations in Iraq and Syria, American personnel provided intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, airpower, special operations capacity, logistics, and local partnerships to local forces. This allowed the U.S. and its partners to monitor and disrupt groups like the Islamic State and defeat its territorial caliphate, while also giving Washington on-the-ground insight into terrorist organizations’ rapidly evolving tactics, as well as local political and security dynamics.
Absent these resources, it is likely the number and severity of ISIS plots and attacks will increase. Washington, its partners, and the Iraqi and Syrian governments must find creative ways to fill the security gaps. Syrian and Iraqi neighbors—Jordan, Türkiye, Lebanon, and other regional players—must begin forging close relationships with Damascus and Baghdad. Without these relationships, the region risks losing years of counterterrorism progress—and the U.S. may be forced to intercede once again.
This commentary is published in coordination with the 2026 Global Security Forum, of which Defense One is a media partner.
Caroline D. Rose is a Senior Director at the New York City-based Soufan Center, a nonpartisan research institution, where she conducts research on the crime-terror nexus, security, counterterrorism, and U.S. defense policy with a focus on Iraq and Syria. She is a Senior Nonresident Fellow at both the New Lines Institute and Orion Policy Institute, both where she writes about trends in terrorism and geopolitics.
Dr. Julie Chernov Hwang is an Associate Professor of Political Science and International Relations at Goucher College. She is a Senior Research Fellow at the Soufan Center & a Harry Frank Guggenheim Distinguished Scholar with over a decade researching terrorist behavior, notably social networks, radicalization, commitment, role assignment, disengagement, rehabilitation, reintegration, repatriation, and deradicalization.

ebe837668f40.text: President Trump is carrying his insatiable appetite for controversy into the most unforgiving stretch of the electoral calendar, fortified by a decade of political survival. "Bottom line, it's gonna all work out. You know why? It always does," Trump told reporters this week. Why it matters: Gone are the days of a single "October surprise," swallowed by a familiar barrage of scandals, provocations and shattered conventions that have persisted in the closing weeks of Trump's final midterm election. The big picture: Axios has documented Trump's steady demolition of presidential norms in his second term, from the transition through his first 100 days and first year in office. This year, even the threat of losing Congress — and with it, much of his ability to pursue his agenda over the next two years — has done little to temper the pace or audacity of Trump's presidency. Consider the first 15 days of October alone, and the succession of controversies that might have shaken the foundation of a more conventional presidency: Raid on a political opponent: Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) home and seized her phone as part of an investigation aimed at stripping the sitting member of Congress of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deporting her, the Wall Street Journal reports. Omar denies wrongdoing. Calls to shoot leakers: Trump declared at an Arizona campaign rally that officials who leak sensitive military information "should be shot," invoking an earlier era when he claimed the government routinely executed leakers. Concessions to Vladimir Putin: Trump eased sanctions ⁠ on Russian diesel, demanded the ouster of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and pressured Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries. Late Friday night, Trump waived sweeping new Russia sanctions ⁠ under a bipartisan law named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that he signed just last month. Taxpayer-funded political ads: Trump spent millions in taxpayer dollars on campaign-style ads promoting his presidency, until a federal judge ordered them halted. He then directed his MAGA Inc. super PAC to finance future spots, drawing a separate complaint alleging violations of campaign-finance law. Federal crackdown on the press: The Justice Department launched an antitrust investigation into ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC after the networks suspended White House pool coverage to protest Trump's ban on three news organizations. $5,000 election promise: Trump pledged to send every adult American a $5,000 check if Republicans retain control of Congress, explicitly tying more than $1 trillion in proposed federal payments to the outcome of the midterms. DOJ intervention in the midterms: With voting already underway, the Justice Department sued California to block 20,000 ballots from suspected noncitizens — the latest escalation in a sweeping campaign to affect American elections. Grisly social-media posts: Trump posted footage of a man being fatally mauled by a tiger, followed by a montage of animal attacks set to upbeat music and an AI-generated video of himself wrestling and embracing a tiger. $333 million in ballroom donations: Secret records obtained by the Washington Post revealed the corporations and billionaires bankrolling Trump's White House ballroom, including donors who benefited from government contracts, regulatory decisions and a presidential pardon involving a family member. The other side: Three October episodes forced Trump into rare retreats — largely of other people's making. A televised execution: Trump scrapped the plan to livestream a convicted mass murderer's execution by firing squad after bipartisan outrage. An ambassador's downfall: Trump forced Kimberly Guilfoyle — who was engaged to his son for four years until 2024 — to resign as ambassador to Greece after reports that she solicited $100,000 from a political donor to cover personal credit-card bills. Guilfoyle denies wrongdoing. A five-day press secretary: Trump ousted Katie Zacharia amid scrutiny of her legal credentials and a widely criticized debut. Axios reports Trump was blindsided to learn that Zacharia — whom he had introduced as an attorney — had never passed the bar exam. What they're saying: Far from seeing October as a month of political peril, the administration is celebrating it as a continuation of Trump's record. "Since Day One of his administration, President Trump has boldly and consistently fulfilled on his campaign promises to protect national security, make America beautiful, secure the border, crack down on crime, ensure free and fair elections, and make life more affordable," White House spokesperson Allison Schuster told Axios. "October is shaping up to be another incredible month," she added. Between the lines: Trump has spent a decade defying political gravity. But the economic strength that helped insulate him during his first term has given way to a deepening crisis of public confidence. A Fox News poll released Wednesday put Trump's approval at 36% — his lowest in either presidency — including a devastating 22% for his handling of inflation. In the same Fox poll, government corruption narrowly surpassed inflation as the issue drawing the most extreme concern from voters. The bottom line: Trump is treating a moment of maximum political vulnerability like business as usual, betting that the instincts that carried him this far won't fail him now.

8f015b3e9d2d.text:
- Published
Pope Leo XIV will be discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday afternoon, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.
The Vatican said the Pope will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing to a crowd in St Peter's Square on Sunday, as he did last week when he surprised the world by announcing the surgery.
On Friday, photographs were released of the Pope celebrating Mass and distributing communion in hospital for staff.
A statement from his doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed "steady improvement" following his operation.
The surgery on Tuesday, which lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The results of further tests to check for any sign that the cancer has spread have not yet been announced.
The Pope also spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in their first call since June 2025. The Vatican said the call was to urge "dialogue and peace".
It came as Russia's bombardment of cities across Ukraine intensifies, with a growing number of civilian casualties and no sign of Putin being ready to halt the invasion.
The Pope also called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy, occupied by Russia and under constant shelling, to allow people to be evacuated and for the urgent delivery of food and medicine. The BBC recently reported on residents there being forced to eat garden weeds to survive.
The Pope's schedule has been cleared completely until 20 October, so his reappearance in public so soon is a surprise and will be some relief for Catholics around the world.
Those close to the Pope said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America, planned for early November and which includes a visit to Peru, where he was a missionary for many years.
It is not yet clear whether he might be fit to travel or require further treatment.

17d02870053d.text: Elon Musk tells biographer Walter Isaacson in a new podcast interview that the fizzled DOGE experiment, which the SpaceX and Tesla CEO once headed, proved there's "no way we were gonna solve the deficit from within the government." "The only way we're going to solve the national debt is with AI and robots," Musk tells the author for a new podcast series, " The Builders with Walter Isaacson ," premiering Tuesday. "We're not gonna solve it by trying to save our way there." Why it matters: Musk's comments to Isaacson — author of the definitive 2023 biography, " Elon Musk " — admit that DOGE was a flop, but point to the chance that some future administration will take a new stab at the problem using ever-more-capable AI. Zoom in: Musk said the appetite to cut spending "is not there at the presidency, the House, the Senate or the judiciary. Basically, no one in authority in the government whatsoever — with maybe a few rare exceptions [like the] Rand Pauls of the world — actually wants to reduce spending." "Maybe if the president made that his primary goal, we could do that," Musk added. "If you try to solve the deficit and stop wasteful spending, you make a lot of enemies. President Trump likes to be liked. He doesn't like people calling him, being upset about ... some funding being stopped." Musk admits he "kinda got carried away, basically" and that he wound up being "gone for too long" from his companies. "What I should have done," he added, "was be more in the background ... and probably only had it last for a month or two" rather than the four months he was formally in the White House. "I should have gone back and focused on AI a little sooner than I did." When Isaacson asked Musk if his time in the West Wing had been too seductive, in a way, Musk replied: "It was, a little bit. I mean, it was kinda cool 'cause ... I'm just there in the Oval Office while all these, like, big momentous decisions are being made." Asked about the time he brandished a chainsaw onstage at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) a month into Trump's second term, Musk said: "That was a weird weekend." Pressed to elaborate, Musk said: "Let's let sleeping dogs lie or whatever." The big picture: Isaacson warned this week that Steve Jobs and the other great creators of the personal computer age would be cautious about autonomous AI agents not tightly connected to human control. Isaacson includes his warning in the new preface to an updated edition, published this week, of his sweeping 2014 history of the digital age, " The Innovators : How a Group of Hackers, Geniuses, and Geeks Created the Digital Revolution." Behind the scenes: Isaacson tells me he launched "The Builders" because he wanted to press the builders of this new AI age on these dangers and hear in their own voices what motivates them. "Musk is an amazing engineer who is pushing us forward with Starship, Starlink, Neuralink, and autonomous EVs," Isaacson said. "But as I describe in my biography, I think he is too prone to darkness and conspiracies when it comes to politics and people. His complexities come through in the interview, as I hope they do in the biography." What's next: Isaacson's podcast series, created by media company Kaleidoscope , includes conversations with Peter Thiel, Alex Karp, Fei-Fei Li, and Dario and Daniela Amodei. A series preview says the tech legends "open up about their ambitions, what frightens them, how they think about humanity, and what drives them to build so big and so fast. The conversations are intimate, charming, and sometimes chilling." Listen to a trailer for "The Builders."

e58d8f156c20.text: Black voters may determine whether Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) can build on breakthroughs in the 2026 elections. Why it matters: This year's primaries showed that DSA's path runs through older Black voters who wield enormous influence in Democratic primaries — particularly in the South — but have been slower to embrace insurgent candidates. By the numbers: Black Democrats are more likely to like than dislike leaders who identify as democratic socialists, but nearly two-thirds remain neutral toward them. 21% of Black Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents told Pew Research Center they like such leaders, compared with 11% who dislike them. Another 65% were neutral. Among Black Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents, 23% of those ages 18–49 like leaders who identify as democratic socialists, compared with 20% of those 50 and older. State of play: Angie Nixon's upset win in Florida's Democratic U.S. Senate primary made the Black state representative the first DSA member to win a major-party statewide nomination. Her politics blend labor organizing and civil-rights protest: The former union organizer fought voting-rights battles with sit-ins and a bullhorn and opened a bookstore amid Florida's school book bans, hosting Black-history workshops and organizing groups. Her vote share rose in precincts with younger and larger Black populations, an Axios analysis of election results found. Donavan McKinney's Detroit victory also showed a DSA-backed candidate can break through in a center of Black political power. The DSA-endorsed state representative defeated Rep. Shri Thanedar 51.9%-48.1% in Michigan's 13th District, pairing deep Detroit roots and a legislative record with labor and local support. Yes, but: A July Redbox Research poll for A Fight Worth Having found former Rep. Cori Bush (D-Mo.) leading Rep. Wesley Bell (D-Mo.) 52%–20% among voters under 35 and 46%–36% among those 35–49. But only 19% of the Black likely-primary electorate in the poll was under 50. Bell ultimately defeated Bush 59%-37%. Zoom out: Nationally, 39% of Democratic-aligned adults under 30 like democratic socialist leaders, compared with 26% of those 50 and older. In 2016, an NBC analysis of 25 state exit polls found Bernie Sanders beat Hillary Clinton 52%-47% among Black voters under 30. In South Carolina's 2020 primary, Black voters made up 56% of the electorate, and 69% of Black voters over 45 backed Joe Biden, according to Edison exit polling . Between the lines: New America's Theodore Johnson tells Axios older Black voters often impose a "viability hurdle" before taking a chance on candidates. Johnson said younger Black voters can be "central" to an insurgent coalition but "insufficient" without broader support. What they're saying: Darius Jones of the National Black Empowerment Action Fund warns against reading frustration with establishment Democrats as socialist conversion. Younger Black voters are "increasingly impatient with the pace of results," he said, but that is "not a wholesale endorsement of the DSA in any way." Marcus Board Jr. , a political science associate professor at Howard University, said DSA's difficulty connecting class politics to race is "definitely a hurdle." The other side: DSA says it is "committed to growing our membership into a more diverse, multiracial, multigenerational movement" by organizing around Black workers, child care, housing and food security.

A nursery owner and five members of her staff have been jailed after they were found to have poisoned more than 200 children with lead-tainted food.
Li Huifang, who operated the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Tianshui, in the Gansu province, was sentenced to life in prison for producing and selling toxic and harmful food, according to Chinese state media.
In July 2025, 247 pupils and staff at the nursery were found to have abnormally high blood lead levels after children began falling ill.
A report into the incident found that chefs at Heshi Peixin had used inedible paint to "enhance the look" of its meals to attract more students - despite the paint being being clearly marked as such.
In addition to the sentence, the Lanzhou Intermediate People's Court also ordered the confiscation of 500,000 yuan (Â£56,200; $74,700) of Li's personal assets, state broadcaster CCTV reported.
Nursery executive principal Zhi Jinglin was sentenced to 15 years in prison and fined 300,00 yuan.
Four other members of staff who worked in the nursery's kitchen received sentences of between six to eight years, according to state media.
The court found the four had been instructed by Li and Zhi to add toxic and harmful ingredients to food served to children and staff.
Food samples were later found to contain lead 2,000 times in excess of China's national safety limit.
The investigation into the poisoning began after 235 children from Heshi Peixin nursery had to be treated for lead poisoning after eating steamed red date cakes and sausage corn buns.
Investigators found that the red date cake and the corn sausage rolls had lead levels of 1052mg/kg and 1340mg/kg respectively, both of which far exceed the national food safety standard limit of 0.5mg/kg.
Lead poisoning is "particularly harmful to young children" and can "severely damage the brain and central nervous system", according to the World Health Organization.
Officials later found that dozens of provincial officials and hospital staff attempted to cover up the incident by tampering with blood tests and accepting bribes from a nursery investor.
China has since published a set of national guidelines for the provision of meals on campuses. Among the measures is the requirement for every new batch of food to be tested, and for flour, rice and cooking oil to be purchased from centralised procurement points only.

A rare pink diamond is going on display in France for the first time since it was stolen almost 100 years ago to the day - the last time it was shown to the public.
The nine-carat, pear-shaped gemstone known as the "Grand CondÃ©" was pilfered in an overnight raid on the ChÃ¢teau de Chantilly in October 1926 and concealed in a hollowed-out apple.
The diamond - one of few royal jewels to survive the French Revolution - was recovered a few weeks later when a hungry maid at the hotel in which the thieves were staying took a bite of the apple.
It will once again be on display in the CondÃ© Museum at the ChÃ¢teau de Chantilly until 3 January.
The museum's director Mathieu Deldicque said that while the apple story may sounds far-fetched, it was widely covered by newspapers at the time.
Deldicque has faced questions about whether the exhibition may be tempting fate, especially given the string of heists on European cultural institutions in the past 12 months, including the daring daylight robbery of jewellery from the Louvre museum in Paris.
While he declined to reveal to CNN how much the diamond was insured for, he noted that extensive academic study into the properties of the diamond had taken place to make it uniquely identifiable.
The results of this analysis, as well as previously unseen archive material about the gem's history and theft, form part of the exhibition, according to the museum.
Naturally occurring pink diamonds are exceptionally rare and often sell for tens of millions of dollars. The highest price ever fetched for one at auction was $71.2m (Â£53.6m) in 2017, according to Sotheby's.
The exact origins of the Grand CondÃ© remain a mystery.
It was first mentioned in 1740 in an inventory of Louis Henri de Bourbon, Prince of CondÃ©, drawn up following his death, the ChÃ¢teau de Chantilly said.
It then became part of the collection of Queen Marie-AmÃ©lie of Bourbon-Sicily, the wife of French King Louis Philippe I, and then her son, Prince Henri of OrlÃ©ans, the Duke of Aumale.
He bequeathed it to the Institut de France, which now owns the ChÃ¢teau de Chantilly, 50km (31 miles) north of Paris, along with thousands of artworks and manuscripts which became the MusÃ©e CondÃ© collection.

a882d846fb06.text: President Trump waived new sanctions on Russia late Friday night, saying it was in the "national interests" to hold off on the sweeping levies under the Graham Act that he signed just last month. Why it matters : Trump is easing American pressure on Russia despite a bipartisan chorus calling for him to do the exact opposite. It comes a week after his surprise deal to let Russia sell diesel internationally, which Republicans have condemned as loudly as Democrats. It also puts Republican candidates making their final midterm sprint in the position of having to defend the president's warmer relationship with a country voters overwhelmingly see as an American enemy . Driving the news: The White House released the text of an executive order late Friday night detailing the implementation of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed in September. The bill, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, imposed broad new sanctions on Russia and countries that do business with it, including buyers of its oil. The order notes that the law allows the president to "waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person, any restriction with respect to a person, and any duty." "I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," Trump said in the order. What they're saying: Democrats quickly blasted the waiver. "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) posted on X. "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin. I hope my Republican colleagues will join me in condemning this craven, cowardly action," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said on X. The big picture: The waiver caps a historic week in recent U.S.-Russia relations, where Trump abruptly eased pressure on multiple fronts. Whether it was the diesel deal, or a fight over Ukraine's ability to use Starlink to defend itself against Russian munitions, or a public denial of Russian involvement in the Iran war, Trump has spent the last few days shifting America's position on an old foe. The bottom line : The louder the bipartisan anti-Russia chorus gets, the more Trump doubles down on pulling back the pressure.

PARIS—By the time Cléo made it to Greek class, she had gone completely pale. It was a Wednesday in June during France’s second consecutive heat wave this year, and the 16-year-old was struggling to cope with the rising temperatures.
She pushed through, thinking she was just tired. But the following day at her sweltering high school on the eastern edge of Paris, nausea and a desperate thirst gripped her. The school nurse, recognizing the signs of heat exhaustion, told her to go home.
This week, as she recalled the experience and worried about more heat waves to come, Cléo and her friends stood by a pile of green garbage cans, blocking their school’s entrance. For the past four weeks, scenes like this have multiplied at thousands of schools across France, where students are protesting to demand better learning conditions and more investment in public education.
These student protests have become one of the most significant social movements in the country’s recent history. They’ve been met with a heavy-handed police crackdown; Roughly 8,000 arrests have been made in three weeks, 85 percent of them minors. Fearing repercussions, Cléo and other underage students who talked to Inside Climate News asked to be quoted using only their first names.
The students’ demands are far-ranging: more teachers, smaller class sizes, a shortened school day and an overhaul of the post-secondary college application system. But the heart of the revolt is indignation over crumbling school infrastructure—a problem laid bare by climate-change-fueled heat waves.
This year was France’s hottest on record, and the country counted 8,000 excess deaths during the summer’s heat waves. In June alone, deaths spiked 11 percent compared to the same month in 2025.
France’s schools, meanwhile, were not built for the hotter world the students have inherited after generations of fossil fuel use have warped the climate. Many buildings were designed to hold onto heat; air conditioning is rare. As classrooms recorded temperature peaks above 100 degrees Fahrenheit this spring, schools reported incidents from fainting to nosebleeds.
Students protesting this week outside high schools in the Paris area described a raft of problems in their buildings that made them feel abandoned by their government, including falling ceilings, moldy walls, out-of-service bathrooms, chair shortages and pest infestations. For many, this year’s record heat waves were a breaking point that highlighted their schools’ inability to keep students safe in a warming climate.
“We’re here to claim our rights, we’re here to make ourselves heard because we’re fed up with this government, we’re fed up with this country and we’ve had enough,” said Koumba, a 16-year-old student at a high school in Montreuil, on the outskirts of Paris.
Schools Built for an Outdated Climate
Marie-Hélène Azam is a professor of engineering science at the National Institute of Applied Sciences and leads a project studying how France’s primary school buildings can be adapted to withstand heat waves.
“We’re realizing that, until now, we’ve designed buildings for energy efficiency in winter,” she said. “We need to find a way to reconcile comfort in winter with comfort in summer, and that means designing buildings a little differently.”
“As soon as the temperature of the building starts to drop, another even more intense heat wave arrives.”
— Marie-Hélène Azam, National Institute of Applied Sciences professor
Traditionally, French schools have large windows to maximize sunlight and warmth. That backfires when temperatures rise, turning classrooms into greenhouses.
And like many older buildings in France, schools are typically heavy structures with “high thermal inertia,” absorbing, storing and then releasing heat. This is beneficial during winter, but it can make classrooms hotter inside than out on high-heat days.
The issue isn’t just extreme temperatures. The way they’re hitting makes it worse.
“With heat waves becoming more intense and lasting longer, we no longer have enough time to cool these buildings down at night or between two heat waves,” Azam said. “As soon as the temperature of the building starts to drop, another even more intense heat wave arrives.”
Among potential solutions: exterior shutters to prevent the sun from heating up windows, ceiling fans to cool students and evaporative cooling technologies that use water to zap heat.
A spokesperson for the Île-de-France region, which oversees public high school infrastructure in the Paris area, said it allocated $1.2 billion to school construction and renovations this year, including upgrades to roofs and windows. During the heat waves, the regional government spent $1.1 million to open additional exam centers and purchase misting devices and fans.
In France, air conditioning has so far been treated as a last resort for climate adaptation. Many worry that widespread installation will worsen the “urban heat island” effect that makes cities hotter than rural areas: AC units push hot air outside, increasing temperatures on the streets. Cost is another barrier, with energy prices in Europe among the highest in the world.

Many of them cite climate change as a source of anxiety about their future, alongside concerns about the economy and how artificial intelligence will affect their job prospects.

From our collaborating partner “Living on Earth,” public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by producer Aynsley O’Neill with Nathan Donley from the Center for Biological Diversity.
Atrazine is the second-most widely used weed killer in the U.S. after glyphosate, which you might know as Roundup. Much like glyphosate, atrazine can disrupt hormones and has been linked to serious health impacts, including cancer. In early October, California’s Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment announced that it plans to list the herbicide as a known carcinogen.
Atrazine is also wreaking havoc on aquatic ecosystems, and recent research from the Center for Biological Diversity has been tracking the extent of the contamination.
Nathan Donley is the environmental health science director at the Center for Biological Diversity and the author of a new study on atrazine. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
AINSLEY O’NEILL: For listeners who aren’t familiar, what is atrazine, and what are the known consequences on human health?
NATHAN DONLEY: Atrazine is an herbicide, so it targets unwanted plants or weeds. It’s a pesticide, and it is the second-most widely used pesticide in this country. We use about 70 million pounds each year, year after year, which starts to add up pretty quickly. It’s used mainly on corn, sorghum and sugar cane.
Atrazine is a carcinogen and is linked to multiple cancers like certain lymphomas and breast cancer. Atrazine is also linked to reduced fertility. Things like decreased sperm counts, irregular menstrual cycling, multiple birth defects are associated with atrazine. We’re talking about harms that can have very tangible consequences and effects on people’s lives.
O’NEILL: A study out of the Center for Biological Diversity recently found that nearly a quarter of all rivers in the continental United States contain levels of atrazine that are found to harm wildlife and human health. Help us understand the scale of this. How much water are we talking about here?
DONLEY: It’s really a striking figure, and one that even as someone who studies pesticides, it just surprised the heck out of me. We’re talking about nearly a million miles of rivers and streams that have really harmful levels of atrazine in them. Keep in mind these rivers don’t just contain some level of atrazine, they have levels that the EPA identifies as high enough to destroy aquatic ecosystems.
We have tens of thousands of synthetic chemicals that are manufactured and released as pollution in this country, and to think that just one of those tens of thousands is single-handedly making a quarter of our rivers and streams dangerous to fish and amphibians and migrating birds is just outrageous, and it makes you just want to scream out the window because so many people live in these areas that are highly contaminated.
The water that they drink and bathe in and prepare food with comes from these highly contaminated rivers. About 20 percent of all drinking water intakes from surface water comes from these rivers that are highly contaminated, so this is really an issue that hits on human health just as much as it does the health of our planet and our natural resources.
O’NEILL: What regions of the country are seeing the most impact from this?
DONLEY: The thing about atrazine is, it’s not spread out evenly across the country. I live in Olympia, Washington, for instance, and I have almost zero exposure to atrazine because there’s really none used around me. But I grew up in Kansas, where I was probably drinking gallons of this stuff every week during my formative years.
The big hot spot tends to be in the Corn Belt, states like Nebraska and Kansas, Missouri, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana. But there are also smaller hot spots around the country. One of those places, for instance, is the Chesapeake Bay watershed. Not many people know this, but corn is very widely grown in the watershed of the Chesapeake Bay. The Mississippi River, where all the runoff from the Corn Belt goes to, is also very highly contaminated.
Lake Okeechobee in Florida, which is the second-largest freshwater lake in the U.S., happens to be surrounded by half a million acres of sugarcane plantations, where a lot of atrazine is used. A place where I used to vacation as a kid, between Galveston and Corpus Christi along the Texas Gulf Coast, is also one of these really highly contaminated regions.

O’NEILL: Atrazine has now been banned in 63 countries, including the European Union. Yet it’s one of the most widely used pesticides here in the United States, just after glyphosate. Why do you think the United States government is so reluctant to ban this pesticide?
DONLEY: We have a very powerful industry lobby in this country: the agrochemical industry, corporate agriculture. They want this pesticide because it lines the pockets of their corporate benefactors, so they lobby hard. They get lawmakers in their pockets, they get presidential administrations to turn a blind eye, and this has been happening for decades. And it’s nearly impossible to get the government to do anything meaningful on atrazine because every time it tries, this powerful lobbying arm comes down on them hard.
The sheer amount of money and power wielded by the corporate agriculture lobby rivals the oil and gas industry, and even when the will of the people want change, the levers remain seized and change never comes. Ultimately what this does is it allows corporations to profit from the pollution that is harming people in this country.
