Plenty of storms have hit Pensacola, Florida’s westernmost city, in the 450 years since its founding, but among the worst has been the storm over the toxic waste site nicknamed “Mount Dioxin.”
Bureaucratic mismanagement led to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency relocating about 400 households from the neighborhoods around the site beginning in the mid-1990s. To date, it’s the third-largest permanent Superfund relocation in U.S. history, after Love Canal and Times Beach.
Thirty years after efforts to relocate residents away from legacy pollution began, the story still isn’t over. Cleanup of contaminated soil was completed in 2010, according to the EPA, but the land remains vacant. Work to clean up groundwater contamination is finally expected to begin this fall.
To understand the scope of the pollution and why the cleanup efforts have been so involved, one first needs to understand the history of the site. From the 1940s to the 1970s, redlining kept Black homebuyers from purchasing houses anywhere in Pensacola except three neighborhoods: Rosewood Terrace, Oak Park and Goulding. Those three neighborhoods were bordered by the CSX railroad and property belonging to the Escambia Wood Treating Company and the Agrico Chemical Company. All of them posed serious, albeit underrecognized, hazards.
Agrico was a fertilizer manufacturer, which left high levels of arsenic, lead, chromium, radium, fluorides and sulfates in the soil and water. The railroad mostly hauled freight, including tank cars carrying hazardous chemicals that sometimes spilled.
And from 1942 to 1982, Escambia Wood Treating produced power poles, railroad ties, pilings and other wood products coated with such health-harming, cancer-causing chemicals as creosote and PCBs to make them last. It was no fly-by-night outfit, either. One of the owners was Charles Soule, Sr., who served as Pensacola’s mayor from 1967 through 1971.
All the managers were white. Nearly all the workers were Black, and many lived near the plant. When they went home after work, they couldn’t get away from the pollution. One later told a reporter: “It was horrible for us all, but we all had to try to make a living.”
After Congress passed the Clean Water Act and other environmental regulations in the 1970s, Escambia Wood’s owners filed for bankruptcy and eventually abandoned the plant. Evidence of their presence remained in the soil and the aquifer.
Escambia Wood had stored the site’s toxic waste—not just creosote and PCBs, but also polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and dioxins—in unlined pits. And in Florida’s porous ground, the waste that workers were essentially ordered to pour into the pits didn’t stay there.
In 1989, Agrico was declared a Superfund site. While EPA personnel were investigating the contamination there, they discovered the situation at Escambia Wood was even worse. Instead of declaring it a Superfund site right away—they were hesitant to establish two next-door sites where the federal government was agreeing to pay for cleanup of toxic material—the EPA ordered an emergency cleanup that required less rigorous procedures.
Because they were in such a rush, the EPA personnel skipped what would normally be procedural steps for such a cleanup. That meant the agency didn’t meet with the Black residents or former employees who offered to show the agency personnel where to find the worst contamination.
Paul Peronard, the assigned EPA coordinator, ultimately worked for the agency for 40 years and now freely admits he handled the Escambia Wood site poorly.
“This was my first [Superfund] site,” he said recently. “I viewed it as an engineering problem, but this site was a social problem … We didn’t explain ourselves well.”
Instead, the EPA sent cleanup crews to excavate the waste as children played just outside the chain-link fence around the property. Before long, the EPA had piled up 250,000 cubic yards of toxic soil, a 60-foot mound locals dubbed “Mount Dioxin.” Sometimes, when the site was unguarded, neighborhood children climbed the fence and slid down the hill.
More than 900 people, many of them Black, lived within one-quarter mile of the site, and within a mile there were five daycare centers, one hospital and three public schools. When clouds of dust blew off Mount Dioxin, it drifted over the neighborhood.
Residents who were already complaining about the high incidence of cancer among their families began complaining of more immediate problems: acute respiratory distress, nosebleeds, headaches, nausea and skin rashes. When they confronted EPA workers with their worries about the dust affecting their health, they were told it was only an odor problem, and thus not a health risk.
One resident, a retired teacher named Margaret Williams, became so frustrated by the perceived inaction in the early 1990s that she helped form and became president of a group called Citizens Against Toxic Exposure (CATE) to advocate for the residents.
“She really had a voice that could make you listen to her,” said her daughter Francine Ishmael, who eventually took over leadership of CATE when her mother’s energy began to flag prior to her death in 2011. “She told me if you speak, speak clearly and speak your truth, and people will listen.”
In 1994, the Escambia Wood site was at last added to the Superfund list. Williams’ group then began pushing for the EPA to buy up the houses around the poisoned site and move everyone someplace safer. At first the agency was reluctant to take such a drastic step, especially to help lower-income Black neighborhoods.
But Williams had cultivated allies, among them Lois Gibbs, the woman who organized the Love Canal homeowners. Gibbs bought a full-page ad in the Florida edition of USA Today the month before the 1996 presidential election. It featured photos of children from around the Escambia Wood site, along with a quote President Bill Clinton used regularly on the campaign trail: “No child should ever have to live near a hazardous waste s

846803d722d4.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/masked-settlers-attack-european-diplomats-in-the-occupied-west-bank Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Masked settlers attack European diplomats in the occupied West Bank World Oct 17, 2026 12:28 PM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — Masked settlers attacked a group of European diplomats during a visit to the occupied West Bank on Saturday, Belgium's foreign minister said, on a second day of high-profile assaults on Palestinians and others during the sensitive olive harvest. READ MORE: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians during West Bank olive harvest and beat U.S. photojournalist At least four people have been killed and more than 100 injured since the harvest began earlier this month, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry. Activists say Israeli authorities do little to stop attacks that involve weapons ranging from slingshots to guns. An attack on Friday seriously injured a Washington Post photographer and others. In Saturday's attack in the village of Taybeh, settlers targeted Belgium's consul general, French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives, Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said. "A French mayor was assaulted and a Belgian vehicle damaged. Our team is safe," Prevot said. He linked the attack to what he called Israel's "illegal settlement policy" and pledged to push for further European Union sanctions. Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians as the "occupying power," Prevot added. "Impunity for violent settlers must end." The attacks came less than two weeks before closely contested elections that could end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's time in office. His government, the most nationalist and far-right in Israel's history, faces domestic criticism over security failures and international criticism over the treatment of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Israel's military called Saturday's attack on the diplomats a "severe act of violence," but said the visit had not been coordinated with it and no soldiers were at the scene. Israeli police said they had opened an investigation. "The Israel Police condemns violence of any kind and will work to complete these investigations until everyone who took part in these cases is brought to justice," the police statement said. "I strongly condemn the severe acts of violence by Israeli rioters," Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said on X, adding that his ministry was in contact with ambassadors from the countries concerned. e49f2c194b86.text: By — Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/house-speaker-mike-johnson-draws-on-faith-as-he-fights-to-hold-the-republican-majority Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter House Speaker Mike Johnson draws on faith as he fights to hold the Republican majority Politics Oct 17, 2026 12:17 PM EDT BANGOR, Maine (AP) — Ever the optimist, Speaker Mike Johnson said he believes Republicans will hold on to their U.S. House majority, defying a surge of Democratic momentum in the final stretch of the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. It's the crowds he says he's seeing as he crosses the country campaigning for GOP candidates. The caliber of recruits and incumbents he calls workhorses, not show horses. And the nearly half a billion he has raised for House Republicans. He also has faith. "We run to win, and that's biblical: You run to win," he told The Associated Press during a campaign stop in Maine. "And I believe that we will." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The speaker of the House is one of the most consequential elected officials in the United States, second in line of succession to the president. While Johnson quipped to Fox News recently that he may return to his hometown of Shreveport, Louisiana, to start a lawn care business if Republicans lose power on Nov. 3, he fully expects to buck an American midterm tradition that often sees the president's party dumped in Congress. It can be said that Johnson, who has drawn so close to President Donald Trump that he routinely fields 1 a.m. calls — they spoke the night before as Trump rallied in Alaska — walks on the sunny side of the street. That's despite voter frustration over high prices and the Iran war, and his own challenge of leading one of narrowest House majorities in modern times. In his three years as speaker, Johnson has pushed past the doubters and naysayers, holding his thread-thin GOP majority together to deliver Trump's agenda. He notably led passage of the big tax breaks and social service cuts bill. Most days he does not have a single vote to spare. WATCH: Democratic and GOP strategists on how Trump's unpopularity is shaping the midterms "So many times everybody had written off, there was no way he was going to be able to pull off a particular vote," said Republican Rep. Mark Harris of North Carolina, who joined the speaker on the campaign swing. "Yet he always seems to pull out the win in the end." In the interview, Johnson did not speak brashly about expanding the House majority on Election Day, as he has in the past. But on track to visit more than 20 states and 40 congressional districts though November, he said the political mood reminds him of the 2024 election that swept Republicans to control of Congress and the White House. "It's not going to be a giant majority," he said. "But I genuinely believe that we will have a working majority." Accidental speaker becomes emboldened by Trump Johnson first fell into the speaker's job almost by accident, a desperate choice by his GOP colleagues after a contingent of renegade Republicans ousted his predecessor, -then-Rep. Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., in 2023. Johnson had been a lower-level member of House leadership, but distinguished himself before the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol by organizing support for Trump's false claims of widespread fraud in the election that he lost to Democrat Joe Biden. In the time since, Johnson has secured proximity to Trump's power. He joined Trump at a UFC fight in New York and once gifted the president a speaker's gavel as Trump signed the "One Big Beautiful Bill" into law. It was a symbolic act, but one that critics saw as giving away the authority of a coequal branch of government. READ MORE: Republicans retreat from battleground districts as lines shift in House races More recently, Johnson abruptly sent lawmakers home early rather than face a vote forced by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as lawmakers tried to halt the Iran war, which has not been authorized by Congress. Over coffee in Bangor, after rallying for House candidate Paul LePage, a former governor, Johnson brushed back criticism that Congress has eroded under his watch as Trump works to amass executive power. "Absolute nonsense," Johnson said. "We did not yield Article One authority to the president," referring to the powers spelled out in the Constitution. "We used our own," he said, to muscle GOP priorities past Democratic opposition. As House majority teeters, Trump's agenda is at risk Johnson has focused the election on Democrats he portrays as "communists." A handful of far-left liberals, backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, are on the ballot. U.S. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the House Democratic leader who is in line for the speaker's gavel if his party sweeps to power, is preparing a first-100 days agenda for when the new Congress convenes in January, if there is a change in control. What the Republicans will do if they retain power is less defined. READ MORE: 5 House districts where Republicans are looking to turn the tables as Democrats eye big midterm wins "Lots of plans," Johnson said, "along the same course of what we've been doing — less taxes, less regulation." 669bd866fd49.text: By — Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-decision-to-waive-russian-sanctions-outrages-congress-but-no-quick-counter-seen Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress, but no quick counter seen Politics Oct 17, 2026 11:57 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation in a bipartisan display of American support for Ukraine in the war with Russia. Lawmakers from both parties blasted the executive order late Friday, the latest in a series of steps that the Republican president has taken drawing the United States closer to Russia's Vladimir Putin. Trump recently announced a diesel deal with Putin to import Russian energy in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices in the U.S. that are roiling the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Beyond irresponsible," said Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., on social media, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed hope that the sanctions that were supposed to take effect Sunday targeting Russian's economy could be revived. "What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Tillis said. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine." Tillis said that if Trump wants to actually bring down energy prices, he should resolve the Iran war, which is largely blamed for the spike at the pump, and "not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin." Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas said "Lindsey would be appalled," referring to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who worked endlessly on the bill before he died this summer. The bill is known as the Lindsey Graham Russian Sanctions Act. READ MORE: Trump's diesel deal with Putin draws bipartisan criticism from a frustrated Congress Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a statement that "by giving the Russian economy life support, Trump's deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier." Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said Trump is "thumbing his nose" at Congress and "enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression." She urged her colleagues to take action to reverse course. Trump's actions come as Ukraine is bracing for a stark winter confronting Russia's ongoing attacks on its energy infrastructure to heat homes and keep the lights on. Zelenskyy, who has endured a rocky relationship with Trump but stayed close to the U.S. lawmakers, urged supporters to speak out on behalf of the sanctions. The next steps are highly uncertain with the House and Senate are on recess until after Election Day. Trump said he was waiving the sanctions indefinitely, citing national security concerns. It is unlikely Congress would be in a position to take any action to challenge Trump's moves until lawmakers return to Washington. Skeptics in Congress warned Trump would not follow the law It took almost a year for Graham to persuade Trump to agree to the Russian sanctions package. It was designed to impose steep tariffs on countries that import large amounts of Russian oil and energy products and was promoted as way to halt the flow of funds fueling Putin's four-year war against Ukraine. But even as Zelenskyy had watched from the visitor gallery as the Senate advanced the package after Graham's death, skeptics in Congress warned Trump would be unlikely to follow the bill once he had signed it into law a month ago. READ MORE: Kremlin relishes in U.S.-Russia diesel deal and Trump's criticism of Zelenskyy Last week, a bipartisan group of senators urged the Trump administration to more quickly clamp down on Russia, particularly the "shadow fleet" of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America's sanctions. The senators noted that the bulk of the new law's provisions were to be effective Sunday. Instead, Trump soon announced the diesel deal with Putin, saying that Russia had agreed to supply tons of fuel to the U.S., where gas prices have skyrocketed in some areas and voters saying affordability issues are a top concern. Outraged lawmakers have pledged to stop the Trump-Putin deal. New York Rep. Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee who had led opposition to the Graham bill — warning that Trump would flout the law — introduced legislation Friday that would block Trump's diesel deal with Putin. "At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cozying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine," Meeks said in a statement. He called the deal "corrupt" and said it "goes against everything the United States stands for." Associated Press writers Kevin Freking and Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report. 25d4fb5fec33.text: By — Colleen Barry, Associated Press Colleen Barry, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-leo-returns-to-the-vatican-4-days-after-lung-cancer-surgery Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Leo returns to the Vatican 4 days after lung cancer surgery World Oct 17, 2026 11:27 AM EDT VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo returned to the Vatican on Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where dozens of well-wishers saw him off with cries of "Holiness." "I am much better, thank you," the pope said when asked how he was as he was driven away in a black SUV. WATCH: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer and prognosis Leo, 71, greeted patients inside the hospital alongside his surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, before waving to well-wishers outside as he walked to a waiting vehicle. He paused when a 13-year-old Ukrainian girl presented him with a homemade papal doll that she said had helped her through successful cancer treatment. She had briefly met Leo at an audience in St. Peter's Square last December — an encounter she told reporters "gave her the strength to overcome the illness." Ten minutes after driving away from the hospital, the pope entered the gates of the Vatican. He is set to resume some duties on Sunday, when he greets the faithful with the traditional Angelus blessing, exactly one week after he announced to throngs in St. Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung — an unusually candid disclosure for a pontiff. Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Since the surgery, Leo has shown signs of recovering well. He had a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, held meetings with senior aides and celebrated Mass in a makeshift hospital chapel. Medical bulletins from his personal physician and surgeon also described a good postoperative recovery, saying he had been able to carry on "normal daily activities completely on his own." On Friday, the Vatican released the first images of Leo since his surgery, showing him in green vestments standing at an altar in the hospital chapel. Doctors said tests confirmed his "continued improvement." READ MORE: What is adenocarcinoma? Here's what to know about Pope Leo XIV's form of lung cancer Leo presided alone over the liturgy and distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes, Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said. In his homily, he thanked hospital staff "for the work they do every day taking care of the sick in their fragility, and in a particular way what they had done for him," Bruni said. The Vatican had initially estimated a weeklong hospital stay and canceled his audiences through Tuesday. Experts said patients could be discharged earlier depending on their recovery, while Bruni said the decision rested with the pope's doctors. Leo's next major engagement is a trip to Latin America from Nov. 6-17, giving him about three more weeks to recover before an ambitious journey that includes a dozen flights and two helicopter trips. The Vatican signaled that preparations were proceeding by publishing on Friday the names of journalists accredited to travel on Leo's plane. Oncology surgeons say patients are generally cleared to fly after three weeks, provided their recovery allows. Doctors are still awaiting test results to determine the cancer's precise molecular and genetic makeup, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether further treatment is necessary. 87fa35c14c7b.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine's use of the Elon Musk -owned SpaceX satellite system remains partially restricted, despite earlier signs this week that it had been fully restored. Why it matters: The current restrictions limit the Ukrainian military from using drones to intercept Russian attack drones and from using its drones to send supplies to soldiers on the front lines, Zelensky said. The intrigue: Ukrainian officials say they are still scrambling to determine whether the restrictions result from a political decision by the Trump administration or Musk. Ukrainian officials have heard different versions of what happened, with the Trump administration and SpaceX executives accusing each other. "SpaceX as a company tells us it is a technical problem. But our contacts in the company say it is coming from the White House. When we ask the White House, they say it is Elon," a Ukrainian official told Axios. Musk said in a Wednesday X post that the U.S. government was involved in disrupting Starshield. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote. President Trump said on Friday that the White House was not involved in restricting Ukraine's use of the system. Behind the scenes: The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk proposed to Trump throttling the Starlink and Starshield satellite networks used by the Ukrainian military. A source familiar with the discussion told Axios that Trump didn't push back on Elon's idea. A White House official denied the Telegraph's account. "This is totally false. As President Trump said, we didn't slow down Starlink at all, and the service is currently operational," the official said. State of play: But the service is not fully operational. Before the restrictions, the Starlink and Starshield network operated even on drones that reached 400 kilometers per hour. Now it is restricted to 161 kilometers per hour, Ukrainian officials say. Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that the Ukrainian military tested the system on Friday in cars in European Union countries. The cars drove 180 kilometers per hour, and the satellite systems continued working. But once the cars crossed into Ukraine, the system disconnected at 161 kilometers per hour. "The conclusion is that the restrictions apply inside Ukraine but do not apply in European Union countries. In other words, this is a planned operation," Zelensky said. Zelensky also expressed skepticism about SpaceX's claim that the speed limit results from technical problems. Catch up quick: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When Starlink doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Ukraine relies on two satellite systems: One is SpaceX's Starlink, which it uses for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes. Ukraine said both systems were restricted. What to watch: On Friday, Ukraine's chief negotiator, Rustem Umerov, spoke with Trump's adviser and envoy, Jared Kushner, to discuss the Starlink issue, Zelensky said. They also spoke about holding a meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian teams next week to continue the discussions on the latest Trump administration proposal for a deal with Russia on ending the war.

ba07609ba187.text: Top Republicans and Democrats alike lined up Saturday to condemn President Trump 's decision to waive recent sanctions on Russia , calling it "irresponsible" and "a deal with the devil." Why it matters : Trump already faces a bipartisan effort to overturn his Russian diesel deal when Congress returns after the election. Now he may have to deal with even broader outrage over sanctions Congress approved just a month ago. Driving the news: Late Friday night, Trump issued an executive order waiving implementation of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which he signed in September. The act would have imposed broad sanctions not only on Russia, but on other countries buying its oil. What they're saying: Democrats forcefully criticized Trump's decision. "By giving the Russian economy life support, Trump's deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier," Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) wrote . "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) posted on X. "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin. I hope my Republican colleagues will join me in condemning this craven, cowardly action," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said on X. Republicans were equally unsparing. "We should be increasing economic pressure on Russia, not easing up. We need to use every tool at our disposal, including fully implementing the Graham sanctions and my REPO Act, to squeeze Putin until he ends his illegal and barbaric war in Ukraine," Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.) wrote . "I have requested a classified briefing on the rationale for this decision." "Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) posted on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day." Sen. John Cornyn (R-Tex.) posted simply: "Lindsey would be appalled." One soon-to-depart congressman , Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), hinted at the trouble Trump may face when Congress returns. "Congress has a lame-duck session. The President has an agenda: supplemental, reconciliation, Ballroom, etc… I think the agenda is dead. Many of us won't fund these things knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus," Bacon wrote . For the record: The White House defended Trump's decision. "President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution," spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement. "Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests." What to watch: The question now is just how hard Congress will push back when it returns in a few weeks.

b6f2f3c1d43b.text: By — Jim Vertuno, Associated Press Jim Vertuno, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/oregon-father-is-the-latest-armed-civilian-to-confront-a-gunman-in-a-u-s-mass-shooting Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Oregon father is the latest armed civilian to confront a gunman in a U.S. mass shooting Nation Oct 17, 2026 3:07 PM EDT Few mass shootings in the U.S. end like the deadly attack on an Oregon elementary school: with an armed civilian opening fire on the gunman. President Donald Trump joined others Friday in praising a father of two girls who confronted a teenage gunman during the attack at Silver Rail Elementary School, which killed three students and a teacher. Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, intervened by firing his own weapon after the shooting began at his daughters' school in the town of Bend. "It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," Trump told reporters at the White House. WATCH: What makes the Oregon school shooting different – and what can be learned Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter who had a .40-caliber pistol legally stored in his vehicle, entered the school, heard shots and fired his gun after seeing a teacher fighting with the shooter, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said. Cases like the Oregon intervention remain rare, according to the Advanced Law Enforcement Rapid Response Training Center at Texas State University. The ALERRT center tracked what it calls "active attack" incidents where the perpetrator used firearms, blades or vehicles from 2000 to 2025. Out of 634 cases studied, 374 ended before police arrived. Among those, 29 ended when armed civilians shot the attacker. In another 31 incidents, civilians subdued the attacker by some other method, such as wrestling them to the ground or removing the weapon. "They recognize they may be the only way to stop it before law enforcement arrives," said James Keith, a spokesperson for the center. The heroic "good guy with a gun" who can stop an attack even before law enforcement can arrive has long been a rallying cry by gun rights advocates, arguing that armed citizens can act as a first line of self-defense and public protection. In some cases, the person who intervenes has had law enforcement or military training. Other times they are just people who reacted in a moment of chaos. WATCH: Oregon school shooter attacked special education classroom, police say In some states, lawmakers have sought to put armed citizens in position to head off an attack as soon as possible in some public spaces. Texas created a school marshal program in 2013 to allow trained teachers and staff to carry concealed firearms on campus. It expanded safety programs and requirements for armed security and personnel at schools after mass shootings at a high school near Houston in 2018, and at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde in 2022. Texas has some of the least restrictive gun control laws in the country, according to the Giffords Law Center to Prevent Gun Violence. The group rates Oregon among the strongest. Some prominent examples of armed citizens who confronted gunmen to help stop mass shootings: Twin Falls, Idaho, In-N-Out A gunman killed three people and wounded seven more at an In-N-Out Burger on Aug. 3. Law enforcement authorities said the gunman may have killed more if not for an off-duty officer who was a customer at the restaurant, and an armed civilian who exchanged fire with the gunman. Jordan Salinas said he didn't hesitate to grab his gun and confront the gunman when he saw people fleeing the restaurant and heard gunfire. Under return fire, the gunman retreated and ultimately killed himself. "He did not like it when bullets started flying both ways," Salinas told the Idaho Statesman. "There's a task that needs to be done, and we're the ones who need to do it." White Settlement, Texas, church shooting In December 2019, a man wearing a disguise and a trench coat pulled out a shotgun and killed two people during a Sunday service at West Freeway Church of Christ before he was killed by Jack Wilson, a 71-year-old firearms instructor who had also been a reserve sheriff's deputy. Wilson stayed calm as worshippers scrambled for cover. "The only clear shot I had was his head because I still had people in the pews that were not all the way down as low as they could. That was my one shot," Wilson said in 2019. Sutherland Springs, Texas, church shooting A gunman killed 26 people at a small-town church in 2017. Stephen Willeford, a former National Rifle Association instructor who lived across the street, grabbed his rifle and ran in his bare feet to open fire at the attacker, wounding him. The gunman fled and Willeford flagged down a passing driver. The two men chased after the gunman, who eventually killed himself. "I kept hearing the shots: pop, pop, pop" when the gunfire started at the church, Willeford said in 2017. "And I knew every one of those shots represented someone, that it was aimed at someone." 34d95b424642.text: By — Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/americas-politically-divided-jewish-community-braces-for-israels-elections Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter America's politically divided Jewish community braces for Israel's elections Politics Oct 17, 2026 2:41 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Jewish Americans feel they have a lot at stake in this month's contentious elections in Israel as three years of Mideast conflicts rile up emotions across the United States, from street protests to the midterm races. But they are sharply divided along political, religious and often generational lines on the preferred outcome in a vote that's perceived as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and held against the backdrop of the enduring trauma of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, which triggered the war in Gaza. Please check your inbox to confirm. Netanyahu's supporters, especially among Orthodox Jews, believe he's protecting a country they love as central to their identity. Many liberal and younger Jewish Americans believe his policies have harmed Israel's global standing, engendering widespread anger that threatens them in the U.S., too. The moment is particularly fraught as antisemitism and antisemitic violence grow. Even harsh critics of Netanyahu's actions, whether over Gaza or Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank, argue that blame for attacks against Jews can't solely be laid at his feet. "A lot of American Jews are really torn. They want to shout from the rooftops, 'Stop the pogroms in the West Bank,' but also yell at everybody, 'Stop with allegations of genocide and double standards against Israel,'" said Rabbi Dan Levin of Temple Beth El in Boca Raton, Florida. Israel is important to Jewish Americans' identity Levin's large Reform synagogue is one of many across the U.S. hosting educational programs this fall because congregants feel "deeply emotionally invested" in the Israeli elections, even if, as non-citizens, they can't vote. Under Israel's complex, multiparty political system, the Oct. 27 election outcome is impossible to forecast. Polls suggest a tight race between a Netanyahu-led bloc and an alliance of rivals for control of the government. Many Jewish Americans have Israeli friends and family. More broadly, support for Israel is a key component of the religious identity of many U.S. Jewish adults ages 45 and older, particularly those who identify as religiously Jewish, according to a recent AP-NORC poll. READ MORE: Arab-led parties could decide the Israeli election, if anyone would partner with them The largest Jewish denomination in the United States is Reform, which emphasizes progressive values. Many Reform Jews see no contradiction between their liberalism and their Zionism — understood as the Jewish people's aspiration "to live as a free people in our land," said Rabbi Josh Weinberg of the Union for Reform Judaism, an umbrella group for more than 800 Reform synagogues in North America. But they worry about the growing power of the ultra-Orthodox in Israel's political and religious life, as well as settlement policies and the treatment of Palestinians in the West Bank, that they perceive as contrary to their values, Weinberg added. "If Netanyahu wins, I worry very much about the young generation of American Jews who may continue to be, I'll put it nicely, disenchanted, and who might just say 'OK, that's it. I'm giving up on Israel,'" he said. Only about 4 in 10 religious Jewish adults under 45 in the United States say that supporting Israel is "extremely" or "very" important for their Jewish identity, prioritizing instead other forms of connection, like celebrating Jewish holidays, according to the AP-NORC poll. Antisemitism is a key concern In the same poll, a majority of Jewish adults said prejudice against Jewish people is an "extremely" or "very" serious problem in the United States today. As the Israeli elections approach, many communities are worrying about their effects on antisemitism. "Some American Jews believe a different style of prime minister, one more similar to earlier ones who constantly talked about the desire for peace, will change the way American Jews themselves are viewed," said Jonathan Sarna, professor emeritus of American Jewish History at Brandeis University. Even Netanyahu critics, however, don't believe antisemitic acts would stop if Israel changes its government, especially when outrage at his administration's actions toward Palestinians is used to incite violence against all Jews regardless of nationality or political leanings. "'There is only one solution, intifada revolution' — we hear that as a call to rise up and use violence against Jews," Weinberg said of a popular protest chant referring to the violent Palestinian uprising. "So when someone says that in Ramallah, that's one thing. When someone says that in Minneapolis, what exactly are they calling for? That seems pretty clearly to us antisemitic." READ MORE: Scars from Oct. 7 fuel deep divisions over Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election But some think different Israeli policies would help stem the tide. "Somebody who decides that they're going to drive a car into a synagogue or attack Jews on the street, that is their responsibility. You can't blame that on Israel's actions," said Rabbi Jill Jacobs, CEO of T'ruah, a rabbinic human rights organization. "But … I think that it's going to be a very scary time for Jews around the world if there's another Netanyahu government and if it continues on its policy of expanding occupation, ethnic cleansing, and forever war." Stanley Weinstein, an Orthodox Jew from Florida, rejects much of the criticism of the Israel

bb564c5aa1b9.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/no-kings-rallies-across-u-s-urge-voters-to-cast-ballots-early-ahead-of-midterms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter No Kings rallies across U.S. urge voters to cast ballots early ahead of midterms Nation Oct 17, 2026 2:26 PM EDT Rallies organized by the No Kings network opposed to President Donald Trump were being held Saturday in cities and communities across the U.S., with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections. The hundreds of planned events were being billed as nonpartisan, though they sought to build on nearly two years' worth of No Kings marches and demonstrations by people upset with Trump's presidency. People gather near the Lincoln Memorial during a "No Kings" protest as part of a nationwide day of action aimed at encouraging early voting ahead of the midterm elections, in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 17, 2026. Photo by Daniel Heuer/Reuters A band entertained what appeared to be a few hundred people in caps and coats Saturday at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C. Despite the chilly weather, many in the crowd danced to the tunes. "VOTE EARLY" and "HANDS OFF MY VOTE!" were among the many signs held aloft. At an Atlanta rally, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd to urge others to vote ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. "The constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?" he asked. "You don't see Superman giving up his power," Bond continued. "You don't see Black Panther giving up his power. You don't see Wonder Woman giving up her magic lasso. So why would you give up your right, your power, your obligation to vote? Be a super hero, use your power. Go to the polls and vote." Demonstrators gather during a "No Kings: Vote Early" protest as part of a coordinated nationwide day of action aimed at encouraging early voting in the upcoming midterm elections in Manhattan, New York City, on Oct. 17, 2026. Photo by Eduardo Munoz/Reuters Trump has long been suspicious of mail voting, and has claimed without evidence that voting fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election. His administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for the midterm elections from people whom the federal government has identified as "likely" noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. On Friday, the Justice Department warned that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution. Earlier Friday, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Dick Durbin, D-Ill., wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified. ed2e16984998.text: By — Susie Blann, Associated Press Susie Blann, Associated Press By — Katie Marie Davies, Associated Press Katie Marie Davies, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/zelenskyy-urges-support-for-new-u-s-sanctions-on-russia-put-on-hold-by-trump Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Zelenskyy urges support for new U.S. sanctions on Russia put on hold by Trump World Oct 17, 2026 2:02 PM EDT KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters Saturday to speak out in favor of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order putting the sweeping restrictions on hold. The White House decision has heightened fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating attacks as winter approaches. READ MORE: Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress, but no quick counter seen Overnight Russian attacks killed at least four people, including an ambulance driver, and wounded dozens, officials said. Ukrainian drones killed a woman in a Russian border region and disrupted flights at Moscow's airports, according to Russian authorities. In a social media statement, Zelenskyy called Trump's decision unfortunate but avoided directly criticizing the U.S. leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days. "A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote. "This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters." He separately thanked Democrats and Republicans who supported the legislation, saying that blocking it would encourage Russia to continue killing and that limiting Ukraine's ability to retaliate would not bring peace. "Nevertheless, we very much hope — and I personally hope — that the president of the United States of America will do everything possible to make (Russian President Vladimir) Putin stop the killing, stop the attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war," he said. Asked about contacts with Washington, Zelenskyy said Ukraine's lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, had met Friday with U.S. presidential envoy Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. Zelenskyy said the U.S. was working to arrange a three-way meeting involving him, Trump and Putin, potentially in the Middle East, Europe or the United States. Critics say Trump's decision helps Putin Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war against Ukraine. The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving. Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. Trump told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details. WATCH: Ukraine resumes strikes on energy targets, saying Russia never stopped its attacks Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, criticized Trump's move, saying the president was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies." "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said. Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine. Republicans and Democrats alike say the purchase will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran. Starlink restrictions were planned, Zelenskyy says Zelenskyy said that Kyiv was investigating sudden speed restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, which is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication. The restrictions, imposed without warning early Thursday, cut the internet data connection when a communication terminal moves faster than 160 kph (100 mph). The cap forced Ukrainian drones to fly slower than usual, making it easier for Russian weapons to target or evade them. Zelenskyy said that there were no similar restrictions in European Union countries and that they apply only to Ukraine. "In other words, this is a planned operation," he said. It was unclear who was responsible. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said this week that the U.S. government owns and controls the system, with decisions about its use resting with the U.S. military and, ultimately, the president. The Pentagon has not answered questions from The Associated Press about the restrictions. Trump told reporters Friday that he did not order restrictions on the system. He also doubted that the disruption came from Musk. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody, but it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. On Monday, voters in Canada's oil heartland will decide whether to take the first step toward a referendum on leaving the country. Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is not voting to leave Canada on Oct. 19. Instead, voters will decide whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, has said that support for starting the separation process, which was around 23% in a recent poll, is "still too high for my liking." READ MORE: Prime Minister Mark Carney says U.S. is trying to break Canada as Alberta votes on separation path Alberta has long feuded with the federal government over oil and federal power. Liberal prime ministers Pierre Trudeau and, decades later, his son Justin became deeply unpopular in the province over energy policy. Justin Trudeau's government imposed a national carbon tax and other climate measures that Alberta leaders said hurt its oil industry. Yet separatist parties typically drew only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney said. Then came the pandemic and the Freedom Convoy, which paralyzed parts of Ottawa, the Canadian capital, and blocked major Canada-U.S. border crossings. "They needed a new cause," Kenney told The Associated Press. "And it naturally morphed into separatism." Pandemic-era restrictions supercharged separatism Men wave Alberta's provincial flags before Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney attends a Forever Canadian Rally, ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty, in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, on Oct. 16, 2026. Photo by Jennifer Gauthier/Reuters Jeff Rath, a leader of the independence movement, said federal vaccine rules preventing unvaccinated Canadians from flying were his breaking point. "If Trudeau won't let me leave Alberta, I'm just going to pick up my whole province and go," Rath recalled telling a friend. "COVID was really the straw that broke the camel's back." "A lot of people were radicalized by the convoy," he said. The 2022 Freedom Convoy began over vaccine requirements for cross-border truckers but grew into a broader revolt against pandemic restrictions. Kenney said people mobilized over anger at globalization, vaccines and pandemic restrictions, while social media allowed previously isolated activists to find one another and organize. Kenney said the movement also became more professional, building organizations, raising money and drawing in political operatives with campaign and fundraising experience. He also sees substantial overlap between separatist activists and people who support Russian President Vladimir Putin or believe conspiracy theories about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Kenney stressed he was describing activists, not typical separation voters, whom he characterized as frustrated Albertans sending Ottawa a message. Kenney said the MAGA movement has been "inspirational" for some separatist activists. He said they "tried to infiltrate with at least some success" the United Conservative Party he founded. Smith replaced Kenney in 2022 after appealing to United Conservative Party members angry over COVID-19 restrictions. "Literally, you can look at the players," Kenney said of the convoy and separatist movements. "It's the same people." Carney finds unusual support in Alberta Prime Minister Mark Carney has made getting Alberta oil to new markets a national priority and backs a proposed pipeline to the West Coast. His more business- and energy-friendly policies, along with his opposition to U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war and 51st-state rhetoric, have made the federal Liberal leader unusually popular in conservative Alberta. Kenney, one of the most prominent conservative critics of Trudeau's approach to Alberta, said Carney "speaks as an Albertan," understands the province's grievances and aspirations, and is moving in the right direction on energy. Rath called Carney a "formidable opponent," saying "every major politician" in Alberta and Canada is against the separatists and acknowledged an uphill battle. He said he would be "thrilled" with more than 30% of the vote — well short of a majority. "Canada is facing real threats to our economy, to our security, to our way of life," Carney said. "We have to be strong and we are stronger together." Activists go to Washington Alberta sends roughly 90% of its crude oil exports to the United States, and separatists have taken their campaign directly to Washington. Rath confirmed he and other independence advocates met with U.S. State Department officials three times and presented a document outlining what an independent Alberta could offer the United States. Rath claimed people involved in the meetings were going directly to the White House and that a possible oil pipeline through the U.S. to the Pacific was "literally a topic of our last meeting with the U.S. State Department." Americans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out.
Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress.
Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome.
Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent.
Midterms come at bad time for Trump
One of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform.
He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s.
It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%.
Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate.
But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years.
The battle for the House
The current Republican majority in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, is as thin as it gets - they have 218 representatives, which is the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them.
Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November.
But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner.
The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party.
Of those 21 toss-ups, 16 are currently held by Republicans and five by Democrats. If the Democrats win four of those on top of 29 districts classed as likely or leaning Democratic, they will win the House.
Historically, the midterms see a high number of seats changing hands in the House, usually in a protest against the White House. The average number lost by the president's party is 27, according to data, external going back to 1934. Of those 23 elections, the president's party has only made gains in three.
The battle for the Senate
The Republicans have a slightly stronger hold on the Senate. They hold 53 of the 100 seats while the Democrats have 45 and two independents who also vote with them.
Members of the Senate serve six-year terms so roughly a third are up for election every two years.
Thirty-five seats are up for grabs in November but analysis by the Cook Political Report suggests that only seven of them are toss-ups that could go either way.
Of those toss-ups, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus the four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.
But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats.
They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.
And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.
But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.
What are the key issues for voters?
Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters.
The president proudly declared that gas was "now below $2.30 [Â£1.74] a gallon in most states" in his State of the Union address on 24 February. But the war with Iran began four days later, disrupting Middle Eastern energy supplies and causing gas to hit $4 (Â£3.03) in the US.
The war became increasingly unpopular as its consequences reverberated around the world and ultimately hit American consumers in the pocket. One poll carried out in August found 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the situation.
Other issues that voters say are important to them include healthcare and immigration.
Trump has recently touted his policies around immigration as a big success, citing significantly lower border-crossing figures than in recent years.
Many Democratic candidates are focusing on the high costs of US health insurance and the impact of Trump's legislation on access to the healthcare system.
Can Trump defy political gravity?
Most signs point towards a successful midterms for the Democrats, but it wouldn't be the first time that Trump and his party have outperformed polls if they do win more seats than expected.
One of the few things in their favour is their huge financial advantage.
At the end of August, the Republican National Committee and its allied groups had more than $600m (Â£455m) cash on hand, while the Democrats had just under $400m (Â£303m).

An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year.
What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.
After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula.
This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.
It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.
The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size.
"In winter, they would keep them at the shipyard. When summer came, they would bring them out and move them to Kim Jong Un's villa or towards Kalma, and use them for swimming and recreation," says Ri Jong Ho.
Ri was once an official at the Workers' Party's Office 39, which is believed to be involved in raising and managing foreign currency for the leadership.
The wealth of those who sit at the top of the secretive North Korean dictatorship is just as hard to pin down as the country's economic figures.
The United Nations and others rely on estimates to classify North Korea as one of the world's poorest countries, with an especially large military budget that funds a sanctioned nuclear programme.
Most North Koreans, according to a 2025 UN report, live under "systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations" with total state control, widespread forced labour, and chronic food shortages that leave an estimated 40% of the population undernourished.
But the regime has long been known to live in luxury.
We don't know the cost of the vessels seen in the satellite imagery, but comparable luxury yachts run from tens of millions to over $100m (Â£75m). Kim's much smaller, 29-metre Princess yacht was previously estimated to be worth about $7m.
While vessel locations alone cannot definitively establish the family's whereabouts, their movements - which overlap with gaps in Kim's public appearances - point to activities that would otherwise remain out of public view.
Wonsan is where Kim Jong Un spent part of his childhood with his mother, according to biographers and intelligence reports, and one expert told the BBC the city has been associated with the family since his father Kim Jong Il's rule.
A defector who served for 13 years guarding residences used by then leader Kim Jong Il - through the 1990s to the early 2000s - told the BBC the villas around Wonsan were used as a retreat by the elite. He recalls seeing dozens of children and teens waterskiing during summer.
North Korean state media rarely publishes reports about Kim being on holiday, instead framing such visits as official inspections or guidance. But defectors interviewed by the BBC appeared to be aware that the family spent holidays in Wonsan, suggesting that at least some North Koreans knew about it.
North Korean state media also claims Wonsan is home to high-rise hotels, restaurants, shops, sports facilities and water parks, and can accommodate nearly 20,000 visitors.
State media and Russian outlets have published images of small groups of Russian tourists visiting the Wonsan Kalma resort, which opened in July 2025. Although developed to attract foreign visitors, the resort is also open to local tourists.
A South Korean news report, citing an unnamed source, says some locals were offered four-night tour packages for around $100, a substantial sum for most North Koreans. The country's per capita GDP - around $667 in 2024, according to the UN - is a small fraction of South Korea's $36,227.
For the majority of North Koreans, holidays are out of reach. And while a growing middle class does exist, they might not have much time for leisure.
Defectors told the BBC that workers, office employees and cooperative farmers are legally entitled to 14 days of annual leave, but this is rarely followed.
Taking consecutive days off to travel is unusual. People typically take weekend trips or travel during national holidays instead of designated "summer holidays".
Even if leave is granted, travel itself is restricted, with official permission required for people to travel outside their city or county. Moving freely is sometimes as much a luxury as the holiday itself.
The BBC tracked four large vessels around Wonsan, measuring approximately 50m, 55m, 60m and 80m. All four vessels repeatedly appeared around Kim's Wonsan villa this year.
The largest vessel showed the clearest activity, moving from the dock to the waters off the Kalma Peninsula, where it has been since July.
Two of the other vessels - 50m and 55m - were repeatedly seen until the end of August around Tae and Sin islands, close to Wonsan.
Satellite images also showed four smaller boats alongside the 50m vessel.
Satellite imagery expert Jeong Seong-hak said the smaller boats ferried people, fuel and supplies to the larger vessel, adding that small islands like Tae and Sin offered "secluded maritime retreats where privacy can be maintained away from public view".
The 60m vessel was repeatedly seen near Kim's Wonsan villa until as recently as last week.
Though North Korea has never publicly disclosed the vessels' official ownership, BBC's analysis of historical satellite imagery found a large vessel with the same distinctive characteristics in Wonsan in 2002, when Kim Jong Il ruled North Korea.
Former NBA star Dennis Rodman, who visited the North in 2013, told The Sun that he had spent much of his seven-day visit with Kim Jong Un around Wonsan, where they went jet-skiing and horse riding.

"They feel like, 'Wait a minute, it can be taken away again.'" At various times over the last decade, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Britain and Israel have carried out punishing air raids on the rebels — only to see them grow even stronger. READ MORE: Saudi diplomat says Iran is encouraging Houthi escalation of attacks on the kingdom The Saudis have struggled to counter the latest attacks, even with far superior U.S.-supplied arms. A senior Saudi diplomat told reporters this week that Iran was encouraging the escalation and that over the summer the Houthis had spurned an offer to negotiate. The Houthis operate in a large and mountainous territory where they can disperse fighters and military infrastructure while threatening major oil facilities and key trade routes. Iran and its allies in Lebanon and Iraq provide expertise, training and sophisticated weapons, according to U.N. and other experts. A recent report found that the Houthis have tried to source parts from Chinese suppliers that are used to make precision-guided ballistic missiles with a range of roughly 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). The rebels are increasingly well-armed The Houthis already have a wide array of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones — many resembling Iranian models — that can reach all the Gulf states as well as Israel. They have also used sophisticated anti-ship missiles and naval drones to strike vessels in the Red Sea, threatening a critical trade route. Iran denies arming the Houthis, which would violate a U.N. embargo. China has not directly responded to the latest report but says it has a "prudent and responsible" approach to military exports. Smuggled Iranian weapons and parts have been seized from numerous Yemen-bound shipments, and a report by U.N. experts in 2024 documented extensive military ties between the Houthis, Iran and its other allies. READ MORE: Iran-backed Houthis strike Saudi oil company Aramco's headquarters, officials say That report estimated that the Houthis had recruited up to 350,000 fighters by 2024, up from just 30,000 in 2015, when Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war against the Houthis and imposed a naval blockade. The Houthis can use relatively inexpensive drones and missiles to target oil and other infrastructure just across the border in Saudi Arabia, as well as tankers off the coast. And while Iran is believed to supply cutting-edge components like guidance systems, the Houthis can manufacture much of their weaponry domestically, and at a much lower cost than the state-of-the-art interceptors used by the Saudis. There are suggestions they may even be using artificial intelligence to try to build better missiles. Saudi Arabia has struggled to respond Saudi Arabia boasts an array of U.S.-supplied weapons, including sophisticated aircraft as well as advanced missile defenses used against Iran at the height of the war last spring. But with supplies of high-end interceptors under pressure, it's unclear how long it can ward off attacks — not only from the Houthis, but from Iran-backed militias in Iraq blamed for an attack that briefly shut down an east-west pipeline crucial for oil exports. In recent days, the Houthis have repeatedly struck King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, leading to a wave of flight cancellations. They have also hit the headquarters of the national oil company, Aramco. Both are several hundred miles (kilometers) from Yemen. At least 19 people have been killed, school classes have been canceled, and the disruption threatens the kingdom's ambitious plans to transform itself into a global hub for business, tourism and sports. Vulnerable assets are scattered across Saudi Arabia's sparsely populated territory, which is roughly three times the size of Texas. Its border with Yemen stretches more than 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) through rugged desert areas. Airstrikes have had limited effect The Houthis, a Shiite religious and political movement rooted in northern Yemen, are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen's internationally recognized government in the civil war. The Sunni kingdom, which has long feared the emergence of a well-armed ally of Shiite Iran on its border, joined the war in 2015 after the rebels seized much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa. Over the next seven years, Saudi Arabia carried out waves of airstrikes against the Houthis, often killing civilians. An array of Yemeni government forces and southern separatists struggled to push the Houthis back, and the battle lines moved little before a 2022 ceasefire. Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row.
Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests.
The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.
Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.
Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.
The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.
During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard.
Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days.
Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic.
Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.
Black smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon.
As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police.
Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation.
The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris.
George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes.
He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June.
In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police.
Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too.
"We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in Franceâ¦ we are trying to make a revolution.
"Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence."
Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana.
She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights."
She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations.
Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades.
The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative?
Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections".
The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join.
In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things".
He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030.
He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind.
The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity.
Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule.
Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni.
She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest.
Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services.
Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups.
Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions.
"Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC.
"He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances."
Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029.
